en: Preface to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* by [Name],
Grand Master of Court Deliberations, Director of the Dragon Diagram Pavilion, Acting Salt and Alum Commissioner for the Circuits of Jianghuai,
Jing, and Xi, concurrently Assistant Commissioner for Transport, Commander-in-Chief of the Upper Guard, and Recipient of the Purple Gold Fish Bag.
Written by Jiang Zhiqi.
Jiang Zhiqi had long found the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* difficult to read and hard to obtain in a fine edition.

It happened that Zhang Gong, the Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent in retirement at the Southern Capital, offered this scripture, which was then transcribed by Su Zizhan of Meishan and carved onto printing blocks.
Considering it a rare treasure to be entrusted to the eternal abode of Mount Jinshan, the Elder of Mount Jinshan, the Great Master Foyin Siyuan, spoke of its wonder, saying:
"Of the twelve divisions of the sutras spoken by the Buddha, there are as many as five thousand scrolls.
Yet, during the time when the True Dharma was circulating, there were those who, upon hearing half a verse or obtaining a single phrase,"

Those who have awakened and entered [the truth] are truly beyond measure. Yet, following the periods of the Semblance Dharma and the Final Dharma, the distance from the Sage has become great, and people have begun to drown in mere words.
They suffer the hardship of attempting to count the sands of the ocean while remaining utterly oblivious to the essence of the One True Body.
It was then that the Patriarchs appeared, pointing directly to the human mind so that one may see one's nature and attain Buddhahood.

It was held that this was a separate transmission outside the teachings, such that during the mere twinkling of an eye or the utterance of a word, those of superior faculties and sharp instruments had already attained it through direct perception.
Thus, Yunmen went so far as to revile the Buddha, and Yaoshan reached the point of forbidding people from continuing the sutras;
both were expressions of this same intent. From this arose the tendency to depart from the Buddha and call it Chan, and to distance oneself from the meaning and call it...
Because of this mystery, those who study Buddhism must disparage Chan, while those who revere the meaning of the teachings must also venerate the mysterious;
the followers of these two schools condemn one another, unaware that they serve each other’s purposes. Furthermore, Chan is one of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā);
how could it possibly differ from the Buddha? Zhiqi believes that Chan originates from the Buddha and the mysterious originates from the meaning of the teachings—not that they are separate.
If one does not abandon dhyāna for the sake of the Buddha, nor abandon the profound for the sake of the doctrinal meaning, then one is close to it.

When Ran Qiu asked whether he should act upon what he hears immediately, Confucius said, "Act upon what you hear. When Zi Lu asked the same, Confucius said, "Your father and elder brothers are still living;
how can you act upon what you hear immediately? Because Ran Qiu was retreating, Confucius encouraged him to advance; because Zi Lu surpassed others, Confucius withdrew him.
How could these doctrines have any fixed standard? They merely serve to remedy specific deficiencies.

When the decline of Buddhist study led people to become submerged in the literal text and deluded by the meaning of individual phrases, such that they failed to embody the profound mystery, the teaching of Chan was propounded to remedy this.

When the decline of Chan practice led people to pursue empty words and dally with clever sophistry, such that they did not understand the ultimate meaning, the teaching of Buddhism was propounded to remedy this. These two approaches alternate...
By saving one another, the Buddha-dharma will be preserved. In the past, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he had already transmitted the Mind-Seal to the Second Patriarch and further said:

"I also entrust to you these four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*; this is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground, intended for all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter.
Thus, the Buddha and Chan were transmitted together, as were the profound mystery (*xuan*) and its meaning (*yi*).
The transmission was handed down together [with other texts], but it was not until the Fifth Patriarch that he changed this and began transmitting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāra-mitā Sūtra* instead.

Thus, when the Sixth Patriarch heard a guest reciting the *Vajracchedikā*, he asked him where he had come from. The guest replied, "I have come from Mount Wuzu, five *li* east of Huangmei County in Qizhou.
The Great Master of the Fifth Patriarch constantly exhorts both monastics and laypeople: 'If you simply uphold the *Vajracchedikā*, you will spontaneously see your own nature.'"

Since the attainment of Buddhahood was thus attributed to those who uphold the *Vajracchedikā*, the *Vajracchedikā* began to flourish widely in the world while the *Laṅkāvatāra* consequently ceased to be transmitted.
That the transmission of the *Laṅkāvatāra* exists today is truly due to the initiative of Master Zhang.
When I, Qi, visited Master Zhang in the Southern Capital, I personally heard his account of the circumstances surrounding the *Laṅkāvatāra*. It all began with Master Zhang himself...
When the Hanlin Academician, who served as Commissioner of the Three Departments, was serving as governor of Chu, he entered a monastery in Langxia one day and saw a scripture case.
Upon opening it and examining its contents, he found it to be the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. He was struck with a sudden realization that this was the very same text he had written in a previous life;
the calligraphy was perfectly intact, clearly manifesting how his spirit had previously received it. Zhiqi heard that when Yang Zhongji (Rang Shuzi) was five years old...
At that time, the wet nurse was asked to retrieve the gold ring he had been playing with. The wet nurse said, "You never had such an object before.
Daohu then went in person to the eastern fence of Li's neighbor's house and retrieved it from within a mulberry tree.

The owner was astonished and said, "This is an item lost by my deceased son; how did you take it away? The wet nurse recounted the story in detail, whereby they came to know that Daohu was the rebirth of his former self.
He was the son of the Li clan. When Bai Lètiàn was first born at seven months of age, his nursemaid pointed to two characters, and though she tested him hundreds of times, he never failed.
At nine years old, he already understood prosody and phonology; the historians considered this a sign of his devotion to literary composition, attributing it to his innate endowment.
Yet Lètiàn himself firmly believed it was due to the karmic conditions of his past practice. Such is the singular truth of man.
The nature of non-extinction undergoes death and birth, coming and going within heaven and earth;
though the number of such worldly cycles were such that one could break all the grasses and trees under heaven into counting sticks and tally-sticks, they could not calculate them.

Yet, because one is submerged in birth and death and the conscious spirit is exhausted and worn out, one can no longer remember them; only those whose minds are perfectly bright and unclouded know this, such as Zhang [Zhan].
His Excellency passed the imperial examinations twice with outstanding essays and grand compositions, ascending to the ranks of the imperial attendants and wielding the central levers of state.
Having served within the court for over forty years, his reputation and achievements have spread to the ears and eyes of all people;

thus, there is no reason to doubt that his former incarnation was once a great spiritual teacher (*mahāsān-kṣiti*). That he is able to recall events from his previous life—is this not truly to be believed?
Therefore, upon reading the new translation of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, I have recorded its causes and conditions at the beginning of this scripture.
Written after the *Laṅkāvatāra-avadāra-ratna-sūtra*:
This *Laṅkāvatāra-avadāra-ratna-sūtra* is the subtle, supreme, true, and definitive meaning taught by the Buddhas of the past.
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Heart-Essence. When the Patriarch Bodhidharma entrusted it to the Second Patriarch, he said:

"I have observed all the scriptures and teachings existing in China; only the four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* can serve as a seal for the mind. From patriarch to patriarch, they have transmitted this as the Dharma of the Mind.
It is like the *Nan jing* of medicine: every sentence contains principle, and every character contains the Dharma. Those of future generations who are enlightened will find it divine..."
To clarify this: it is like a pearl rolling upon a platter, or a platter rolling around a pearl; there is nothing that cannot be done.

If one conceives a new idea and discards prior learning as useless, they are either ignorant and foolish or merely mad. In recent years, students have each followed their own masters, striving for simplicity and convenience;
having grasped a single phrase or a single verse, they claim to have attained realization, even going so far as to involve women and children.
The disciples clapped their hands and laughed as they vied with one another to discuss the joy of Chan; those of higher standing sought fame, while those of lower standing sought profit.

As this secondary current and its lingering influence spread everywhere, the Buddha-Dharma declined. It was like a vulgar physician who, without relying on medical treatises, directly transmits prescriptions and remedies;
though he may occasionally hit upon the right treatment when curing illness, he lacks the ability to respond appropriately and make a definitive diagnosis whenever he encounters a disease.
To discuss death and rebirth is not to be compared in the same breath with those who have mastered the classics and studied antiquity.

When people see that [the *Nan jing*] possesses a singular efficacy or is more expedient than the works of the ancients, they claim that the *Nan jing* can be understood without study; how mistaken this is!

The meaning and intent of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* are profound and subtle, and its phrasing is concise and archaic; if readers cannot even parse its sentences, how much less [can they grasp its meaning]?
Is it not because those who seek the meaning through the words forget the meaning to realize the mind that this work has remained so obscure in the world, nearly lost yet barely surviving?

Mr. Zhang Gongdao, the Grand Guardian of the Crown Prince and Master Lèquán, having attained a vast and expansive mind and realized pure awakening, once visited a monk’s quarters in Chūzhou during the Qìnglì era and happened to encounter this text.

When the scripture came into my hands, I was suddenly struck with the realization that I had recovered an old possession; before I had even finished opening the scroll, my long-standing karmic obstructions were dissolved like ice.

Examining the calligraphy closely, the hand of the author was vividly present, and I sighed with a mixture of sorrow and joy. From this point on, I gained insight and have constantly used the four verses at the beginning of the scripture to elucidate the essential points of the mind.
I have been a disciple in the Master’s gate for thirty years, and this year in the second month, I passed through the Southern Capital.
I visited the Honored One at his private residence; at that time, he was seventy-nine years old, and all traces of illusion had utterly vanished, his wisdom-light being perfectly round and complete.
As for me, Su Shi, I too am worn out by misfortunes and my hundred thoughts have grown cold as ashes.

The Honored One, deeming me one who could be instructed, bestowed this scripture upon me and provided three hundred thousand coins to have it printed and distributed throughout the Jianghuai region, with the Elder Foyin of Jinshan serving as the supervisor.

The Great Master Sizi Yuan said, "If one merely prints and distributes [this text], it will eventually be exhausted; however, if it is transcribed and carved into printing blocks, it will be inexhaustible.

Shi then transcribed it for him, and Yuan sent his attendant Xiaoji to Qiantang to seek a skilled craftsman to carve the woodblocks, which were subsequently established as the permanent property of Jinshan Temple.
On the ninth day of the ninth month of the eighth year of the Yuanfeng era, [the text was completed by] Chao Feng Lang, newly appointed as Prefectural Governor.

Preface to the *Lengqie Tongyi* (Comprehensive Meaning of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra), written by Su Shi—Knight Commander (Qiduwei) with the rank of Borrowed Crimson, concurrently serving as Military Governor of Dengzhou and Commissioner for Encouraging Agriculture within the jurisdiction:

The Tathāgatagarbha-mind has never had any entity from the outset; that which is called the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two forms of selflessness [are likewise devoid of intrinsic being].

From this emerges the great purport of the *Lankāvatāra-sūtra*, the Heart of the Buddha’s Words. Therefore, when speaking in terms of the departure from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), even correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) must all be departed from;
yet when speaking in terms of the identity with nature (*dharmatā*), there is not a single name, characteristic, or conceptual construction that is not itself identical [to it].
Thus, the refutation of characteristics is exhaustive, and the manifestation of nature is all-pervasive, as the text repeatedly investigates and analyzes through a process of dialectical inquiry.
The principles herein are subtle and profound; this sutra encompasses and preserves them. Is it not the ultimate exposition for exhausting principle and perfecting nature?

Thus, Bodhidharma transmitted it, Mazu demonstrated it, Zhang Wen-ding Gong attained a deep affinity with it in his youth, and Su Wen-zhong Gong elucidated it, whereupon it began to circulate widely in the world.
People came to admire and yearn for it; yet its text is concise and archaic, and the translator likely intended to lead those above [the common folk] toward it.

The roots of understanding and the depth of realization are attained through self-mastery; if these are not transmitted to future generations through the medium of written words, they will not fall into superficiality or dilution.
Consequently, those of inferior or middling faculties are often unable to even parse the sentences and look upon the work with awe-struck hesitation.

Among the commentators, there are certainly those who offer illuminating insights, yet they frequently obscure the intended meaning of the teaching and remain dark regarding the purpose of the text, failing to distinguish between what is correct and what is erroneous.

When I observed that the confusion regarding the unsurpassed, ultimate teachings had not yet subsided, I privately felt deep concern. I attempted to select one or two instances to reflect upon at leisure;
finding them difficult to set aside, I proceeded to investigate the beginning and end of a single scripture, examining its sections, phrases, and the origins and conclusions of their meanings.

Following the rules and general principles of our Tiantai school, I expounded upon its essential tenets and titled this work *Tongyi* (Comprehensive Meaning). Drafting it and then transcribing it, a full year passed.
When the work was finally completed, he once presented it to others, who remarked, "The intent of the Buddha is profound and deep, while the sentiments of ordinary people are shallow and crude;
how could one not invite derision from those of great learning? He replied, "Is this so? To look at the Sage through the lens of an ordinary person—I dare not do so.
To look at one person through the lens of another—I have not been overly modest. Others again said, "If the intention of the translator did not lie [in literalism]..."

If one simplifies what was ancient, then having observed the doctrines of the present, the obscure becomes clear, the obstructed becomes unblocked, the circuitous becomes direct, and the difficult becomes easy;
would this not be to commit an offense against the ancients? I reply: "Whether they understand me or blame me, let that rest with the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (Chunqiu);
I truly dare not decline [this responsibility]."
The Third Day of Mid-Winter in the Jia-si Year of the Jiading Era.
Preface by Baiting Shan-yue to the *Lengqie abatuo luo bao jing tongyi*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Baiting Shan-yue of Siming.
Chapter One, Part One: The Heart of All Buddha-Speech.
This great original version of the sutra exists in its entirety in India;

however, because the volume was so extensive and this chapter was the most essential—sufficient to serve as a seal for the mind—it was transmitted separately to this land. It has been translated four times, three of which remain [the first being by Guṇabhadra].

[Translated by Bodhiruci in the Song dynasty; translated by Śikṣānanda in the Wei dynasty; translated by Dharmakṣema in the Northern Liang dynasty. Is it not appropriate that the Song translation has become widely prevalent?
This is the general catalog of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* in its Great Version. "Laṅkā" refers to a mountain so loftily isolated that none may go there except through supernatural powers (*abhijñā*);
thus, it is translated as "Inaccessible" (*avata*) to signify that it transcends the path of the mind.
"Jue" (Ultimate) refers to the place where this sutra was preached. In the Sanskrit original, it is *Avatāra*, which translates as "entering and roaming.

Therefore, both translations refer to it as the *Laṅkāvatāra* (Entering Laṅkā). In terms of principle, it means entering and roaming within the realm of self-realized noble wisdom (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara*) while preaching this sutra;
this is also like what the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says regarding "roaming in the unconditioned."
The "measure" (pramāṇa) is the profound nature of reality (dharmatā). Alternatively, it may be translated as "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*);
thus, it should properly be called *Anuttara*, though it is likely a corruption. As for the word "jewel" (*ratna*), it signifies being precious and honorable.

Because there is nothing that can surpass the jewel of the supramundane Dharma, worldly jewels are borrowed as a metaphor. When establishing a title using the categories of person, dharma, or analogy, this [title] takes the location from the dharma.
This is also an example of the method of using both doctrine and parable. "Sūtra" is explained as usual.

"The Chapter on the Heart of All Buddha-Speech" is the specific title of this single chapter. As for "all," what does it not encompass? The Buddhas of the three periods of time have all realized this mind together and spoken this Dharma together.
Now, though it is pointed out specifically, it refers first to Śākyamuni; although it applies generally to the Dharma, it is nonetheless nothing other than the mind. From... [text ends]

To provide a general overview, it is called the "Chapter on the Essence of the Buddha’s Words" (*Buddhaguhya-hṛdaya-parivarta*). This refers to the meaning of "classification," signifying that [the teachings] are gathered into categories to form this chapter.

Following its specific title, I shall now apply the Fivefold Profound Meaning (*pañca-vidha-gambhīrārtha*) according to the Tiantai school. The first is the title based on the characteristic of the separation between person and dharma:
"all Buddhas" refers to the person, while "essence of the words" (*guhya-hṛdaya*) refers to the dharma; these are all characterized by their mutual separation from marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
This precisely accords with the title of the work; for the Buddha is one who has attained the ultimate fruit, and thus he is ultimately free from signs (*nimitta*).

As one who is free from signs, he teaches the Dharma that is free from signs. This Dharma is itself the mind, and the mind is also free from signs. Being free from signs means being signless (*animitta*), and even this signlessness is transcended.
It is on this basis that the name of the Dharma may be understood. Second, it is said that the primary meaning of the mind (*paramārtha-citta*) constitutes its essence.

This is precisely what is named the "referent-essence" (*abhidheya-svabhāva*). Now, although the meanings of "mind" (*citta*) are manifold, that which is here named is the *tathāgatagarbha*, the intrinsically pure ultimate mind (*paramārtha-citta*).
Therefore it is said: "This is the nature, the self-nature, and the ultimate mind of all Buddhas of the three periods.
This mind is the most central and supreme; like a sovereign or a father, it is the nature of all minds, wondrous and singular.
To establish all phenomena and all meanings as the ultimate destination and essence of all dharmas—this is what is meant by "essence" (*tattva*).

Third, taking the realization that delusion has no intrinsic nature as the thesis (*siddhānta*): it is through this thesis that the essence is revealed. If various delusions were present, the essence would not manifest of itself;

it is only through the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*svasaṃvedana-āryajñāna*) that one realizes the lack of intrinsic nature in delusion, whereby delusion itself reveals the True. Do not... [text ends]
It is for this reason that it is said, "deluded thoughts have no intrinsic nature," and also, "external natures have no intrinsic nature"; these are all the essential tenets of this sutra.
Its fourth section, titled "Refuting the External and Distinguishing the Erroneous," is intended to manifest the fundamental principle.
Since wisdom must be clear and luminous before it can be functional, one uses it to refute the external; thus, internal and external are distinguished, and through this, the erroneous is discerned.
When the crooked is set against the straight, both are fully revealed;

just as when a mirror is bright, it does not deceive regarding the beautiful and the ugly, and when a plumb line is established, it does not err regarding the curved and the straight—thus, nothing fails to attain its proper measure. Its fifth [section] states: "The Vaipulya Universal Vehicle constitutes the characteristics of the teaching.
Formerly, all took this sutra to be a discourse on the sudden and great [teaching], yet they did not realize that it primarily discusses illusory phenomena.
The meaning involves the Vaipulya gate; the capacities it reaches still extend to those of the three vehicles, and the stages it discusses encompass all ten bhūmis.
Therefore, when judged by period, it belongs to the Vaipulya division among the four periods; as for its categories, it comprehensively includes all Mahāyāna teachings.
As for the teaching itself, it is a "universal vehicle" (pāramitā-yāna) that connects the preceding and succeeding periods, simultaneously subsuming the three vehicles and the four teachings.

According to this school’s judgment, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* is categorized as belonging to the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*) while being interpreted according to the Perfect Teaching (*yüan-chiao*).

Although this method of explaining the essence (*ti*) appears particularly unique, it follows from what the school venerates. The five meanings do not go beyond the three dharmas, and the three dharmas are rooted in the one mind;

by using this to explain the title of this work, its underlying purport becomes even more manifest. Furthermore, regarding the name of this chapter, according to the specific text below, it has a single name.
The *Āryajñānavastuvikalpasvabhāva-sūtra*, also known as the *Pañcadharmasvabhāvaparīkṣā-sūtra* or the *Abhilāpavikalpalakṣaṇacitta-sūtra*, further elaborates upon what has been taught;
in brief, there are four topics: the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the eight consciousnesses, and the two forms of selflessness (*anātman*).
These constitute the structural outline of this chapter and the key points for establishing its doctrinal principles.

While one might distinguish various titles based on their specific meanings, none are as comprehensive and all-encompassing as the title "The Buddha Speaks of the Mind," for it simultaneously encompasses both phenomena and principle;
therefore, this title alone has been adopted.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling atop Mount Laṅkā on the shore of the Southern Sea, amidst various precious flowers.
To adorn [this assembly], together with a great community of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas who had come from various diverse buddha-fields—
these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possessing the power of mastery over immeasurable samādhis and sporting in supernatural transformations,
with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati as their leader— all of whom were consecrated upon the crown of their heads by the hands of all the Buddhas.

They skillfully understand the meaning of the objective realms that are manifestations of one’s own mind; they universally manifest according to the various types of beings through various minds, forms, and immeasurable gates of deliverance;
and they ultimately and thoroughly penetrate the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.

The sutra indeed states it clearly: "The one who preaches the Dharma neither speaks nor demonstrates; the one who hears the Dharma neither hears nor attains. This is the Tathāgata preaching through non-preaching, and Ānanda hearing through non-hearing. The sutra indeed states it clearly: "The one who preaches the Dharma neither speaks nor demonstrates; the one who hears the Dharma neither hears nor attains. This is the Tathāgata preaching through non-preaching, and Ānanda hearing through non-hearing. The phrase "it is thus" (*evam*) refers to the Dharma that was heard; it is a term expressing faith and compliance. "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) means that Ānanda heard and upheld this Dharma from the Buddha.

In the commentaries of the Tiantai school, based on the four phrases of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*—namely, "birth," "birth of birth," and so forth—the terms "I," "I," "heard," and "heard" are interpreted accordingly to accord with the Four Teachings.
"At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) signifies the harmony between hearing and upholding.

At the opportune moment when conditions converged, the Buddha, having already perfected the Way, expounded the Dharma according to the capacities of beings to guide and benefit all classes of sentient beings.
Other meanings are detailed in other texts. "Dwelling on the summit of Mount Laṅkā by the southern sea" refers to the location where the teaching was given;
according to the Tang translation, this is called Mount Malaya within the city of Laṅkā, as the subsequent text also mentions Laṅkā.
The country of Malaya—this term "Laṅkā" refers to the mountain named after the capital city, or it may be used as an abbreviation;
it is adorned with various precious flowers to demonstrate the excellence of that place. Alternatively, it may be explained according to its symbolic meaning.
Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, he is listed among those who heard the teaching; the text first praises the assembly’s virtuous conduct.

Regarding the virtues of the Bodhisattvas, the statement that they have come from various and diverse Buddha-fields serves to illustrate the principle that by mentioning the distant, one knows the near;

furthermore, it speaks of other directions rather than excluding this land. This is because the capacities and conditions (*indriya-pratyaya*) are immeasurable. Thus, the samādhis and so forth are praised as his true virtues:

the first phrase refers to concentration (*samādhi*), the second phrase refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), and the third phrase refers to the transformation of others (*parārtha*). It does not, however, praise his voice.
In what has been heard, the intent of praise and censure is present; the reason these are listed first is that they are presented by way of their physical appearance and attire.
Next, there is a distinct eulogy of the Great Wisdom (Mahāmati) who is the foremost leader, stating that all Buddhas pour water upon his crown, which clarifies the high rank of his position.
It is said that this Bodhisattva possesses the virtue of a "subordinate sage" (ya-sheng), and thus he is designated as having received the office through consecration (abhiṣeka).
The matters [concerning] this will be seen in the subsequent text. Regarding "the realm manifested by one's own mind," this is where the primary purport of the entire sutra first appears.
By stating that "Mahāmati has well understood," it indicates that his wisdom and virtue are preeminent.

Since there are various minds and forms according to the various sentient beings, there are distinctions among the seeds of the five aggregates, such as good and evil. Mahāmati, through immeasurable gates of liberation...
To respond universally is for the Dharma-gate to be profound and vast; to achieve ultimate penetration into the fivefold equality is likewise to have universal mastery over all Buddha-dharmas.
It is fitting that such a person should lead the assembly to initiate the teaching and proclaim the wondrousness of the Way, for there are matters beyond the reach of the ordinary multitude.
This is because they are endowed with the two kinds of adornment, and are thus able both to question and to answer—this is what is meant by "great."
"Wisdom indeed exists therein. [This concludes] the first chapter.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, together with the Bodhisattva Maitreya, while traveling through all the Buddha-fields, rose from their seats by the Buddha’s spiritual power, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and joined their palms in reverent salutation.
Verses in Praise of the Buddha:
The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky; though wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to great compassion.
All phenomena are like illusions, transcending mind and consciousness; though wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to great compassion.

Distant from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, the world is always like a dream; through wisdom one finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet gives rise to the mind of great compassion.

Knowing that both persons and phenomena lack self-nature (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), and that afflictions and their residual traces are eternally pure and signless (*animitta*), one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.

All things are without *nirvāṇa*, for there is no *nirvāṇa* apart from the Buddha; there is no Buddha apart from *nirvāṇa*. One remains far removed from both the awakening and that which is to be awakened.
Whether there is existence or non-existence—having abandoned both of these, the Sage observes with tranquility; thus he is far removed from arising.
This is called "not grasping at purity in this world or the next."
In general, when praising the Buddha, how could one below fathom that which is above and thus exhaustively describe his *dharmamukhas*?

To say "by receiving the Buddha's spiritual power" (*buddhānubhāva*) is to recount what the Buddha has realized in order to praise the great purport of a single sutra; this is also generally seen in this verse.

There are two parts in total: first, praising the merit of distancing oneself from [defilements] to accomplish the welfare of both self and others; second, extolling tranquility (*śānti*) to conclude with the correspondence between name and reality.
The virtues of this distancing are fivefold: namely, the world, mind-consciousness, permanence and annihilation, the two obstacles, and the awakened and that which is awakened.
There is indeed a sequential order to these textual meanings. First is the world, which refers to the objects of perception;

although the objects of perception are distanced, mind-consciousness has not yet perished, and thus the subject that perceives still persists—therefore it follows next. Once mind-consciousness is distanced, [the next stage follows].
This is the root of false views; because there is false view, there are the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

Furthermore, these extremes of annihilationism and eternalism arise from the view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), which can obstruct the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and constitute the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Next, regarding the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):
if one is separated from the obstacle, that is awakening; awakening is itself *nirvāṇa*. If the subject-object duality still persists, it is not originally quiescent.

Therefore, when one ultimately departs from both the perceiver and the perceived—these five being perfectly detached from spatiality—one is named a Buddha; thus, there is no difference in terms of sequential stages.
Nevertheless, the world is fundamentally a law of arising and ceasing, which only a Buddha can fully comprehend as being like flowers in the sky or dreams within a dream.
Because one departs from them by not departing—that is, by seeing through the mind-consciousness and its perceptions of that world—it is said to be "like flowers in the void."
Since they are called "flowers in the sky," they are neither existent nor non-existent; this is why this wisdom cannot be categorized as either existence or non-existence.

Speaking from this perspective, it may be said that even a Buddha does not abide within the three realms. Yet, because sentient beings have not yet awakened, the Tathāgata takes pity on them and, out of great compassion, establishes teachings for the world.
These are like illusions and dreams: the principle is one, though the meanings differ. This is fully explained [in the scriptures].

Regarding the "Ten Similes of the Mahāyāna" (and so forth), the textual meaning of "being free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism" originally derives from the Āgamas within the section on being free from annihilationism and eternalism;

what is stated here is that while the objects to be abandoned are proximate, the capacity to abandon them is truly far-reaching—there is no dualistic view, whether partial or biased, that is not abandoned.
The principles of the non-self of persons and phenomena, as well as the two obstacles, shall be clarified later; [in this context], all things are non-existent.
Nirvāṇa is so called because all phenomena, by virtue of their equality, are fundamentally quiescent; thus, there is neither nirvāṇa nor one who attains it.
As Vimalakīrti said: "All sentient beings are themselves the mark of nirvāṇa and cannot be extinguished further.
Precisely because they are the very mark of nirvāṇa, there is no nirvāṇa; and because they cannot be extinguished further, there is no Buddha-nirvāṇa.
To be far removed from both the awakener and that which is awakened—this may be explained directly as being neither Buddha nor Nirvana;
this is "non-existence," yet it is not merely the absence of existence. Ultimately, since both are described as quiescent, it is said:
"Whether there be existence or non-existence, the Muni is free from both. This is a concluding eulogy of the Muni’s tranquil contemplation. That is to say, the Muni.

Because it is named "Silent Quiescence," to contemplate in this manner is precisely the contemplation of stillness. This contemplation and its virtue both arise from the aforementioned "separation" (*viveka*).
If one were to say they arise from the separation of arising and ceasing, it would merely be redundant with the preceding text.
It is because these two—separation and stillness—are mutually manifest that not a single dharma can be grasped; thus, there is neither grasping nor non-grasping.
There are three meanings: taking that which is not taken, not taking that which is taken, and neither taking nor not taking.
These are fully explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* according to the verse on the fire-pile (*agnirāśi*), which exhausts their intent (and so forth).
This is why the Tathāgata has attained ultimate quiescence and reached the pinnacle of absolute purity. [End of] Chapter Two.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahamati had praised the Buddha with verses, he announced his own name: "I am named Mahamati; I have attained mastery of the Great Vehicle. Now, with these one hundred and eight points, I respectfully inquire of the Most Honored One among the supreme, the Knower of the World. Having heard those spoken verses, the Buddha observed the entire assembly and addressed the sons of the Buddhas, saying: [The remainder of the text follows: "Excellent, excellent, Mahamati! You have asked this question out of a desire to benefit and gladden all beings, and to bring peace and happiness to gods and humans. Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it to you. Mahamati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are the four? They are: the self-nature of imagined characteristics (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-svabhāva*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are five kinds of knowledge (*jñāna*). What are the five? They are: the knowledge of dharma (*dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of meaning (*artha-jñāna*), the knowledge of conventional expression (*nirukti-jñāna*), the knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the non-duality of subject and object (*advaya-jñāna*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are three kinds of mind-only (*cittamātra*). What are the three? They are: the mind-only of the world of appearances (*nimitta-cittamātra*), the mind-only of the world of names (*nāma-cittamātra*), and the mind-only of the world of reality (*tattva-cittamātra*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). What are the two? They are: the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of nirvana. What are the two? They are: the nirvana of the extinction of the aggregates (*skandha-kṣaya-nirvāṇa*) and the nirvana of the non-extinction of the aggregates (*askandha-kṣaya-nirvāṇa*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the Tathagata-garbha. What are the two? They are: the Tathagata-garbha that is the cause of samsara and the Tathagata-garbha that is the cause of nirvana. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). What are the two? They are: the transformation of the basis of the cessation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the transformation of the basis of the cessation of the obstacles to what is known (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*). What are the two? They are: the realm of reality as the sphere of the Hearers (*śrāvaka*) and the realm of reality as the sphere of the Buddhas (*buddha*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the path (*mārga*). What are the two? They are: the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the fruit (*phala*). What are the two? They are: the fruit of the cessation of the afflictions and the fruit of the cessation of the obstacles to what is known. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*). What are the two? They are: the body of liberation characterized by the cessation of the afflictions and the body of liberation characterized by the cessation of the obstacles to what is known. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). What are the two? They are: the Dharma-body of the teachings (*deśanā-dharmakāya*) and the Dharma-body of the realization (*adhigama-dharmakāya*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). What are the two? They are: the Great Vehicle of the teachings and the Great Vehicle of the realization. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the Bodhisattva. What are the two? They are: the Bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stage of certainty (*niyāma*) and the Bodhisattva who has entered the stage of certainty. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the Buddha. What are the two? They are: the Buddha of the transformation (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) and the Buddha of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-buddha*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the wheel of the Dharma (*dharmacakra*). What are the two? They are: the wheel of the Dharma of the Hearers and the wheel of the Dharma of the Buddhas. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha*). What are the two? They are: the cessation of suffering through the exhaustion of the causes of suffering and the cessation of suffering through the exhaustion of the manifestation of suffering. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). What are the two? They are: the path of seeing through the direct perception of the truths and the path of seeing through the direct perception of the non-arising of phenomena. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the path of cultivation. What are the two? They are: the path of cultivation through the removal of the afflictions and the path of cultivation through the removal of the obstacles to what is known. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the ultimate truth. What are the two? They are: the ultimate truth of conventional designation and the ultimate truth of the ineffable reality. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the non-self (*anātman*). What are the two? They are: the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). What are the two? They are: the view of self regarding persons and the view of self regarding phenomena. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). What are the two? They are: the grasping at the extreme of eternalism and the grasping at the extreme of nihilism. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the view of clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). What are the two? They are: the clinging to views regarding the self and the clinging to views regarding phenomena. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the view of attachment to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). What are the two? They are: the attachment to precepts and vows regarding the self and the attachment to precepts and vows regarding phenomena. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). What are the two? They are: the view of a self regarding the aggregates and the view of a self regarding the elements. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the view of a person (*pudgaladṛṣṭi*). What are the two? They are: the view of a person regarding the internal and the view of a person regarding the external. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*). What are the two? They are: the view of existence regarding the past and the view of existence regarding the future. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the view of non-existence (*nāstidṛṣṭi*). What are the two? They are: the view of non-existence regarding the past and the view of non-existence regarding the future. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). What are the two? They are: the view of permanence regarding the self and the view of permanence regarding phenomena. Furthermore, Mahamati, there are two kinds of the view
"You sons of the Buddhas, you may now all ask whatever you desire; I shall explain for you the realm of self-realization.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having received the Buddha’s permission, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and questioned him with these verses:
How is mindfulness purified? How does mindfulness increase? What is seen as delusion? How does delusion increase?
For what reason are there lands, transformed appearances, and various non-Buddhists? What is the state of non-reception (*anupādāna*)? Why is it named "non-reception"?
Why is one named a "Son of the Buddha" (*jinaputra*)? To what place does liberation extend? Who is bound, and who is liberated? What are the realms of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)?
How are there three vehicles? We pray that you will explain this for us. From what do the dependent originations arise? What is the agent and what is the action?
What are the various differing explanations? How does growth occur? What are the formless attainments and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)?

What is the cessation of perception (*saṃjñā-nirodha*)? By what cause does one awaken from concentration? What is the arising of the performed action, and how does one go forward and maintain the body?
What is manifest discrimination? How are the various stages produced? Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence? What is the body and where does it reside?
How does one go forth to rebirth, and to what destination does one arrive? Who are the most excellent sons [of the Buddha]? By what cause do they attain supernatural powers, mastery, and samādhi?
What is the most excellent mind of samādhi? Tell me this! What is called the "storehouse" (ālaya)? What are the mind (manas) and consciousness (vijñāna)?
What are arising and ceasing? What is the seeing and returning [to the source]? What are the lineage (gotra) and the non-lineage, and what is the measure of mind (cittamātra)?
How are characteristics established, and what is the meaning of non-self (anātman)? Why is there no sentient being? What is conventional discourse?
How do the views of annihilationism and eternalism not arise? And how is it that the Buddhas and the non-Buddhists do not differ in their characteristics?
What are the various diverse sects of future ages? What is emptiness, what is its cause? What is momentary destruction?
What is birth from a womb? Why is the world unshakable? What is the cause for [the world] being like an illusion, a dream, and a city of the Gandharvas;
like a mirage in the heat of the world, and like the moon’s reflection in water? For what reason are the factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga) and the limbs of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) taught?
What is the turmoil of the lands? How does one come to have views of existence? How is it that there is neither birth nor cessation, like flowers in the sky? How does one awaken to the world?
What is meant by teaching the departure from letters and the departure from false imagination? Who is it? And what is space? For example, how many kinds of realities are there?
How many *pāramitās* are there? What is the nature of the mind? By what cause are the various stages (*bhūmis*) traversed? Who reaches the state of non-apprehension?
What are the two kinds of selflessness? How is it so? How many types of purified wisdoms are there? How many kinds of precepts are there? What is the nature of sentient beings?
Who produces the various natures of jewels, such as mani-gems and pearls? Who produces all languages and the various natures of sentient beings?
By whom are the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) and the arts (*śilpa*) revealed? How many kinds of verses (*gāthā*) are there—long stanzas, short stanzas, and prose?
How many kinds of beings are there? What is called "treatise" (śāstra), and how does it arise? How do food and drink, as well as various sensual desires, arise?
What is meant by kings, wheel-turning monarchs (cakravartin), and minor kings? How do they protect the kingdom? How many kinds of devas are there?
What are called the earth, the constellations (nakṣatra), the sun, and the moon? And how many kinds of those who practice for liberation (vimukti) are there?
How many kinds of disciples are there? What is an *ācārya*? Furthermore, how many kinds of Buddhas are there?
How many kinds of Māras and various heterodox teachers (*tīrthika*) are there? Each of them has how many kinds of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and mental states (*citta*)?

Each of those, again, has how many kinds? How are the measures of conventional designation (*prajñapti-mātra*) established? I pray that the Most Victorious One will explain: what are emptiness, wind, and clouds? And what is the clarity of mindfulness and hearing?
What are forests and trees? What are creeping vines? What are elephants, horses, and deer?
How are they captured? What constitutes the base and lowly? By what cause does one become base and lowly? What is comprised within the six categories?
What are icchantikas—men, women, and those who are neither male nor female—and how are they all born? What is the regression of practice? What is the arising through practice?
By what dharma does the Dhyāna Master establish which classes of beings so that they are born into the various realms of existence? What are their characteristics and what are their likenesses?
What constitutes wealth, and by what cause is wealth attained? What is the Śākya clan, and by what cause does the Śākya clan exist?
What is the Ikṣvāku lineage? O Unsurpassed Honored One, please explain! What is the Long-Suffering Rishi, and how does he instruct others?
How does the Tathāgata, at all times and in all lands, manifest surrounded by various classes of sons of the most excellent lineage?
Why do you not eat meat? How did you prohibit and sever the eating of meat? For what reasons do various types of beings eat meat?
Why are there lands shaped like the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, or lotuses, as well as those with the superior marks of lions, those situated sideways, and those that are inverted?
Like Indra’s net, or like various precious jewels, lutes, hourglass-shaped drums (*kinnara-vīṇā*), and *tantrī* drums;

or like various kinds of flowers that are free from the light of the sun and moon—such as these, they are immeasurable. What is a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*)? What is a reward-born Buddha (*vipāka-ja-buddha*)?
What is a Buddha of suchness (*tathatā-buddha*)? What is a wisdom Buddha (*jñāna-buddha*)? Why does one not attain equal and perfect enlightenment in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
For what reason does one attain awakening after becoming free from desire in the Akaniṣṭha heaven? How long will the Sugata remain in parinirvāṇa? Who shall uphold the True Dharma?
For how long will the Teacher of Gods and Men abide, and for how long will the True Dharma remain? How many types of *siddhāntas* and views are there?
Furthermore, how many divisions of the *vinaya* and of monks are there? By what causes and conditions do those most excellent sons—the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas—arise?
For what reason are there one hundred transformations? What is meant by the one hundred non-apprehensions? What is mundane penetration? What is supramundane? What are the seven stages?
We pray that you will explain these for us. How many kinds of Saṃgha are there? What constitutes the schism of the Saṃgha?
What is the treatise on medical formulas? Furthermore, by what causes and conditions did the Great Muni proclaim such words?
Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni—why do you say that I teach both permanence and annihilation, as well as self and non-self?
Why do you not always expound the true meaning, yet instead analyze and explain for sentient beings the "measure of mind" (cittamātra)?
For what reason are there forests of men and women, harītakī, āmalaka, and kīra trees, as well as the various mountains such as Cakravāḍa and Vajra?
It was filled with immeasurable, jewel-adorned sages and gandharvas.
The Unsurpassed Knower of the World, having heard the verses spoken by them—the foremost gateway to the Mahāyāna perfections and the heart of all Buddhas—exclaimed, "Excellent, excellent!
He then addressed Mahāmati: "Listen attentively; I shall now explain to you in due order that which you have asked."
Birth and non-birth, nirvāṇa, emptiness, moments, the lack of intrinsic nature, the Buddhas, the various pāramitās,
the sons of the Buddha, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the various non-Buddhists, as well as those who practice in the formless realm—
such diverse things as Mount Sumeru, the great oceans, mountains, continents, islands, lands, the earth, the stars, the sun and moon, and the non-Buddhists, devas, and asuras.
Liberation, mastery, supernormal powers, dhyāna, samādhi, cessation, the bases of psychic power, the factors of enlightenment, the various stages of the path,
the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the aggregates, bodies, coming and going, meditative attainments, the attainment of cessation,

the arising of the mind, and the teaching on the mind, mentation, and consciousness— all are without self. Furthermore, there are the five natures, perceptions, that which is perceived, and the two views of appearance.
Vehicles and the various lineages, gold, silver, and mani-jewels; the great elements of the icchantikas in turmoil, and the singular Buddha-wisdom;
the attainment of the radiance directed toward sentient beings; the existence or non-existence of elephants, horses, and various birds and beasts—how are these captured?

Through the establishment of causes and the *siddhānta*, as well as the agent and the acted-upon, the forest of delusions is realized as being nothing but the manifestation of the mind-only (*cittamātra*), which does not truly exist externally.

The mutual non-attainment of the various stages; the hundredfold transformations and the hundredfold absences of sensation; the medical treatises, the sciences of craftsmanship, the various fields of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*), and the arts;

the dimensions of the mountains, Mount Sumeru, the earth, and the great oceans; the measurements of the sun and moon; the respective number of atoms (*paramāṇu*) in the bodies of sentient beings—low, middle, and high;
the number of atoms in each *kṣetra*; how many *dhanus* are there in a *dhanus*; how many *hasta*, *pada*, *krośa*, *ardha-yojana*, and *yojana* are there?
How many rabbit hairs, window-dust particles, nits, sheep’s wool, barley-dust particles, *pṛthak*, *aḍhaka*, *droṇa*, *khāri*,
*kuṭapa*, and so on, up to *bimbara*— how many of each of these are there?
How many *anūpa* are called one *śalīśarpa*, and how many *śalīśarpa* constitute one *ratni*?
How many *laitya-māṣas* are there in one *māṣa-dhāna*, and how many *dhānas* make one *kāriṣāṇa*? How many *kāriṣāṇas* constitute one *pala*?
What is the measure of these accumulated quantities? How many *palas* are there in Mount Meru?
These are the things you should ask; why must you inquire about other matters, such as the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, buddhas, and the supreme sons [of the Buddha]?
How many are there for each body? Why do you not ask this: how many *āyutas* are there in this flame, and how many *āyutas* are there in the wind?

Furthermore, how many faculties (*indriya*) are there, and how many *āyutas* are there in each faculty? How many pores are there, and how many are there in the eyebrows? What is the King Vaiśravaṇa, the Sovereign Lord, and the Wheel-Turning Sage King?
How does a king provide protection, and what constitutes liberation? These matters—both the detailed exposition and the summary phrasing—are as you have asked.
What are the various desires and various foods and drinks of sentient beings? What are the groves of men and women, and the adamantine firm mountains?
How are they like illusions, dreams, and the analogy of the wild deer’s thirst? What are the mountains adorned by celestial seers, *devas*, and *gandharvas*, and where does liberation reach?
Who is bound and who is liberated? What are the realms of dhyāna, transformations, and the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)?
What is action without cause? What is action with cause? What is action both with and without cause? And what is that which is neither with nor without cause?
What is that which has already ceased after manifesting? How are all cognitions purified? How do cognitions transform, and how do they transform their respective activities?
How are all perceptions severed? Who is it that arises from samādhi and shatters the three realms of existence? Where does this occur, and by what body?
How is it that there are no sentient beings, yet one speaks of a self? How does the worldly convention speak?
We pray that you will extensively analyze the characteristics of what is asked. What is "not-self"? What are the embryonic matrix (*garbha*) and the various different bodies?

What are the views of annihilationism and eternalism? How does the mind attain meditative concentration? What are speech, the various wisdoms, the precepts, and the spiritual lineage, O Son of the Buddha?
What is accomplishment, and what is the treatise? What are the various teachers and disciples, and these diverse sentient beings?

Furthermore, what are they? What constitutes food and drink? What is the clever Māra’s contrivance? What are the trees and creepers? What are the questions asked by the Son of the Most Victorious One?
What are the various buddha-fields? What is the long ascetic practice of the sages? What constitutes a clan, and from which teacher did one receive instruction?
What is meant by "ugliness"? What kind of person practices in the desire realm? Why does one not awaken to Akaniṣṭha? What is mundane supernormal power? What is a bhikṣu?
What is a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*)? What is a reward Buddha (*vipāka-buddha*)?
What is a Tathatā Buddha? What is a Buddha of equal wisdom? What is the Sangha of the Buddha-sons? Thus you ask, O Son of the Buddha.

In the Vīṇā-dhvaja drum-flower buddha-field, there are seven points concerning the ground of the mind that transcends light; these questions, as well as many others, are all asked according to reality.

These and other numerous sons of the Buddha should each ask their respective questions, which correspond to the characteristics [of the truth], are free from all views and errors, and transcend verbal expression through the *siddhānta*.
I shall now reveal them by establishing the sequence of the verses. O sons of the Buddha, listen well and attentively!
These one hundred and eight phrases are as taught by all the Buddhas:

the phrase of non-arising and the phrase of arising; the phrase of permanence and the phrase of impermanence; the phrase of characteristics and the phrase of characteristiclessness; the phrase of abiding-change and the phrase of non-abiding-change; the phrase of momentariness and the phrase of non-momentariness;
the phrase of intrinsic nature and the phrase of being apart from intrinsic nature; the phrase of emptiness and the phrase of non-emptiness.

The phrase of cessation and the phrase of non-cessation; the phrase of limit and the phrase of no-limit; the phrase of middle and the phrase of non-middle; the phrase of permanence and the phrase of impermanence;
the phrase of condition and the phrase of non-condition; the phrase of cause and the phrase of non-cause; the phrase of affliction and the phrase of non-affliction;

the phrase of craving and the phrase of non-craving; the phrase of skillful means and the phrase of non-means; the phrase of artifice and the phrase of non-artifice; the phrase of purity and the phrase of non-purity.
The phrase of accomplishment and the phrase not of accomplishment; the phrase of analogy and the phrase not of analogy; the phrase of disciple and the phrase not of disciple;

the phrase of teacher and the phrase not of teacher; the phrase of spiritual lineage and the phrase not of spiritual lineage; the phrase of the three vehicles and the phrase not of the three vehicles;

the phrase of possession and the phrase not of possession; the phrase of aspiration and the phrase not of aspiration; the phrase of the three spheres and the phrase not of the three spheres; the phrase of characteristics and the phrase not of characteristics.

The category of existence and the category of non-existence; the category of both and the category of neither; the category of the bliss of the present life realized through one’s own noble wisdom and the category of the lack of such bliss in the present life;
the category of buddha-fields and the category of non-fields; the category of *ābhāsa* (appearance) and the category of non-*ābhāsa*;

the category of water and the category of non-water; the category of the bow and the category of non-bow; the category of reality and the category of unreality; the category of number and the category of non-number, and number itself.
The phrase and the non-phrase; the phrase of illumination and the non-phrase of illumination; the phrase of space and the non-phrase of space; the phrase of clouds and the non-phrase of clouds;

the phrase of arts, crafts, and fields of knowledge and the non-phrase of arts, crafts, and fields of knowledge; the phrase of wind and the non-phrase of wind; the phrase of earth and the non-phrase of earth;
the phrase of mind and the non-phrase of mind; the phrase of designation and the non-phrase of designation; and intrinsic nature.
The phrase of non-intrinsic nature; the phrase of the aggregates and the phrase of non-aggregates; the phrase of sentient beings and the phrase of non-sentient beings;

the phrase of wisdom and the phrase of non-wisdom; the phrase of nirvāṇa and the phrase of non-nirvāṇa; the phrase of suchness and the phrase of non-suchness; the phrase of external paths and the phrase of non-external paths;
the phrase of chaos and the phrase of non-chaos; the phrase of illusion and the phrase of non-illusion; the phrase of dreams and the phrase of non-dreams.
The phrase of flame is not the phrase of flame; the phrase of image is not the phrase of image; the phrase of wheel is not the phrase of wheel;
the phrase of gandharva is not the phrase of gandharva; the phrase of deva is not the phrase of deva; the phrase of food and drink is not the phrase of food and drink;
the phrase of sexual desire is not the phrase of sexual desire; the phrase of view is not the phrase of view; the phrase of pāramitā is not the phrase of pāramitā; the phrase of precept is not...
The phrase of precepts; the phrase of sun, moon, and stars; the phrase of non-sun, moon, and stars; the phrase of truths; the phrase of non-truths;

the phrase of fruits; the phrase of non-fruits; the phrase of cessation and arising; the phrase of non-cessation and non-arising; the phrase of remedies; the phrase of non-remedies; the phrase of characteristics; the phrase of non-characteristics;

the phrase of branches; the phrase of non-branches; the phrase of fields of specialized knowledge (*śilpasthāna*); the phrase of non-fields of specialized knowledge; the phrase of meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*); the phrase of non-meditative concentrations; the phrase of delusion.

The phrase is not a deluded phrase; the manifesting phrase is not a manifesting phrase; the protective phrase is not a protective phrase; the clan phrase is not a clan phrase; the seer phrase is not a seer phrase;
the king phrase is not a king phrase; the embracing phrase is not an embracing phrase; the jewel phrase is not a jewel phrase; the prophetic phrase is not a prophetic phrase;
the icchantika phrase is not an icchantika phrase; the phrase of woman, man, and neuter.

The phrase of neither female nor male nor neuter; the phrase of flavor and the phrase of non-flavor; the phrase of phenomena and the phrase of non-phenomena; the phrase of the body and the phrase of non-body;

the phrase of awakening and the phrase of non-awakening; the phrase of movement and the phrase of non-movement; the phrase of faculties and the phrase of non-faculties; the phrase of the conditioned and the phrase of non-conditioned;
the phrase of the unconditioned and the phrase of non-unconditioned; the phrase of cause and effect and the phrase of non-cause-and-effect; and the phrase of the Ultimate of Form (*Akaniṣṭha*).

The phrase that is not a phrase; the ultimate phrase that is not an ultimate phrase; the section-phrase that is not a section-phrase; the thicket-and-vine phrase that is not a thicket-and-vine phrase;
the miscellaneous phrase that is not a miscellaneous phrase; the explanatory phrase that is not an explanatory phrase; the Vinaya phrase that is not a Vinaya phrase;
the bhikṣu phrase that is not a bhikṣu phrase; the locus phrase that is not a locus phrase; the syllable phrase that is not a syllable phrase. Mahāmati, these are the one hundred [phrases].
These eight statements were previously taught by the Buddhas; you and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study them.

Herein begins the main body of the text, which consists of three parts: the request, the granting of permission to speak, and the actual discourse. The text says: "Now, by means of one hundred and eight points, I respectfully consult the Most Honored One among the Honorable"—this is the *request*.
"I shall explain for you the realm of self-realization"—this is the *granting of permission to speak*. The following is the *discourse*.
Furthermore, the first of the two [sections] provides a general inquiry and a summary conclusion by means of verses, stating: "How does one purify mindfulness? and so forth—this is the inquiry.

"Arising and non-arising," and so forth—this is the summary. It is also an explanation. "The phrase 'non-arising' and the phrase 'arising,'" and so forth—this is the concluding reference that reveals the meaning.
In total, there are one hundred and eight phrases of meaning, together with the five dharmas, the three natures, and the eight consciousnesses.
Although the enumerations of the two kinds of non-self differ in their breadth and brevity, their essential meaning is identical; the general purport of the sutras is summarized therein.

To demonstrate this briefly for now: since it is called "the realm of self-awakening" and "that which was taught by the Buddhas of the past," and is the foremost among the various gates of the Mahayana perfections—the very heart of all Buddhas—then it is that which is realized by the unsurpassed awakened mind.
The realms of the three periods of time, the path of penetration, and the immeasurable gates of liberation—what could possibly surpass these?

Nevertheless, as for this Dharma, it possesses principle and phenomena; it possesses nature and cultivation; it possesses the true and the false; it possesses delusion and awakening (the meanings of defilement and purity, bondage and liberation, opposition and conformity are as above;
regarding delusion and awakening, etc.); it possesses teaching and practice; it possesses cause and fruit; it possesses essence and function; it possesses identity and difference.
The meaning of the single chapter on "Illuminating Being and Non-being" can be understood as encompassing the beginning and the end (etc.). Question:
Since both the questions posed and the responses received proceed toward the fundamental [truth] without a fixed sequence, it is improper to demand a definite number of sections or their synthesis.

It is only when reaching the final summary and pointing back that one says: "I shall now manifest the sequential establishment of the phrases," which serves as a general conclusion to the preceding questions and responses.

The one hundred and eight phrases demonstrate the establishment [of the system]. (Note: According to the current Song edition of the main text, there are only one hundred and four phrases; by adding the four phrases from the *Vimalakīrti* [Xiānchā], the number of phrases becomes complete.

For instance, beneath the phrases "existence" and "non-existence," the *Vimalakīrti* renders them as "existence-phrase and non-existence-phrase" and "non-existence-phrase and not-non-existence-phrase. Furthermore, the phrase "the bliss of the present dharma through the manifestation of one's own noble wisdom" is expanded by the *Vimalakīrti* into two phrases.

Likewise, the phrase "arising and ceasing" and "not arising and ceasing" are also divided into two phrases. Finally, beneath the phrase "explanation" and "not explanation," the *Vimalakīrti* further adds the phrases "definitive" and "not definitive," totaling four added phrases. And...
The enumeration reaching this number may also symbolize the one hundred and eight dharmas that correspond to the one hundred and eight afflictions;
thus, the numerical meaning is complete (and so forth). Having already grasped the general framework at the outset, the subsequent sections shall now be explained in detail.
"How does one purify mindfulness? is a question posed from the perspective of awakening. "How does one perceive delusion and confusion? is a question posed from the perspective of delusion.

Because all defiled and pure phenomena are established from these two minds, there are further two phrases regarding their increase, which can be understood through the one hundred and eight questions.
Their summary explanation states: "Birth and non-birth.
Birth refers to all phenomena within delusion, which are fundamentally based on momentary false thoughts; non-birth refers to that which is not so.
Thus, because one awakens to the fact that all phenomena ultimately converge upon the principle of the emptiness of *nirvāṇa*, it is called the "emptiness of *nirvāṇa*.
"Momentary convergence" (*kṣaṇa-gati*) means that there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). "Convergence" (*gati*) signifies "going," while "reaching" (*prāpti*) signifies "extreme limit.

Both of these convergences reach their ultimate limit in a single principle; this single principle is the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature. Because there is no intrinsic nature, there is arising.
Since even non-arising does not arise, and that [non-arising] likewise does not arise, he knotted his fingers and said: "The phrase 'non-arising,' the phrase 'arising,' and so forth.
This indicates that the questions, the responses, and the concluding summary of the knotted fingers share a single, unified purpose.

Consequently, all subsequent matters and phrases are subsumed under the category of "arising," while all non-phrases are subsumed under the category of "non-arising"; it is simply a matter of realizing that all phenomena are non-arising.
That "arising" and "non-arising" are both solely one's own mind, and that all principles emerge therefrom—these one hundred and eight phrases are summarized in a single word.

However, the intention to mutually clarify those points that specifically contradict the following phrase is first indicated here; thus, it merely serves as a concluding summary for the subsequent questions. Although they are not explained separately, the underlying principle is contained therein, as the ancients have said: [The original Chinese text follows: 而生生而不生皆唯自心及出諸理則一百八句一言蔽之矣而特與次句反者互顯之意首示於此故至後問領結而已雖不別釋理在其中舊謂 **Translation:** "That 'arising' and 'non-arising' are both solely one's own mind, and that all principles emerge therefrom"—thus the one hundred and eight phrases are summarized in a single word. Yet, the intent to mutually manifest those [points] that specifically contradict the subsequent phrase is first shown here;
therefore, it merely serves as a concluding summary for the later inquiries. Although they are not explained individually, the principle is contained within them, as the ancients have said."
As for the answer being found in the subsequent text: later on, there is a separate question and a separate answer; because it arose from a renewed request, it is not related to the previous intent.

Furthermore, there are names and characteristics that are difficult to understand, and those who provide explanations may mistakenly point to various other commentaries. Moreover, since this is a text of inquiry, it is not necessary to be exhaustive in detail.
All of these are teachings where the response to the capacity of the audience is without fixed form; the translators have retained or omitted them as appropriate to the circumstances.

Regarding the textual meanings of the secular classics, if one were to correlate them one by one, it would only increase the proliferation of names and concepts; therefore, it is sufficient to omit them.
Second, as for the separate questions and separate answers in the prose section, they follow the sequence of the text. [End of] Chapter Three.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are there for the various consciousnesses?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing for the various consciousnesses;

they are not to be known by means of discursive thought. There are two kinds of arising for the various consciousnesses: namely, arising as a continuous flow (*pravṛtti*) and arising as manifestation (*nimitta*). There are two kinds of abiding: namely, abiding as a continuous flow..."

Regarding abiding and the abiding of characteristics, there are two kinds of cessation: namely, the cessation of the stream and the cessation of characteristics. Mahāmati, the various consciousnesses have three kinds of characteristics:

namely, the characteristic of transformation, the characteristic of activity, and the characteristic of reality. Mahāmati, briefly stated there are three kinds of consciousness; explained in detail, there are eight aspects. What are the three?
They are the true consciousness, the manifesting consciousness, and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena.

"All phenomena are mind-only; they arise through the transformation of the mind. This is taught because it clarifies that the mind encompasses all things, thereby showing that consciousness is fundamentally rooted in the mind.

Although consciousness manifests in various forms, the mind itself is non-dual. This passage clarifies the characteristics of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the various consciousnesses, and its intent is threefold:

first, to provide a general demonstration of the characteristics of all consciousnesses; second, to specifically clarify the sequential order of the present sense organs and their objects; [and third, to explain the nature of the transformation of the support].

Rebirth is based upon the beginningless *ālayavijñāna*; thus, the three [aspects] manifest the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) as non-extinguished, establishing the core tenet of the Sūtra as the "Heart of the Buddha’s Words.
Regarding the initial question by Mahāmati, the meaning of "characteristics of consciousness" refers to the arising and ceasing of mental conceptions; hence the various questions.

In the response, first the characteristics are briefly shown, and subsequently the meanings are explained in detail. Within the brief exposition, it is stated that "the various consciousnesses exist..."
The two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing that cannot be known through discursive thought refer to the two types: the continuous flow (*pravṛtti*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because they are difficult to discern due to their subtlety and coarseness, they cannot be clarified by means of identity or difference, or conjunction or separation.

Furthermore, because these marks of consciousness are subtle, they are the domain of the Buddhas; only through wisdom can they be fully exhausted, for they are beyond the reach of other conceptualizations, emotions, or notions.
To speak briefly regarding that which is unknowable, it is said: "The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising," and so forth.
Although the text lists them separately, in total there are only two characteristics: the characteristic of continuous flow (*pravāha-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of arising (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*).

As for the continuous flow, it refers to the aggregate of consciousness within, which continues from moment to moment without ever pausing, as described in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* as being like a rapid stream of water. When viewed...

Regarding "tranquility" in terms of consciousness: the eighth ālayavijñāna is characterized by its manifestations appearing externally, dwelling within the sense organs and their objects, and undergoing arising, ceasing, and transformation.
In terms of consciousness, this refers to the sixth manovijñāna, which includes the five sensory consciousnesses and also secondarily encompasses the seventh vijñāna.

Although they are thus distinguished through their functions of discernment, their substance is fundamentally not different. When each is said to undergo arising, abiding, and ceasing, it is merely... [the general case].
Conditioned phenomena possess the three phases from beginning to end, alternating between arising and ceasing;

when the characteristic of change (*anyathātva*) is added, they are further said to be the "eight phases that transform things," consisting of the great and the small. It is also said that the various consciousnesses have three phases, and that three consciousnesses have eight phases;
thus, the consciousnesses and their phases are described with varying degrees of detail. Regarding the phase of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), there are six.

The meaning of consciousness (*vijñāna*) arising sequentially in relation to the sense organs and their objects is also called the "aspect of activity" (*karmalakṣaṇa*) of the *vijñapti-matratā-vibhāga-śāstra*.
This refers to what is stated in the *Awakening of Faith*: "Because of non-enlightenment (*abodha*), the mind moves; this is called 'activity' (*karman*).
It is also termed the "manifesting consciousness" (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*), which is the eighth consciousness. This sutra does not establish a ninth consciousness separately.

Because consciousness [is the same as] the true aspect, the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) exists within the eighth [consciousness], yet there are distinctions such as phenomenon and principle, essence and function, coarse and subtle, and sequential priority and posteriority;
thus, the mutual manifestation of benefit, root, and branch is merely the revealing of their respective aspects.

The commentator’s treatment of manifest karma in contrast to the seven consciousnesses implies that the eighth consciousness is purely "true" (*zhen*), which reverses the conventional path and also clearly contradicts texts such as the *Zongjing lu*.

Regarding what is currently being addressed, it does not reach the level of the seven [consciousnesses]; the meaning will be clearly elucidated later when one sees the detailed explanation of the characteristics of cognition in other texts (1).
Mahāmati, just as a bright mirror holds all forms and images, so too does the manifesting consciousness appear in its locus; Mahāmati, it is just like this.
