The manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the consciousness that discriminates objects (*vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*)—these two possess characteristics of being perishable and imperishable, and they serve as mutual causes for one another.
Mahāmati, the inconceivable perfuming and the inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness.

Mahāmati, the grasping of various sense-objects and the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization are the causes of the consciousness that discriminates objects. Mahāmati, if those various unrealities obscure the true consciousness...
When all false imaginings cease, then all sense-faculties and consciousnesses cease; this is called the cessation of characteristics (*nimitta-nirodha*).

Mahāmati, as for the cessation of continuity (*saṃtati-nirodha*), when the cause of continuity ceases, then continuity ceases; when that from which it proceeds and its object of perception cease, then continuity ceases.
Mahāmati, why is this so? Because these are its supports. "Support" refers to the conditioning influence (*vāsanā*) of beginningless false imagination.
This refers to the deluded conceptualizations regarding the objects of the consciousnesses, such as the "seeing" of one's own mind.
Next, the meaning is explained in detail through further analysis. Regarding the terms "arising and ceasing": while the names are the same, their meanings differ from what was stated above.

Previously, it was explained generally that the characteristics of consciousness involve arising and ceasing, and having ceased, they arise again; therefore, arising and ceasing constitute delusion. This [section], however, [addresses] the single reality.

The characteristics are manifested through the statement that "extinction" means the extinction of delusion, which constitutes the true; thus, extinction without extinction is itself quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).

Within this, first the reason for the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) is clarified to reveal its fundamental capacity to give rise [to phenomena], stating: "For example, like a bright mirror," etc.

This correctly explains that the clarity of the mirror can manifest all forms and images without error; therefore, it corresponds to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), which acts as the objective support (*ālambana*).
When the manifestations of form appear, because the six consciousnesses depend upon both the primary and secondary [realms], one knows that the subject and object cannot be conflated as one.

Next, regarding the meaning of the manifestation and the causal nature of the objective consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*), it is said: "These two are mutually causes, characterized by the destructible and the indestructible;

this is because the objective consciousness is destructible, as its consciousness perishes along with its objects, and thus possesses the quality of destruction, whereas the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) is not [destructible]."

Because it is indestructible, maintains its support, is not lost, and is absolutely non-extinguished, although there is a distinction between destruction and non-destruction, they are mutually dependent causes;
thus they are neither different nor non-different. The sequential discussion of the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses should also be understood in this way, as will be clarified later.
Regarding the three types of causes for each of the two consciousnesses, it is said: "inconceivable perfuming," etc.; the term "inconceivable" refers to that which cannot be conceptualized.
This discussion refers precisely to what was previously termed "neither identical nor different, neither combined nor dispersed. Therefore, there is no perfuming, yet there is perfuming;
it is perfumed within the unchanging *tathatā* (suchness), which changes to become ignorance (*avidyā*). This constitutes the cause of the *darśana-vijñāna* (manifesting consciousness).

Furthermore, the apprehension of sensory objects by the five faculties, the discrimination of the beautiful and the ugly, and the remote tracing back of beginningless false conceptualization—all these constitute the causes of the *viniścaya-vijñāna* (discriminating consciousness of phenomena).

Regarding the term "cause," the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) can be known; in relation to the preceding [characteristics] of abiding and ceasing, all of those are the characteristic of arising.
Next, regarding the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*): if the aforementioned characteristics and the continuous flow (*pravāha*) all cease, it is called "cessation.

As for the phrase "if it covers that true consciousness" (*tattva-vijñāna*), "covering" means to obscure; that is, because the various false delusions that are able to cover that true consciousness are extinguished, the nature of the true consciousness becomes manifest.

The faculties, objects, and consciousnesses will no longer arise; this non-arising is what is called "extinction. Regarding the explanation based on the principle of mutual reversal, that interpretation is somewhat circuitous.
That being so, how does one extinguish delusion? It is simply by illuminating that the deluded consciousness is fundamentally empty.

As for the extinction of the continuity [of consciousness], it refers to the aforementioned characteristic of the flowing consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); because it arises from causes and conditions, its extinction likewise follows.
Because it continues to cease, it is called "the cessation of the cause," and so forth. The "cause" refers to beginningless false conceptualization (*anādikāla-vikalpa*);
this is what is meant by the "basis" (*āśraya*) mentioned in the text. The "object-condition" (*ālambana*) refers to the objects of the consciousnesses of one's own mind, such as seeing and hearing;

this is what is meant by the "conditioned. Furthermore, the mention of "false conceptualization" includes both the subject that perceives and the object perceived, for when these two are combined, there subsequently arises the sequence of [phenomenal] existence.
If one seeks reality within these three—the marks of false conceptualization and consciousness—it cannot be found; thus, the limits of the past and future are severed.
The marks of the continuous consciousness will no longer continue. This non-continuation constitutes cessation, not the cessation of an inherent nature.
The text that interrogates and explains this is manifest. (2)
Mahāmati, it is like this: a lump of clay and its atoms are neither different nor non-different; so too is the case with golden ornaments.
Mahāmati, if the lump of clay were different from its atoms, it would not be composed of them; yet in reality it is composed of them, therefore they are not different.
If they were non-different, then there would be no distinction between the lump of clay and its atoms. Thus, Mahāmati, does the transformation occur.

If the true nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) were different [from its manifestations], the storehouse consciousness would not be their cause. If it were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cease, the storehouse consciousness should also cease;

yet its own true nature does not actually cease. Therefore, Mahāmati, it is not the cessation of the storehouse consciousness in its own true nature that occurs, but rather the cessation of its karmic aspect (*karmalakṣaṇa*).
If the storehouse consciousness were to cease in its own true nature, then the storehouse consciousness itself would perish, Mahāmati.
"Mahāmati, the doctrine of cessation is no different from the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists. Those non-Buddhists maintain such a theory as follows:
'When the grasping of objects ceases, the flow of consciousness also ceases. Mahāmati, if the flow of consciousness were to cease, then the beginningless flow would have to be severed.
However, Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists do not say that the cause for the arising of the flow is the convergence of eye-consciousness, form, and light."
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other causes for birth; those causes are said to be the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*), the Person (*puruṣa*), the Lord (*īśvara*), Time (*kāla*), or atoms (*paramāṇu*).

The three types of knowledge [of the Vedas] clarify that consciousnesses are neither different nor not different, precisely manifesting that the true nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is non-extinguished.
Is this not what is meant by the "Buddha’s Mind-Essence," the central tenet of this sutra? The text first establishes a simile, stating:
"It is like a lump of clay and its subtle particles, or like gold and its ornaments. These are intended to clarify that they are neither different nor non-different;
for if they were different, the lump of clay would not be composed of subtle particles, yet in reality it is formed from them.

If they were not different, then their association would not be distinct; therefore, their characteristics are distinguished to clarify that they are not the same, while their essence is one to clarify that they are not different.
This is the general purport of the analogy. Next, the detailed explanation clarifying the phenomena states: "In this way, Mahāmati," and so forth.
The meaning intends to show that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) are neither different nor non-different in their true nature.

If they were different, then the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) would not be the cause; for that which is not a cause cannot be the cause of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). Upon initial examination, this is not so.

If they were not different, then when [the evolving consciousnesses] cease, they would cease simultaneously; it should not be that the store-consciousness also ceases, because the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the store-consciousness is indestructible.
Thus, its non-identity is clarified by the fact that the evolving consciousnesses exist because they have the store-consciousness as their cause; its identity is clarified...
Since it is neither different nor non-different, it is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished.

Because it is not extinguished, it is not annihilation; because it is not non-extinguished, it is not permanence. Being neither annihilation nor permanence, the nature of the single truth exists herein;
in reality, it cannot be extinguished. Thus, what is called "extinction" merely refers to the extinction of the marks of ignorance and karma. Therefore, it is said:

It is not that the consciousness of the self-characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) ceases, but rather that its aspect of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) ceases. The reason it ceases is that the cessation occurs through the transformation of the aspect (*lakṣaṇa-parāvṛtti*), not through the destruction of the nature (*svabhāva*).
If both nature and aspect were to cease together, one would fall into the nihilistic view of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which is not what is meant by the Buddha-dharma.
Those various non-Buddhists merely emerge from external calculations, asserting nothing more than that there is an object to be grasped and experienced.
Because the elements cease, the flow of consciousness ceases; thus, by the cessation of the objects and the cessation of consciousness, one falls into the view of annihilationism.
How could such a person know that the nature of the flowing consciousness arises from the beginningless *ālayavijñāna*?

Furthermore, when they say that the cause for the arising of the flow is not something distinct from the four conditions such as the eye, but rather that there is no other separate cause—how could there be a separate cause that is not subject to annihilation?
If "superior," "wondrous," and so forth are precisely those imagined causes, they are designated as distinct characteristics (as stated in the third and fourth [sections]).
○ This concludes Chapter Four.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*), namely: the self-nature of accumulation (*saṃbhāva-svabhāva*), the self-nature of nature (*svabhāva-svabhāva*), and the characteristic of self-nature (*lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*).
The nature of self-nature, the great element of self-nature, the cause of self-nature, the condition of self-nature, the accomplishment of self-nature, and the self-nature itself.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*):

namely, the realm of the mind, the realm of wisdom (*jñāna*), the realm of knowledge (*vidyā*), the realm of vision, the realm that transcends the two views, the realm that transcends the stages of the sons [of the Buddha], and the realm of the Tathāgata’s own attainment.
Mahāmati, this is the mind of the ultimate reality of the intrinsic nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.
By means of the mind of the ultimate reality of the intrinsic nature, they accomplish the worldly, the world-transcending, and the world-transcending-superior dharmas of the Tathāgatas.
With the noble eye of wisdom, they enter into and establish the specific and general characteristics exactly as they have been established.
Mahāmati, how is it that one shares the evil views of the treatises of the outsiders?
It is because they do not realize that what appears as their own objective realm is a manifestation of their own mind; they fail to understand the limits of this and thus do not penetrate [reality].
Mahāmati, foolish ordinary people formulate dualistic theories regarding existence, non-existence, and the self-nature of things, concerning the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The previous statement that the single nature is indestructible differs from that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), yet the reason for this difference has not been fully exhausted. This is now correctly clarified:
the Tathāgata’s self-nature, the ultimate reality mind (paramārtha-citta), does not share in common with non-Buddhists or ordinary beings.

Since this ultimate reality transcends the realm of the stages of the sons of the Buddha (bodhisattva-bhūmi) and even surpasses that of the Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), how much more so does it transcend that of non-Buddhists and ordinary beings?
Regarding the names and meanings of these seven types, if one were to explain them solely in terms of delusion, it would not constitute a definitive conclusion.

Since it is stated that "this is the self-nature and first-principle mind of the Tathāgatas of the three periods" and also that "ordinary beings lack self-nature," does this not simultaneously conclude that the meaning of "nature" applies both to the sage and the ordinary person?
Thus, it is appropriate to explain them collectively according to the perspective of the sage. Within this, the former...
The sixth is the non-emergence of cause and effect, which refers to the nature of the accumulation of self-nature (*saṃbhāra-svabhāva*). This is the cause for the gathering of all virtues;

because of this accumulated cause, there is both nature (*svabhāva*) and appearance (*lakṣaṇa*), with nature being internal and appearance being external. The nature of the great elements (*mahābhūta-svabhāva*) is the fruit.

While the great elements are fundamentally universal, here they refer specifically to the noble retribution, namely "constant form" (*nitya-rūpa*) and so forth; these are the five aggregates of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā-skandha*).
Because it is a fruit, there are causes and conditions; the cause is primary while the conditions are auxiliary.

That which is accomplished by cause and condition is the accomplishment of the nature of self-nature (*svabhāva*), that is, the accomplishment of the subsequently attained ultimate mind (*paramārtha-citta*). Next, the seven kinds of ultimate truth are explained;

following the above, these should also be interpreted solely in terms of awakening, with both general and specific aspects. The first six apply generally to the lower stages, reaching them through one's own effort.
The ultimate limit of the realm exists only in the Buddha; furthermore, what is called the "realm" refers to the realm of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
This serves as a general conclusion summarizing what preceded, and it also functions as a further explanation of the preceding meaning, stating:
"This is the Tathāgata’s mind of the primary meaning," which refers to his own arrival at that realm. It also concurrently transcends the realm of the mind of the stage of the *putra* (son).
This is the objective realm of the mind itself. "Accomplishing the eye of wisdom" refers to *prajñā* (wisdom); "entering into specific and general characteristics" refers to *jñāna* (knowledge);
"that which is established as it is" refers to vision (*darśana*); and "not sharing in the evil views of external paths" refers to transcending the two types of views.
Thus, the names and their meanings may be understood. By means of this mind, one accomplishes the noble eye of wisdom of the Tathāgata.

Inferring the effect from the cause and the cause being manifested in the effect also indicates that cultivation is identical to the nature (*dharmatā*), and the nature is perfected through cultivation.

Therefore, when the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is opened, it arises entirely from the manifestation of the nature; even the eye of knowledge (*jñāna-cakṣus*) is insufficient to be called the perfection of virtue through the nature.
Thus it is said: "Entering the establishment of self-characteristics and common characteristics," while simultaneously referring to the mundane and supramundane. (1)

The profound necessarily encompasses the shallow; secondly, the object [of contemplation] pervades all, wherein entering the particular is the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), and entering the common is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
The single mind as the three truths is precisely this principle: the one is the general characteristic and the three are the particular characteristics.
Based on these three truths, various names and terms are established, namely: the "Mind-Only Dharma-realm" (*cittamātra-dharmadhātu*) as the great general characteristic.

Are the gates and so forth not shared with the non-Buddhists? However, if one were to clarify only what is unique and fail to mention what is shared, then the realms of ordinary beings and sages would be utterly severed;
how could that possibly be the truth? Therefore, the text asks "How so? below and further investigates and explains the reason for their being shared.
This intention reveals that what is unique is also shared, and what is shared is also unique; thus it says, "that which is called one's own realm."

Regarding the views based on the false discrimination of the elements (*dhātu*), they claim that their own objective realm is identical to the objective realm of one's own mind; from the very beginning, these have never been different.

Yet, those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) give rise to false discriminations of difference within this ultimate identity, and thus cannot realize that all objective realms are merely manifestations of one's own mind.
How much less could they immediately understand that what they perceive is nothing other than the mind?

Regarding "nature" (*prakṛti*) and "limitations" (*pradeśa*) being non-penetrating: this refers to the fact that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) themselves have no penetration regarding the limitations of their own minds;
because they give rise to views of limitation within what is actually without limitation, they cannot penetrate it.

As for "the self-nature of the naturelessness of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana-niḥsvabhāva-svabhāva*): it does not mean that there is no nature at all. Rather, because they are deluded and lack awakening, one uses the term "non-existence" as a derogatory expression. These are the two types of dualistic views.
This term should encompass two meanings: namely, the duality of existence and non-existence, and the duality of mutual relativity.
While the duality of mutual relativity is only fully exhausted upon attaining Buddhahood, the duality of existence and non-existence is already present from the initial stage of the path.

Although current usage mostly relies on the former meaning—whereby that which is to be abandoned remains relatively near—it must also be understood that when speaking of the ultimate Middle Way, it too must transcend all relativity. [End of Chapter Five]

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain how the suffering of the three realms of existence, which arises from false discrimination, is extinguished; how ignorance, craving, and karma—the conditions for rebirth—are extinguished;
and how the illusory objects manifested by one's own mind are seen according to their appearance.

Mahāmati, if there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who wish to establish the manifestation of cause and effect as having either no seed or having a seed, or who maintain that things abide through conditions, aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, or who claim that once born they perish; [all such views are based on false discrimination].
Mahāmati, whether it be continuity, entities, birth, existence, nirvāṇa, the path, karma, its fruit, or the truths—these are the doctrines of nihilism that destroy [reality].
Why is this? Because they cannot be apprehended in the present, and because seeing a beginning is not possible.
Mahāmati, for example, a broken jar does not perform the function of a jar, nor does a scorched seed [produce a sprout].

"Mahāmati, such is the nature of the 'tooth' (the causal basis). If the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases has already ceased, is now ceasing, or will cease, then because one's own mind’s false conceptualization sees no cause, they cannot arise sequentially.

Mahāmati, if you further claim that consciousness arises from the conjunction of three conditions—whether there be no seed or there be a seed—then a tortoise should produce hair and sand should yield oil; your own doctrine would be destroyed and would contradict your own resolution."
Regarding the definition of "having seeds" and "being without seeds," such assertions entail these faults: all performed activities become entirely empty and meaningless.

Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists who claim that things arise from the conjunction of three conditions—asserting that the characteristics of causes, conditions, and effects, as well as their own specific marks (*svalakṣaṇa*), exist in the past, future, and present;
and that whether characterized by having seeds or being without seeds, they have been established through a continuous succession of causal efficacy since time immemorial, and are thus perceived.

Mahāmati, those foolish ordinary people who are consumed by evil views, who are crooked, deluded, intoxicated, and devoid of wisdom, falsely claim to speak as an Omniscient One because they have turned their perceptions toward the ground [of reality] and perceived their own habitual tendencies. Thus it is said.
The illusory realm manifested from one’s own mind is singular, yet there are those who see it and those who do not, those who awaken to it and those who do not;

this is because deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) acts as an obstruction, preventing awakening. Since the very substance [of the realm] transforms and ceases, it follows that what is seen is also not far away.

This is because the preceding text states that due to seeing through deluded conceptualization, one does not realize it is a manifestation of one’s own mind; thus, it is said that [the realm] must cease.
Only after delusion ceases does one perceive that the three paths of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) are obstacles; because these obstacles are extinguished, wisdom manifests.
This is why this illusory realm of one's own mind appears accordingly, as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream-event.
By contrast, when delusion has not yet been extinguished, all objective realms are nothing other than real.
The text first briefly indicates that the extinction of the suffering of the three realms of existence through false conceptualization refers to the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*).

Ignorance, craving, and karma constitute the two paths of affliction and karma (*kleśa-mārga* and *karma-mārga*). These evolve across the three periods of time to form the twelve links of dependent origination;

by investigating and deconstructing them, one speaks of the "extinction of conditions. "Following what is seen" means seeing according to the point where those conditions have been extinguished. The three paths are fundamentally identical to the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).

Why wait until after cessation to see this? This is said in contrast to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); thus, although it speaks of "extinguishing" as a way of eliminating the illness, it does not mean that the dharma is eliminated.
Next, in the section clarifying the correct meaning, one first sets forth the externalist calculations to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox, stating:
"If there are śramaṇas, etc. Since this corresponds to the subsequent text, it refers to the views of the non-Buddhists; thus it is known.

This name applies both internally and externally. To cause the manifestation of causes and effects—whether they possess seeds or lack seeds—one reckons that what lacks seeds arises spontaneously (*svabhāva*), while what possesses seeds is reckoned as having causes such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) or the *prakṛti* (primordial nature). Thus, by desiring the production of effects, causes and effects manifest in succession.
Furthermore, one reckons that [the self] abides in dependence upon things, events, or time, or else takes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its conditions.

Those who claim that things arise and abide here [in this world] hold the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), while those who say they perish after arising hold the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
To refute the calculation of eternalism through repeated arguments, the text states: "If there were a continuity," and so forth. This means:

if there were a continuity of cause and effect, or if things, or their arising and abiding, were all existent, then regarding what is now called the four [states], such as nirvāṇa, etc., [the same logic would apply].
If one asserts that the phenomena of the Truths (satya-dharma) are non-existent, it results in the nihilistic view of annihilationism;
therefore, he further interrogates and explains its meaning, saying: "Why is this so? Because those [phenomena] do not exist within these present Four Truths.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "seeing the beginning as non-apprehendable" (*ādi-anupalabdhi*), it means that when one seeks the origin of the self at the very outset and does not find it, one then makes such a calculation.

To reckon that there is a seed when there is no seed, or to attain [a result] when one has not attained it, are all false reckonings; they do not constitute the causal factors for liberation in the present.

For example, it is like a broken jar. Next, the following refutes the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Two analogies are established at the outset: the first analogy shows that it is not a fruit, and if it is not a fruit, then there is no cause;

the second analogy shows that it is not a cause, and if it is not a cause, then there is no fruit. These are also discussed in terms of the characteristics of what has already ceased, what is presently ceasing, and what is about to cease.

Because their expectations are shattered, it is said: "If one reckons that the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases is such that what has already arisen and ceased is 'already ceased,' then there is no cause;
if what is currently ceasing is 'without fruit,' then there is no cause for its imminent cessation.
By this reasoning, all these are but the deluded perceptions of one's own mind. Since they lack a cause, there can be no sequential continuity of arising."
How could one even conceive of its cessation? If you further claim that there is a seed-consciousness, we shall again refute that calculation.
To say that consciousness arises from the combination of the three conditions—the self, the sense organs, and the objects—is as impossible as a tortoise growing hair or sand producing oil;
such a principle simply does not exist. Since each of these three is individually unobtainable, how could they exist when combined?
Therefore it is said: "To deviate from the definitive meaning, if one lacks its fundamental basis, then the activities performed will likewise lack real significance.
It is further said: "Those various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) repeatedly assert their own calculations in many ways;

for instance, they claim that things arise through the conjunction of three conditions, as calculated above, or they claim that seeds exist across the three periods of time—past, present, and future—in terms of both existence and non-existence."
If one speaks in terms of "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), it refers to what is proximate; if one speaks in terms of "phenomena" (*dharma*) established from the beginning, it refers to what is remote.
In either case, they all proceed based upon the stage of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

This refers to the meaning that eighty thousand kalpas ago, from the primordial darkness (*ādi-tamas*), consciousness (*buddhi*) arose, and through successive transformations, the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) were produced. All of these arise from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of past perceptions.

Because it is merely the result of false views and deluded conceptualization, it is said to be "harmed by evil views"; alternatively, the original text says "shì-shì" (噬噬), which also means "to harm" (1).
Mahāmati, furthermore, if other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas perceive that which is devoid of self-nature as being like clouds, a whirling firebrand, or a [mirage-like] pillar...
The city of Gandharvas, the unborn, illusions, mirages, water-moons, and dreams—all these are manifestations of the internal and external mind, born of beginningless false discrimination.
They do not exist apart from one’s own mind; they arise through the causal conditions of false discrimination. When these are extinguished, one speaks of the cessation of false discrimination.

Regarding the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which establishes the body for the sake of experience, there is no mutual relationship between the objects grasped within the realm of consciousness and the grasper.
Mahāmati, one should enter into the discernment that arises from one’s own mind, which is free from the objective realm of non-existence and detached from arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Mahāmati, before long, that bodhisattva shall attain the great wisdom of the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, as well as skillful means that are unconditioned.
Mahāmati, for them, all realms of sentient beings are entirely like an illusion; they do not exert effort regarding causes and conditions, nor do they distance themselves from them.
Free from internal and external objects, seeing nothing outside the mind, one enters successively into the signless state;
one enters successively through the stages of samādhi, proceeding from stage to stage.

Next, to clarify the correct teaching of the Buddha-dharma, it is said: "Furthermore, as for the other śramaṇas and so forth," which refers extensively to the aforementioned illusory phenomena manifested within one's own mind.
"Seeing that they are devoid of self-nature" means seeing that all dharmas are entirely devoid of self-nature, as well as devoid of other-nature, common nature, and causeless nature;
now, to summarize briefly, we speak of "self-nature" because [all] natures are devoid of [inherent] nature.

Therefore, the dharmas of non-arising are like illusions; they are compared to floating clouds, fire-wheels, the moon in water, dreams, and so forth—all of which serve as metaphors for the illusory objects perceived, being one and the same.

If one realizes that illusory objects are fundamentally without interior or exterior, then one sees that what appears as interior and exterior is merely the mind manifesting through deluded thought. Yet all these are formed by beginningless falsehood and do not depart from the self.
When the mind is naturally detached from its own nature, becoming increasingly manifest as illusory, then the causes and conditions of deluded thought are extinguished;
this is what is called the extinction of the suffering of the three realms of existence caused by deluded thought. Thus, while not departing [from reality], one departs [from delusion];

one departs from both the discourse and that which is discoursed upon, as well as the contemplation and that which is contemplated. Ultimately, one departs from everything, including the ālayavijñāna—the storehouse consciousness that establishes the body for experience. Yet, even so, it remains.

The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is truly not something to be abandoned; rather, it is the storehouse consciousness as it manifests—namely, the body, the objects of enjoyment, and the environment—that is to be abandoned.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the objects of consciousness and so forth," "objects" refers to the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), and "appropriation" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). As for "appropriation," this refers to the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*).

This is because, as previously explained, once one is detached from the views [of self], the objects of consciousness cannot be apprehended; therefore, [the notion of appropriation] is inconsistent [with the ultimate state].
Thus, objective realms are non-existent; within that state of non-existence, how could there be arising or ceasing?
Therefore, having transcended the notions of arising, abiding, and ceasing, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the self-mind subsequently arise and enter into all objective realms.

When one discriminates with correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), there is nothing that is not an illusory manifestation of the mind; thus, what is called the illusory manifestation of the self-mind is perceived according to its appearance.

Since the stages (*bhūmi*) are still the preliminary characteristics (*pūrvanimitta*) of the ground (*bhūmi*), it is further clarified that when one proceeds toward the fruit, gives rise to function, and realizes entry into the realm of self-awakening (*pratyātma-gocara*), it is said:

"That bodhisattva will before long attain equality," meaning that this bodhisattva first manifests wisdom by extinguishing delusion, and subsequently enters into the equality of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa; by means of this, two kinds [of realization] are attained.
Expedient means (*upāya*) refers to the skillful means of great compassion, which is the function of transforming sentient beings;
"non-development" expedient means refers to the wisdom that realizes principle.

However, since the realization of principle fundamentally arises from development, the term "non" is used precisely to indicate that there is no development—development being extinguished within the nature (*prakṛti*), such that both self and other are understood as one.

Because the entire realm of sentient beings is like an illusion, there is no need for deliberate mental effort; it proceeds spontaneously through causes and conditions, remaining far removed from internal and external objects.
Yet, one still perceives that there are objects to be abandoned. As one advances in this state, there is only this single mind and nothing further to be seen.
This is the entry into the signless realm (*animitta*), which is the perfect first stage of dwelling—namely, entering the gate of the letter *A*.
Since all dharmas are inherently non-arising, one naturally enters subsequent stages;
thus, there are samādhi-realms that progress from stage to stage, increasing in excellence by degrees until reaching the ultimate limit. (2)
By discerning and observing that the three realms are like an illusion, one shall attain the illusory samādhi;
by transcending what appears to one's own mind as non-existent, one abides in the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Having abandoned those [delusions], one employs skillful means (*upāya*) born of that [realization]—the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*)—and accordingly enters the body of the Tathāgata, enters the transformations of suchness (*tathatā*), and attains mastery over supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), compassion, and skillful means.
Having thus become fully adorned, they enter all Buddha-fields and the abodes of non-Buddhists, transcending mind, thought, and consciousness.
Mahāmati, it is through this gradual transformation that the Bodhisattva attains the body of a Tathāgata.

Therefore, those who wish to attain the Tathāgata’s body of conformity should remain far removed from the false notions of arising, abiding, and ceasing, as well as from the mind, the aggregates, the elements, the sense-bases, and the causal conditions produced by expedient means.

Contemplating that conceptualization is false and is merely mind, one proceeds directly to observe the beginningless habit-energy of false discrimination as the cause of the three realms of existence.
By reflecting on the non-existence [of these realms], one reaches the Buddha-ground of non-arising and attains the noble path of self-realization.
Having attained mastery over one's own mind, one enters into the subtle minds of sentient beings like a mani jewel that assumes the colors of whatever it encounters.
The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) accords with the measure of the mind to gradually establish the stages (bhūmi) in continuous succession;
therefore, Mahāmati, you should diligently train in your own established tenet (svasiddhānta).

When the causal practice has reached its limit and one is about to enter the realization of the fruit, one further reveals the realm of the aforementioned samādhi as being solely what is manifested by one's own mind.
Since even this manifestation that has just appeared cannot be apprehended, it is said that one "transcends the manifestations of one's own mind.
"Transcendence" (*tīrṇa*) carries the meaning of surpassing; when nothing exists, there are no longer various marks.

It is only from the perspective of the cause that it is called the "illusion-like samādhi," whereas at the stage of the fruit, it is said that one "attains the abiding in prajñā," which is the singular wisdom of signlessness (*animitta*).
In the realm of signlessness (*animitta*), one does not perceive even the distinction between produced phenomena and non-produced phenomena; it is in this way that one is detached.
As for what is called "abandoning the skillful means (*upāya*) regarding production," if one were to apply skillful means toward produced phenomena, that would constitute "action" (*kṛtya*);
however, this [state] is the skillful means of non-production and non-cultivation. This is revealed by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
The power and function are also obtained through the samādhi attained at the final moment of the Vajra-like mind; therefore, it is called *samādhi*.
Because of this samādhi, one enters the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) and attains the perfect realization of the single body, the all-bodies, and the three bodies;

therefore, it is called "entering accordingly" (*anupraveśa*). "Tathāgata-body" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "Suchness" (*tathatā*) refers to the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); and "transformation" refers to the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is supernatural power (*abhijñā*).
The Dharma-gates of mastery (*vaśitā*) and so forth involve both transformation and equality; they equally enter all Buddha-fields and the abodes of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Wherever there are sentient beings with the karmic conditions to be transformed and delivered, there is no realm—whether the realm of Māra, the realm of Buddhas, or the realm of non-Buddhists—that is not entered.
Therefore, it is said that they "equally enter. Only by ultimately transcending mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) does one attain the state of non-duality.
Only one who realizes through the wisdom of discernment (*viveka-jñāna*) and manifests the universal form-body (*sarva-rūpa-kāya*) is capable of this;
otherwise, how could one achieve the non-obstructed, equal entry into the identity of Māra and Buddha? This concludes the gradual stages of the Bodhisattva. Furthermore, it is said:

"Those who wish to attain the Tathāgata’s body that enters according to conditions must rely upon the dharma of the fruit to demonstrate the causal cultivation. Briefly stated, there are five [points], beginning with "distancing oneself from... [and so forth].

Regarding the observation, realization, and activation of function, the exhortation to remain distant states that one "should distance oneself" from the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and the mind;
these do not go beyond the dharmas previously identified as objects to be abandoned. This refers to the observation of "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) and "direct advancement" (*pratyakṣa-praveśa*).

That which is "mind-only" means there is no external perception of phenomena; "direct advancement" means not traversing other paths. In this way, one directly observes the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
That which is fundamentally non-existent is the fault of beginningless falsehood, which is affliction (*kleśa*). The cause of delusive thoughts and habitual tendencies is the path of karma.
The three realms of existence are the path of suffering. Contemplating and observing this, one realizes that nothing exists;
thus, one distantly accords with the Buddha-ground of non-arising and reaches the realm of the self-realized noble state—this is "accordance and realization. This alone.
When one attains one's own mind, there is no entry that is not self-attained; thus, all things are sovereign.

Only after this realization and verification does one proceed to function, which is called "reaching the practice of non-development. This means that when a Bodhisattva attains this realized wisdom, they are like a mani jewel that reflects various colors;
with subtle wisdom, they enter the subtle minds of sentient beings and, according to the measure of those minds, teach the absence of [inherent] existence.
The gate of measurement (*pramāṇa*) also causes the recipient to establish [the teachings] through the gradual succession of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the words of the exhortation, "that which is excellent according to one's own *siddhānta*": the word *si* means "pervasive" (*vyāpin*), and *tan* is translated as "giving" (*dāna*).

This refers to the Tathāgata’s pervasive bestowal of the four dharmas, such as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), upon sentient beings, enabling them to obtain the four benefits; this is called the general sense of *siddhānta*.
Since this [text] exhorts the cultivation of both self and others, it is the meaning of one’s own *siddhānta* (established tenet);

furthermore, because there is nothing that is not cultivated through the mind alone, the various schools’ interpretations based on the meanings of "tenets" (*śāsana*) and "seals" (*mudrā*) are erroneous. (3) The above is Chapter Six.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what has been taught—the mind, the thought, the mental consciousness, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the characteristics;
the sphere of activity of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the non-conjunction with objects perceived as one's own mind;
the manifestation of all teachings as the realization of the true nature; and the heart of all Buddha-words—this is for the sake of Laṅkā."

At that time, while the great bodhisattvas dwelling on Mount Malaya in the midst of the ocean were expounding the realm of the *ālayavijñāna*—the ocean-like waves praised by the Tathāgata as the *dharmakāya*—the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "For four causes and conditions, the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arises. What are these four? They are:
the non-awakening to the grasping of what appears as one’s own mind; and the fault of beginningless false discrimination regarding form."
"Mahāmati, due to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), clinging, the nature of consciousness, and the self-nature of desire to see various forms and appearances—
these are called the four causes and conditions by which waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) within the stream of water.
Mahāmati, just as the visual consciousness arises, so too do all the sense organs, atoms, and pores arise simultaneously, following their respective objects."
Having heard that the eight consciousnesses and other such dharmas are the sphere of practice for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
because they do not depart from the objective realms perceived by the minds of sentient beings and are each devoid of characteristics, and thus are not in conjunction;

and because both delusion and enlightenment proceed from the same source and both truth and falsehood emerge together, yet there is a distinction between their conjunction and non-conjunction— the latter, being a false conjunction, is delusion.
That which is non-composite consciousness is true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*). When revealed by means of this, all that has been taught is the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
this is the great essential core of the heart of the speech of all Buddhas.

Having thus set it forth, [the author] requests that for the sake of those who have not yet heard it, the Great Wisdom (*Mahāmati*) be correctly established as the primary subject for the kingdom of Laṅkā, and that the various dharmas previously mentioned be explained.
I wish to hear why the ocean waves and the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) are praised as the realm of the *dharmakāya*.

This means that the ocean waves do not depart from the six consciousnesses within the eight consciousnesses; and that the *ālayavijñāna* reaches the ultimate limit of the eight consciousnesses, being fundamentally indestructible.
It is in this way that they constitute the realm of the *dharmakāya*; this is the reason for such praise and exposition.

In response to your request, I shall first explain that the four conditions, such as the eye and so forth, indicate that the evolving consciousnesses arise based upon the store-consciousness (ālayavijñāna). Thus it is said:

"By means of the four causal conditions, visual consciousness evolves," and so on. What is meant by "the non-awakening to the grasping of what is manifested from one's own mind" refers to the condition of the sense organs (*indriya*).

Because one does not awaken to the fact that [objects] are fundamentally manifestations of one's own mind, they merely function as the condition of the sense organs through grasping; in reality, they do not exist.

Regarding the phrase "originating from the habit-energy of beginningless false delusion," it should properly be stated as "that which is produced by habit-energy" being the causal condition of form (*rūpa-pratyaya*).

Regarding "clinging to the intrinsic nature of consciousness," this is the causal condition of consciousness (*vijñāna-pratyaya*). Regarding "desiring to see various forms and characteristics," this is the causal condition of desire-to-see (*darśana-kāmatā-pratyaya*).

All of these together are described as "manifestations of one's own mind" and "non-enlightenment," though the text is merely abbreviated. It is by means of these four conditions that [the world arises].

When visual consciousness arises, its fundamental cause is traced back to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); therefore it is said that "where the water flows, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise from the storehouse consciousness.

According to this later analogy, the substance of the mind is like the ocean, the eight consciousnesses are like the flowing water, the seventh consciousness is like the turbulent current, and the six consciousnesses are like the waves.
Now, based on the movement of these eight consciousnesses, visual [consciousness] comes to exist.
The arising of the waves of the evolving consciousnesses—such as visual consciousness and so forth—is analogous to the eye;

by using the eye as an example for the other sense organs, it is shown that down to a single atom or a single pore, all arise simultaneously with consciousness. Therefore, they are able to perceive and know just as visual consciousness does.

If it is the case that they arise in succession according to their respective objects, then external objective realms must also arise simultaneously with consciousness and be capable of being cognized through its perception.
Dust is also consciousness; that all phenomena are but consciousness is seen herein (1).
For example, just as a bright mirror manifests various forms and images, so too does the wind of external objects blow upon the ocean of the mind, causing waves of consciousness to arise incessantly.
Because the characteristics produced by these actions are neither different nor non-different, they combine with karma to give rise to profound appearances.
Because they enter into attachment and are unable to comprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth, the five bodies of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) arise.

Mahāmati, one should know that the cause for the arising of those very five bodies of consciousness is the differentiation of causal conditions and the perception of segmented characteristics; it is due to that body [of consciousness] that they arise.
They do not have the thought: "We arise through mutual causality, turning upon the false discrimination and attachment to what is manifested by our own minds. And yet, they do so.
Each [consciousness] functions with its own distinct characteristics, simultaneously discerning objects through the differentiation of temporal segments;

that is, as those [consciousnesses] evolve, they proceed like a practitioner entering the meditative absorption of *dhyāna-samādhi*. Subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) evolve, yet one does not perceive them, thinking instead:

"Consciousness has ceased, and only then do I enter meditative absorption. In reality, consciousness does not cease when one enters meditative absorption, because the seeds of habitual tendencies have not been extinguished.
Because it is extinguished, it is not extinguished; for it is extinguished because the objects of perception that cause its grasping are no longer present.

Mahāmati, such subtle Ālayavijñāna reaches an ultimate limit that cannot be measured or fully determined by the power of the wisdom obtained through samādhi by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or practitioners of external paths, except for the Tathāgatas and those bodhisattvas who dwell on the stages.

There are two types of metaphors: first, the metaphor for the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) being endowed with all the various consciousnesses, like a mirror manifesting images; this is also like the aforementioned manifestation of the evolving consciousnesses.
Second, the metaphor for the various [evolving] consciousnesses depending on the storehouse consciousness to function, like wind blowing over the ocean;

that is to say, because the winds of external objects—the six sense-fields—agitate the ocean of the eight consciousnesses, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses and so forth arise in continuous succession.

Regarding the non-interruption of the causal activity and its characteristics being neither different nor non-different: this means that the cause is the *ālayavijñāna*, which gives rise to the various evolving consciousnesses;
thus, there is the characteristic of activity. This cause and the characteristic of activity are fundamentally neither identical nor different.

Because they are neither identical nor different, they are not conjoined yet are conjoined. This is why one deeply enters into and becomes attached to the characteristics of the arising of those activities and their causes.

Because one knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth is empty, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, arise in succession within the body—the "body" having the sense of being an aggregate (*kāya*), meaning a collection of various objects of perception (*viṣaya*).
Once the five consciousnesses have arisen, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises simultaneously with them, taking the same objects;
therefore, it is said that these very five bodies of consciousness are accompanied by [the mental consciousness] which discriminates and segments the five sensory objects.
To discern and understand these characteristics as the five consciousnesses is because they turn from the five consciousnesses to enter the sixth consciousness for the sake of discrimination;

therefore it is said that they turn based on those [five]. As for the phrase "it does not form such a thought," when the various consciousnesses arise in succession, if it were not for the objective fields (*viṣaya*), the consciousnesses would not themselves claim to be mutually dependent in their successive arising.

Because one clings to the objects before them through the false imaginings manifested by one’s own mind, and because those objects undergo arising and ceasing, consciousness likewise evolves in accordance with them;
thus it is said that "those various signs of disintegration evolve together," meaning that consciousness evolves either because those objects possess various signs of disintegration,
or because consciousness arises through the differentiation of perceived objects— both of these are cases of such evolution.
Arising and ceasing in accordance with objects, it undergoes transformation; yet apart from these external conditions, it cannot be found through the false conceptualization of one’s own mind.

Next, as for the practitioner, this passage relies on the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) to demonstrate the meaning that the limit of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is not extinguished.

That is to say, when a practitioner of dhyāna reaches the ultimate limit of the cessation of perception, because of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they do not perceive the characteristics of consciousness.
Subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) follow along with meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); because of non-awakening, one thinks that consciousness has ceased.
Thus, when entering meditative absorption, consciousness in fact does not cease; it is said that "it does not cease" because the seeds of habitual tendencies have not been extinguished.

Since the seeds still remain, it has never truly ceased; yet, because one abides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), all perceptions (*saṃjñā*) regarding the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) do not arise.
When the objective sphere turns toward the mental objects (*dharmas*), and because the apprehension of sense-organ and object is incomplete, it is extinguished.
Know by this analogy that as for the subtle *ālayavijñāna*, its ultimate limit—whether it is extinguished or not—is likewise so.
Since the flow of one's own mind no longer continues and consciousness transforms into wisdom, once it has ceased to continue, how could it not be extinguished? Since it has [ceased]...
How could wisdom be extinguished? This extinction and non-extinction are so subtle as to be difficult to know;
therefore it is said that such a subtle storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) reaches its ultimate limit.
With the exception of the Tathāgatas and those equal to them, who are able to know this, the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others are unable to know it. If one knows the reason for its limit, then—
The *dharmakāya* of the objective realm is present therein; that it is not explicitly stated while directly answering the request is indeed full of profound intent.
(2) In the remaining stages, the characteristics of wisdom and skillful means distinguish and resolve the meanings of the phrases, thereby perfecting the most supreme and boundless roots of goodness.

Having thoroughly abandoned the false fabrications of the delusive imaginings manifested by one’s own mind, while dwelling in mountain forests in meditative seclusion, those who cultivate the lower, middle, and superior stages are able to perceive the continuous flow of their own mental delusions.
They receive the empowerment of the Buddhas from immeasurable lands, attain the power of mastery, supernatural faculties, and samādhis, and become spiritual friends and sons of the Buddha.
This is the self-nature manifested by their own mind, which consists of the mind, thought, and consciousness.
Having already transcended such causes as the false conceptions of objective realms, the ocean of birth and death, karma, craving, and ignorance, for this reason, Mahāmati,
practitioners of the path should draw near to the most excellent spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
It is like the great waves of the ocean, which arise from a violent wind; as the vast billows surge through the dark abyss, there is no time when they cease.
The ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* is eternally abiding, yet moved by the winds of objective realms, the various waves of consciousness leap forth and arise in succession.
There are all manner of colors—blue and red—as well as conch shells, milk, rock honey, bland flavors, and various flowers and fruits; it is like the sun and moon together with their radiance.
Neither different nor not different, as waves arise from the ocean, so too are the seven consciousnesses; they arise in conjunction with the mind.
Just as the ocean transforms into various shifting waves, so too do the seven consciousnesses arise in conjunction with the mind.

That is to say, within the locus of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the various consciousnesses evolve; it is by means of that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that one conceptualizes the meanings of various signs.

The unchanging characteristics are eightfold, yet they are signless and even signlessness itself. Just as there is no distinction between the ocean and its waves, so too there is no difference among the various consciousnesses and the mind;
their diversity cannot be apprehended. "Mind" (citta) is called the gathering of karma; "intellect" (manas) is called the extensive gathering.
The various consciousnesses perceive their respective objects, such as the manifest realm, which are explained as five.

Regarding the characteristics of the remaining stages (*bhūmi*), these refer to what remains of the characteristics of the stages—that is, the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
For anyone who practices according to reality based on perfect understanding, there are four matters by which they are also able to perceive the flow of the delusive thoughts of their own mind;

this is what is called the "limit" (*paryanta*). These are: first, wisdom and skillful means that skillfully penetrate the true meaning of the phrases; second, the roots of goodness... [text truncated].
Second is maturation; third is being free from the delusions of one’s own mind; fourth is practicing according to one's faculties while dwelling in mountain forests.
As for the merit thus obtained, it is inconceivable and beyond cognition; therefore, it is called "immeasurable.

Regarding "the Buddhas of the various lands bestowing empowerment," this refers to the stage of receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Regarding "sovereign spiritual powers," these refer to the dharma-gates that have been attained. All...
"Virtuous friends who are sons of the Buddha" refers to those who have entered the lineage of the noble ones (*āryagotra*).

"Their mind, thought, and consciousness, and so forth, have all completely transcended" means that they are free from the three paths of suffering caused by the delusions of self-nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
Therefore, the practitioner is cautioned to draw near to them; if one relies upon such persons, the path and its practice can be discerned. (Verse 8a)
The preceding verse and its commentary can be understood through the analogies of blue, red, and various other colors; these encompass the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

This recalls the previous phrase regarding the "wind of objective spheres," which refers to the external conditions of the six sense objects arising from the transformation of the six consciousnesses—this is precisely the first [verse] concerning form (*rūpa*).
*Kha* refers to the sound of a jeweled pendant; *candana* refers to the fragrance of sandalwood and milk; *mora* refers to rock honey.

Tangibility is the earth element, and taste is the flowers, fruits, and other such phenomena; this is because these six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) can give rise to the six consciousnesses (ṣadvijñāna).
(This is according to the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*, which explains as follows...

The sun and moon with their radiance, and the waves of the ocean—these two metaphors precisely illustrate that the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*) and the six consciousnesses arise together, being neither different nor non-different; yet it is said that there are "seven" [consciousnesses].
The term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is spoken of in reference to both the fundamental and the derivative; it does not refer to the seventh consciousness. Furthermore, it says:

"For example, the transformation of seawater," etc. Based on the preceding [analogy], the analogy of the waves is further opened into two meanings. First, regarding the analogy of the distinct phenomena, the text states:

"That is to say, in the locus of the *ālayavijñāna*," etc., because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) contemplates the various marks of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), [the transformation] is established.
Regarding the sequence of analogies for the distinct meanings, the principle that they are not different from the primary teaching is stated as follows:
"The unchanging marks are eightfold," meaning the unchanging marks are fundamentally only the eight consciousnesses; because the branches are traced back to the root, it is said there are eight.

Because the characteristics of all consciousnesses are identical to their reliance upon the *ālayavijñāna*, and because the *ālayavijñāna* is without characteristic (*animitta*), all consciousnesses are likewise without characteristic; thus, it is said they are "without characteristic" and also "characteristicless. As it is said: "Like space, it is without characteristic."

Although the waves of the ocean differ, they are all equally characterized by the nature of moisture and thus lack distinction; this serves as a metaphor for the fact that all consciousnesses are "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) and likewise lack any difference in their essential character.

Furthermore, when the eight consciousnesses are derived from the six consciousnesses, they are distinct; yet when the six consciousnesses are derived from the eight consciousnesses, they are not distinct.

This should also be understood through the analogy that illustrates the dharma. The designation of "mind" (*citta*) as the "accumulator" (*saṃgrāhaka*) is based on the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) doctrine.
This means that the eight consciousnesses are able to collect the seeds of all phenomena and give rise to all phenomena; thus, karma is also a phenomenon.

As for "mind" (manas), it refers to the seven consciousnesses which, taking the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and so forth as their objects, constantly and critically deliberate and calculate them to be the self; therefore, they are further called "the broadening of the various consciousnesses.

Regarding "that which is cognized by consciousness," this refers to the six mental consciousnesses (manovijñānas) cognizing their respective objects and discriminating what has been apprehended by the five sensory consciousnesses.
Because they take objects such as forms and so forth as their domain due to the presence of dust [sensory objects], the five are spoken of; that is, the five consciousnesses.
(3) At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati asked in verse:
"Blue, red, and all other forms and images cause sentient beings to give rise to various consciousnesses, like waves. How is it that these manifold dharmas exist? I pray only that you will explain."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"The various colors, blue and red, and all waves are entirely non-existent; yet it is taught that the mind accumulates karma to awaken ordinary people.
That karma is entirely non-existent, for it is subsumed within one's own mind. Being free from what is grasped and having nothing to grasp, it is identical to those waves."
The establishment of the body through experience is the manifest consciousness of sentient beings, in which various karmas appear, just as waves arise upon water.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva spoke again in verse:
"The nature of the waves of the great ocean is surging and can be distinguished; how is it that the storehouse [consciousness] and its karma are not likewise perceived?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
Ordinary beings lack wisdom; the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is like a vast ocean, and the characteristics of karma are like its waves. This analogy applies to all cases.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva spoke again in verse:
Just as the rising sun shines equally upon sentient beings of low, middling, and superior capacities, so does the Tathāgata illuminate the world;
having taught the truth to the ignorant and already categorized all phenomena, why does he not speak of the ultimate reality?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"If one speaks of reality, that mind has no reality; It is like the waves of the ocean, The images in a mirror, and dreams— All appear simultaneously.
The realm of the mind is likewise so; Because objects are not simultaneous, Karmic activity arises in succession."
"Consciousness" refers to that which is cognized by consciousness, and "mind" refers to what is intended; thus, these five [aggregates] manifest without any fixed order.
Below this, there arise three further rounds of question and answer to re-explain the preceding meaning. Regarding the first question:

since it was previously used as an analogy that form and so forth give rise to consciousness like waves, what is the intent behind this? In the response, the statement "all are non-existent" intends to reveal...

Both the phenomena and their metaphors are unattainable; thus, the waves are unattainable because they depend entirely upon the great ocean, and the consciousnesses and their objects are unattainable because they are rooted in the eight consciousnesses.
Therefore it is said that the "gathering of karma" refers to the mind and its associates;

although the six consciousnesses possess the function of gathering, the merit (the actual agency) resides in the eight consciousnesses, for the nature of the eight consciousnesses is detached from [duality], and thus they are what is subsumed.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata of No-Marks (Animitta) uses this to awaken ordinary beings, causing them to know that the marks of the present faculties, objects, and consciousnesses, as well as the karmic manifestations they produce, are all unobtainable and are merely empty—just like those waves which fundamentally do not exist.
If the wind of no-marks ceases, there is only the ocean of the single nature; this is the meaning of "not being different from what preceded. As for the enjoyment [body]...
The establishment of the body and so forth is also merely what is manifested by the manifesting consciousness (*vijñapti*).

Although these manifestations appear as if they were distinct, they are like those waves—this refers to the meaning of their prior difference. Yet, since the manifesting consciousness is fundamentally empty, how could they possibly exist?
The intent behind saying this is simply that the false consciousness is empty. Mahāmati then raised a second question.
This means that while the metaphor can be seen, the dharma cannot be known. The World-Honored One answered that ordinary people lack wisdom;

they know only proximate matters but do not know distant principles. Therefore, he employs metaphors to correspond with the dharma so that, by relying on the analogy and extending it through inference, [the meaning] may be understood.
As stated in the text at length, Mahāmati again raised a third question, the intent of which was precisely to request [further clarification].
Regarding the teaching on the *dharmakāya* as the objective realm, it should have been explained according to the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Yet, the Tathāgata has never spoken thus;
instead, he has merely categorized the various phenomena by describing the characteristics of consciousness through analogies such as the "store-consciousness being like a great ocean.

Since we have not yet heard the reason for explaining the true reality, I shall reiterate my fundamental position and request that you first provide an analogy—just as the sun illuminates all things—to illustrate the Tathāgata, so that the Truth may be explained.
If one asks why this is not actually stated in the response, the answer is that it is not that it is not stated; rather, it is difficult to state because there are many meanings involved.
First, because the mind has no reality, it is said, "That mind lacks true reality," and so forth.
If one were to say, "Although the Tathāgata wishes to speak the truth, he does not speak because the listener’s mind lacks true reality," this [explanation] remains consistent.
The meaning of the current passage is precisely to clarify that the *ālayavijñāna* arises like waves;

therefore, it is said that this mind has no reality, being compared to the ocean, waves, reflections in a mirror, or dream-objects. Although these appear simultaneously, they are all devoid of reality;
thus it is said: "The objects of the mind are likewise. That is to say, the objects of one's own eight consciousnesses are also just like this. It is simply because those objects...
Because they lack substantial reality and merely arise in succession according to the transformations of their respective objects, the six consciousnesses merely discern what they perceive.
As for the "mental" (manas) consciousness, it likewise follows the discernment of the mental consciousness, merely perceiving that such is the case.
The five sensory consciousnesses, however, manifest according to their objects; thus, they have no fixed order. It is said that all of them lack substantial reality.
Thus (four). It is like a skilled painter and his apprentice who spread colors to depict various forms; my teaching is also like this.
The colors originally have no patterns; it is neither the brush nor the canvas that creates them. Yet, for the sake of pleasing sentient beings, they are interwoven to paint various images.
Discourse is a distinct practice; reality is free from names and conceptual discrimination. One should first practice the preparatory stage to reveal reality.
Reality is the state of self-awakening, free from the perceiving subject and the perceived object. For the sons of the Buddha, this is taught; for the ignorant, there is extensive conceptualization.
All these various things are like illusions; though they appear, they lack reality. Thus, through various explanations, provisional designations are established according to specific circumstances.

What has been taught is not what should be taught to them; for them, it would be inappropriate. Just as a skilled physician prescribes various remedies according to each individual patient, so does the Tathāgata teach sentient beings according to their mental dispositions and capacities.
This realm of false conceptualization is not the domain of the Śrāvakas, nor is it their portion;
it is the realm of self-realization taught by the Compassionate One.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to know the realm of false discrimination consisting of the grasped and the grasper as manifestations of one’s own mind, he should avoid social gatherings, worldly customs, and sleep;
throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, he should constantly awaken himself and practice skillful means.
He should also avoid the discourses and doctrines of those with evil views, as well as those of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
One should thoroughly penetrate the characteristics of the false imaginings that appear as one's own mind.
Second, regarding the teaching that these are not real, it says, "For example, like a skilled painter," which correctly reveals the meaning that words and letters lack substantial reality;
for colors themselves have no patterns, where "patterns" refers to literary compositions produced by means of colors.
Once it is completed, the colors are not the painting itself; just as reality is manifested through verbal expression, yet the expression is not reality itself.
The analogy of the brush and the canvas is likewise: although the image emerges from the brush and canvas, in truth it is not the brush or the canvas;
they are merely used to paint the image for the sake of pleasing sentient beings. If one considers the image, it too is not [the reality].
In reality, that which is expressed by verbal discourse is not the true meaning; this is also seen in the subsequent text.

Discourse, distinct practices, and so forth, when combined, are not real. This means that while verbal teachings are provisionally established outside of reality, reality itself does not reside within verbal discourse, because that which is truly real is free from names and words.
Thus, the *tathāgatagarbha* is the true nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Since [these] may not be real, they are further dispelled. Just as attachment arises from verbal expressions and one falls into the mind-measure (*cittamātra*) of continuity, so too is that not real.
Therefore, such conceptualization is intended only for beginners;
"beginners" refers to those with a new mind, as in the phrase "the beginner of the Three Vehicles. Even for practitioners, it is shown [as such].

When one realizes true reality (*tattva*) through self-awakening, one knows that true reality is free from the conceptualizations of the subject and object of cognition; how much more so regarding verbal expression?
For those who are disciples of the Buddha, this is the extent of what can be said. Ultimately, true reality cannot be expressed in words;
it is only by attaining the state of self-awakening through direct realization that it is called "true reality," which alone accords with the intent of the sutras. As for anything else...
Because the ultimate principle has not yet been realized as reality, the foolish engage in extensive conceptual proliferation.

To further clarify the initial statement regarding "action" (*karma*), although it is extensively analyzed through various verbal teachings, its actual nature is not true; it is just like a magical illusion, which appears yet lacks reality.
Thus, these various explanations and so forth should be understood as collectively revealing this point. Thirdly, the explanation of what is inappropriate.
Therefore, since we have already analyzed this extensively, what prevents us from speaking of the ultimate reality? Thus it is said: "That which is spoken is not what is appropriate;

for them, it is a false teaching. This is merely an explanation to dispel doubts, as in the saying: "If one preaches the Dharma without adapting to the capacities of the listeners, it conversely becomes a great falsehood.
Therefore, it is compared to a skilled physician who prescribes medicine according to the illness; so it is with the Tathāgata.

The verbal teachings are spoken according to the measure of the mind; since they do not fall within the scope of ordinary people or those of the Lesser Vehicle, it is said that "deluded thoughts are not their realm," and so forth.
From this perspective, that which is called "reality" is simply the realm of self-realization attained by the Tathāgata, which can ultimately never be explained to those who have not yet reached it.
If so, by what means can ordinary, ignorant sentient beings come to know the truth?

Because it is the reality, he offers this exhortation: if you wish to know the manifestation of one's own mind as false imagination (*vikalpa*) and the point where such false imagination ceases, then you will know that which is real.
Nevertheless, while one is within delusion, one does not recognize that state as delusion;

only by departing from dullness and distraction, emerging beyond false imagination, and awakening to what is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*)—the great skillful means—does one finally come to know this.

As for that delusion: while one uses the scriptures and treatises of external paths and evil views, as well as the marks of emptiness of the Two Vehicles, to obscure oneself, one does not even know it;
only after awakening will one depart from it and be able to achieve thorough penetration.
(5) ○ This concludes the Seventh Chapter.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, having established himself in the characteristics of wisdom, he should diligently cultivate the three characteristics of supreme noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
What are these three characteristics of supreme noble wisdom that he should diligently cultivate? They are:

the characteristic of non-existence, the characteristic of the sphere of the self-vow of all Buddhas, and the characteristic of the ultimate realization of the noble wisdom of self-awakening. One should cultivate them.
Having practiced this, one is able to abandon the mind of a lame donkey; through wisdom, one attains the eighth stage of the Supreme Son (Bodhisattva).
Then, regarding the cultivation of the three marks above that: the mark of "non-existence" refers to the marks of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists;
the mark of "the sphere of one's own vows" produced by the cultivation of great wisdom refers to the [marks] of all previous Buddhas.

Mahāmati, the ultimate characteristic of self-realized noble wisdom cultivated through practice in various states consists of non-attachment to the characteristics of all phenomena and the attainment of the body of the Illusion-like Samādhi.
Mahāmati, this is called the threefold characteristic of noble wisdom that leads to progress toward the stages of the Buddhas.
