If one accomplishes these three characteristics of noble wisdom, one will reach the culmination of self-realized noble wisdom.
Because the ultimate object of experience is such, Mahāmati, one should diligently cultivate and study the three characteristics of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
As previously stated, the realm of self-realization cannot be realized by anything other than wisdom;

thus, the characteristics of wisdom are established as being no more than three, serving as the dharmas in which the practitioner should abide. If one merely abides [in them] without practicing, by what means could [realization] be attained?
Because one is able to reach [the goal], it is called "abiding. Having abided therein, one should diligently cultivate and study the three marks of the supreme noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
If there are those who can cultivate and study these three marks, they shall attain the realm of the supreme self-realized noble wisdom.
In the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary), the statement "having attained this through cultivation, one is able to abandon the mind and wisdom of the lame donkey" is an illustration.

This further clarifies the exhortation. Some write "hui-zhi" (wisdom), but I fear this would manifest a mistaken inversion. The two vehicles cannot advance at this point; they are likened to lame donkeys.
The term "Sons of the Most Victorious One" refers to the eighth stage of the Bodhisattva, as it is not shared with the two vehicles;

therefore, it is said that they "are able to relinquish. If one distinguishes between the Ten Stages of the Separate and Perfect [teachings], these stages are entirely sacred from beginning to end, and thus it should not be said that [the relinquishment] begins only here.

Because it abandons the two vehicles, we know that prior to this point [the teaching] was still shared with them; thus, although this sutra is a sudden Mahāyāna, it also encompasses the *tong* (common) vehicle—this is the first point.
Regarding "the mark of non-existence," this refers to ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
To speak of the marks of the two vehicles and external paths is to refer to what is absent; it means that in the practice of the Bodhisattva, those two do not exist.
Because one mounts upon emptiness and the false characteristics of external paths, it is called the "characteristic of non-existence.
Although this differs from those [external paths], it nonetheless arises from the false to produce emptiness, and through emptiness, one attains the ultimate characteristic of non-existence;

therefore, it is said that "the place of the former Buddhas' original vows produced by cultivation" refers to the inconceivable characteristic of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). All such things...

In the causal stage of the Buddha, there is no lack of wisdom; his vows accord with the realm of truth (satya-dhātu), which constitutes the locus of his vow. Because he initiates practice from this state, it is called "cultivation arising [from the vow].
As for the ultimate characteristic of self-awakened noble wisdom (svapratyātma-āryajñāna), it is the characteristic of the Middle Way of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
When one has no conceptual attachment to the characteristics of any phenomena, then non-attachment is the meaning of the Middle Way, and so forth.

Although these words are concise, their principle is profoundly deep. To have no grasping or attachment toward any objective realm or phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is precisely to reach the stage of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*); how could this not be the ultimate essential?

By means of this, one attains the body of the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), whereby one is able to universally manifest emanations; furthermore, one attains the stages of the Buddhas and proceeds therein. From this point onward:
Because these three characteristics are present in all phenomena without exception, there is nothing that surpasses emptiness (*śūnyatā*) for destroying all delusions;
nothing more magnificent than the provisional (*prajñapti*) for establishing all virtues; and nothing greater than the middle way (*madhyamā*) for reaching the ultimate realization of all principles.
This constitutes the fundamental characteristic of wisdom; thus its accomplishment is as described above, and the concluding exhortation may be understood accordingly. Chapter Eight.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of great Bodhisattvas,
and empowered by the majestic spiritual authority of all Buddhas, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
we pray that you will expound for us the *Āryajñānavastuvibhāgasvabhāva-sūtra*, which distinguishes the basis of the one hundred and eight phrases."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, based on this, analytically explains how Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter into the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of both specific and common characteristics.
Because he analytically explains the imagined nature, they are able to thoroughly know and universally observe the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*),
thereby purifying their delusions, illuminating the various stages (*bhūmi*), and transcending all sounds.
Having heard of the joy of the meditative concentrations of the pratyekabuddhas and various non-Buddhists, and having fully observed the inconceivable sphere of activity of the Tathāgata,
they definitively abandon the five dharmas and the self-nature (*svabhāva*). Adorned by the wisdom of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas,
they give rise to illusory realms and ascend to all Buddha-fields, from the Tuṣita palaces up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Ultimately, within the celestial palaces, one attains the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharma-body.
That which distinguishes self-nature is the object of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). For this reason, it is called a sūtra; know that this constitutes the general purport of this single scripture.
Mahāmati, having thus introduced the subject, he asked a question. At the beginning, he first recounted what the assembly was reflecting upon, namely, "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).

As for "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), it is correctly termed "the nature of false discrimination" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). However, false discrimination does not arise of itself; its arising must necessarily depend on conditions.
Furthermore, were there no false discrimination, intrinsic nature could not be established. Therefore, by mentioning one, both are simultaneously implied.

Next, responding to the request for further explanation, he says: "The basis upon which the hundred and eight phrases are distinguished" means that the hundred and eight phrases are used to distinguish intrinsic nature.

"Because it serves as the basis [for the teaching], please explain in detail the nature of the false discrimination of self-characteristics and common characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa-vikalpa-svabhāva*).

This is a general statement regarding the basis of the entire sutra. These phenomena of self- and common-characteristics exist in all things, and they are the source from which both delusion and awakening arise.
The commentators take the distinctness of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to be self-characteristics, while their combination to form a single body is taken as the common characteristic.
This understanding merely involves calculating and clinging to names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*); one has not yet realized how to employ discernment (*vibhāga*) to shatter delusion.
One should know that these characteristics cannot coexist, for their meanings mutually cancel one another out. Thus, by means of them, one may shatter delusive characteristics:

if one uses the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) to subvert its mark, the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) fails to be established; conversely, if one uses the general characteristic to subvert the specific characteristic—
Since self-characteristics do not establish themselves, how could such conceptualized delusions exist? Therefore, one who employs them skillfully may take a bandit as a general;
one who employs them unskillfully may find medicine to become a disease. Is the analogy of ice and water far removed from this truth?

Although this passage primarily addresses the literal text, it simultaneously refutes the underlying intent. One who grasps its essential meaning can apply this principle by analogy to other cases of conceptual differentiation.

The subsequent statement concerning the characteristics of benefit has four aspects: first, through skillful discernment, one is able to correctly understand the selflessness of persons and phenomena, thereby purifying deluded conceptualization;
second, illuminating the various stages (*bhūmi*), one gives rise to and transcends the bliss of all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*);
third, observing the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata, one abandons the five dharmas and the three natures (*svabhāva*).
Fourth, the manifestation of the fruit-stage *dharmakāya* is well-adorned by the wisdom of the *dharmakāya*.

If the benefits are such as these, how can one fail to clarify their source? As for the claim that it is "separate from the five dharmas and self-nature," once all objects of negation within the various gates of antidotes have been exhausted, the negating subject itself vanishes; this is entirely described in terms of the Tathāgata’s realm.
Ultimate detachment is merely the equality of a single nature—detaching from that which is to be detached.
This is as stated in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*: "The Tathāgata ultimately accords with Perfect Enlightenment. Furthermore, it says:

"As for the arising of illusory realms, all inconceivable transformative functions on the level of fruition are established without exception by relying upon the illusory realm. This is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This clarifies the point (1).

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There is a class of non-Buddhists who, through their false conceptualization and attachment to 'nothingness,' perceive that because the cause is exhausted, they form the notion that a rabbit has no horns.
Just as a rabbit has no horns, they claim that all dharmas are likewise so. Mahāmati, there is yet another [class of non-Buddhists]..."

Other non-Buddhists, having perceived the various distinctions among the seeds, qualities (*guṇa*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), substances (*dravya*), shapes, locations, and transverse phenomena, become attached to them.
They conceive of the existence of horns on a cow based on the perception of transverse phenomena that do not exist in a rabbit’s horns. O Mahāmati, they fall into these two views;

failing to understand that it is merely the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*) and the objective realm of one's own mind, their delusions increase, and they establish the delusions of the body, its experience, and its foundations.
Mahāmati, the nature of all dharmas is likewise; being free from existence and non-existence, one should not form conceptualizations regarding them.
Mahāmati, if one were to form the conceptualization that "a rabbit has no horns" while remaining detached from existence and non-existence, this is called a false conceptualization.

Because it arises from dependent observation, one should not form the conceptualization that "a rabbit has no horns," for even down to the most subtle atom, the nature of things as objects of discrimination cannot be found.
The noble realm of wisdom is free from the improper conceptualization that "cows have horns.

In the response, the primary aim is to refute externalist views; for one cannot understand the nature of false imagination (*vikalpa*) unless one penetrates its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Since the root of false imagination lies in the absence of intrinsic nature, it concludes: "One should contemplate that which is manifested by one's own mind."
As for deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), its fundamental nature can be understood as follows:

first, regarding the conceptual attachment to non-existence, it is said that "the causes of awakening and knowledge are exhausted," meaning that apart from awakened thought, there are no further causes;

this is illustrated by the notion of a rabbit having no horns, and all phenomena are likewise so. Second, regarding the conceptual attachment to existence, it is said that "one seeks the seeds through vision."
Those "elements" (mahābhūta) refer to the qualities (guṇa) that depend upon the substantial entities (dravya)—this is what is meant by "dust" (rajas), or as some say, "the master.
To "reckon perversely" means to falsely reckon what is not a dharma as being a dharma. Such a person perceives the substratum of the elements as ultimately consisting of atoms;
regarding every place possessing form, they recklessly differentiate them, yet they still maintain that the prior notion of a rabbit having no horns is incorrect.

Therefore it is said: "There are no horns on a rabbit, yet one recklessly conceives the notion that a cow has horns and considers this to be correct. Next, the Tathāgata refutes this error in three ways:
first, by refuting those who do not understand their own minds, he says, "They fall into the two views," and so forth;

this means that their reckoning of existence and non-existence is nothing other than the views of annihilationism and eternalism. They merely fall into the perception of external objects apart from the mind, regardless of whether those objects actually exist.
All that is non-existent is merely conceptual construction; therefore it is said that one does not understand the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*) and the realm of one's own mind.
Speaking from the perspective of the realm of one's own mind, there is not a single dharma existing outside the mind.

Yet, speaking from the perspective of the proliferation of conceptual construction, the body, objects of enjoyment, and so forth are all external things; thus they constitute the root-measure of conceptual construction. This is why there is existence and non-existence.
None of these are as [you think]. If you know that all phenomena are nothing other than your own mind, then you will naturally not fall into views such as existence or non-existence.

Even if you speak of existence or non-existence, there is nothing that is not [the mind]. Why is this? Because when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise—is this not existence being the mind?
And when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease—is this not non-existence being the mind? It is not that they arise apart from the mind.
Because the essence of non-extinction is itself the Middle Way, although there is existence and non-existence, one does not fall into dualistic views.
Applying this principle to all dharmas, it is said: "The nature of all dharmas is likewise so.

Since the nature of the mind is not different from the nature of dharmas, and the essence of the nature of dharmas is subtle and wondrous—being precisely the Middle Way—one should not form conceptions of existence or non-existence. (3) This is the section on the nature (*svabhāva*).

To depart from and refute their calculation, it is said: "If one further departs from existence, non-existence, and so forth—since their nature is already free from existence and non-existence, yet they still form perverted conceptions, all such views are termed 'erroneous conceptions. Their calculation that a rabbit has no horns is based on the dependence upon the cow having horns;
if that cause [the cow's horns] were absent, what else would there be to depend upon for them to say the rabbit has no horns? Therefore, it says: "That..."
Because they exist through dependence upon observation, as stated in the *Mahā-śāstra*, there is currently neither dependence nor any established phenomenon.
Since a cow’s horn does not exist apart from the rabbit’s horn, the notion that "the cow has horns" is likewise dependent;

even the analysis of the horn into its constituent parts results in no horn at all, so one should not form such conceptualizations. Thus it is said: "down to the subtlest atom, discrimination is still a process of analysis."

Since the nature of phenomena is entirely unobtainable, they are likewise non-existent. Furthermore, it is said that the realm of the Sage is free from [conceptualization], and one should not form the notion that "a cow has horns.
Previously, the absence of intrinsic nature was used to refute non-existence; here, the realm of the Sage is used to refute existence.
Thus, the texts present these perspectives alternately. (2)
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, when one who is free from false conceptualization perceives that conceptualization does not arise, does he subsequently employ inference, deliberation, and investigation to conclude that false conceptualization is non-existent by saying 'it does not exist'? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"It is not through investigation that one concludes false conceptualization does not exist and says 'it does not exist. Why is this? Because false conceptualization arises dependent upon those [objects]."
Therefore, based on those horns, conceptual construction arises; because conceptual construction arises based on the horns, it is said that it depends on causes.
Because it is neither different nor non-different [from its cause], conceptual construction does not arise through investigation; thus, O Mahāmati, one says "there are no horns.

Furthermore, O Mahāmati, if conceptual construction were different from the horns, it would not arise based on the horns; if it were not different, then because it would be identical to them, it would exist even down to the level of atoms.
When analyzed and investigated, neither is found to exist, for they are not distinct from the horns; therefore, they are both without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

If both are without intrinsic nature, what dharma exists, and for what reason do you say they are "non-existent"? Mahāmati, if one says "there are no horns" because they are non-existent, yet observes them as existent and thus says "the rabbit has no horns," one should not form such a conceptualization.
Mahāmati, it is due to incorrect reasoning that one speaks of both existence and non-existence.
This is not established.

Since you have already rejected the externalist views that both existence and non-existence are causes, when the present orthodox teaching says that one who has attained freedom from false conceptualization is one who has seen that conceptualization does not arise,
this is precisely what must be understood as being like those externalists [who argue] by means of rabbit horns and the like.
Observing through analogy, one does not give rise to deluded thoughts; this is called "non-existence" because it is intended to distinguish [reality] from the absence of deluded conceptualization.
Therefore, this question is asked. In the Buddha’s response, he first correctly excludes what is not [the truth]:

it is not merely that at the site of deluded thoughts nothing with self-nature can be found—that is itself non-arising. Why wait for such an observation of non-arising before declaring that they do not exist?

It is said: "As for 'conceptual construction' (*vikalpa*), because it arises dependent upon that [object], it is called conceptual construction; it does not exist of itself, but must arise dependent upon that.
Although it is not exactly like that [object], taking that very horn as an analogy, the horn serves as the causal basis for the conceptual construction.

To speak of it as a 'basis' means that the conceptual construction is not separate from the horn, yet the horn is not the conceptual construction; therefore, they are neither identical nor different."

This distinction clarifies that when there is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), no self-nature can be found; how then could it be necessary to observe its non-arising to say that "horns do not exist"?
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "conceptual construction is distinct from the horns," this explains the meaning of being neither distinct nor non-distinct from what precedes it.
The phrase "it is because of that" means simply that it arises dependent upon that [the horns]; it does not mean that the horns are themselves the conceptual construction—such is their reckoning.
The claim that there are no horns is incorrect. If one analyzes and investigates until reaching the subtlest particles (*paramāṇu*), nothing can be found;

thus, there is no distinction to be made between having horns and not having horns. Therefore, it is said that they are not different from horns. Consequently, those [horns] are also not intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*);
how much more so the horns of a rabbit? "Not being an intrinsic nature" means lacking a real nature. Thus, it is reiterated: "If both are non-existent."
As for "nature," it is neither existent nor non-existent; by what dharma and for what reason could one say it is non-existent?

Because the teaching of the Dharma is true, one speaks of existence and non-existence. If it were as you previously conceived—that the non-existence of horns is understood by observing the non-existence of horns in that which *does* have horns—then such a conceptualization should not be formed.
This has already been refuted as before; how much more so, then, is this false conceptual discrimination not [the truth]?
Since both [positions] are unestablished by means of the correct reason (*samyag-hetu*), one knows that those [opponents] possess nothing but false conceptualizations (*mithyā-parikalpa*).
Apart from the three previously refuted meanings and the one correct reason—that there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—all else is merely false conceptualization.
By simply excluding those [false views], their own [erroneous] conclusions will naturally fall away, and the meaning of the refutation becomes manifest. (3)

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other outsiders who, clinging to views, do not properly understand the limits of space (*ākāśa*) regarding matter, emptiness, objects, forms, and horizontal phenomena;
they maintain the false discrimination of a view that matter arises apart from space.
Mahāmati, space is included within matter, as it enters into the elements of matter. Mahāmati, matter is space, for it is established by the nature of the container and the contained.

One should understand the differentiation of the phenomena of form and emptiness, O Mahāmati: when the four great elements arise, their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are each distinct, and they do not abide in space;
yet it is not that space does not exist therein. Likewise, O Mahāmati, one observes that because the cow has horns, the rabbit has no horns.
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, if the horn of a cow is analyzed into atoms (*paramāṇu*), and those atoms are further analyzed, they do not abide for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
"Based on what observation do you say that [things] do not exist? If you say it is by observing other things, then those [other] phenomena are likewise [unreal].

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "You should abandon the false views and conceptualizations regarding rabbit horns, cow horns, space, form, and color.
You, all you Bodhisattvas and Mahāsattvas, should contemplate that these are the false manifestations of your own minds."
He causes them to enter into contemplation as the most excellent sons of all buddha-fields, instructing them through the skillful means of the manifestations of their own minds.
He again raises the externalist arguments regarding the meaning of form and emptiness to distinguish their errors; by citing examples, he refutes the previous faults, stating: "Form and emptiness..."

As for "the matter," it refers to those who falsely conceptualize emptiness as being distinct from form and characteristics, reckoning them as either existent or non-existent, and failing to realize that form and emptiness are fundamentally without boundaries. Therefore, to refute their lack of skill regarding these boundaries, it is said:

"If empty space were form," meaning that emptiness is one of the manifest colors (*vyañjanavarṇa*), and that there is no entering into the four great elements or the categories of form that does not involve emptiness.
If there were function, then form would not exist outside of space. Furthermore, it is said that form is held by space;
that which is established in the locus of being held refers to the fact that if form were without space to hold it, then all forms would be established in a locus of being held [without support].
Thus, there is no form outside of space. How then can one speak of form arising apart from space and perceiving its boundaries? This is due to a correct cause.
He pointed it out to them, saying: "Regarding the nature of form and emptiness, you should understand that 'nature' refers to true nature, which is the fundamental emptiness of form and emptiness.
Furthermore, the four great elements upon which [form] depends each have their own characteristics when they arise—solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion.

Although the characteristics of form and emptiness differ, their nature does not exist apart from one another; therefore, it is said that they likewise do not abide in empty space, nor in form and emptiness."

The characteristics are distinct, yet it is not that space lacks the nature of space; nor do they exist apart from one another. One should understand that such distinctions are as detailed [in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*] (and so forth).
By analogy, when observing existence and non-existence through mutual dependence (*apekṣā*), there should likewise be no difference.
Therefore it is said: "O Mahāmati, when observing that a cow has horns and so forth, this is spoken in dependence upon the existence of the cow's horns; thus one says that a rabbit has none."
If one were to break a horn into minute particles, and further divide those particles until reaching the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal), then the horn itself would no longer exist as a horn.
Since a momentary abiding characteristic (*kṣaṇasthiti-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be found, what reliance could there be?
Therefore it is said: "What does it observe? and so forth. If this observation of dependence were like observing in relation to other things...
Those who expect the emptiness of present form to differ from it, yet find that its actual existence and non-existence are similar in principle, say:
"That dharma is likewise so. This is known as the first false conceptualization (*parikalpita*). Therefore, he concludes by exhorting one to abandon these two kinds of views. Furthermore, he says:

"One should contemplate that [all things] are the false imaginings manifested by one's own mind. If one wishes to know the reality of whether these false imaginings exist or not, one should simply turn back upon oneself.
Contemplate this with the mind as the primary focus: Is it existent, or is it non-existent? Is it both existent and non-existent, or neither existent nor non-existent?
Examine this and you will realize it for yourself. One should likewise teach others by means of this;
therefore it is said that "entering accordingly" constitutes being the most supreme son of all buddha-fields, even as a son of the Buddha. (4)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

Form and so forth, as well as mind, are devoid of form and so forth; they nourish the mind, body, and experience, establishing the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). They manifest for sentient beings as mind, thought, and consciousness.
The self-nature of phenomena consists of five categories, two kinds of selflessness, and two kinds of purity—thus has it been extensively taught by the Speaker.

Length, shortness, existence, non-existence, and so forth, arise from one another in mutual succession; through non-existence existence is established, and through existence non-existence is established.
When the analysis of atoms ceases, the conceptualization of form no longer arises. The mind-measure (*cittamātra*) is the locus of establishment. One must see that which is not desired;
for the realm of sensory perception and conceptualization is not the true domain. This is likewise true for the Śrāvakas. This is what the Savior has taught as the realm of self-realization.
The verse stating that "form and so forth, as well as mind, do not exist" is a summary of the aforementioned nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

It indicates that these do not exist apart from external objects such as form and internal consciousness. Speaking in terms of ultimate principle, they have never existed from the beginning; this single word "non-existent" is a sharp blade for severing delusion, surpassing which there is nothing more effective.
Once one takes full responsibility for this realization, what deluded thought will not be eliminated? It is only because ordinary beings do not understand this that [delusion persists].
Because of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one conversely grasps [objects] to nourish one's own mind; thus, through the self-enjoyment and so forth, the fundamental basis is established.
Speaking in terms of what is manifested by the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the eight consciousnesses and so forth are established in succession.

Regarding the five factors of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-dharma*), these are named according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): the five factors, such as name (*nāma*) and so forth, as well as the two forms of selflessness (*anātman*).

These matters—length and shortness, existence and non-existence, and so forth—as explained by the Tathāgata in his extensive teachings, as well as the re-establishment of these points through analogies and verses, show that all conceptualizations of existence and non-existence, as well as [the notion of] mutual dependence, fail to attain correctness.

In this world, there is nothing characterized by existence, non-existence, length, or shortness that does not arise through mutual causal dependence and the production of names; the Dharma is likewise. Therefore:
It is said that existence is established through non-existence, and so forth; if existence and non-existence were fixed, then existence and non-existence would not be established.
Since they are established through mutual dependence, they fundamentally lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is why the heterodox views that fixate on existence and non-existence are incorrect.

Thus, that which possesses existence does not exist as existence, and that which possesses non-existence does not exist as non-existence. To be neither existent nor non-existent is called the Middle Way.
Therefore, all dharmas must ultimately be rooted in the Middle; that the Middle itself does not constitute a "middle" is what is called the supreme subtlety.

This is how the True Teaching differs from the non-Buddhist paths by a vast distance. The phrase "analyzing atoms so that the conceptualization of form does not arise" means that "analysis" refers to both discernment and disintegration.
The verse [above] regarding the analysis of horns shows that when there are no horns, one is not permitted to give rise to the false conceptualization of form.

Regarding the "contemplation of analyzing phenomena" (*dharmapratyavekṣā-saṃjñā*), the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) calculate that the fundamental principle of this sutra’s core tenet is that all things are directly devoid of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);

what need is there to analyze them before they fail to arise? However, we merely analyze whether there is the correct or the false; if one borrows their method of analysis to refute their errors, what fault is there?

Furthermore, it is intended as an aid for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to destroy their deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*). As for the "establishment of the scope of the mind" (*cittamātra-vyavasthāna*), it refers to the aforementioned...
Contemplate that one's own mind is utterly devoid of existence and non-existence; that which is merely the measure of one's own mind is the locus for establishing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is not a realm to be relished by those of inferior or small views who perceive through conceptualization and imagine that phenomena exist external to the mind.
The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly. (5) The Ninth Chapter concludes here.
