The Buddhas and noble ones, having departed from all false imaginings regarding all phenomena, manifest only their own intrinsic nature;

therefore, there is nothing that is not perfect and nothing that is not accomplished—there is nothing that is not the perfection of suchness, and nothing that is not the accomplishment of correct gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*).
Thus it is said that "that which is attained by noble gnosis" refers to correct gnosis, as well as the sphere of activity reached by the noble gnosis of self-realization.
This refers to *tathatā* (suchness). When the aforementioned two dharmas are unified into a single self-nature, this constitutes the *tathāgatagarbha-citta* (the mind of the Tathāgata-garbha).

However, since it was previously explained that all five dharmas must be transcended, if even *samyagjñāna* (correct wisdom) and *tathatā* are to be transcended, then the *tathāgatagarbha* must also be transcended.
To this, it is said: Only by being transcended does it receive the name "Tathāgata-garbha. Furthermore, as for whether it is transcended or not transcended, it is merely... [text ends]

If one investigates provisional names to reach their reality, there is from the beginning no fixed dharma; in terms of separation, all are separated, yet even the Tathāgatagarbha mind has never not been separated.
In terms of identity, all are identical, yet how could names, marks, and false conceptualizations ever be identical?
Ultimately, whether it is separation or non-separation lies neither here nor there. By means of the five dharmas, one realizes the three natures; thus, as for "perception" (vikalpa):
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) differs from them only in name. Regarding the exhortation to practice:

although what is taught throughout this sutra applies generally to the five dharmas, when one follows the ultimate [teaching], it refers solely to the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), as stated in the text, and so forth. [End of] Chapter Seventeen.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully contemplates the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*). What are the two kinds of selflessness?

They are the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). What is the selflessness of persons? It refers to the absence of a self and what belongs to a self;

it is the arising of consciousness through the grasping and attachment to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), which are clusters of ignorance, karma, and craving, such as the eye and forms.
All sense-faculties are manifestations of one's own mind; they are the storehouse of the body and the world, established and displayed through the marks of one's own false imaginings.
They are like a river, like seeds, like a lamp, like the wind, and like clouds—momentarily perishing as they successively arise, restless and turbulent. Like monkeys, they delight in impure places;
like flies, they are never satiated; like wind and fire, they are caused by the beginningless habit-energies of falsehood.
The water-wheel of the cycle of birth and death, the wheel of existence, and the various forms and colors that arise like illusions, spells, or mechanical devices—
skillfully understanding their characteristics is called the wisdom of the non-self of persons.

The first five dharmas and so forth still pertain to both delusion and awakening; because they consist exclusively of the wisdom of the two non-selves (pudgala- and dharma-nairātmya) that arises from awakening, they are explained by means of the latter three dharmas.
In other texts, these are called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) or the emptiness of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*);
here, however, they are called "non-self" (*anātman*), and "non-self is also empty. However, ordinary beings [cling] to the provisional and the real...
Because my own views were so biased, I have collectively referred to this as "non-self" (*anātman*). If one penetrates non-self, then there is no attachment to anything.

The first explanation concerns the characteristics of the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*): that which is free from "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*). "Self" is merely a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), whereas "what belongs to the self" is considered substantial.

Furthermore, apart from a single "self," everything else is "what belongs to the self. Now, a provisional designation does not exist independently; it is grasped [only in dependence upon something else].
Because the real exists through the provisional, one must seek the person in its reality; if reality itself were non-existent, the provisional would perish.

Therefore it is said that the aggregates of the sense bases and elements (*āyatana-dhātu-skandha*), as well as ignorance, craving, karma, and birth, constitute the reality of this single body, yet they do not exist of themselves.

Furthermore, it is said that the arising of consciousness through the grasping and attachment to the eye, forms, and so forth, constitutes the reality of the conscious mind, yet it does not exist of itself.
Furthermore, if one asks what constitutes these [phenomena], it is said that all sense-faculties (*indriya*) are manifestations of one's own mind.

To speak in terms of their fundamental basis, they all manifest from the eight consciousnesses. If one asks whether these eight consciousnesses possess any substantial reality, it is further said that there are the "receptacle," the "body," and the "storehouse.
Here, the "receptacle" refers to the body of the preceding aggregates (*skandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), which is like a vessel; the "storehouse" refers to...
The storehouse of the eight consciousnesses of one's own mind is all established and manifested through the characteristics of one's own false imaginings; what reality could there be?

Therefore, there are five metaphors such as a flowing river to illustrate the characteristic of momentary destruction, and three others—such as being like empty space, being characterized by agitation, and so forth—to illustrate that these are likewise the characteristics of false consciousness.
Thus, they are compared to a monkey and other such things; yet all are beginningless and empty.
Because the cause of false habitual tendencies leads to the revolving cycle of birth and death within the various realms of the triple world, it is compared to a water-drawing wheel.
As for the various bodily forms, the preceding analogy referred to deluded consciousness, whereas this refers to the illusory body;
it is like a magical art that can trigger a mechanical device through divine mantras to make an elephant rise, or like a spell that can raise a corpse—such are its categories.

One who knows in this way is said to "skillfully know their characteristics. This means that if one knows according to the characteristics of those various analogies, then the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are all seen as empty fabrications.
Since their root is empty, from whom could they provisionally arise? Thus, one immediately realizes the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya). (1)

What is the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*)? It is the realization that the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) is devoid of a self or what belongs to a self.
One understands that the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are merely accumulations produced through mutual conditioning by the ropes of karma and craving; they are without movement.

All phenomena are likewise devoid of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and are unreal, being the marks of false imagination. It is through the power of such false imagination that ordinary beings [arise].
Now, birth is not [the domain of] sages or worthies, for the mind, intellect, consciousness, and the five dharmas are inherently free from self-nature.
Therefore, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, you should skillfully discern that all phenomena are without self and that even wholesome phenomena are without self.

Before long, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva shall attain the first stage of a Bodhisattva; through the contemplation of non-existence, observing the characteristics of the stages, they shall awaken and experience great joy.
Advancing by stages, he transcends the characteristics of the nine stages and attains the Dharma-Cloud stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).

There, within a great jewel palace adorned with immeasurable precious ornaments, which is like a great king of jewel lotuses and is a realm produced through the cultivation of the illusory nature of reality, he is born and seated;
surrounded by a retinue of sons of the Conquerors (*jinaputra*) of the same class, he comes from all Buddha-fields.

When you come to receive the empowerment of the Buddha’s hand—like the consecration of the crown prince of a universal monarch (cakravartin)—you shall transcend the stage of the Buddha’s sons and reach the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
You shall attain the sovereign Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata;

because you see the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), this is called the characteristic of the non-self of phenomena. You, all you Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, should practice and study this. (Note: Below "the characteristic of the fundamental ground" [本地相], there is the character "clear" [明].)
Because the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is directly revealed according to reality, it is called "awakening to the imagined nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.

This means that if one awakens to the fact that the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are merely imagined and lack a real intrinsic nature, and realizes they do not exist, then even the self postulated based on reality cannot be found;
this is the selflessness of phenomena. As with the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, the same applies to the persons above.
The contemplation of non-self (anātman) is free from "self" and "what belongs to self" because the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases arise through a successive, reciprocal causal process.

When one investigates their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), arising is found to be non-arising; because there is no arising, there is no movement, and thus one does not perceive any characteristic of agency or volitional activity.
By analogy, the contemplation of the non-self of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) is likewise fundamentally without reality; therefore, it is called "all phenomena" (dharmas).
It is likewise: the dharmas previously awakened to are devoid of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and are therefore unreal.
By knowing the unreality of dharmas, one knows the non-self (*anātman*) of the self. Observing it from this perspective, the two modes of observation have never failed to be mutually dependent.

Thus, what is called the characteristic of false conceptualization (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*) and the power of false conceptualization, which—as previously stated—binds one like the ropes of craving and karma, are all...
That which is produced by ordinary beings is not that of the noble sages; since the noble sages have transcended all things, how could there be any power of deluded thoughts or appearances?
Therefore it is said: because the mind, consciousness, the five dharmas, and the self-natures are all transcended. This so-called "transcendence" does not necessarily mean physical separation;
it refers to realizing that their nature is non-existent. In the section on the marks of the exhortation to benefit, it says "non-existence."
All those who contemplate the signs of the stages (*bhūmi*) do so by means of non-existence; this contemplation of the signs of the stages is precisely the sign of non-arising of the first stage.
Through such observation, one awakens; through awakening, one rejoices, and thus progresses sequentially, transcending the signs of the [remaining] nine stages.

"Clarity" (*vidyā*) refers to the various realized dharmas, such as the clarity of power (*bala-vidyā*) and so forth; however, regarding the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), [this clarity is established].
The specific conclusion regarding the benefit of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) is made because it is attained by Bodhisattvas at a single time; therefore, it is concluded later.
Since it is said that one "gradually advances" and yet also "leaps over," the meaning of "ascending progress" is not one of skipping stages.
Regarding the arising through the cultivation of the illusory nature of the realm: all resultant functions and inconceivable matters proceed from this.
The establishment of the same class of elephants refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body; other matters concerning the empowerment (abhiṣeka) are as stated in the text.
(2) [End of] Chapter Eighteen.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, please explain the characteristics of establishing [right views] and of slandering [the Dharma]."

"I only pray that you will explain this for me and for all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, so that we may leave behind the two extremes of the evil views of superimposition and denial, and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having awakened, we shall remain free from the views of eternalism through superimposition and nihilism through denial, and thus not slander the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having received the request of Mahāmati Bodhisattva, spoke.
The verse says:
"Establishment and denial do not exist for that mind; the body and its enjoyments are established by the mind, yet the mind cannot know them.
Through delusion and lack of wisdom, one engages in establishment and denial."
Within the realm of true purity, even "non-existence" is not applicable, much less can one speak of "existence"; thus, fundamentally, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
That which is the natural state of existence and non-existence refers to the two truths; to assert existence or to assert non-existence refers to the two views.
By means of the two truths, the principle does not contradict one another: they are one in essence while responding to duality. By means of the two views, however, [the matter is otherwise].
Those who possess signs grasp at their partiality and fail to attain the whole;

this is why Mahāmati inquires of the World-Honored One regarding the characteristics of establishment and slander, intending to lead Bodhisattvas away from those two views and enable them to reach the Right Path.
Thus it is said, and so forth. To speak of "leaving behind the view of eternal establishment and the view of nihilistic slander" means that "eternal" refers to...

To establish [a view] that negates [causality] is to slander the cause. Thus, there are those who hold to both existence and non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, or combinations of these single and dual aspects, as well as views beyond words;
all of these are rooted in the two extremes of views and none constitute the True Dharma.
To claim they are real is to slander it to what extent? What kind of view could possibly avoid slandering the True Dharma? One should reflect upon this carefully. (Verse)
To speak of establishing [existence] or slandering [non-existence] while claiming that there is no such thing as "mind-only" is incorrect; for both establishment and slander are indeed mind-only.
Within the nature of true quiescence, there has never been any reality of that mind-only from the beginning.

The Tathāgata has directly pointed this out from the outset, intending for deluded ordinary beings to realize that fundamentally nothing exists; thus, one becomes free from all false views and leaves behind body and sensation.
Regarding the statement "by means of establishment and mind," these dharmas are precisely the locus from which the two views arise;
yet they themselves do not claim to exist or not to exist, and thus one cannot know them. Nevertheless, within the absence of fixed dharmas, fixed views arise.
As the teaching states: "How have all dharmas ever claimed to be identical or different? All are merely the conceptualizations of the mind."

To know that they are foolish and ignorant is so; thus, that fundamentally not a single dharma exists is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), while that all dharmas appear as they are is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The wise attain this and practice both the ultimate and the conventional together, whereas the ignorant fail to comprehend it and fall into the discourse of dualistic views.
Truth and view differ by only a single interval. (1)
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify the meaning of these verses, addressed Mahāmati, saying:

"There are four kinds of establishment regarding what does not exist. What are the four? They are: the establishment of non-existent characteristics, the establishment of non-existent views, the establishment of non-existent causes, and the establishment of non-existent natures.
These are called the four kinds of establishment. Furthermore, as for 'denigration,' it refers to..."
To engage in slander by observing that which has been established as unobtainable when it is not one's lot [to perceive it] is called the characteristic of establishing through slander.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of establishing that which does not exist? It refers to the attachment to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as having self-characteristics or common characteristics when they do not exist;
to think "it is thus" and "it is not otherwise"—this is called the characteristic of establishing that which does not exist.

Mahāmati, this "establishment of the characteristic of non-existence" arises from the attachment to various habitual tendencies and the false fabrications of beginningless time; it is born of the proliferation of delusive thoughts regarding characteristics that do not exist.

Mahāmati, as for the establishment of the characteristic of the view of non-existence: if one establishes views such as the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), the sense-bases (*āyatana*), the self (*ātman*), the person (*pudgala*), sentient beings (*sattva*), life-span (*jīva*), nourishment (*poṣa*), or the spirit (*puruṣa*), this is called the establishment of the characteristic of the view of non-existence. Mahāmati.

The characteristic of establishing what is not based on causes refers to the initial consciousness arising without a cause, which is subsequently unreal like a magical illusion and fundamentally unarisen;

that the elements of the eye, form, and light, along with mental attention, arise moment by moment and, having arisen, truly disintegrate—this is called the characteristic of establishing what is not based on causes.
Mahāmati, the characteristic of establishing what does not exist as a nature refers to space, cessation, and parinirvāṇa, which are not produced.

Based on the nature of conceptual attachment, one establishes this state of being free from existence and non-existence; all phenomena are like the horns of rabbits or horses, appearing like floating hairs.
To be free from both existence and non-existence is called the characteristic of establishing the nature of non-existence.

This establishment and denial arises from the false imaginings of the foolish, who do not skillfully examine that which is the manifestation of their own minds; they are not noble sages. Therefore, it is free from such establishment.
One should study the refutation of slanderous and evil views.
Generally speaking, there are many ways of establishing [doctrines], yet to speak in opposition to these is not to avoid slander; therefore, its characteristics are briefly shown.

It consists primarily of the view of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-dṛṣṭi*). Regarding the general statement that [things] do not exist, those who establish them as existing claim that what was originally non-existent...
As for the existence of "existence," once one has clearly understood that it is not so, to further slander it by demonstrating the characteristics of such slander means:
having established [the object] as existing and then failing to find it through investigation, one concludes that nothing exists at all;

this is the arising of the view of slander because the observation was directed toward what is not its proper domain. In the commentary, the phrase "establishing characteristics" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*).
To enter into and give rise to conceptual attachment regarding what is fundamentally neither self-characteristic nor common characteristic— saying "it is thus" or "it is not otherwise than thus"—
such that the self-characteristic is not distinct from the common characteristic, is precisely to give rise to the perception of existence where there is no existence. Furthermore,
because it arises from the habitual tendencies of false delusions since beginningless time, one knows it to be a false vision.
The latter three examples are likewise so; "view" refers to views such as those of a self, a person, or sentient beings, which arise in relation to actual dharmas;
therefore it is said: "If those [views] are thus, the aggregates, elements, and bases are also examples.
Regarding the statement that the initial consciousness arises without a cause, this means that some reckon there is a cause, while others reckon there is no cause—both are [erroneous].
Regarding its characteristics, one directly refutes their position, saying:
"If you claim that the initial consciousness arises without a cause, then it would be unreal later on; being like an illusion, how could there be arising?
If there were a causal moment prior to the four conditions such as the eye, then once it has arisen, it would be real; yet once it has become real, it must eventually perish. This is...

Because they involve arising and ceasing, all such views are incorrect. Regarding the "establishment of a nature" (svabhāva-vyavasthāna)—such as the extinction of space and so forth—these are the attachments of those non-Buddhists who conceive of the three unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) as having a nature that is not produced. To rectify this through correct reasoning, it is said:
"This is free from both nature and the absence of nature. This means that although the unconditioned dharmas are empty, they are not identical to emptiness itself.
All phenomena are like the horns of a rabbit or a horse, which do not exist, yet they are not like the appearance of falling hairs, which exist [as a perceptual error].
Therefore, it is said that one is "free from existence and non-existence. How could one take what is uncreated and conceive of it as having an intrinsic nature?

Furthermore, the statement regarding "establishment and denial" is a summary refutation; it arises because one does not skillfully contemplate that the manifestation of one's own mind is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent.
To calculate and cling to existence and non-existence is not the way of the sages; therefore, one is exhorted to abandon these two views and practice and study in this manner.
(2) ○ This concludes the nineteenth chapter.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thoroughly understands the mind, the thought, the mental consciousness, the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness.
Having reached the ultimate goal, he manifests various kinds of forms for the sake of pacifying sentient beings, just as the nature of false imagination abides in the realm of dependent origination;
like a multicolored wish-fulfilling gem, he universally manifests all the Buddhas.
In all Buddha-fields, the great assemblies of Tathāgatas gather therein to hear and receive the Buddha-dharma.

That is to say, regarding all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, reflections, and the moon in water; regarding all phenomena as being free from arising and ceasing, and free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence;
and having transcended the dharmas of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they attain hundreds of thousands of samādhis, even up to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas.
Having attained samādhi through that samādhi, he travels to various buddha-fields to make offerings to the Buddhas, is born in the palaces of the devas, and proclaims the Three Jewels.
Manifesting the body of a Buddha, surrounded by a great assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, he liberates sentient beings by means of the measure of what is manifested within their own minds.
He analytically expounds upon the non-existence of external natures, causing all to distance themselves from views such as existence and non-existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The world is the measure of the mind; O Son of the Buddha, observe it! Having abandoned the body of various types and the performance of conditioned activities, one attains power, supernormal faculties, and mastery, achieving fulfillment."

To awaken those who have not yet awakened by means of one's own prior awakening is the heart of the benevolent person; to first deliver oneself and subsequently deliver sentient beings is what is meant by a Bodhisattva.

Since this [text] has already been verified and expounded as the Bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the eight consciousnesses and so forth, which can lead to the stage of ultimate peace and bliss, it further exhorts all Bodhisattvas to employ this very path in return.
The ultimate transformation of others for the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings is manifested through the appearance of various kinds of forms;

thus, the path of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others is complete. To say that it is "like the state of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) based upon dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva)" serves as an analogy for how a Bodhisattva necessarily gives rise to responsive transformations whenever there is a karmic opportunity, just as the deluded imaginings of ordinary beings do.

Regarding dependent origination, it is further said: "For example, like a mani jewel that manifests various colors" means that a Bodhisattva, by means of a single body, universally manifests as all bodies throughout all Buddha-lands.

This is just as the light and reflections of a precious jewel pervade and encompass everything, each according to its own nature; therefore, two analogies are used. Appearing according to color is fundamentally like a *maṇi* jewel.
Now, since these [forms] are commonly employed, how could there be anything that cannot manifest according to one's wishes?
Yet, the reason one must listen to and receive the Dharma within a Buddha-field is that Bodhisattvas—both self and others—still abide in the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*).

Without serving the Buddhas and hearing the Dharma to awaken the mind, it is insufficient to attain the various *samādhis*. Therefore, it was said previously that they "manifest various kinds of elephant forms."

The subsequent passage states: "Manifesting the Buddha-body is precisely the causal stage of the Bodhisattva; once the transformation is accomplished, one ultimately employs the transformation of the fruit. Such is the natural principle of the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "measuring sentient beings by means of the self-mind’s direct perception (*svacitta-pratyakṣa*)," this clarifies the re-establishment of the fundamental school through the deployment of transformative teachings.
Now, if one saves sentient beings by means of "Mind-Only," there is no being who is not saved; if one preaches the Dharma by remaining detached from inherent nature, then it is thus.
Because all that is seen is detached from [subject and object], one knows that for the Bodhisattva, both self and other, from beginning to end, are fundamentally based upon this. The verse says:
"The world is a measure of the mind. This means that the Bodhisattva, through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of their own mind, observes all worlds;

for those who can be transformed, they manifest bodies of various kinds to respond universally to them. Yet all of these arise from the power of unconditioned compassion (*nirnimitta-maitrī*), and thus they are detached from the perceived object.
The performance of practices is also established and accomplished by attaining the power of the illusion-like samādhi and other such states.
[End of Chapter Twenty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for our sake..."
"I teach that all phenomena are empty, unarisen, non-dual, and devoid of the characteristics of intrinsic nature, self, and so forth.

When I and the other bodhisattvas have awakened to this emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and absence of intrinsic nature, we shall swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by abandoning the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati.
The Bodhisattva said: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well; I shall now explain it to you in detail.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Mahāmati, that which is called 'emptiness of emptiness' (śūnyatā-śūnyatā) is precisely the locus of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva). Mahāmati, for one who clings to the imagined nature, [the teachings of] emptiness, non-arising, and non-existence are taught."
Second is the characteristic of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
First, regarding the discourse on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one must not fail to exhaustively grasp the principle of emptiness;

for if one does not fully comprehend these principles, there are those who often fall into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) or become mired in partial emptiness. They give rise to dualistic views, becoming attached to the characteristic of emptiness and unable to liberate themselves from it.
Because these exist, there is what is called emptiness—non-arising, non-duality, and the departure from the marks of self-nature.

This is requested so as to exhaust their principles and reach the limit of their afflictions. The Tathāgata tells them that "emptiness" is precisely the locus of the self-nature of deluded thought (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, he says that emptiness is taught for those who are attached to deluded thoughts. These two are mutually related.
Because they engage with [phenomena], they do not penetrate emptiness, and thus deluded thoughts arise; when deluded thoughts reach their limit, one then realizes emptiness.
This is merely the matter of emptiness and deluded thoughts entering and exiting one another. This is the purport of the Tathāgata’s response to Mahāmati.

As for the term "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), it refers to that which was previously described as "emptiness," "non-arising," and so forth—namely, the emptiness of that which is already empty, or the non-arising of that which is already empty.
Non-duality and the absence of intrinsic nature—these are exhausted in a single phrase.
Since false conceptualization can arise from emptiness itself, this emptiness must therefore exhaust its own principle; if its principle is not exhausted, emptiness will again become a sickness.

If one merely reaches the point where false conceptualization is exhausted and identifies with emptiness, one must nonetheless exhaust that sickness to its limit; failing to exhaust it, [it remains a hindrance].
As for that illness, the emptiness encountered therein must necessarily be partial; thus, it is through the mutual necessity of these two that clarity is attained.
Furthermore, if deluded thoughts arise from emptiness, then deluded thoughts are fundamentally void.
If one knows that the Tathāgata taught emptiness as a remedy for delusion, then what further phenomena could there be? In this way, the faults of emptiness are more than half-removed.
(1) Mahāmati, those seven kinds of emptiness are briefly stated as follows:

the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of activity (*kriyā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-activity (*akriyā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression (*sarvadharma-nirabhilāpya-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the ultimate reality of noble wisdom (*paramārtha-āryajñāna-mahā-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of this and that (*itaretara-śūnyatā*). What are their characteristics?
"Emptiness" refers to the emptiness of all natures in terms of their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

This is because, when one contemplates them as mutually accumulated, they are devoid of the nature of specific and general characteristics through conceptualization; because the nature of self, other, or both does not arise; and because characteristics do not abide.

Therefore, it is said that all natures and characteristics are empty; this is called the "emptiness of characteristics. What is meant by the "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)? It means that the intrinsic nature of itself does not arise.
This is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all dharmas; therefore, it is said that their intrinsic nature is empty. What is the emptiness of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*)?
It refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), which are devoid of "I" and "mine," and which arise through causes, conditions, performed actions, and skillful means.

This is called the emptiness of conditioned formations. Mahāmati, this very emptiness of conditioned formations, being a dependent origination of successive conditions and lacking an intrinsic nature, is called the emptiness of non-conditioned formations (*asaṃskāra-śūnyatā*).
What is the emptiness of all phenomena as being beyond verbal expression? It refers to the fact that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is inexpressible;

thus, the state wherein all phenomena are beyond verbal expression is called the emptiness of all phenomena as being beyond verbal expression. What is the great emptiness of the ultimate reality and noble wisdom (*paramārtha-āryajñāna*)?

It refers to the attainment of the noble wisdom of self-realization, wherein all views and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are empty; this is called [the emptiness of the ultimate reality and noble wisdom].

Regarding the great emptiness of the ultimate noble wisdom of all dharmas, what is meant by "emptiness of this or that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*)? It refers to the emptiness of something in relation to the absence of another;
this is called "emptiness of this or that. Mahāmati, for example, it is like saying a house belonging to the mother of a concubine's son is empty of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth.
This does not mean that because there are no bhikṣus, the house itself is empty, nor that the nature of the house is empty, nor that the bhikṣus themselves are empty.
The emptiness of intrinsic nature is not the absence of elephants and horses elsewhere; this is called the self-characteristic of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

That something is absent in a certain place is called the emptiness of that in relation to that (*itaretara-śūnyatā*). These are the seven kinds of emptiness. Among them, the emptiness of that in relation to that is the coarsest form of emptiness;
you should distance yourself from it.
Because emptiness has both extensive and concise [explanations], the various sūtra teachings do not present the meaning of emptiness in a single uniform way.

Here, I shall briefly set forth seven kinds of emptiness, beginning with the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). "Characteristics" refers to all natures—both specific (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—which are empty because they are unobtainable. Thus it is said:

by observing that [phenomena] are accumulated through mutual succession, one analyzes the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), discussing their mutual opening and closing.
Turning one's observation toward them, they are found to have no accumulation at all; yet when each part is analyzed individually, they are found to lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Because self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) do not arise, they are non-arising, and this non-arising is emptiness—this is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaśūnyatā*). Furthermore, by investigating through the nature of self, other, or both, [intrinsic nature] cannot be apprehended;
thus, it does not abide in the characteristics of self, other, or both—this is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇaśūnyatā*). As for the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāvaśūnyatā*), it means:
The non-arising of self-nature is emptiness by virtue of its non-arising; furthermore, it is said that "the nature of all phenomena is empty of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-śūnya*).

Because this applies both specifically and universally, all phenomena are non-arising. Although emptiness was previously discussed, the present mention of "emptiness of intrinsic nature" is as follows:
whereas the former involved an analytical investigation leading into emptiness such that both nature and characteristics were [examined], this [latter]...
Since they are fundamentally empty of both [subject and object], their nature and characteristics are both identical to the true nature; this serves as the boundary for distinguishing them.

Regarding the emptiness of practice and the statement that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are devoid of "I" and "mine": the aggregates are fundamentally what belongs to the "mine," yet their nature is fundamentally detached from it.

Thus, the "I" is established based on the aggregates, and practice arises from the "I"—all of these are without exception empty. Therefore, it is said: "The means of action consist of the objects produced by causes."
"Arising" refers to that which is produced; "that which belongs to me" refers to karma, and "action" (saṃskāra) arises from the fundamental aggregates.

This is the emptiness of action. As for the emptiness of non-action: it means that one does not depart from the previously performed actions, yet through the successive conditions of dependent origination, no intrinsic nature can be found.
Thus, while there is action, there is no action; therefore, non-action is also empty. Regarding the emptiness beyond verbal expression: as for all words...
Because conceptualization arises from deluded thought and the self-nature of that conceptualization is non-existent, there is likewise no verbal expression.
If one contemplates all phenomena as being without self-nature, then verbal expression naturally falls away; this is precisely the emptiness that transcends verbal expression.

As for the Great Emptiness of the Noble Wisdom of Ultimate Reality: the noble wisdom of self-realization is fundamentally not something that should be made empty, yet it is able to empty those [false] views.
The habitual tendencies of the past are named "empty" based on that which is emptied; since that which is emptied is already empty, how could that which empties it not be empty?
This is precisely what is meant by "ultimate emptiness. As for "emptiness of this and that," this refers specifically to the emptiness imagined by non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
When contrasted with the self, it is merely empty of "that" while not being empty of itself; therefore, it is said that "in that, there is the emptiness of that," and thus it falls [into error].
The negation of non-existence is precisely for the sake of not [falling into] self-emptiness; if both that and the self were empty, then who would there be to fall [into such an error]?
Therefore, by means of the analogy of the son of a concubine and the mother’s house, the meaning is that although there are no elephants or horses, there is a community of bhikṣus.
While the absence of elephants and horses is the emptiness of those objects, the presence of the bhikṣus is not likewise [empty].
If one cannot [realize] self-emptiness, and furthermore says that "the nature of the house is empty" rather than "it is not a house," then this is to dismiss [the argument] by concession;
for even if one house were taken as empty, it does not necessarily follow that all other houses are empty.

If one uses this logic to claim that although there are bhikṣus, the nature of the bhikṣu is empty, it does not necessarily follow that every single bhikṣu is empty. If one proceeds in this way, there would be nothing at all.

Elephants and horses are empty, yet they are not non-existent in other places; this is because when each of these is analyzed, the various characteristics of subject and object, self and other, remain distinct.
Therefore, it is said: "This is called the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena," which does not mean that they are empty.

Thus, he concludes with a refutation, saying: "That [is] in that [place], there is no that," and so forth. The first "that" refers to the opponent (the outsider), who merely— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
"That which does not exist there cannot be said to make this non-existent" and "the emptiness of this and that" (itaretara-śūnyatā) are the coarsest forms of emptiness;
from these, one can understand how externalist calculations are refuted. (2)
Mahāmati, [dharmas] do not arise from themselves, yet they are not non-arising, except when abiding in samādhi; this is called "non-arising. To be free from self-nature is precisely non-arising.
Because all natures manifest as momentary continuities, successions, and variations, they are free from self-nature;
therefore, all natures are free from self-nature. What is meant by "non-duality"? It refers to all dharmas being like the aggregates (*skandhas*).
O Mahāmati, all phenomena are non-dual—neither in terms of heat, nor length, nor shortness, nor black, nor white.
Nirvāṇa is not distinct from saṃsāra, nor is saṃsāra distinct from nirvāṇa, because they exist as causes for differentiated characteristics. This is called non-duality.
As it is with nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, so it is with all phenomena; therefore, they are empty, unarisen, non-dual, and devoid of the characteristics of self-nature.
One should train in this way. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I have always taught the Dharma of emptiness, which is far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence. Birth and death are like illusions and dreams, yet karma is not destroyed.
This is also true for space and nirvana; both are likewise so. Fools create deluded thoughts, but the noble ones are free from existence."
"No. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:

"Mahāmati, emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the departure from the marks of self-nature universally enter all the sūtras of the Buddhas; indeed, whatever sūtras there may be, they all expound these."
This meaning is explained and revealed through various sūtras according to the aspirations of sentient beings;
however, the true reality does not reside in words, just as the mirage of water deceives a herd of deer.
The deer, clinging to the appearance of that sign as being water, perceive it as such, yet no water exists there. In this same way, all that is taught in the sūtras...
The Dharma is intended to inspire joy in the foolish; it is not that true noble wisdom resides in verbal expression.
Therefore, one should rely upon the meaning and not cling to words.
Having already clarified that all phenomena are empty, this further specifically addresses the meaning of non-arising and so forth, all for the purpose of providing a detailed exposition.
The principle of emptiness may also be elucidated through these four meanings; this is the purport of the text.

Regarding "not arising from self" and so forth, it should be understood according to the verses in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;
they do not arise without a cause; therefore, they are said to be unarisen. Now, to explain this comprehensively: "not arising from self" does not mean that they are not produced at all.
This means that it is not the case that nothing whatsoever arises. To speak according to principle, there is non-arising, yet there is nothing that does not arise.
Yongjia said: "If in reality there is no arising, then there is nothing that does not arise. Thus, what is called "non-arising" refers merely to abiding in samādhi;
therefore it is said: "Except for abiding in samādhi. Next, the meaning of being "devoid of self-nature" is explained by again referring to non-arising.
For this reason, it is said that being devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vivikta*) is itself non-arising.
"Devoid of intrinsic nature" refers to the mind as a momentary, continuous, and flowing stream, as well as to phenomena such as those appearing as distinct natures.

This means that because the mind undergoes transformation, all phenomena appearing as distinct natures likewise lack intrinsic nature. As for the question, "How is there non-duality?", this is a subsequent explanation of non-duality.
The text first indicates the two aspects by way of phenomena (*dharma*), stating that "all dharmas are like a mass of heat," which means that phenomena cannot help but be distinct.
It further states that "all dharmas are non-dual," which means that principle (*li*) cannot help but be one.
Because this single principle integrates those distinct phenomena, all dharmas are non-dual; they are non-dual.
Emptiness itself is neither nirvāṇa nor saṃsāra; these are likewise external objects.

This is not the same as the view of ordinary outsiders, who, because they perceive saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as mutually distinct, claim that there are external characteristics and causes, and thus maintain that each possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Therefore, it is said that there are no two, concluding with the unification [of all things] as an illustration to exhort practice, and so forth. The first verse summarizes the emptiness that is free from [duality].

Regarding the severance of [the views of] permanence and annihilation: so-called "non-arising" and "being devoid of intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) also entail being devoid of [these extremes]; this is explained sequentially.

It clarifies that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are each free from the extremes of permanence and annihilation. Thus, saṃsāra is not permanent because it is like an illusion, yet it is not annihilated because its karma is indestructible.
Nirvāṇa is likewise not permanent because it is like an illusion, yet it is not annihilated because it is not the same as the extinction of ashes.
When the text speaks of *nirvāṇa* and space, it refers to the three unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Because birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is neither interrupted nor eternal, it is itself *nirvāṇa*; because *nirvāṇa* is neither interrupted nor eternal, it does not exist outside of birth-and-death.
Yet, due to their deluded conceptualizations, the ignorant give rise to views of annihilation and permanence; the Noble Ones, however, remain free from existence and non-existence.

Thus, there is no difference between these two dharmas. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in general terms of emptiness, non-arising, and so forth, as they constitute the essential purport of all great teachings;
therefore, it is said that [this teaching] universally enters into all sūtras.

If one uses this principle to seal and determine its exposition, then the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox will not be erroneous; otherwise, it would be the teaching of external paths. It is further said that, following...

Regarding the phrase "because of the aspirational minds of sentient beings": this means that although one may provisionally manifest emptiness and other such principles through verbal expression, these do not truly exist within the expressions themselves.
If one were to stubbornly cling to them, one would not only lose the underlying principle but also fail in the verbal teaching itself;
therefore, this serves as a warning to remain free from verbal expression. What is it that must be left behind? It is simply non-attachment. This is the nature of words and letters.
Is it not this very detachment that is meant? One who grasps this is like one who understands the finger pointing at the moon.
(3) The above is the twenty-first chapter. The First Fascicle of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra is hereby completed.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Volume Two, Chapter One:
The Essence of All Buddha-Speech, Part Two.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has spoken in the sūtras..."

The *tathāgatagarbha* is pure by nature; it manifests the thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings, just as a precious jewel of great value may be wrapped in soiled garments.

The *tathāgatagarbha* is likewise eternally abiding and unchanging, yet it is enveloped by the soiled garments of the aggregates (*skandhas*), elements (*dhātus*), and sense-bases (*āyatanas*), and defiled by the dust and toil of unreal conceptualization—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion.
"What has been proclaimed by all the Buddhas—why, World-Honored One, do you speak of a *tathāgatagarbha* in the same way as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) speak of a self (*ātman*)?
World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also speak of a permanent agent that is free from *guṇas*, omnipresent, and imperishable.
World-Honored One, they say there is a self. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "My teaching of the *tathāgatagarbha* is not the same as that of the non-Buddhists."
Mahāmati, when I have spoken of the "self" using such terms as space, signlessness, wishlessness, the reality-limit, the dharma-nature,
the dharma-body, nirvāṇa, being devoid of intrinsic nature, non-arising, non-ceasing, primordial quiescence, and parinirvāṇa by its very nature—
it was after having thus explained the Tathāgatagarbha that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha did so in order to sever the fear of selflessness in foolish people.
Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgatagarbha-gate, which is free from false conceptualization and has no objective realm, is taught for this purpose.
Mahāmati, future and present Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should not form attachments based on the view of a self (*ātman*).

It is, for example, like a potter who, from a single lump of clay, uses human effort, water, wood, a wheel, and a cord as skillful means to produce various vessels; the Tathāgata is also just like this.

Regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which is free from all marks of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*), through various forms of wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he sometimes speaks of the *tathāgatagarbha* and sometimes speaks of selflessness (*anātman*).
For these reasons, he speaks of the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is not the same as the "self" (*ātman*) spoken of by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This is called teaching the *tathāgatagarbha* in order to attract and lead those non-Buddhists who cling to a self.
The Tathāgatagarbha causes one to abandon the false imagination of an unreal self-view and enter the sphere of the three gates of liberation;
it inspires the aspiration to swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has spoken thus regarding the Tathāgatagarbha.
Were it not so, it would be identical to the views of the non-Buddhists. For this reason, Mahāmati, [it is taught as such].
In order to abandon the views of the non-Buddhists, one should rely upon the Tathāgata-garbha, which is selfless.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The person, the continuity, the aggregates, conditions, atoms, the Primal Lord (Pradhāna), and the Creator—these are all the products of the mind’s measure of false imagination."
It must be distinguished that there are cases where things appear similar but are actually different, and where statements seem distinct but are fundamentally the same;
for if one does not clearly discern this, the heterodox will surely be confused with the orthodox.

Thus, Mahāmati asks whether the Buddha’s teaching on the *tathāgatagarbha*—which remains immutable even while enmeshed in afflictions—is identical to the *ātman* (self) postulated by non-Buddhists. The text first recounts the Buddha’s teaching, stating: "The Tathāgata..."
Regarding the naturally pure *tathāgatagarbha*: the essence of the *garbha* is fundamentally empty and has never been defiled;
thus it is called "pure. This nature is common to both sentient beings and Buddhas. When manifested by the Tathāgata, its thirty-two marks appear in their entirety;

when present within the nature of sentient beings, it remains eternally and unchangingly enshrouded by the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*). This demonstrates that cause and effect are non-dual.

It is said: "The turning and entering [of the Tathāgata] is, in its true essence, entirely the substance itself; it is not that there is a real characteristic of turning and entering. This is just as the Sūtra says:
"The Buddha’s Dharma-realm body enters into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings. This can be understood through the application of analogies such as the "highly priced jewel" and so forth.
The phrase "How is it, World-Honored One... and below is the formal conclusion of the inquiry. It further states: "The non-Buddhists also... [and so on].
To say that there is a permanent agent is to conceive of the *ātman* as being permanent and acting as an agent;

it is held to exist apart from the conditions of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, and because its nature as a self is all-pervasive, it is said to be "apart from qualities" (*guṇa*) and all-pervasive without perishing.
Regarding the claim that this is identical to the *tathāgatagarbha*, the response first distinguishes them by means of the Dharma, stating: "I... [The text continues with the distinction].
It is taught that the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally devoid of the characteristics of a self;

however, it is spoken of as "self" in order to manifest its virtues and to refute delusion, for this "self" and "non-self" are not the same as the fixed conceptualizations of a self held by non-Buddhists.

Therefore, it is said that there are times when such phrases as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—that is, through the meaning of these terms—are used to speak of the Tathāgatagarbha as "self" within the context of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
The full manifestation of all virtues is the meaning of the True Self (*ātman*); these are identical in substance though different in name, and they stand to one another as name and reality.

Furthermore, for the sake of deluded beings who cling to a self and fear the term "selflessness," [the Buddha] taught that the realm free from conceptual construction and devoid of existence is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha;
this is the meaning of selflessness. Nevertheless, since all of these can serve as gateways to communicate through conventional designations, they are all "gates."
Since it is merely a matter of principle, it is said that the gateway of the *tathāgatagarbha* does not mean that the Tathāgata is exclusively located within the self;
therefore, one should not harbor attachments through the view of a self. Thus we know that the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox lies in the reality itself, not in names.
Next, he cites an analogy to conclude and clarify this point, saying: "It is like a potter who, from a single heap of clay... Now, the heap of clay is one; fundamentally, there is no [distinction].

Because the vessels for concentration are fashioned through skillful means, the various forms of these vessels serve as metaphors for the single nature of *dharmanairātmya* (the selflessness of phenomena).

Originally there is no fixed name, yet through the skillful means of wisdom, various names are established—just as the previously mentioned emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), up to the nirvāṇa of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-nirvāṇa*). Therefore, the conclusion clarifies: "Or it is said to be like..."
Regarding the *ālayavijñāna*, it is sometimes said to be "non-self" (*anātman*). If one speaks of non-self in contrast to the *tathāgatagarbha*, then the *tathāgatagarbha* would be the self.
Since it is also said that it is "sometimes spoken of as non-self," this implies that the self itself is non-self.
Thus, those who speak of it as being the self do so in order to guide those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cling to a self, leading them from their false notion of a self to realize the truth.
The statement that the true self is taught as "non-self" is intended to cause one to abandon the false conceptualization of a self and enter the three gates of liberation;
thus, from the very beginning, there has never been a fixed doctrine [regarding a self]. Furthermore, it may be analyzed through the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), such as:

"Non-self" is used to refute the notion of a self, and so forth. Moreover, the phrase "hastening to attain [enlightenment]" and so on serves to reaffirm the fundamental tenet and provide a concluding demonstration. That is to say:
Although this explanation is generally applicable, if one is to depart from external views, one should rely on the *tathāgatagarbha* as being without self;
thus, we know that the name "garbha" truly encompasses two meanings and is not the same as the "self" imagined by non-Buddhists. The verse states:

"The person, the continuity, and the aggregates" refers precisely to the basis upon which non-Buddhists imagine a self; it does not exist apart from the five aggregates, for the "person" is also the "self. This is the condition.

The notion that atoms are the creators [of the world] is a calculation of the non-Buddhists; however, because it does not transcend the delusive imaginings of the mind-measure (*cittamātra*), it is incorrect. [End of] Chapter One.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, observing future sentient beings, again requested of the World-Honored One: "I only wish..."

The Buddha told Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: "I shall explain the uninterrupted practice for those who practice like the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, which constitutes the great skillful means. What are these four? They are:
(1) skillfully discerning that what appears is one's own mind; (2) observing that external objects have no inherent nature; (3) being free from views of arising, ceasing, and abiding."

Attaining the sublime bliss of the noble wisdom of self-realization is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the four dharmas that constitute the great skillful means of the practitioner.
What is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s skillful discernment of what is manifested by one's own mind? It is to contemplate in this way:
the triple world is merely the limit of mind; it is devoid of "I" and "mine," free from fluctuation, and free from coming and going, having no beginning.

The manifestation that arises through the entry of false imaginings— established by the body and wealth and bound by the various forms and activities of the three realms, which are perfumed by the habitual tendencies of falsehood—
is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful discernment of what is manifested as his own mind.
Those who aspire to the Great Way ought to engage in great cultivation; those who hope for the Great Fruit must possess great skillful means.
If one cultivates yet lacks skillful means, it will be difficult to achieve the fruit of the Way despite one's desires.

Having heard that Mahāmati would swiftly attain Bodhi, and observing that there were those in future generations with the potential to enter the Way, he requested instructions on uninterrupted cultivation.
The Dharma teaching states that "uninterrupted" refers to being without interruption or intermixture. When there is no intermixture, one is refined;

when there is no interruption, one progresses. Since one is both refined and progressing, what practice could one not master? In the response, it is said that one attains the practitioner through the accomplishment of four dharmas.
"Great skillful means" (mahopāya) is a synonym for "skillful means" (upāya), or it may be used in contrast to the "real."

Wisdom (*prajñā*) and either the preliminary or the actual contemplation are all skillful means (*upāya*). While there are many doors to skillful means, these four dharmas are the greatest among them;
therefore, they differ from others and are specifically elucidated. These four do not go beyond the cultivation of the nature of cause and fruit:
the nature of goodness is that by which one cultivates well, and the good cause is that by which one attains the good fruit, up to the ultimate fruit.
If it is good, then there is nothing that is not entirely good; this is why these four constitute the sequence.

"First, the excellence of discerning what is manifested by one's own mind" means that one contemplates in this way that the three realms are merely the limit of mind (*cittamātra*). Here, the three realms are the object of contemplation, while "merely mind" constitutes their limit.
Now, the three realms are fundamentally non-existent; they are solely false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and false conceptualization is without marks (*animitta*).
Because nothing arises apart from one’s own mind, the limits of "mind-only" are precisely the limits of one’s own mind.

Since one realizes that there are no phenomena external to the mind, and because one is free from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," being solely the aspect of suchness (*tathatā*), those who seek motion, agitation, coming, or going cannot find them;
how then could there be any false manifestation? It is merely due to the perfuming of beginningless false habits that the form-and-color (*rūpa*) of the three realms [appears].
The activities of conceptualization follow into one's own mind, manifesting as speech, form, and activity; here, "activity" briefly refers to two of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Because of these aggregates, one is bound to the body and material wealth, which includes both speech and enjoyment.

Since the body serves as the basis for their establishment, if one knows that all phenomena arise solely from the perfuming of delusion and manifest back from one's own mind—and that this mind is fundamentally quiescent—what further need is there for action?
To analyze it in this way is excellent (1).
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully contemplate that external natures are non-natures?

It means that all natures—such as mirages, dreams, and so forth—are beginningless, false, and caused by the habit-energy of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). By contemplating the self-nature of all natures in this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva acts.
Thus, skillfully observing that external natures are without intrinsic nature is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful observation that external natures are without intrinsic nature.
How does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully abandon views of arising, abiding, and ceasing?

It is by seeing that all natures—whether produced by self, other, or both—are non-arising, because they enter into the limits of one's own mind; thus, one sees that external natures are without intrinsic nature.
When one perceives that consciousness does not arise and conditions do not accumulate, and sees that the imagined nature of dependent origination cannot be found within or without the three realms;

when all views regarding the arising of things are abandoned and their lack of intrinsic nature is realized; when one knows that all phenomena are like illusions and attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
and having attained this patient acceptance, one is free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing—this is called a bodhisattva.
Mahāsattvas are skilled in discerning and departing from views concerning arising, abiding, and ceasing. How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the sublime joy of the noble self-realized wisdom?

It means attaining the stage of non-arising dharma (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), entering the eighth bodhisattva stage, and attaining detachment from mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*), as well as the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
They then attain the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), O World-Honored One; this is the mind-made body.
For what reason did the Buddha tell Mahāmati that the "mind-made body" (manomaya-kāya) is called "mind-made" because it moves as swiftly and without obstruction as thought?
It is like the movement of the mind; it is like a stone [thrown] in that it is unimpeded across immeasurable *yojanas* in other directions.
Because of what was previously seen, one remembers it without forgetting, and as the stream of one's own mind flows without interruption, birth occurs within the body without obstruction.
Mahāmati, in this way, the various types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) attained by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas arise simultaneously.
These mind-made bodies—adorned with the power of the illusion-like samādhi, mastery over supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), and sublime marks—arise all at once as a noble lineage of beings.

Like the arising of a mind-made body, they are without obstruction; according to their recollections and the spheres of their original vows, they manifest for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.

Having attained the excellent bliss of the noble self-realized wisdom born of birth, such a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the stage of non-arising dharma-patience and dwells in the eighth bodhisattva ground;

there he completely relinquishes the mind, mentation, and consciousness, the five dharmas, the three natures, and the characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness, and attains the body of mental origination (manomaya-kāya), thereby obtaining the excellent bliss of the noble self-realized wisdom. This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
One who accomplishes these four dharmas attains the great skillful means of a practitioner; they should train in this way.
Having already understood one's own mind, what external nature could there be?

To say that one contemplates the non-existence of external natures means to understand that there is nothing internal or external, and thus to look outwardly at things such as mirages and dreams—all natures are fundamentally rooted in beginningless false habituation.

Because causes and conditions are unreal—like illusions, dreams, and the like—one now contemplates in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*). Thus, one contemplates that the self-nature of all phenomena is itself no-nature;
this is the contemplation of non-arising, such as the principle that things do not arise from themselves.

Within the view of being free from arising, abiding, and ceasing, it is said to be "like illusions, dreams, and so forth," which reiterates what was stated above. Regarding the statement "one sees that consciousness does not arise," this correctly demonstrates the freedom from views.
Due to the aforementioned contemplation, one internally perceives that consciousness does not arise and external objects do not accumulate;
because the real nature of each and every thing cannot be found upon investigation, it is said that "non-arising arises.

Because all phenomena within and without the three realms are produced through the conditions of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), they share the same ground and principle; thus, being entirely unattainable, they are nothing more than the departure from inherent nature.
When one sees that nature is detached, seeing itself is also detached; because both dependent origination and seeing are entirely quiescent, it is said that "birth and seeing are both extinguished.
To realize and know the self-nature of all phenomena in this way is the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Since there is no arising, there is no cessation;
thus, the views of birth, abiding, and cessation are all without exception transcended. One who attains the sublime bliss of the noble wisdom of self-awakening is...

Regarding the "Dharma-joy obtained upon dwelling in the eighth stage," according to the Tiantai school’s clarification of the stages, it is only from the eighth stage onward that one attains non-arising (*anutpāda*).
This is generally said to pertain to the Shared Vehicle (*sādhāraṇayāna*), or else to the paths of the Distinct (*biejiao*) and Perfect (*yuanjiao*) teachings.

Furthermore, since these four dharmas are all explained as being like illusions and transformations, we know that the Shared Vehicle encompasses both the Distinct and the Perfect; this is the second point. It does not state what is "enjoyed," but rather...
"Detaching from mind, thought, and consciousness" means that detachment itself is the bliss; it does not mean there is some other separate object of enjoyment.

This refers to the single moment of transformation where one abandons such phenomena as these. When all factors of the remedial gate—both subject and object—are entirely detached, the noble wisdom of self-realization is thereby attained.
Thus, one should know that the locus of realization lies solely in the locus of detachment; by detaching from this, one attains it. If...
Now, when one perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm and does not perceive that there is a single dharma to be attained, what could be said regarding the sublime bliss of noble wisdom?
Yet, it is specifically stated that attaining the "mind-born body" (manomaya-kāya) is the foundation for the arising of transformations.

This is also like casting away the mind to subsequently attain the function of the mind; this involves three meanings: the meaning of swiftness, the meaning of non-obstruction, and the meaning of recollection.
The meaning of what was previously observed is as stated in the text, etc.: "the flow of one's own mind is uninterrupted" refers to the *manas* (mind).
"Birth occurs without obstruction in the body" refers to birth; that is to say, when the *manas* departs, the body must attain birth.

Only sages and those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are capable of this. If discussed in terms of ordinary beings, it is not necessarily the case that when the *manas* arrives, the body arrives; it is said that they are simultaneous.
This refers to the preceding statement that the mind-born [body] has no before or after. When the Bodhisattva’s mind-born [body] arises, it is again brought forth in accordance with the Dharma;
this means that even through the sovereign supernormal powers of the Illusion-like Samādhi, it is capable of being produced.
The body of the noble lineage, adorned with wondrous marks, is the very body thus produced. Furthermore, because these arise simultaneously, there is no before or after. It is just as...

The "birth according to one's wishes" (*yathābhiprāya-janman*) and so forth can be understood accordingly; the phrase "accomplishing sentient beings" (*sattvaparipācana*) also obtains this characteristic of bliss.
The characteristics of identity and difference shall be further clarified later. If one follows the principles of the Tiantai school, the true and the semblance are distinct;

the Buddha’s intention was to act according to what is appropriate, and there was never a fixed position from the outset. This [present work] is for the purpose of explaining the sutras rather than exclusively adjudicating the teachings, and thus it may be set aside [as such].
[Section] Two. Chapter Two.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again entreated the World-Honored One, saying: "I pray that you will explain the characteristics of the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*) of all dharmas.
By awakening to the characteristics of causal conditions, I and the other bodhisattvas shall become detached from all natures."
There is the view of non-existence and the view of false imagination; there is the view of non-imaginary conceptualization, arising either gradually or simultaneously. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"All phenomena have two kinds of causal conditions, namely external and internal. External conditions refer to the production of a jar through various expedient means such as a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, a string, water, wood, and human labor—just as a clay jar arises from these factors.
Internal conditions refer to things such as thread and cloth, grass and mats, seeds and sprouts, or curd and butter."
The dependent origination of external conditions is also like this; this is called the sequential arising of external conditions. What are internal conditions?

They refer to dharmas such as ignorance, craving, and karma, which receive the name "conditions. From them arise the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—these dharmas receive the name "arisen from conditions.
Although they are without distinction, deluded worldlings falsely conceptualize them; this is called the dharma of internal conditions. Mahāmati, as for those causes:

There are six kinds, namely: the cause of what is to be (bhaviṣyat-hetu), the cause of continuity (saṃtati-hetu), the cause of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-hetu), the cause of activity (kriyā-hetu), the cause of manifestation (prabhāvana-hetu), and the cause of dependence (apekṣā-hetu).

The "cause of what is to be" refers to the production of internal and external phenomena once the cause of activity has been performed. The "cause of continuity" refers to the production of internal and external phenomena once the object-condition (ālambana) has been grasped.

The "cause of characteristics" refers to the production of the characteristics of the aggregates (skandha-bīja) and so forth. The "cause of activity" refers to the production of uninterrupted succession. The "cause of manifestation" refers to the performance [of the act].

Regarding the causal factor of sovereignty, as exemplified by a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), once the phenomena of conceptual construction have arisen, their characteristics manifest and perform their functions, like a lamp illuminating forms and other objects.
Regarding the causal factor of cessation, when these cease, the continuity is severed and the nature of non-conceptualization arises.
The doctrine of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is indeed the fundamental basis for the arising of all phenomena in Buddhism; it also encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
In terms of their meaning, there are distinctions of intimacy and distance, while in terms of their function, they necessarily complement one another.
There has never been a case where a cause exists without conditions, nor where conditions exist without a cause; there is nothing that can achieve its purpose apart from these two.
Even that which seeks the true dharma within these very conditions cannot be found; this is the reason why phenomena are established through causes and conditions, thereby giving rise to principle.

As with the four aforementioned dharmas, there is no expedient means that is not a cause and condition; it is simply that the meaning of "causal conditions" (pratyaya-hetu) has a sequence of priority and posteriority.
Therefore, Mahāmati again requested an explanation of the characteristics of causal conditions, [the Buddha] saying: "One must thoroughly understand the causes and conditions of all dharmas."
That which is accomplished is free from all false imaginings of existence and non-existence, and is also free from the views of gradualism and simultaneity;

therefore, it is called the absence of false imaginary views. The meaning of gradual and simultaneous arising will be explained later in the commentary. Regarding what is called the "two kinds of conditions":
external conditions refer to using phenomena to clarify principles, such as a lump of clay and so forth; internal conditions specifically point to ignorance (*avidyā*).

In this context of the karma of craving, the conditions themselves are taken as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and the phenomena arising from those conditions are taken as that which is accomplished (*sādhya*).

For example, when a jar is produced through various causal conditions, the jar itself is what is accomplished; likewise, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are also phenomena that are accomplished.
Other examples, such as thread and cloth, may be understood by analogy. As for the statement regarding "successive transformation and production":
To speak briefly according to the facts, it is as stated; however, based on what follows, it says:

"That is without differentiation," meaning there is no distinction between simultaneous (*sahaja*) and gradual (*kramika*) [arising], and this also serves to eliminate the sequence of the lower [stages]. Next, to clarify that its causes are of six kinds:

these are the causes of those conditions, which should be discussed in relation to the preceding [section] regarding the sense of directness (*pratyakṣa*) and remoteness (*parokṣa*). As for the statement "there shall be a cause," it refers to the single [cause].

With mindfulness as the cause, there arise internal and external phenomena consisting of the faculties and their objects; because the cause is designated by the name of the fruit, it is called the "mark of future continuity.

This means that once one has performed an act of mental apprehension (*ālambana*) toward the preceding faculties and objects, the seeds and other fruits of the subsequent aggregates (*skandha*) continue to arise in accordance with wholesome or unwholesome karma.
Furthermore, regarding the "cause" (*hetu*): immediately after the performance [of the action], it exists.
Regarding the "cause that functions as a cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*) among the succession of good and evil phenomena:
