it acts as a cause upon the cause itself, like a Wheel-Turning King who, having already achieved victory, further performs sovereign deeds. Regarding the "cause that manifests" (*vyañjana-hetu*):

whenever any imagined phenomenon arises, there must necessarily be a manifestation of its characteristic, just as when a lamp illuminates a form, it becomes clearly visible within the relationship between the agent and the object acted upon. Regarding the "dependent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*): it is precisely this delusion.

The statement that "the false arises in dependence upon one another" means that when false conceptualization ceases, the nature of non-conceptualization acts as the continuity of false conceptualization;
yet when there is no false conceptualization, it is severed. Therefore, it is said that at the time of cessation, it acts as the continuity and the severance.
This is because the meaning of the false depending on the non-false implies that the nature of non-conceptualization arises [from the false]. (1)
Mahāmati, those deluded ordinary people who perceive the marks of their own false imaginings do not arise either gradually or simultaneously. Why is this?

If they were to arise simultaneously, there would be no distinction between the agent and the object, and the characteristic of causality could not be established. If they were to arise gradually, the characteristic of selfhood could not be established.

Just as a father cannot exist without a son, Mahāmati, there is no such thing as gradual arising. Thus, it does not arise. Mahāmati, it is like the name "father" being non-existent if there is no son.
The notion that there is a gradual arising through a process of continuity is not so; it is merely a false imagination (*vikalpa*).

Because what is produced arises from conditions such as objective referents (*ālambana*), sequential conditions (*anuloma-pratyaya*), and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), Mahāmati, the gradual arising does not exist because of the attachment to the nature of false imagination.

Furthermore, neither gradual nor simultaneous arising exists, for they are the manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya*) experienced as enjoyment. Thus, external natures—whether characterized by specific marks (*svalakṣaṇa*) or common marks (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—are non-existent.

Mahāmati, because the arising of characteristics occurs through the non-awakening to the manifestations of one's own mind and through false discrimination, both gradual and simultaneous production are eliminated.

Therefore, one should abandon views of gradualism and simultaneity regarding the functioning of causes, conditions, and skillful means. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
All things are without arising and without the extinction of causes and conditions; yet within that arising and extinction, one gives rise to the conceptualization of causes and conditions.

This is not to deny extinction, but rather to show that the continuity of causes and conditions arises. It is solely for the purpose of severing the delusive ignorance and false imaginings of ordinary fools regarding the dependent origination of existence and non-existence.
These phenomena are entirely without arising; it is only through being deluded by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that they revolve. From these three realms of existence (*bhava*), they manifest.
In reality, there is no arising, nor is there any cessation of conditions; one contemplates all conditioned phenomena as being like flowers in the sky.

One neither grasps at nor abandons that which is grasped, for one has abandoned the vision of delusion. There is nothing that has already arisen, nor anything yet to arise, and furthermore, there are no causes or conditions;
all things are non-existent, and these are merely conventional designations.
Next, [the text] refutes the notion that causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) do not give rise to the two kinds of characteristics of birth.

It states that those who are "fools characterized by their own deluded imaginings" regarding causal conditions—meaning those who perceive the characteristics of gradual or simultaneous arising—are all merely discriminating through their own deluded imaginings;
they are also made to form deluded imaginary characteristics by fools. This is a deliberate inversion of words; in reality, neither [gradual nor simultaneous] is appropriate as the two.
Regarding their arising from seeds, the investigation states: if they were to arise simultaneously, there would be no distinction between the agent and the acted-upon;

thus, cause and effect would be conflated, and the specific characteristics of the cause could not be discerned. If they were to arise sequentially, there would necessarily be a priority and posteriority;
this characteristic would be perceived by the ignorant, yet it is not perceived by me—meaning that in the Tathāgata, no such priority or posteriority is seen.

One should consider that [the subsequent moment] can be obtained in relation to [the preceding one]; if it were pronounced with a level tone (i.e., as a single word), then they could not be related to one another in the sense of "self" and "other.

Therefore, the subsequent analogy of father and son is introduced: "Just as if no son is born, there is no name 'father,' so too, if the subsequent thought has not yet arisen, the preceding thought cannot be called [a 'father'].
This conversely clarifies that if the preceding thought has ceased, there is likewise no subsequent thought to continue it; this serves as an illustration for the case of father and son.
Since its meaning is thus, it is said that gradual succession is a provisional means (*upāya*). Otherwise, it would not be the true meaning;

it is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that speaks of "arising. Furthermore, because conceptual construction relies upon the four conditions (the names and meanings of the four conditions are as explained elsewhere), one perceives the appearance of gradual arising.
When examined through this lens, no characteristic of arising can be found; therefore, it is correct [to say there is no such thing].
The summary states: "Gradual arising and non-arising, etc. Thus, there are two modes of arising:

first, that which arises gradually due to attachment to the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); second, that which arises simultaneously due to the manifestation and enjoyment of one's own mind.
This means that while all phenomena manifested by one's own mind may appear to arise simultaneously, [in reality...]
When one mutually examines both [subject and object] and finds that external existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended, then neither of the two arises.

Furthermore, it is said that because one does not perceive the delusive conceptualization of what is merely a manifestation of one's own mind, the arising of characteristics is resolved back into the two aforementioned meanings.
To speak in terms of principle, since nature is fundamentally unarisen, phenomena have no intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); and since phenomena have no intrinsic characteristic, then—
In this state of non-attachment, one naturally does not destroy conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) while realizing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Thus, observing all things in their totality and being free from views, the verse says: "All things are entirely without arising. This means that neither gradual nor simultaneous arising occurs.
Since even arising itself cannot be found, how could there be causes and conditions for cessation? How much less, then, could there be such arising?
Can the perception of causes and conditions arise within cessation? To speak thus as a "remnant" does not mean that one negates the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing;

rather, it is spoken from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), for there is not even a single dharma that is not discarded. If everything were simultaneously discarded, it would result in nihilism.

It is only for the sake of severing the false attachments of the ignorant that this statement is made. Thus, what is it that conditions are severed? One relies upon conditions [to effect their cessation].
Because of the contemplation of cessation, it is said that there is no dharma of dependent origination with objective conditions; all things are entirely without arising.
It is only through the deluded turning of habitual afflictions that the three realms are perceived, whereas within the nature of true quiescence, there is fundamentally no arising or ceasing.

Therefore, by means of non-arising, one contemplates conditioned phenomena as being like flowers in the sky, seeing neither existence nor non-existence, nor any delusive confusion, within the objects of the grasper and the grasped.
As for characteristics, whether already arisen, about to arise, or otherwise—all such things do not exist; they are merely conventional designations expressed through names and words.
(2) [End of] Chapter Three.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the nature of speech."

The Sūtra on the Mind that Manifests the Characteristics of Discursive Thought. "World-Honored One, if I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas skillfully understand this Sūtra on the Mind that Manifests the Characteristics of Discursive Thought, we shall be able to penetrate the two kinds of meanings—namely, speech and that which is expressed by speech—and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
By means of these two modes of speech and its expression, we shall purify all sentient beings."
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you.

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are four kinds of conceptualization regarding the characteristics of speech:
namely, speech regarding characteristics, speech regarding dreams, speech regarding the attachment to false conceptualizations, and beginningless conceptualization."
Discourse based on the characteristics of verbal expression arises from attachment to the forms of one’s own false imaginings;

discourse like that of a dream arises from recollecting objects previously experienced; discourse arising from the absence of intrinsic nature in objects perceived after waking arises from the attachment to past false imaginings;
and discourse based on beginningless false imagination arises from recollecting the actions performed by former enemies.

Arising from the habitual tendencies of one's own seeds due to the faults of beginningless false fabrication and attachment—this is called the fourfold characteristic of conceptualization through verbal expression.
That which is the natural state of dharmas is perfected through the Way; that which is indicated by verbal expression is deficient in its principle.
Thus, do the sages have any intentional purpose in speech? It is because sentient beings are deluded and do not know the Way that they are compelled to speak.
Therefore, speech may serve as a means to manifest the meaning, but one should not become stuck in the teaching while forgetting the principle.
Unfortunately, ordinary people cling to these words and give rise to frivolous arguments, which conversely obscure the Way.

This is why the sages are especially cautious regarding speech. Mahāmati, because there was previously this statement that "speech is merely conventional expression," speech constitutes the characteristic of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

It is for this reason that this sutra speaks of "names, characteristics, and conceptual construction" to reveal the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-citta*); thus it is called the *Vikalpalakṣaṇacittasūtra*.
Mahāmati, having already used speech to express his intent, [he now asks: (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
When one explains the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is meaning in the speech and what is spoken, and there is a purpose;

if one can skillfully penetrate this, one may attain the Buddha-way and purify the defilements of all sentient beings. Thus, while it is conceptualization (*vikalpa*) in its verbal expression, it is no longer mere conceptualization.
If it were merely conceptualization, it would be insufficient to demonstrate the ultimate truth, yet by means of it, one does so.

Regarding the statement that "the title of this scripture is not heterodox," as for those points where its progression and regression are questionable, the answer first distinguishes their characteristics:

it states that discursive conceptualization (*prapañca*) is not the Way, whereas speaking of the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the Way. If one is skillful in the underlying meaning, one will not be far from the Way;
thus, it may also purify the deluded thoughts of sentient beings. However, if one clings to the speaker [as being real], [it is not so].
Thus, one loses what has been taught; even when the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is spoken, the mind is not truly real.

Herein, the characteristics of conceptualization through verbal expression (*abhilāpa-vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*) are first clarified, consisting of four types of characteristics. As for "verbal expression," it arises from attachment to the forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) of one's own conceptualizations.
It is like the subsequent production of sound based on the conjunction of seven factors, and because of this, there is the characteristic of verbal expression.
Next, regarding "dream speech," this refers to recollecting previously experienced objects and subsequently manifesting them within a dream;
because there is speech, yet upon waking no real object can be found, it is said that it arises from the absence of intrinsic nature in the objects perceived after waking.
It is also identical to the time before dreaming. One should know that appearances are like dreams and dreams are like waking; thus, all are [equal].
Regarding the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the latter two types of verbal expression are as follows:

first, that which arises from the karmic actions performed by former enemies—namely, when a person who was previously hostile inflicts harm upon another and harbors it within their heart, only to suddenly give vent to words of resentment at a later time;
second, that which arises from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of one's own seeds since beginningless time—namely, the ordinary, mundane verbal karma of the present. And...
The reason these four are specifically singled out is that they sufficiently encompass the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*):

namely, the first two belong to the neutral nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*), the latter two belong to the evil nature (*akuśala-svabhāva*), and when combined with the preceding [terms] which express wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*), the three natures are fully represented. (1)
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again requested the World-Honored One on this matter, saying:

"I pray that the World-Honored One will further explain the realm manifested by the conceptualization of speech. Where, for what reason, in what manner, and by what cause does the conceptualization and speech of sentient beings arise?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It arises from the conjunction of the head, chest, throat, nose, lips, tongue, palate, and teeth."
Mahāmati uttered these words: "World-Honored One, are verbal expression and conceptual construction different or not different?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Verbal expression and conceptual construction are neither different nor not different. Why is this? It is because they arise from the same causal characteristics.
Mahāmati, if verbal expression were different from conceptual construction, then conceptual construction would not be its cause; if they were not different," [the text continues].
"Because speech does not manifest the ultimate meaning, yet it does manifest it; therefore, it is neither different nor not different. Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, is speech itself the ultimate truth (paramārtha), or is that which is expressed by speech the ultimate truth?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Neither is speech the ultimate truth, nor is that which is expressed by speech the ultimate truth."
Why is this so? That which is called the "ultimate truth" (paramārtha) is that which is entered through the noble discourse of bliss; it is not discourse itself that is the ultimate truth.
The ultimate truth is that which is attained through the self-realization of noble wisdom; it is not the realm of realization through the conceptualization of discourse.
Therefore, the conceptualization of discourse does not manifest the ultimate truth, for discourse is characterized by arising and ceasing, and is in flux.
If it arises through successive causal conditions, then it does not manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), Mahāmati,

because the self-nature and other-nature of phenomena are non-existent. Since the characteristics of verbal expression do not manifest the ultimate truth, furthermore, Mahāmati, because one enters into the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind,
the various characteristics of external existence and non-existence are merely the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of verbal expression.
Because it reveals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), Mahāmati, you should abandon all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding verbal expressions.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
All natures are without intrinsic nature and likewise beyond verbal expression; this profound meaning of emptiness within emptiness cannot be fully understood by the foolish.

That all natures, their own-nature, and the dharma of verbal expression are like shadows—this is the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) taught by me, for the sake of the sons of the noble ones who possess self-realized wisdom.
Next, he requests an explanation of the objects manifested by verbal expression—that is, the objects consisting of the principles of good and evil matters as they are spoken of.

Having already heard the explanation of good and evil within the four kinds of verbal expressions as clarified above, he further requests an explanation of the objects of *vikalpa* (conceptual construction) and the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth) based on this same principle. In total, there are four questions; what are they?
Regarding the first answer concerning "where," it means that sound arises from the conjunction of the wind of the breath with seven locations, such as the head;
since it arises dependent upon various conditions, sound is illusory. Because there is a second question asking whether [sound] is different or not different from its cause, the answer states:
"Because it has the characteristic of arising from those causes, it is itself that very conceptual construction."

Because the characteristic of verbal expression arises from causes, it is neither different nor not-different [from them]. If it were different, then conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would not be the cause;
if it were not different, then verbal expression would not be a characteristic, being merely the speech-activity of conceptual construction and unable to manifest meaning.
Since it nevertheless possesses the characteristic of manifestation, it is not the same as conceptual construction. If reality cannot be sought through identity or difference, then—
Since that which is neither different nor non-different approximates the truth, he again poses a third question. The Buddha replies:
"Both the speaker and the spoken are not the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Even if one speaks of principle, it is not the subtle state of self-attainment;
thus, it may appear to be so but is actually false. Only that which is entered through the speech of the noble bliss of self-realization is called the ultimate meaning."
The "meaning" (*artha*) of the noble joy is the sphere of realization for noble wisdom; it is entered through verbal expression, yet once entered, it is no longer verbal expression.
Therefore, because it is not a sphere of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), verbal expression does not reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
To directly explain the question regarding the cause [of this], there are three points stated: first, that verbal expression arises from birth.
First, because the cessation of fluctuation and the chain of dependent origination is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Second, because self and other lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is merely verbal discourse and inquiry; thus, self and other are mere appearances and are not the true nature.

Third, because one enters according to the measure of what is manifested within one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*); that is to say, whatever is spoken does not transcend the measure of what is manifested within one's own mind.
If one analyzes the nature of self-nature as being non-existent, then external nature is likewise non-existent; thus, neither is sufficient to manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
However, when speaking from the perspective of the direct cognition of what is manifested by one's own mind, all phenomena are established in their own nature.
How could there be such a thing as "external nature" or "non-nature"? This is merely a provisional teaching given in opposition to delusion; in reality, it is all but one’s own mind.
Beyond this, all natures whatsoever are non-natures; because it is correctly stated that no external nature can be found, it is said that "external natures are non-natures.

Hereafter, all cases shall follow this precedent. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, "Apart from the true mark (*dharmatā*), everything else is the work of Māra," and as the Tiantai school says, "to use principle to exclude emotion"—the essential meaning of these is quite similar. Thus, if speech is...

If it is asked: "Should not the mind of ultimate reality (paramārtha-citta) be entirely omitted from the discussion of mere conceptual construction (vikalpa)? The answer is: The mind as it has been described is not without its underlying principle;

however, because it is the bliss of the noble ones' self-realization (pratyātma-ārya-sukha), it transcends verbal expression. Furthermore, if one follows what has been said according to the characteristics of verbal expression, that is not the case.

If one realizes that the nature of verbal expression is itself detached [from duality], that is precisely the ultimate reality (paramārtha). How, then, could there be anything wrong with it? Therefore, [it is not excluded].

It is said: because one must depart from the characteristics of all conceptual proliferations (*vikalpa*) of verbal expression, one knows that by merely departing from conceptual proliferation, verbal expression perishes of its own accord;

it is because the essence itself is devoid of [intrinsic nature] that there is nothing else [to exist]. The first four lines of the verse correctly state that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
thus, verbal expression is not verbal expression, which is precisely the point where nature perishes. This is the ultimate truth of the principle of absolute emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
It is said: "The meaning of the profound *śūnyatā-śūnyatā* (emptiness of emptiness) is the reverse of the preceding long prose section; it also serves to clarify the subsequent meaning.
As for the latter four lines, they mean that if all phenomena possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then verbal expression would likewise not be like a shadow that lacks a physical form.

It does not manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for the ultimate truth is that which is attained solely by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*); therefore, it is called 'self-realization' (*pratyātma-vedya*)."
"The sons of the noble ones and others correspond to the preceding passage" (2). ○ The above is Chapter Four.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us that which is free from all external paths—whether it be identity or difference, both or neither, existence or non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence or impermanence."
The practice of the noble wisdom of self-realization, which transcends the imagined nature of individual and common characteristics, enters into the meaning of the supreme reality.

It is the characteristic of progressive purification through the continuous succession of the stages (*bhūmi*), advancing ever higher; it is the characteristic of entering the stage of the Tathāgata, which is uncreated and like the manifestation of one’s original vows, resembling the infinite manifestations within the realm of the *māyā-vaśitā* (power over illusion).

"The severance of the path of language and the cessation of mental activity is the realm personally attained by the sages, as well as the field of realization for those in training.
As has been clarified above, how could it be that the path of language is severed while mental activity is not likewise ceased?

It is simply because Mahāmati wishes to investigate its meaning that he again requests an exposition of the method of transcending the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*); first, [the text] sets forth this transcendence."
Regarding the fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) concerning existence and non-existence, the establishment of the fundamental [principle] is the starting point.

Alternatively, based on the remainder of the "original non-existence," the commentator provides an explanation by means of three sets of fourfold propositions: namely, identity and difference (the fourfold proposition of identity and difference);

existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence (the fourfold proposition of existence and non-existence); and permanence and impermanence (the fourfold proposition of permanence and so forth). These are presented in successive order with gradual abbreviation, so as not to burden the text with excessive detail. This is it.
The various fourfold propositions (*catuskoṭi*) each have their own tenets; these are omitted here for brevity (*etc.*).

Next, within the formal request, the initial petition concerns the method of the Bodhisattva’s own practice on the causal ground, free from [extreme] propositions, which states: "That which is not practiced by any non-Buddhists," and so forth.

This is because non-Buddhists are precisely stuck in views; even when they reach the ultimate state of ineffability, they do not transcend views. Therefore, to be free from views—[the text continues as follows:]
That which is not the domain of others, but the domain of the noble wisdom of self-realization alone, transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations.
By acting through non-action, one enters the ultimate realm of the sages. Although this is the cause for oneself, it also leads to the fruit.

Regarding the statement that one is "separated from the self-characteristics and common characteristics of false conceptualization," it is because one has transcended the four propositions that one does not perceive the existence of self- or common characteristics.
When one attains this, all [phenomena] are transcended, and one subsequently enters the ground of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
One traverses the various stages until reaching the supreme, progressive marks of purity;

this is what is meant in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* by "purity that surpasses the practices of all bodhisattvas. Next, I shall request the four aspects of transforming others from the ground of fruition.
When teaching the Dharma, it is said that one enters the stage of the Tathāgata by conforming to its characteristics.

While for oneself one has already entered the self-realized, wondrous detachment through a single gate, one further uses the power of original vows to speak where there is no speaking to awaken sentient beings.

As for the meaning of "no [speaking]," it is as previously explained: while one’s own practice is already free from the four attachments, there is no hindrance to the four [attachments] when transforming others.
It is said that, although the four propositions are one and the same, they are grasped as four views; thus, they enter as four gates. The Dharma has no orientation or aversion;
it is people themselves who are enlightened or deluded. Therefore, it is compared to the various colors manifested by a mani jewel: there is nothing that is not fully revealed.
The "limitless marks" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "practices" (*caryā*) and so forth are the phenomena being illustrated. "Marks" refers to the marks of the stages (*bhūmi-lakṣaṇa*), and "practices" refers to...
That is to say, although the practices one cultivates are boundless, they all manifest from one’s own mind.

To enter into the characteristics of those respective categories means that all phenomena—ranging from existence to neither-existence-nor-non-existence—are each comprised of specific classes and limitations;
may he explain all such dharmas. Within the triple request, there is also a dual summary of the dharmas of oneself and others, as stated in the text.

[Cloud] (1). The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! That you are able to ask me about such a meaning will bring great peace and happiness, and will be of great benefit and advantage, out of compassion for all devas, humans, and worldlings.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall analyze and explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!

We shall surely receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Ignorant ordinary beings, not knowing the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*), grasp at internal and external natures based on [the concepts of] identity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence and impermanence, and inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)."
Due to attachment to false conceptualization, it is like a herd of deer driven by thirst who, seeing a mirage in the springtime, perceive it as water;

deluded and frantic, they rush toward it, unaware that it is not water. In this same way, foolish people, conditioned by false conceptualizations from beginningless time, have their minds scorched by the three poisons;
delighting in the realm of forms, they see arising, abiding, and ceasing, and grasping at internal and external natures, they fall into [the cycle of existence].
The perceptions of oneness, difference, both, neither, existence, non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence, and impermanence are all comprised within false views.
Just as a city of the Gandharvas appears to the ignorant and witless who conceive the notion of a city due to beginningless habitual tendencies,
yet that city neither exists nor does not exist— so too do the outsiders, based on their attachment to the deceptive habitual tendencies of beginningless time, manifest such appearances.
One cannot comprehend that which is characterized by identity, difference, both, or neither; existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence;

nor permanence or impermanence—these are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind, like a person who dreams of men, women, elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, cities, gardens, mountains, rivers, and bathing pools, all variously adorned, and enters into them, yet upon waking remembers them. O Mahāmati, what do you think? Is this real?
"How is it that such a person, not relinquishing the recollection of what was previously dreamed, is considered wise but not of great wisdom?
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "In this way, ordinary people are devoured by evil views;

the wisdom of the outsiders does not know that things are like dreams, being the manifestation of one's own mind, nor do they rely on [the categories of] identity, difference, both, neither, existence, or non-existence."
Neither existent nor non-existent, neither eternal nor non-eternal; it is like a painted image that is neither high nor low, yet foolish commoners conceive of it as being high or low.

In this way, those future followers of external paths, filled with the habitual tendencies of evil views, rely on views of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, or impermanence; thus they destroy themselves and others, while remaining apart from the truth that is free from existence.
The proponents of non-arising also say that there is no [arising], which is a slander against cause and effect; it uproots the roots of goodness and destroys the pure causes.

Those who seek excellence should distance themselves from such talk. Having fallen into the false imaginings of existence and non-existence regarding both self and other, they fall into the extremes of superimposition and denial.
Due to these evil views, they shall fall into hell, just like those with cataracts in their eyes.

Seeing what appears to be hanging hair, he says to the multitude: "You all observe this; yet this hanging hair is ultimately neither an existent nature nor a non-existent nature, because it is neither seen nor not seen.

In this way, those of external paths, based on false views and expectations regarding identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence, as well as the views of permanence and annihilation, slander the True Dharma, thereby sinking themselves and leading others to sink as well.
It is like a fire-wheel: it is not a wheel, yet the foolish perceive it as a wheel, while the wise do not.
In this same way, the evil views and aspirations of the outsiders—based on notions of identity, difference, both, or neither; existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence;

and permanence or impermanence—regard all natures as arising. It is like a bubble of water that resembles a mani-jewel; the ignorant and small-minded, lacking wisdom, perceive it as a mani-jewel and fixate upon it.
Just as one pursues a water bubble, thinking it might be a mani jewel, yet it is neither a mani nor not a mani because it is neither grasped nor not grasped;

so too, those of external paths, perfumed by the habitual tendencies of false discrimination and evil views, speak of birth where there is nothing to be born, and speak of cessation where there is a causal condition for existence.

In the initial general explanation within the response, it says: "Foolish ordinary beings who do not know the measure of the mind" refers to those ordinary beings who, due to two reasons, conceive of the fourfold views (*catuskoṭi*).

First, because they do not understand that all phenomena are manifestations of their own minds—equal to space and pervasive throughout the *dharmadhātu*, such that there is no phenomenon that is not of the nature of mind—they confine their own minds to the aggregates (*skandha*) and the physical body.

Because there is an internal [self], one perceives external phenomena; therein, one grasps at the nature of the internal and external. Based on their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), one gives rise to the view of identity;
based on their distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), one gives rise to the view of difference; and based on both together, one gives rise to the view of simultaneity.

Apart from these three, one gives rise to the view of non-simultaneity. This applies analogously to impermanence and so forth (and so on). By means of this causal perception, attachment is established.
Because one clings to the arguments of established doctrines and causal theories, there arise right and wrong; because of this right and wrong, there arise likes and dislikes.
Once likes and dislikes have formed, the afflictions of craving and views arise, and thus birth and death become endless. This is fundamentally due to this; how can one not investigate its origin?

Regarding these two—the nature-in-itself (*svabhāva*) and the habitual cause (*vāsanā-hetu*): if it were only the former sense, then the failure to know the measure of the mind would be identical [to the latter]; how could there be any difference?

Regarding these various attachments, they all arise because of past habitual causes; thus, if one calculates existence from beginning to end, one calculates existence, and if one calculates non-existence from beginning to end, one calculates non-existence.
Both "both" and "neither" are nothing other than what has been perfumed by former habits;

otherwise, ordinary worldlings who are merely indolent would not necessarily give rise to such views, nor would they be the first among the heterodox. Next follows a separate illustrative explanation consisting of twelve metaphors.
Each has its own dharma, analogy, and synthesis; the significance of employing these analogies is not without points of similarity and difference.
Whether a dharma is applicable or not is to be understood according to the text. The phrase "like a herd of deer" refers to the analogy. The phrase "thus, the foolish person" refers to the dharma.
What is called "perfumed by false conceptualization" (vikalpa) refers to the meaning of the habitual cause of self-nature (*svabhāva-vāsanā*). The three poisons burn the mind.
The preceding passage constitutes the analogy; taking up the equality of internal and external natures correctly corresponds to the arising of views.

The brief statement does not correspond to the initial meaning, but the subsequent text should be understood accordingly. Within the analogy of the city of Gandhāra, it is said that "that city neither exists nor does not exist":

the ignorant view it as existing, yet in reality it is fundamentally non-existent. When both aspects are taken together, they signify that it is neither [existent nor non-existent]; those who cannot comprehend this are called ignorant.

The phrase "the objective realm of one's own mind" combines the first two meanings. Within the analogy of the dream, the addition of "not abandoning recollection" implies that it is not [mere] wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, it is said: "If one does not know that the nature of one's own mind appearing as a dream is such, then one knows the nature of the dream is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent.

In the analogy of the painted image, the statement regarding other proponents of the doctrine of non-arising who are free from existence and non-existence refers to the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).
Furthermore, because they will align with their own views, they also claim that there is no superior seeking; that is, those who seek the supreme Dharma should abandon such evil views.
It is said that this falls into the views of self, other, or both, and the text states that it "falls into establishment and denial.
This means that those with the view of existence follow by establishing [existence], while those with the view of non-existence follow by denying it. Furthermore—

Regarding the statement that one falls into evil through the view of causes, it is said so as to instill fear in them. In the analogy of the hanging hair, it says "neither existent by nature nor non-existent by nature" because of seeing and not seeing;
this means that because it is seen, it is not non-existent by nature, and because it is not seen, it is not existent by nature.
Other passages may be understood by analogy. In the analogy of the water bubble, the statement "to speak of arising within what does not exist" is seen in the text.

In this context, although other metaphors are indeed applicable, there is none that better expresses the refutation of asserting existence where there is no existence, nor the refutation of claiming annihilation regarding that which exists through causes and conditions;
for such views are all the inverted perspectives of the non-Buddhists (2).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three kinds of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*). Having established these respectively, one attains the self-realized noble wisdom (*āryajñāna-svasaṃvedana*), which is free from the two natures (*svabhāva*).
Yet, one still clings to the false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of existence regarding phenomena.

Mahāmati, when the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*) undergo transformation, and the manifestations of one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśya*)—including the grasped and the grasper—are severed, all false conceptualizations cease, and one reaches the stage of the Tathāgata, the self-realized noble wisdom.
The practitioner does not conceive of those [objects] as having the nature of existence or non-existence.

If, however, a practitioner gives rise to the perception of grasping at the characteristics of existence or non-existence within such a realm, Mahāmati, that person is grasping at nourishment and grasping at a self and a person.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one speaks of their intrinsic nature, self-nature, or specific and general characteristics, all of these are spoken by the *nirmāṇa-buddha* (transformation buddha) and are not spoken by the *dharma-buddha*.
Furthermore, all verbal expressions arise from the expectations and views of the ignorant;
they do not establish the self-nature of the dharmas that lead to the dwelling in the bliss of the samādhi of noble wisdom’s self-realization.
For example, when the reflection of a tree appears in water, it is neither a reflection nor a non-reflection, neither the shape of a tree nor a non-tree shape; such is the case with the outsiders.

Those who perceive through the habitual熏 (vāsanā) of false conceptualization and attachment—relying on notions of identity, difference, both, or neither; existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence;
permanence, or impermanence—are unable to know that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds.

It is like a bright mirror which, according to conditions, reflects all forms and images without false conceptualization; those images are neither images nor non-images, yet one perceives them as images and non-images.
Foolish people with false imaginings form conceptions of images;

likewise, the evil views of the non-Buddhists are the manifestation of images within their own minds, which they falsely imagine and cling to based on notions of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, or impermanence.
For example, when wind and water meet, sound is produced; that sound is neither a substantial nature nor a lack of nature. Such is the delusion of the evil views of the non-Buddhists.
Perceptions based on identity, difference, both, or neither; existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence;

and views of permanence or impermanence—these are like a great earth where there is no grass or wood, or like a mirage with flowing streams and surging waves of clouds. They are neither of the nature [of reality] nor not of the nature [of reality], because of the presence of greed and the absence of greed.
Thus, foolish people, perfumed by the habitual tendencies of beginningless falsehood, engage in false conceptualization and attachment.

Based on the gates of arising, abiding, and ceasing; unity and difference; conjunction and non-conjunction; existence and non-existence; neither existence nor non-existence; permanence and impermanence;
and the self-abiding nature of things, it is likewise like a mirage or a wave.

For example, it is like a person using incantations or mechanical devices to cause a *piśāca* spirit—which is not a sentient being—to move and act through skillful means; this is merely the deluded imagination of the foolish and ignorant.

Mahāmati, such externalists, clinging to false views and hopes based on the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of oneness and otherness, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, and the views of permanence and annihilation, establish what is unreal through their attachments.

Therefore, one who wishes to attain the reality of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) must abandon birth, abiding, and cessation; oneness and otherness; bothness and not-bothness; and existence and non-existence.
It is not a false conceptualization of evil views such as existence, non-existence, permanence, or impermanence.

Regarding this analogy, it generally refutes those who give rise to views—whether mundane or heterodox—in three ways: first, they deviate from entering the Path; second, they fall into the view of self (*ātman*);

and third, they equate [the truth] with provisional teachings. Therefore, it is said: "There are three kinds of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*). (The definitions and characteristics of the three cognitions and the five members)
As explained elsewhere), this is a preliminary exposition of the tenets of the treatise.

Although each [system] establishes its own position, when one attains the realization of the path, one acquires the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) which is free from the two kinds of self-nature and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Yet, those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to false conceptualizations regarding the existence of a self-nature;
thus, they deviate from the single principle of entering the Path. This also serves as an appropriate explanation to resolve their latent doubts (and so forth). It further states:

Regarding the transformation of mind, intellect, consciousness, body, and phenomena: this "transformation" refers to awakening from one's own delusion and realizing that all dharmas are manifestations of one’s own mind.
Thus, the various false imaginings of the grasped and the grasper—the sense organs and their objects—are severed.
This is the practice of those who rely on the stage of the Tathāgata; they never give rise to notions of existence or non-existence regarding those objective realms. Furthermore, if...

Secondly, if one differentiates within such objects by grasping at existence and non-existence, or at the arising of being and non-being, this constitutes attachment and nourishment of the notions of "self" and "person.
Though one may claim to be practicing, if the notions of self and person are not eliminated, they will all result in views and craving;
thus, one falls into the view of self. Furthermore, it is said: "If one speaks of that nature, intrinsic nature, or the specific and general characteristics..."

This means that if one were to say merely that those various phenomena possess an intrinsic nature with its own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common-characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), such statements as these are all spoken by the *nirmāṇabuddha* (emanation Buddha).
Furthermore, the claim that all verbal expressions arise from the ignorant and so forth implies that speech exists because of grasping and attachment;
this is not the case here, for this sutra establishes that it clarifies how all phenomena ultimately converge within one's own mind.
For those who have attained the dwelling in the bliss of the samādhi of self-awakened noble wisdom, the true analytical exposition is identical to the provisional teaching in three ways.
Generally, whenever heterodox and false views are refuted, they are examined by means of these three teachings, from which there is no escape for their errors.
In the analogy of the mirage, it is said that views arise based on arising, abiding, and ceasing; furthermore, it is said that conditions abide in themselves.

Regarding the "gate of phenomena" (*vastu-mukha*), speaking of it in the present context, it does not, in its entirety, transcend the objects of arising, abiding, and ceasing—whether internal or external, self or other—upon which views are based, such as that [illusory] mirage.
However, because the textual expressions are abbreviated, the first passage mentions only arising, abiding, and ceasing without stating that these are objects of another;
the subsequent passage mentions only the gate of one's own abiding phenomena (*sva-vastu-mukha*).
Yet, it does not speak of arising and ceasing as mutually manifest; such discourse merely pertains to the gate of the phenomena of arising and ceasing within the self and the other.
According to the Tang translation, it says: "Within the gate of the dharma-nature realized by the noble wisdom itself, one perceives arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Although this was produced by the translators, there may be points that are not yet certain; those [translators] merely saw the words "self-abiding" (*svayam-sthiti*) in the Sanskrit manuscript and lost sight of the [correct meaning].
Having investigated this thoroughly, I have found that even the self-realized dharma of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) cannot be expressed in words;

how, then, could it be possible for ordinary people or outsiders (*bāhya*) to give rise to views through conceptualization? This is an extreme impossibility, and therefore I have set it forth briefly.
For this reason, I shall conclude with an exhortation: who among men does not desire to attain the noble wisdom of self-awakening and thereby abandon evil views and delusions?
Alas! The affliction lies in not being self-illuminating; thus, external objects, mental states, and habitual tendencies are able to obscure it.
Having already explained how that which obscures and that which is obscured are thus, there remains the further affliction of not being able to separate from them.
If one were to know this and separate from it, what would hinder the attainment of so-called "self-realized noble wisdom"? There is no greater essential point for exhortation than this.

Regarding this, although according to the text one ought to further respond to the requests of the four aforementioned propositions, the reason they are not discussed is due to three general considerations.

First, these four propositions concern the transformation of others (*parārtha*) at the level of fruition, rather than being the essential points of what is known during the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*). Second, if one’s own practice (*svārtha*) is free from conceptual phrases and transcends emotional attachments, then the four propositions for transforming others will be attained spontaneously.

Third, [the text] intends to clarify that the ultimate meaning of the Dharma is beyond words and cannot be fully expressed through speech. Thus, it is for these reasons that they are not explicitly stated.
Second, furthermore, speaking in terms of the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the four explanations do not go beyond the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*);

yet, if one clings to them, the four views become rigid, while if one enters through them, the four gates open wide. Thus, by turning what is contrary into what is compliant and reversing delusion into awakening, the explanation is contained therein. Third. (3)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Like an illusion, a dream, a reflection in water, the shadow of trees, a mass of hair, a mirage in the heat—thus one should contemplate the three realms of existence (*trisaṃsāra*) to ultimately attain liberation.
Just as a deer’s thirst causes deluded and wandering thoughts, and the deer perceives it as water though in reality there is no substance of water."
In this way, when the seeds of consciousness move and encounter objects, the deluded ordinary person gives rise to false conceptualization.

Just as one who is afflicted by cataracts perceives what is not there, they cling to and grasp at the nature of things within beginningless birth and death. By using a wedge to extract a wedge, one abandons the grasping of desire;
by contemplating things as being like illusions, spells, mechanical devices, floating clouds, dreams, or flashes of lightning, one attains liberation and forever severs the three continuities.
In that state, there is no agent; it is like a mirage or space. To know all phenomena in this way is to have nothing further to know.
Teachings are merely provisional names, and they too lack any intrinsic characteristic.

Within that state, one gives rise to deluded conceptions regarding the aggregates and formations, which appear like falling hairs, like painted falling hairs, like illusions, dreams, gandharva cities, fire-wheels, or the shimmering heat-mirages—appearing to sentient beings though they do not exist.

The same applies to permanence and impermanence, identity and difference, bothness and neitherness. Since beginningless time, the continuity of faults has led the deluded and ignorant to produce false conceptualizations.
Just as various colors appear within a bright mirror, water, a clear eye, or a wondrous *maṇi* jewel, yet in reality nothing exists there;
so too do all natures manifest. They appear like a mirage in the heat of the day, with various colors appearing, yet they are non-existent, like a dream.
The verse states: "Like illusions, dreams, water, and tree-reflecting shadows," etc. This stanza summarizes the preceding text;

however, because the metaphors are repeated and the textual structures intersect, it is somewhat difficult to clarify. I shall first provide a commentary on this: there are three instances of repetition in the verse.
Specifically, the metaphors of the cataract-afflicted eye seeing falling hairs and the dream appear four times, while the metaphors of the mirage and the illusion appear three times.
The *Marīci* (mirage) and *Bimba* (reflection) appear twice; those with single verses above are four, such as the *Gandharvanagara* (city of the gandharvas) and others;

those missing verses are two, such as *Śabda* (sound) and *Budbuda* (water bubble); those appearing separately are six: like a wedge, like a floating cloud, like lightning, like water, like the pure eye, and like a mani-jewel—none of which exist in the prose (*gadya*).
Next, regarding the sequential commentary: at the beginning of the verse is "dream" (*svapna*).
Since these four similes are all non-juvenile, they are headed by the single character "illusion" (māyā).

However, while the prose version clarifies that ordinary people and outsiders give rise to views, here, using the simile of illusion to contemplate the three realms of existence (tridhātu) serves to mutually corroborate and clarify this point.

It is precisely because one does not penetrate the principle of illusion that the fourfold conceptualization and the four views arise; if these were extinguished, there would be no birth, and that is the principle of illusion.

The fact that this passage is consistent with other sections on dharmas and similes, despite some textual disarray or separate expositions, is precisely because the points being illustrated vary in what they include or exclude;

by examining how they mutually clarify one another, the meaning becomes clear. Thus, the combined explanation of the seeds of consciousness and so forth clarifies the two meanings mentioned above—essential nature (*svabhāva*) and habitual causes (*vāsanā-hetu*).
It is solely because one does not know the measure of the mind (*citta-mātra*) that one perceives objects external to the mind.
The realms (*dhātu*) are like being obscured by a cataract; this refers to beginningless birth and death, which is the meaning of "succession.
The wedge is originally a metaphor for greed; because of greed, there is birth and death. Now, using the teaching of illusion to cause one to abandon it is like "a wedge driving out a wedge.
Regarding the phrase "severing the continuity of the three," according to the subsequent text, these are the three poisons. Within them, there is no agent.
"Like a mirage in empty space" means that by means of the characteristic of a mirage one comes to know all phenomena; thus one knows there is nothing to be known.

This is not called "ignorance," for knowledge is itself ignorance. "Verbal teachings are merely provisional names" means that verbal teachings regarding existence, non-existence, and so forth—the four propositions—are fundamentally only provisional names and possess no real characteristic. It is precisely because of this lack of understanding that delusion arises.
Consider how the aggregates such as formations are like falling hair, or like the illusion of falling hair seen during the day;

in total, seven analogies are employed to clarify that [the aggregates] fundamentally do not exist yet appear to sentient beings. This applies equally to the categories of permanence and impermanence, as can be understood from the preceding verses.
Although the mirror, water, the pure eye, and so forth—collectively serving as metaphors—manifest various forms, they possess no [intrinsic reality].

The statement that "the manifestation of all natures is like the day and so forth," while "the appearance of form is like a dream and thus non-existent," serves to mutually illustrate these two points and concludes the intent of this single section (4).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is free from these four positions: namely, identity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence;

as well as permanence and impermanence. It is free from the extremes of existence and non-existence, and it transcends the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of false views, attachments, and the aggregates.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma takes as its primary focus suchness—neither a substantial nature (*svabhāva*) nor a self (*ātman*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, for the sake of purifying the obscurations of afflictions and cognitive hindrances, I teach the Dharma through a succession that is neither causeless,
nor atomic, nor temporal, nor inherent in nature. Just as a merchant chief establishes one hundred and eight propositions in successive order,
I skillfully differentiate the characteristics of the various vehicles and the various stages.
From here below, the text generally demonstrates that the true teaching transcends the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).

Since the ground is thus, the path of cultivation is thus, and the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is thus realized, the establishment of the teachings to suit the capacities of sentient beings must necessarily correspond to this. Therefore, it is said at the outset:
"When I sat upon the site of enlightenment, I did not obtain a single dharma; it was an empty fist used to deceive small children, a means to entice and deliver all beings."
In the *Dharmapada*, it says at the conclusion: "Arising cannot be spoken of, even down to non-arising and non-non-arising cannot be spoken of.
This sutra, however, says: "Within these two intervals, not a single word has ever been spoken.
It is for this same reason that [the former] can be thus, yet cannot be as that; it is like being free from affirmative propositions while still not being free from negative propositions.
It is further said that because there are causes and conditions, it can also be spoken of; yet, this does not hinder the making of various explanations.

Since both "it can" and "it cannot" are applicable, there is neither being nor non-being. This is first called the inconceivable teaching of no fixed direction, which has already transcended the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).
It is further said that one is free from existence and non-existence, establishing [the truth] while avoiding slander. As for those who slander, they are subsumed under the above.
The fact that all views do not transcend the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism confirms the validity of the previously established foundational doctrine;

this is because they are free from the characteristics of the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*). Thus, such analytical compilation is itself the dependent origination of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

the term "dependent origination" encompasses both suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), and it follows that all Four Noble Truths are ultimately true. Such analytical discernment of the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) is itself liberation.
The Way of liberation and cessation likewise simultaneously reveal that all four truths possess the characteristic of liberation.
Yet, if one speaks of dependent origination without reference to the Truth of Cessation, it is erroneous; if one speaks of liberation without reference to the Path and Cessation, it is delusory.

Taking these Four Truths as the foremost of all teachings on the Dharma, the doctrine of "non-arising" and "separation from nature" is thereby distinguished from and set apart from heterodox schools. Thus...
Because it is not a doctrine based on the nature-imaginations of non-Buddhists, it is said to be "neither nature nor Īśvara," etc. (The meanings of terms such as "nature" are as explained elsewhere).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in order to purify the obstacles of afflictions and cognitive hindrances," this again specifically reveals that this sutra exists for the purpose of purifying the two obstacles;

it also establishes all phrases through the state of detachment and non-arising, reaching the realization of non-existence, just as in the following example: [as in the verse: "Just as a painter... and so forth.
Because the merchant leader is able to show, to guide, and to demonstrate, he establishes the one hundred and eight points of meaning in successive order;
because he is able to guide, he ultimately causes [beings] to reach the ground of non-existence and non-arising.
That he is thoroughly proficient in discerning the various vehicles (*yāna*) and the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*) is due to this principle (5). This concludes the fifth chapter.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are the four? They are:

the dhyāna practiced by foolish worldlings, the dhyāna that examines meanings, the dhyāna that takes suchness as its object, and the Tathāgata-dhyāna. What is the dhyāna practiced by foolish worldlings?

It refers to the practitioners among śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists who contemplate the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), as well as specific and general characteristics, the skeleton, impermanence, suffering, and so forth.
Taking attachment to the signs of impurity as primary, such signs are not seen as distinct from one another, and one proceeds through successive stages without eliminating them;

this is called the "dhyāna practiced by fools. What is the "dhyāna that observes meaning"? It refers to the realization that there is no self of persons (pudgala-nairātmya) regarding both specific and general characteristics, and that externalists' notions of self, other, or both lack inherent nature;
having thus observed the selflessness of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya), one gradually [penetrates] the meaning of the characteristics of those stages.
Advancing in this is called the dhyāna of observing meaning (*arthapravicaya-dhyāna*). What is the dhyāna of taking suchness as its object (*tathatālambana-dhyāna*)?
It refers to the non-arising of false discrimination within the true state of the two kinds of selflessness; this is called the dhyāna of taking suchness as its object. What is the Tathāgata-dhyāna?

It refers to entering the stage of the Tathāgata, attaining the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization, abiding in the three kinds of bliss, and accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
The contemplation of conceptual objects is called the Tathāgata-dhyāna. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The dhyāna practiced by fools, The dhyāna of observing the characteristics of objects, The dhyāna of taking reality as its object, And the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata.
For example, like the forms of the sun and moon, the lotus, the deep abyss, space, and the extinction of fire— when a practitioner contemplates these various signs,
such as the external paths, the common meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), and likewise the realms of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
by abandoning all of them, one enters that which is "without anything at all. Then, in all lands, the Buddhas, with inconceivable hands...
At one time, he stroked [the disciple’s] crown of the head, causing him to enter accordantly into the mark of suchness (*tathatā*).
This principle cannot be harmonized without dhyāna; transformation cannot be accomplished without samādhi.

As for what was said previously—that being free from the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) means the cessation of the sphere of mental activity—this is the principle reached therein. Were it not for the Tathāgata-dhyāna, how could one reach it? Furthermore, it brings about the accomplishment of all...
The manifestation of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable deeds is his transformational power; were it not for the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, how could such things be established?
Therefore, following this, the four kinds of dhyāna are further elucidated. Since the profound cannot be clarified without the shallow, these three types are mentioned together.
As for what is called "the dhyāna practiced by foolish people," this refers to the contemplation of the non-existence of a person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) by the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists.
Regarding their own nature, they are unable to comprehend that all is merely the measure of one’s own mind, and thus fail to know that external natures are non-existent;
because they do not practice according to reality, they are all disparaged as "fools. The meaning of specific and general characteristics is as explained previously.

As for the "chain of bones," this refers to the Hīnayāna practice of fixing the mind on the contemplation of impermanence—the visualization of a skeleton of interconnected white bones—which serves as an antidote to attachment. This contemplation resides in [the realm of] conceptualization.
Initially, as a skillful means, one practices both [the sign and the contemplation] as auxiliary practices; because this is explained from the perspective of the initial stage, it is called "primary.

Regarding the statement that "these signs are not different from the contemplation," this means that when the signs seen within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are not distinct from the contemplation, it is the sign of having perfected the contemplation.

Although there is progressive advancement through successive stages, because the conceptual mind (*saṃjñā-citta*) has not yet been eliminated, this is not yet the contemplative meaning of the higher concentrations (*dhyāna*).

This refers to the "selflessness of persons" (*pudgala-nairātmya*) mentioned above as that which is to be abandoned. Regarding the "self and other" of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), it means that they take what is actually other to be the self.

Once both [Buddhists and non-Buddhists] have realized the nature of the selflessness of persons, [the Buddha] specifically instructs the Bodhisattvas to contemplate the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
By sequentially observing the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*), their realization progressively deepens without regression; this is its defining characteristic.
Furthermore, regarding "clinging to objects through meditation on Suchness" (*tathatā*): in contrast to the above, this refers to the practice of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle].

"Delusive thoughts" (*vikalpa*) refers to the aforementioned two types of grasping at phenomena and persons by ordinary beings. The "delusive thoughts regarding the two kinds of selflessness" (*nairātmya*) refer to the aforementioned contemplation of the two selflessnesses;

as long as one has not forgotten the objects of focus and remains within the realm of duality and opposition, involving acceptance and rejection, all such states are considered delusive thoughts. Yet, it is precisely these that constitute the bodhisattva’s creation of objective realms.
Because within the midst there is no lack of true reality and nothing exists outside the mind to be observed, it is called "the state of suchness.

Because one does not give rise to deluded thoughts therein, and because even at the point of objective clinging one realizes that there is nothing other than the single suchness, it is called "clinging to suchness" (*yathābhūta-tathatā*).
As for the Tathāgata-dhyāna, both the object of observation and the deluded thoughts of the observer, as well as the term "suchness," are entirely transcended; it is simply called "entering."
To believe and know with certainty that the sphere of mental activity has ceased within the stages of the Tathāgata, and that there is only the single True Suchness—this is the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
It is what is called the state where recollection, conceptualization, and observation have been eliminated, and the pure mind is eternally uniform.

Only such a venerable and wondrous person can perceive Prajñā; such a one may be said to approximate the Tathāgata-dhyāna. As for the three kinds of joyful abodes, they merely lead toward the state of a Sage.
The three characteristics of wisdom, when spoken of by the Tathāgata, are the Great Samādhi;

because they ultimately accord with the principle of the three truths through the three types of wisdom, they are called the "three kinds of joyful abodes. This is precisely the meaning of what was stated in the preceding text:

"If one accomplishes these three characteristics, one can reach the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization. In the verse, four types of dhyāna are first presented in general, followed by a specific [treatment].
Emerging from the signs of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-nimitta*) to demonstrate gain and loss— such as forms resembling the sun or moon— means that within the concentrated mind,
one may see forms like the sun or moon, or a *padma* lotus, or perhaps the appearance of a deep and treacherous sea, or like empty space,
or like a fire being extinguished until it becomes mere embers. Practitioners who cultivate the path observe these various kinds of signs in this manner.
One should not grasp at what appears; for such grasping leads one to fall into the paths of externalists, which are the tracks of deviant ways, or into the realms of the two vehicles.
All of these arise from failing to settle the mind properly within the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), or because conceptual thought and the mind have not yet been forgotten.
Therefore, all must be relinquished. When not even a single dharma is seen as obtainable, then no objective realm exists. This is [the state].

To accord with and enter into the mark of suchness (tathatā) is precisely what is endorsed by the Buddha regarding the latter two types of dhyāna-marks; thus, he demonstrated this by placing his hand upon [the disciple's] head.

Therefore, one should know that when only a single phenomenon manifests before one, it is not necessarily the true state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:

"If one does not form a conception of holiness (*ārya-adhimukti*), it is called a 'wholesome state' (*kuśala-viṣaya*); if one forms a conception of holiness, one will immediately be possessed by various demons. This is why [the Buddha] showed [the mark].
This may indeed be called the Dharma. [End of] Chapter Six.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what you speak of as 'Parinirvāṇa,' what dharma do you designate as Nirvāṇa?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is all self-nature, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the mind (*manas*), and the mental faculty (*manovijñāna*)."

The transformation of the habitual tendencies of consciousness and views is called *nirvāṇa*. For all Buddhas and for me, the nature of *nirvāṇa* is the sphere of reality (*dharmadhātu*) which is empty of intrinsic being.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, *nirvāṇa* is the sphere of the self-realization of noble wisdom; it is free from the false imaginings of annihilation and permanence, and is neither existence nor non-existence. Why is it not permanent?

Because the false imaginings regarding specific and general characteristics have been severed, it is not permanent. Why is it not... [annihilated]? Because... [the continuity of the stream of consciousness remains].
"Severance" refers to the fact that all noble ones—past, future, and present—attain self-awakening; it is not a severance, Mahāmati. Nirvāṇa is neither destroyed nor does it die.
If nirvāṇa were subject to death, one would have to undergo rebirth and continuity once again.

If it were subject to destruction, it would fall into the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, nirvāṇa is free from destruction and free from death; thus, it is the refuge for practitioners. Furthermore..."
Furthermore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is neither abandonment nor attainment, neither annihilation nor permanence, neither a single meaning nor manifold meanings;

this is called nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is the realization of their own specific characteristics and common characteristics, the non-frequenting of objective spheres, and the absence of inverted views and the non-arising of false conceptualization; they regard that state as nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, what are the two characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*)? What are the two? They are:

attachment to the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-abhiniveśa*), and attachment to the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-abhiniveśa*).

Attachment to the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of verbal expression arises from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless false speech. Attachment to the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of things arises from the failure to realize that [the world] is one's own mind.

The manifestation of the limit arises. There are three kinds of *nirvāṇa*: first, the *nirvāṇa* falsely imagined by non-Buddhists; second, the *nirvāṇa* realized and attained by those of the two vehicles;
and third, the ultimate *nirvāṇa* in which the Tathāgata dwells in peace. Although these three share the same name, they differ greatly in reality. If one does not...
If one rectifies the names according to the Dharma, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata might become confused with the empty delusions of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles;
how could this not be distinguished? Therefore, Mahāmati asks in order to examine the reality of the matter.

In the response, [the Buddha] first demonstrates the self-nature of ultimate nirvāṇa, stating that the transformation of all self-natures and habitual tendencies constitutes the form-dharmas of the nine realms.

The transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), the mental faculty (*manas*), and the perceiving consciousnesses (*vijñapti*) refers to the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors.

What, indeed, is not encompassed by the term "all"? Nevertheless, because they all arise from being permeated (*vāsita*) by beginningless false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), they are collectively termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).

When these two types of transformation reach the state where no further transformation occurs, this is precisely the *nirvāṇa* attained by the Tathāgata; therein, from the very beginning, there has never been a single dharma.
All phenomena converge within it; though they are fully endowed with manifold wonders, they all return to the signless (*animitta*).
Therefore, it is called the "realm of empty affairs. What is meant by "empty affairs" is that all phenomena are characterized by quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*).
Since they are said to be quiescently extinguished, they are fundamentally without arising; even all sentient beings are, in their very nature, the mark of *nirvāṇa*.
What transformation could there be? It is precisely because transformation reaches its ultimate limit that it converges with fundamental quiescence;
when these two are non-dual, one may call this "perfect consummation," which can be apprehended through the mind.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the following passage demonstrates that Nirvāṇa is free from [extremes], meaning that the realm of the self-awakened noble wisdom is free from such things as annihilationism and eternalism. The sūtra itself explains its meaning as follows:

Regarding the statement that because one attains self-awakening it is not "annihilation" (*uccheda*): this means that the nature of awakening attained is not subject to transition across the three periods of time, and thus it is not annihilation or abandonment.
As for those who claim it is either annihilation or destruction, I now say they have misunderstood; rather, one should correctly say it is "abandonment.
Furthermore, the statement that it is neither annihilated nor eternal, neither a single meaning nor manifold meanings, serves as a general conclusion.
The superior meaning states that by negating [the extremes of] annihilation and permanence, as well as identity and difference, the ultimate and profound mystery of *nirvāṇa* is further revealed;

yet, it is simply by negating what is incorrect that the principle of *nirvāṇa* is attained. Regarding the statement that the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles involves awakening to self-characteristics and common characteristics:

it is precisely because they have awakened to the emptiness of self-characteristics and common characteristics—that is, their lack of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—that they are called those who see without inversion. This refers to the voice [of the Buddha].
"One who hears [the teachings] but does not give rise to false conceptualization because they do not associate with or approach sense objects is a Pratyekabuddha.
This statement in the text means that because they form conceptualizations regarding the state of non-arising, they differ from ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

It should be understood that this merely distinguishes them from the externalist calculations of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); as with the subsequent distinction, this is stated briefly here. Following this, it speaks of the "two natures" (*svabhāva*).
Regarding the aforementioned "all intrinsic natures," if one observes their origin: all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) possess both names and reality.
