Names arise from the false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of verbal expression; reality arises from the deluded manifestation of the boundaries of one's own mind.
Since both are merely false habits, knowing them to be the transformation of the nine realms of existence is itself *nirvāṇa*.
This can be understood from the preceding discussion. ○ If it is the seventh chapter:
*The General Meaning of the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Fascicle Two;
*The General Meaning of the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
The First Chapter of the *Sarvabuddhahṛdaya*, Part Two (Continued).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata establishes Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas through two kinds of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-bala*) so that they may prostrate before the Buddhas and listen to and inquire about the meaning of the Dharma.
What are these two kinds of supernormal powers by which they are established? They are: first, the meditative absorption of samādhi (*samādhi-samāpatti*); and...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having attained the first bodhisattva stage through the Buddha’s spiritual power—
namely, by entering the bodhisattva Great Vehicle Illumination Samādhi— and having entered this samādhi, all Buddhas of the worlds of the ten directions,
through their supernormal powers, manifest for him: the spiritual power of manifesting all bodies, faces, and speech, as well as the spiritual power of hand-consecration.
The speech from all their bodies and faces is like that of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have likewise accomplished such marks and virtues;
O Mahāmati, this is called the first Bodhisattva stage,
wherein the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains the samādhi and supernormal powers of a Bodhisattva, having accumulated roots of goodness over hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Having accomplished the successive stages, he thoroughly penetrates the antidotes and their opposing factors until reaching the ultimate stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
There, dwelling in a subtle and wondrous palace of great lotuses, he sits upon a great lotus jewel lion-throne,
surrounded by a retinue of similar Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, his body adorned with various precious necklaces like golden *campaka* flowers.

The radiance of the sun and moon, along with all the most supreme hands, comes from the ten directions and bestows empowerment upon the crown of his head as he sits upon the throne of the great lotus palace.
It is like the empowerment of the crown prince of a sovereign wheel-turning monarch or of Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Mahāmati, this is called the bodhisattva’s power of hand-empowerment; this is known as the two kinds [of empowerment] of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Regarding spiritual power: if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in two kinds of spiritual power, they behold the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, face-to-face;

if it were otherwise, they would not be able to see them. Furthermore, Mahāmati, all the various practices of dharmas—such as samādhis and the bases of psychic power—which are conceptualized by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of these abide entirely within the two kinds of spiritual power of the Tathāgata.

"Mahāmati, if Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas were able to expound and explain by their own power, apart from the Buddha’s spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), then all ordinary worldlings should also be able to speak. Why is this? It is because they do not abide in spiritual power.
Mahāmati, mountains, stones, trees, musical instruments, cities, and palaces all manifest spontaneously through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata upon his entering a city."
The sounds of music issue forth; how much more so for those with minds! Countless beings who are deaf, blind, or mute are all liberated from their immeasurable sufferings.
The Tathāgata possesses such immeasurable supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and Bodhisattvas..."
When the Bodhisattva dwells in samādhi-samāpatti, as well as at the time of the empowerment upon the stage of supreme advancement, the Buddha bestows his supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*) upon him.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "In order to be free from the karmas and afflictions of Māra, so that he does not fall into the dhyānas of the Śrāvaka stage, so that he may attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, and so that he may further advance in the dharmas already attained—for these reasons, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, and [the others]..."
All the Perfectly Awakened Ones establish all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas by means of their supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*).

If they were not established by supernatural power, they would fall into the false views, delusions, and expectations of the various śrāvakas and māras of external paths, and would fail to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For this reason, all the Buddha-Tathāgatas employ their supernatural power.
At that time, when the World-Honored One wished to restate this meaning for the sake of embracing all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he spoke these verses:
"The One Honored Among Men, by his supernormal powers, has completely purified his great vows; through samādhi and empowerment, [he encompasses] the first bhūmi and the ten bhūmis."

The Buddha possesses great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) capable of establishing the conditions for those with karmic potential, while Bodhisattvas possess the power of empowerment through the perfection of their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Thus, if the Buddha did not establish them through his supernormal power, he would be insufficient to manifest his spiritual transformation;
and if the Bodhisattvas did not receive empowerment, they would be insufficient to accomplish their task and advance swiftly toward Bodhi. Therefore, the Buddha...
Because they attain the opportune moment, they are like fish that think of their offspring; because Bodhisattvas respond accordingly, they are like bees that think of the honeycomb.
Such is the way in which they mutually assist and sustain one another.

The preceding chapter clarified that Tathāgata-dhyāna can accomplish inconceivable deeds for sentient beings, yet it did not reveal the specific nature of those deeds that are accomplished. Therefore, this [chapter] follows.
He informed them that the Tathāgata possesses two kinds of spiritual power: the power of samādhi-attainment and the power of hand-consecration;

thus, both reside in the Buddha. Furthermore, it is said that when a bodhisattva abides in the Buddha’s spiritual power, it means that they must rely on the Buddha’s power to achieve the merit of being perceived, while also relying on the bodhisattva’s own samādhi and roots of goodness to effect the response.
Because it reaches the limit, it is called "entering. The Bodhisattva’s Mahāyāna Illumination Samādhi takes "illumination" as its meaning, which refers to the capacity for seeing.
By means of this samādhi, one is able to evoke the bodies, faces, and speech of all Buddhas;

as in the case of Vajragarbha in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, who was empowered [by the Buddha]. Taking one instance as an example for all others, it says "and the rest," and further says "at a hundred..."

The roots of goodness accumulated over a thousand kalpas and the penetration of the characteristics of the antidotes for the various stages, as elucidated in such sections as the "Ten Abodes" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, can further evoke the power of the roots of goodness of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

This means that although the Noble Ones possess the power to bestow their grace upon those who are receptive, it cannot be evoked without the roots of goodness; likewise, bodhisattvas of the same kind are all [governed by] the Dharma.
The Great Being’s body is like that of Maheśvara and others, wherein the matter of repeated empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) is manifested.

If it were not thus, one would be unable to see; this is a general summary and conclusion showing that if one does not internally rely on the power of the roots of goodness from samādhi, but instead externally relies on the Buddha’s spiritual power, then one cannot achieve the manifestation of the signs of realization through the resonance of the single limit (*ekānta*). Whatever... [text ends]... all such things.
The meaning of this subsequent "reversal and further illustration" (*paryudāsa*) is as follows:
whatever dharmas such as samādhis a bodhisattva explains are all due to abiding in the Buddha’s spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*).

Thus, by taking the ordinary person as the case to illustrate the noble one, it is explained in reverse: if a bodhisattva were apart from that spiritual power, they would be unable to accomplish anything at all.
How much more so for ordinary beings? If one attains supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), even insentient things become useful;
how much more so for those with consciousness—how could they not be able to escape suffering? This refers to the meaning that if the Buddha bestows his knowledge, even insects know it;
if the Buddha does not bestow it, even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) do not know it. Yet, [the sūtra] speaks of "all ordinary beings."

Regarding those who do not abide in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), if we speak for the moment according to the principle that the holy supersedes the mundane, there are many sentient beings and the Buddha does not abandon them;
thus it is said, "The Tathāgata possesses such supernatural powers," and so forth.

Generally speaking, supernatural power arises from *samādhi* and *samyaksamāpatti*, which is precisely the Tathāgata’s dhyāna and the Great Quiescent Samādhi (*mahāśānti-samādhi*). It is quiescent yet ever-present.
Illuminating, abiding, functioning, and conforming to the nature—when these are provisionally established in their myriad aspects, there is nothing that is not possible;
yet how could there be any intentional thought within them? Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, asking further about the reason for this empowerment.
The answer does not go beyond these four meanings, as can be known from the detailed explanation. Otherwise, if it were contrary to this, one would perceive loss or gain. [Verse:]
The verse is easily understood. [End of] Chapter Eight.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Buddha speaks of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), he is speaking of causes and conditions;
he does not speak of it as his own self-originated path. World-Honored One, even the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) speak of causes and conditions, such as the Primal Lord (*Īśvara*)."

At that time, from subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), such various natures arise; yet, regarding what the Blessed One calls the arising of all natures through causes and conditions, there are discourses concerning the *siddhānta* of inquiry and the *siddhānta* of immediate realization.
Furthermore, the Blessed One, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also speak of the arising of existence and non-existence;

the Blessed One likewise speaks of the non-arising of what has arisen, and that once arisen it ceases—just as the Blessed One has taught, beginning with "ignorance is the condition for volitional formations" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) and so forth.
"Old age and death—this is what the Blessed One has taught as being without cause, not as having a cause.

The Blessed One establishes this teaching: 'Because this exists, that exists. He does not establish a view of gradual arising; rather, he refutes the superior claims of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), for they do not accord with the Tathāgata’s teaching.
Why is this? Because the causes taught by the non-Buddhists do not arise from conditions, yet they claim there is something produced. The Blessed One [teaches otherwise]."

To say that one observes conditions through the existence of things and observes things through the existence of conditions—such a causal relationship is confused and thus leads to an infinite regress.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not teach that there is no cause, nor do I teach a confused causal relationship.

When it is said 'because this exists, that exists,' this refers to the non-existence of the grasped and the grasper, which is the realization that the great measure is but the manifestation of one's own mind. Mahāmati, if one is attached to the grasped and the grasper...
Failing to realize that external objects—which are merely manifestations of one's own mind—are neither existent nor non-existent, they fall into such errors.
It is not my teaching on dependent origination that I am refuting; I constantly state that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and are never produced without a cause.
When the True Eye is not clear, heterodox views become delusions; once such false doctrines have been produced, doubts and suspicions must inevitably be resolved—it is essential to understand this.
Therefore, Mahāmati juxtaposed the Buddha’s teachings with those of the non-Buddhists to challenge them.

First, he compared them through the lens of causality (*hetu-pratyaya*), stating that the Buddha’s teaching on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and so forth means that dependent origination is precisely the meaning of causes and conditions. However—
Since he does not separately state the reason for establishing [the teaching], it is said that he does not speak of his own path;
for while the non-Buddhists speak of a supreme Īśvara and so forth, is it not also the case that they speak of the meaning of causes and conditions regarding the arising of all natures?

Is there a difference between this and the Tathāgata’s own established doctrine (*siddhānta*) concerning the arising of all natures through causes and conditions, or is there no difference? Next, by means of...

If one argues that the simultaneous existence of both causelessness and [causality] constitutes a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) view—since they also claim that existence arises from non-existence, which is merely causeless—and that the Buddha likewise taught that there is no arising and that what has arisen ceases, as in "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations" (*avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*), is this not also the Buddha’s teaching of causelessness?
Third, regarding the objection of confusion, it is said: "The world..."
The Venerable One established the intention behind the statement that "because this exists, that exists," which refers to simultaneity rather than the gradual arising of successive stages;

it is not merely a matter of parallel occurrence. Furthermore, this was intended to demonstrate the superiority of the Buddhist teaching over the claims of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), for their assertions maintain that effects arise from causes that are distinct and do not originate from conditions (*pratyaya*), thereby rendering the relationship between cause and effect entirely disconnected.

It may be argued that since the Buddha spoke of "this being, that arises" and so forth—observing that causes have effects and that these are mutually dependent—this would result in confusion and the fault of an infinite regress.
In response, the text first generally refutes this objection and subsequently provides an explanation of the Buddha’s words.
The Buddha stated, "Because this exists, that exists," meaning that because these six sense faculties exist, those six sense objects exist.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "Cognition arises from objects, and characteristics exist because of the sense faculties. Thus, the faculties and objects arise in mutual dependence;
if they did not depend on one another for their arising, then the grasped object and the grasping subject would lack inherent nature.

When such awareness is realized as arising from the self-manifestation of one's own mind, it is simply emptiness. Otherwise, it merely reveals the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who fail to perceive this principle. Such is the case.
How does this fault relate to the present explanation of dependent origination? Therefore it is said: "It is not I who speak of dependent origination;

rather, what is called 'observing that there is an effect because there is a cause' means that by observing past causes, there is a present effect—the effect being like the result—and further, from the present effect, there is a future cause.
This is precisely the characteristic of dependent origination across the three times; how could it be confused?"
"The underlying principle of disorder, though not explicitly explained here, exists within the remaining texts; therefore, it is treated briefly (and so forth). Furthermore, it is said:
'I have always taught that the harmony of causes and conditions is precisely the response to the question regarding the absence of cause.

How could this be the same [as spontaneity]? Since the two differences have been distinguished, the coexistence of causes and conditions with spontaneity can be understood on its own; thus, it is not shown separately. (1)
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is it not the case that because speech has an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), all things have an intrinsic nature?
World-Honored One, if there were no intrinsic nature, speech would not arise; therefore, because speech has an intrinsic nature, all things have an intrinsic nature. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Speech is produced regarding that which lacks an intrinsic nature—such as the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise. These are instances where speech is currently manifest in the world."
Wisdom is neither existence nor non-existence; it is merely a verbal expression.

As for what you have said—that because there is verbal expression there is existence, and because there is verbal expression all things exist—your own thesis is thereby undermined. Mahāmati, not all Buddha-fields possess verbal expressions;
verbal expression is merely a form of activity. There are some Buddha-fields where the Dharma is revealed by a mere glance, or by gestures, or by raising an eyebrow.
There is the movement of the eyes, or smiling, or yawning, or clearing the throat, or recollecting buddha-fields, or physical gestures;

O Mahāmati, it is like the world of Gandhavatī and the land of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra, where by a mere glance all bodhisattvas attain the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and various supreme samādhis.
Therefore, there is no inherent nature in verbal expression, nor is there any [inherent nature] in existence.
The Great Wisdom of Universal Nature beholds this world and sees that such sentient beings as mosquitoes, gnats, insects, and ants perform their respective tasks without any speech.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

Just as with space, a rabbit’s horn, and the son of a barren woman—things that do not exist yet are spoken of—so too, ordinary fools give rise to false imaginings regarding the dharmas produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions;
they cannot know them as they truly are, and thus they wander through the cycle of existence within the house of the three realms of being.
The previous statement held that all phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions;

yet, because of doubts regarding the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) based on verbal expression, one might ask whether there is also an "all-nature" [intrinsic nature]. To state the opposite: if there were no intrinsic nature, verbal expression would not arise.

If both were to possess intrinsic nature, then that nature would become a substantial reality—would this not contradict the principle of dependent origination? This objection contains an implicit dilemma regarding both positions.
Buddhabhadra replied that although there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is still verbal expression;

that is, because causes and conditions are fundamentally without intrinsic nature, it is not obstructed by using verbal expressions to demonstrate them. How could verbal expression itself be the intrinsic nature?

Just as in the world one currently speaks of "tortoise hair" or "rabbit horns," which are also fundamentally without intrinsic nature yet possess verbal expression, so too it is neither nature nor non-nature; one speaks of "non-nature."
Thus, since it is not a real statement and yet it is not the case that there is no nature [of speech], such that its expression still exists, it is said: "It is merely verbal expression.
The concluding censure, "Your treatise is then destroyed," means that the doctrine of co-arising nature (*sahabhū-svabhāva*) is destroyed.
This implies that not only are causal conditions devoid of intrinsic nature, but even verbal expression is not permanent; thus it further says: "It is not in all buddha-fields."
There are those who say that correct speech is not necessarily verbal expression; since such speech is not constant, it is merely an activity performed in accordance with conditions.
Because this activity is not fixed, how could it possess an inherent nature? Alternatively, there may be Buddha-lands where the Dharma is manifested through gazing, and so forth.

These all vary according to the different modes of transformation for those beings; they do not rely exclusively on verbal expression, yet the essence of the six sense objects is fully present therein.

All of these can manifest the Dharma and lead one into the Way, just as those in the Chan school employ the striking of the mallet, the raising of the whisk, or the lifting of eyebrows and blinking of eyes to receive and guide others;
for indeed, it is from this that they emerge. To say that such principles do not exist would be impossible, yet people fail to realize that these too are the teaching.
Is it not narrow-minded to regard only verbal discourse as the teaching? Furthermore, it is said: "It is like looking intently."

In the *Asphāraṇa* (Not-Winking) World, the preceding section merely provides a general indication; here, it specifically distinguishes this region by naming its land and the *Gandhottarakuru* World, where the Buddha’s work is performed through fragrances, and so forth.
By these examples, one can understand how other realms establish their transformations.

However, the act of "gazing" serves to further clarify the characteristics of the superior land and its transformative activities. Why stop at the mere fact that the Sage establishes transformations for illumination? It extends even further.
Sentient beings and even subtle categories of things also possess those that can be distinguished without relying on verbal expression;

thus it is said, "Seeing the mosquitoes, gnats, insects, and ants of this world. From this we know that within every land and every atom, down to the most minute particle, there exists a realm of ultimate transformation.
Therefore, what is called "verbal expression" is merely one aspect of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
How can the ears be sufficient to determine the reality of a nature? The verse says "the son of Paṇḍu";

according to the Tang translation, this refers to the "son of a stone woman" (a barren woman's son), rabbit horns, and the like—all of which are metaphors for that which is fundamentally non-existent yet expressed through verbal designation.

Likewise, phenomena are fundamentally without intrinsic nature, yet through deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one speaks of their nature; therefore it is said: "Such natures are [products of] deluded conceptualization," using these as examples to illustrate the harmony of causes and conditions.

It is naturally so that because the deluded thoughts of ordinary fools cannot know things as they truly are in accordance with their nature, there exists the phenomenon of saṃsāra within the three realms of existence (2). [End of] Chapter Nine.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the term 'constant sound,' what does it refer to?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It refers to delusive confusion (*bhrānti*). While this delusive confusion appears even to the Noble Ones (*ārya*), it is not a state of perversion (*viparyāsa*).
Mahāmati, it is like a mirage in springtime, a fire-wheel (*alātacakra*), falling hair, a city of the Gandharvas, an illusion, a dream, or a reflection in a mirror—such is the world."
"Inversion is not the mark of a wise person; yet, Mahāmati, it is not that this delusive confusion does not manifest.

That delusive confusion manifests in various ways, and it is not the case that delusive confusion itself constitutes impermanence. Why is this? It is because it is free from both existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati, what is meant by being free from existence and non-existence? It refers to the various objective realms of all foolish common people."
The sound of permanence, in contrast to impermanence, gives rise to delusion within the realm of illusions;

yet, if one does not speak of permanence by means of impermanence, then permanence remains undifferentiated, and if one does not speak of delusion by means of the realm of illusions, then delusion lacks its cause.
This is why the sound of permanence constitutes delusion, and why delusion is caused by the realm of illusions. Thus it is observed.
Now, this text suddenly asks: "What is the meaning of the statement that sound is permanent?

Its intention is that since the speech previously heard was not permanent, does it mean that there is only the phenomenon itself while the statement regarding "permanent sound" remains? The Buddha answered that this is a delusion;
because it is precisely a delusion, he spoke of "permanent sound," but this does not mean that the sound is permanently present within the speech. Indeed, it is a delusion.

This means that because deluded views arise from illusory objects and are taken to be impermanent, one uses those very objects to demonstrate permanence, so that one may realize that illusory objects have no nature other than impermanence;
thus, one departs from the inversion of regarding things as impermanent—this is the intended meaning. First, to explain the principles of permanence and impermanence in general, it is said:
"By means of that confusion and so forth," meaning that the illusory objects are fundamentally one for both the sage and the ordinary person.
To perceive that which is distinct as being either permanent or impermanent is what is called "delusion. This refers to the following passage: "like the heat haze of springtime," and so forth.
This is because these illusory objects do not fail to appear even within the sphere of experience of the noble ones (*ārya*). Thus it is said that they appear to the noble ones as well;
however, because they do not grasp them as erroneous, they are not inverted. That which is non-inverted is precisely the permanent. As for the phrase "like springtime":
At that time, the flames and so forth truly emerge from the illusory realm; wherever such various analogies exist, the worldly foolish and ignorant are deluded and take them to be inverted.
This is precisely impermanence. Although it is not something reached by the wise, it is not as if it does not manifest;
thus, its nature is simply constant. Therefore, he concludes both points together, saying: "Those who are deluded and confused have various manifestations"—this refers to ordinary worldlings.
To perceive it as inverted is not delusion; rather, it is the deluded mind that creates impermanence. When the Sage perceives it, he regards it as constant.
To see it as constant is to know that its essence is fundamentally not inverted; to perceive it as inverted is to know that its illusory nature is fundamentally constant.
Yet, within this illusory realm, it is still termed "delusive confusion," for this serves to show that inversion is not separate from the realm, so that one may come to understand it.
The objective realm is fundamentally non-perverted. Why is this so? The text below interrogates and explains its meaning by stating, "Because it is free from existence and non-existence.

This means that an illusion cannot be definitively established as either existent or non-existent in its reality; thus, the existence and non-existence that are free from both existence and non-existence constitute the eternal nature (*dharmatā*).
Now, since it has already been stated that it is free from existence and non-existence, why is it nevertheless perceived as a delusion?
Delusion is the domain of the foolish; therefore it is asked: "How can one be free from the delusion of existence and non-existence?
(1) Just as hungry ghosts see the Ganges while others do not, there is no nature of delusion for those [ghosts], yet it is not non-existent because it appears to others.
Likewise, for the noble ones who are free from inversion, this delusion is not inverted; therefore, delusion is said to have the characteristic of permanence.
Because their characteristics are not destroyed, Mahāmati, delusion is not the destruction of the various characteristics of conceptual construction; therefore, Mahāmati, delusion is eternal.
Mahāmati, how is delusion real? Furthermore, regarding this delusion, the noble ones do not give rise to a perverted cognition, nor do they give rise to a non-perverted cognition.
Mahāmati, with the exception of the noble ones, there is no one who [perceives] even a slight [portion] of this delusion.
Mahāmati, the conceptualization of distinctions is not the object of noble wisdom; whatever exists as such is the false discourse of fools, not the speech of the noble ones.
Furthermore, regarding the view of fools, I have cited the hungry ghosts at the Ganges as a metaphor: although they are near the Ganges, they do not see the water.
While there is this difference between seeing and not seeing, the nature and substance of the river remain constant as before; therefore, there is no delusion.
The nature of delusion means that it does not exist because of being seen, nor does it cease to exist because of not being seen.
Speaking from the perspective of its being seen, it is not the case that the Gaṅgā River is non-existent; therefore, it is said that because it appears to others, its nature is not non-existent.

This delusive confusion is explained as the constant meaning of delusion, in that all noble ones (ārya), by virtue of having abandoned both inverted and non-inverted views, [perceive] that very [reality].
The essence of delusion is eternally abiding because its characteristics do not perish; it is not that the various conceptualized characteristics of delusion perish and yet are called eternal.
Thus, this nature of eternity resides in the object and not in the person, for it is the Sage who can accord with the object.
Conversely, this reveals that inverted views reside in the person and not in the object, precisely because they reside in the person.
Those who are deluded perceive various manifestations; however, because these do not exist as objective entities, they are not produced by delusion.
According to the principle of impermanence, one speaks of neither "existence" nor "non-existence," thereby collectively demonstrating that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
How could a person then have a fixed view? If a person holds a fixed view, it is merely an inversion. Thus, the Sage is free from inverted views. May it be so!
Furthermore, it is also free from non-perverted views. Generally speaking, that which grasps the reality of phenomena is called non-perversion, while otherwise it is a perverted view.
For the Noble Ones (*ārya*), that which grasps the principle (*tattva*) is non-perversion, while otherwise it is a perverted view.

If the Noble Ones were to actually possess a "view," then that view would constitute perversion; therefore, in order to manifest that they have attained the vision of the principle rather than a mere [subjective] view, both [aspects] must be negated.
The previous citation of the Sage as a non-perverse example was made in reference to phenomena (*vastu*) in contrast to delusion;
now, however, we specifically discuss the Sage from the perspective of principle (*tattva*). Therefore, both examples are set aside to clarify the meaning of reality.
Thus it is asked: "What is the reality of delusion? It is said that the permanent is precisely reality; hence, the permanent is cited as the example. Now, regarding delusion...
The objective realm is fundamentally real, yet ordinary beings do not know it; therefore, by relying upon the various sages, it is revealed through the causes and conditions for seeing reality.

If one were likewise to neither give rise to inverted nor non-inverted cognitions regarding the locus of delusive confusion, then the reality of delusive confusion would not be restricted to the sages alone.
Taking this as an analogy, what was previously clarified regarding the constancy of delusive confusion does not apply solely in contrast to [the state of the sages].
To speak of it is already to entrust the sacred to manifest the mundane; if one were to focus exclusively on the sacred, the common person would be excluded from any share.
Thus, we know that the words "causes and conditions" possess a profound significance. Furthermore, the phrase "excluding all the sages" serves to eliminate confusion and excess;
it means that although the sages employ causes and conditions to demonstrate the starting point, in reality, they do not [rely upon them].
Setting aside the various sages and speaking directly of ordinary beings, even those who do not harbor exhaustive conceptualizations cannot yet achieve such realization;

therefore, it is said that setting aside the sages, if one possesses even a slight degree of conceptualization regarding these delusions and confusions, how could the characteristics of phenomena possibly be considered truly real?

Furthermore, when it is said that "ordinary beings possess existence," it refers precisely to those who have a slight degree of conceptualization, yet who wish to equate themselves with the wisdom of the sages.
That which concerns the true nature of phenomena is a false discourse of the deluded, not the speech of the noble ones (2).
Those who are confused give rise to two kinds of natures—delusive and non-delusive—based on inverted and non-inverted perceptions: namely, the nature of the noble ones and the nature of the deluded.
As for the nature of the noble ones, it is distinguished into three types: the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle.
How is it that the deluded give rise to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle through false imagination?
It is called giving rise to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle through false imagination when one adheres to the grasping of self-characteristics and common characteristics.

Mahāmati, from that very same confusion and false imagination, one gives rise to the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; this refers to not closely adhering to the self-characteristics and common characteristics of that very same confusion.

What is the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle that arises from delusion? O Wise One, it is that very same delusion which gives rise to the lineage of the Buddha vehicle—namely, awakening to the fact that external objects are merely the manifestation of one’s own mind, and that they lack intrinsic nature; by not conceptualizing these appearances, the lineage of the Buddha vehicle arises.

This is called the lineage of the Buddha vehicle arising from that very same delusion. Furthermore, the deluded thoughts of ordinary beings regarding the various natures of phenomena give rise to ignorance.
Now, Mahāmati, that which is the lineage (gotra) is neither an existing entity nor a non-existing entity; this is the meaning of "lineage.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, that which is the nature of the transformation of the self-nature of dharmas—the delusive confusion that is not conceptualized by the mind, mentation, and consciousness of the noble ones, and which is free from the habit-energies (vāsanā) of past errors—is called suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, when I speak of "being apart from the mind," this phrase reveals being apart from conceptualization; it is precisely the teaching of being apart from [conceptual] thought.
Regarding all perceptions:
the meaning of the three types of lineages is that those who are inverted are the ignorant, while those who are not inverted are the noble ones. Even the Tathāgata lineage can be eliminated;
all others are termed "inverted. Although both are called "false conceptualization" (*vikalpa*), this is stated from the perspective of their respective causes. Correctly so.
As stated in the *Mahā-śāstra*: "The two dharmas of the Buddha and sentient beings both arise from false dharmas. This refers to the arising of the dispositions (*gotra*) of śrāvakas and others;
it also describes them as the "deluded imaginings of fools" because they are based upon fools, yet they are not themselves the disposition of fools.
Furthermore, this is said in contrast to the Buddha-disposition (*buddha-gotra*); thus, one should know that the meaning of the Two Vehicles involves a formal negation. It says:
Regarding "clinging to specific and general characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*):

this refers to śrāvakas who, being attached to the specific and general characteristics of the five aggregates and other phenomena, fail to realize that their fundamental nature is empty, and thus give rise to weary detachment. This constitutes the lineage of the śrāvaka.

As for the pratyekabuddha, what is termed "specific and general characteristics" here has the same meaning as that which they abandon; however, they differ in that they delight in cultivating seclusion and add the term "not associating with others."
Regarding the phrase "within the lineage of that Buddha," it specifically refers to the "wise one" (*jñānin*) in order to distinguish them from the two vehicles;

the meaning of "realizing that which appears as one's own mind" and so forth has been explained previously. Furthermore, "the nature of various phenomena" refers to the lineage of the foolish (*bāla*), who, through their deluded conceptual minds, adhere to things according to their objects and thereby establish their nature.
The phrase "they do not possess actual entities" serves as a general conclusion, pointing back to all the preceding points.
Although the meanings of the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) are distinct, that delusion is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent, and no real entity can be found;

it is only because of the divergence between delusion and awakening, or turning toward and turning away from them, that they differ. Therefore, it is said: "This is called the meaning of the spiritual lineage. Furthermore, it is said:
"That very delusion is not the conceptualization of the various sages," which serves to reveal that the spiritual lineage of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna-gotra*) is not limited to those alone.

Not only does one cease from conceptualizing regarding delusion, but one also undergoes a complete transformation of all dharmas, including the faults and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).
Upon reaching the ultimate limit of this transformation, one arrives at the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*); therefore, there is nothing that is not suchness.
This is as stated in the preceding text: "The transformation of all self-natures and habitual tendencies, up to and including the habitual tendencies of views, is called *nirvāṇa*."

The phrasing is merely different; however, because the mental conceptions of the nine realms are all without exception transcended, it is said that "as one is detached from the mind, one is also detached from thought.
To speak of this phrase means it is the phrase for transcending the mind and severing thought, which corresponds to what is called in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"True Suchness is free from thought; when one turns toward it, the mind is severed. Since it is called "True Suchness," then—
Because all phenomena are truly such and as they are, there is neither negation nor establishment; why then do you speak now of transformation and the departure from mental conceptions?
Wherein lies their being "truly such"? It is said: Transformation is precisely the means by which one enters true suchness.
Without relying on transformation, how could one accord with suchness? Once one accords with suchness, even "suchness" itself vanishes of its own accord—how much more so words?
"Even when separated, it is simply a separation from that which, in its own essence, is without separation" (3).

Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, is delusion existent or non-existent? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is like a magical illusion, devoid of the characteristics of conceptual attachment.

If delusion possessed the characteristics of conceptual attachment, then for one who possesses such attachment, its nature could not be extinguished, and dependent origination would [cease to function]."
Regarding the statement by the non-Buddhists that phenomena produced by causes and conditions are like illusions, Mahāmati said to the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, if delusion is like an illusion, it should then act as a cause for other delusions. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "An illusion is not the cause of delusion, because it does not give rise to faults.
Mahāmati, an illusion does not give rise to faults, nor does it possess false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Mahāmati, an illusion arises from the clarity of another; it is not [self-originated]."
"Because it arises from the locus of the habitual tendencies of one's own false imaginings, it does not give rise to faults, O Mahāmati;
this is a deluded attachment of the minds of fools, not that of the noble ones. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Noble One does not perceive delusion, nor is there a real interval between them; if delusion were truly real, it would be abandoned as such.
If any characteristic arises, that too is delusion and impurity, like a visual impairment.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is not that there is no resemblance to illusion; one sees all phenomena as being like an illusion. Mahāmati addressed the Buddha:

If it is said that the Blessed One teaches that all dharmas are like illusions because of attachment to various illusory appearances, or if it is said that all natures are like illusions because of attachment to diverse characteristics—if this were so, Blessed One, there would be some natures that are not like illusions. Why is this?
It is because the various characteristics of form do not arise from causes; Blessed One, form has no cause.
"World-Honored One, various marks appear like illusions; therefore, there is no attachment to the similarity between various illusory marks and all phenomena.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not that all phenomena are like illusions because of attachment to the similarity with various illusory marks.
Mahāmati, rather, all phenomena are unreal and perish as quickly as lightning; this is what makes them like illusions. Mahāmati, it is, for example,"
A flash of lightning appears for a mere instant, and having appeared, it immediately vanishes; it does not appear to the foolish.

In this same way, all natures are observed to be devoid of self-nature through their own imagined self-characteristics and common characteristics; they are not appearances of form, nor are they attachments to such appearances.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Since that which is not illusion has no analogy, the Dharma-nature is said to be like an illusion—unreal and as swift as lightning;
therefore, it is described as being "like an illusion. Next, there are four sections of challenging objections: first, the objection concerning the existence or non-existence of delusion.

Previously, delusion was treated as permanent and real, yet it was also considered a false imagination; thus, one asks whether its fruit exists or does not exist, and so forth. The Buddha answers with the analogy of an illusion.
"Phenomena are like illusions and lack the characteristic of attachment" means that if one definitively asserts existence or non-existence, there will be attachment;

and where there is attachment, the nature [of phenomena] cannot be extinguished. Therefore, they are described as being like illusions: although there is delusive confusion, their nature cannot be apprehended, and thus they lack the characteristic of attachment.
If they were to possess the characteristic of attachment, then dependent origination would be identical to that of the non-Buddhists. (Second Objection)
Regarding the statement that "delusion is like an illusion," if one follows the current text, one might ask:

"If delusion is taken as being like an illusion, then since delusion gives rise to faults, would the illusion also act as a cause for other delusions? In the response, it says that "the illusion is not the cause of delusion";

this specifically means that the illusion is not the cause of delusion, though the wording here is inverted. This is because the single term "illusion" (māyā) has three meanings: [1] the illusory appearance itself; [2] the magical artifice; and [3] the mental state of being deceived.

Although the illusory object (*māyā-vastu*), the illusory phenomenon (*māyā-dharma*), and the illusory contemplation (*māyā-darśana*) are three distinct things, they are all alike in that no fault arises;

thus one knows them to be illusions and is without false conceptualization—this is "contemplation" (*darśana*). Furthermore, it is said that "the illusion" refers to that which arises from another source of clarity, which is the "phenomenon" (*dharma*).
This admits of two interpretations. According to those two translations, both treat it as "illusory phenomena arising from the clarity of incantations," which refers to the five [aggregates].
When one clearly perceives that which is like an illusion as being illusory, it arises from the clarity of wisdom;
it is not produced from the habitual tendencies of one's own deluded thoughts, and therefore it is not a cause of affliction.

To say that this is the "deluded attachment of the minds of foolish people" means precisely that while the illusory phenomena of confusion do not themselves give rise to faults, the mind’s deluded attachment to them constitutes the fault. For the sages and worthies, however, this is not so.
The first four lines of this verse praise the absence of attachment to the characteristics of illusion;
it means that because the Sage can realize that delusive confusion is like an illusion, he perceives therein no real dharma that can be apprehended.

Conversely, if one were to hold a conceptual attachment, then the nature of delusive confusion could not be extinguished, and it would consequently become a real dharma. This is certainly not the same [as the former].
The first [verse] concerns the reality of delusion; the subsequent four lines of verse address the non-arising of faults regarding illusion.
This means that if one realizes things are like illusions, one abandons all marks of delusion and does not perceive even a single dharma as obtainable.
If there still appear to be marks of arising, this is because delusion has not yet been exhausted; it is like having a cataract in the eye, whereby one sees things as impure. Furthermore...
Next, Mahāmati, [the Buddha] again demonstrates below that illusion is not non-existent.

Because of the preceding statement, "like an illusion, there is no attachment," etc., those who might be confused could think that illusion is simply non-existence; therefore, he takes the example of illusion as a cause and further refutes this, saying:
"It is not that illusion is non-existent. This is because seeing all phenomena as like an illusion means that illusion is not identical to non-existence.
There is a similarity [between phenomena], which gives rise to the notion that they are unreal, like the analogy of lightning. Mahāmati, for this reason he raises the third question:
Is it because all dharmas share the same illusory characteristic that one clings to them as having distinct characteristics?
Or, if one were to calculate them based on their identical characteristics, since the various dharmas perceived before us are not necessarily all unreal like mirages and the like?
It is said: "There are natures that are not like illusions. If one speaks generally, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) should have no distinct causes;
yet, in the world, there has never been a caused phenomenon that is entirely like an illusion.

Since this uses the dissimilar to challenge the similar, it should likewise use the similar to challenge the dissimilar. [The text] is brief here; in the response, the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) are correctly negated, and furthermore—
Taking up a different meaning: all phenomena are unreal and perish as swiftly as lightning, being like an illusion;

therefore it is said, "like a flash of lightning," and so forth. Since an illusion is already a metaphor, this further uses a simile to clarify the metaphor, showing that the rapid arising and ceasing in a single moment can only be understood by the wisdom of the noble ones (*ārya*) and is not perceived by ordinary people (*bāla*). Such is the manifestation of appearances.

The phrase "the nature of all things is ultimately revealed" means that when one observes all phenomena upon the substance of one's own deluded thoughts through their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), no real nature is found;
thus, they are like illusions. This is not a statement based on attachment to the similarities or differences of perceived forms as if they were real.
The verse says, "There is no analogy for illusion," meaning that even an analogy is merely a semblance; it does not mean that [phenomena] are not illusions.
"Because there is no analogy for non-existence.

(4) Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what the World-Honored One has taught—that all natures are unarisen and like illusions—will this not result in a contradiction between what was previously said and what is now said?
You have taught that the nature of things is unarisen and like an illusion. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"O Mahāmati, it is not because my teaching on the nature of non-arising is like an illusion that there is the fault of contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Why is this?
It is because the realization of arising and non-arising is merely the manifestation of one's own mind; external entities and their non-existence are non-existent.

Non-arising manifests, O Mahāmati, and thus there is no fault of contradiction between what I have said before and after. Rather, it is in order to refute the causal arising of the outsiders that I teach that all natures are non-existent."

Mahāmati, the foolish masses of non-Buddhists give rise to great delusion, desiring that existence and non-existence arise from birth; they cling to various conceptualizations based on their own false imaginings.
Mahāmati, I do not hold that there is arising from existence or non-existence; therefore, I teach by means of the doctrine of non-arising.
Mahāmati, when I speak of "nature," it is for the purpose of gathering in those in the cycle of birth and death, and to destroy the views of nihilism and annihilationism for the sake of my disciples.
Because it encompasses the various karmic bases for rebirth, the term "nature" (*svabhāva*) is used to describe the grasping of birth and death.

it is spoken of as being like an illusion or a dream because fools, falling into the characteristics of evil views and longing for them, do not understand that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds, and they remain attached to the characteristics of self-nature produced by causes and conditions.

“Mahāmati, regarding the characteristic of intrinsic nature, one should not allow foolish people with evil views to harbor hopes for or become attached to all dharmas—whether to oneself or to others—but rather see all dharmas as they truly are in their actual state, thereby avoiding improper discourse.

The non-arising of that which is not of the nature of existence is subsumed within the nature of existence; this is the observation of saṃsāra as being like an illusion and so forth, wherein one does not falsely conceptualize regarding characteristics.

In response to the doubt that there might be a contradiction between existence and non-existence, first there is a general summary, followed by a specific analysis. Within the general summary, it says:
Regarding "arising is non-arising," the principle is fundamentally one; it is spoken of as threefold according to its various meanings.

First, that arising is itself nature (*dharmatā*) means that one awakens to the manifestation of one's own mind as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such that what exists is not truly existent—this is the meaning of being like an illusion. Second, because external natures lack inherent nature, there is no principle of arising;
this is the meaning of manifestation being non-arising. Since these three are mutually identical, the single principle remains without contradiction. This is the general intent.
Furthermore, within the specific explanation, the initial exposition of "non-arising" has two meanings. First, it is to refute the externalists' view that things arise from causes;
because they postulate that various distinct causes give rise to things, [the Buddha] says that all natures are non-arising to destroy that [view].

Moreover, he intends to show that if things were to arise from themselves, they would simply be arising from non-existence, which is nothing other than reckoning them as causeless—this is not a reckoning based on one's own false imagination.

The attachment to dependent origination is not thus in the present case. Generally speaking, when we speak of "arising" and "non-arising," there is both the phenomenal aspect (*dharma*) and the principle (*tattva*).
As for the principle, arising is itself non-arising; therefore, I say that I preach non-arising by means of non-arising. This is not the same as causeless arising.
Phenomenally, things arise from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and do not arise from some other cause. Is this not, then, different from the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*)?
Next, regarding the explanation of the meaning of "nature" (*prakṛti*): it refers to the teaching that all phenomena possess the nature of being either wholesome or unwholesome.
This is for three reasons: first, so as to provide a destination for the birth-and-death of sentient beings; second, to counteract and refute the nihilistic views of non-Buddhists;
and third, so that disciples of the internal teaching may understand that they receive rebirth according to their karma. As the text says: "The nature... and so forth.
Regarding the sound "as before," it refers to the constant sound. To explain the meaning of "illusory" (*māyā*) within this context, there are two points.

First, because one knows that its nature is detached, it is said that the illusory nature is itself the self-nature (*svabhāva*). This is because knowing the self-nature of illusion is precisely the detachment from self-nature; thus, the reason for speaking of "illusion" is for the sake of detachment.
As the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "To know illusion is itself detachment; no further expedient means are required. Second, [the second point follows].
In order to shatter the grasping at signs by foolish people, there are three further [points], and for this reason it is said that they "fall into the evil views of fools," etc.:
first, they do not know that all is the manifestation of one's own mind; second, they destroy the arising of phenomena produced by primary causes and conditions;
third, they cling to the characteristics of the nature of conditions as being truly existent. Therefore, it is taught that all dharmas are like illusions.

To shatter the appearances of dreams so as not to allow the foolish to fall into the error of attachment, and to manifest virtue by not allowing them to grasp at any phenomena—whether self or other—is the opposite of the second and third faults mentioned above.

To prevent them from engaging in improper discourse of existence or non-existence regarding the state of reality as it is, is the opposite of the aforementioned failure to understand that all is a manifestation of one’s own mind. These are all intended to prevent such [faults].
It is also said that "to see all dharmas as they truly are" means to see them in accordance with reality;
thus, all dharmas are no longer [grasped as] all dharmas. Therefore, one transcends the measure of what appears to one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-pramāṇa*).

Otherwise, if one still dwells within the realm of self and other, or existence and non-existence, it will not serve to refute divergent views or manifest the true principle. However, the preceding passage further states:
All [the scriptures] alike state that one awakens to the manifestation of one’s own mind; this particular text alone speaks of "transcending," yet there is no contradiction between them.
This is because while one may know [the truth], if one has not yet transcended it, the mind still persists; only when one transcends and further detaches from it does one reach the ultimate.
What is there to transcend? It is simply the One Suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, it is to counteract the delusion of attachment to external objects that the self-mind is thus demonstrated.
Furthermore, when one realizes that one's own mind naturally subsides both internally and externally, one comes to know that these two meanings share a single principle.

The verse states, "Non-arising is non-nature," which praises the meaning of non-arising; that is, arising from non-arising means that every phenomenon (dharma) is non-nature, and "arising" is also [the state of] non-nature.
The remaining verses concerning the two meanings can be understood accordingly. (5) ○ This concludes Chapter Ten.

The distinctions between the body of names (*nāmakāya*), the body of phrases (*padakāya*), and the body of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) are objects of attachment for ordinary, deluded people, like an elephant sinking deep into the mud.

The conventionalities are not real and thus cannot be established [as such], yet the real is not manifested without the conventional. The two serve as mutual causes and supports for all verbal teachings.

The entire body [of this teaching] possesses the virtue of being endowed with the nature of manifesting and clarifying, yet there is both gain and loss. Gain arises through the underlying meaning and leads to Bodhi;
loss arises from clinging to the literal language and results in frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).

Since gain and loss take form, one must surely deeply clarify their respective origins. As for the statement that "words follow into the entry of meaning, while phrases take shape as the body," it means:

The phrases that accord with the underlying meaning are not meaningless phrases; by means of them, one realizes that awakening is not far off, and there is nothing other than this principle for awakening others.
"Word-body" (*nāmakāya*) refers to establishing names based on phenomena; that is, names express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Phrase-body" (*padakāya*) refers to phrases possessing a body of meaning; that is, phrases express specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*). This definitively establishes intrinsic nature.

Regarding the definitive ultimate: since the nature of words (*pada*) consists in their function of signifying specific meanings, when they are definitively ultimate and not mutually confused, this is the function of the collection of words (*padakāya*).
As for the "collection of forms" (*vyañjanakāya*), it refers to that which manifests names and phrases;

"form" (*vyañjana*) is also called "syllable" (*vyañjana*), meaning written characters. It is precisely through these characters that names and phrases are manifested, and names and phrases are likewise accumulated [to form them].
Regarding the "body" (*kāya*) of phonemes (*vyañjana*), it is called a "body" because it serves as the basis for both phonemes—which are what constitute written characters—and words (*pada*).
This is because its meaning is that of an accumulation of similar elements. Furthermore, the "body of form" (*rūpa-kāya*) is used as a metaphor to illustrate this;

just as a person's physical form has length, shortness, height, and depth, one relies on phonemes to understand phrases (*pada*). Moreover, the "body of phrases" (*pada-kāya*) is likened to a "track" or "footprint," as follows:
To know the elephant, horse, and so forth by their tracks is like seeking the meaning by following the phrases; this is specifically stated in contrast between form (*rūpa*) and phrases (*pada*).

To rely upon this for reflection and cultivation is precisely the intention of the Tiantai school regarding the contemplation of dharma-characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Because those who are attached to the grasped and the grasper do not understand that all things are merely manifestations of their own minds; therefore, I refute them.

The Buddha’s teaching on transcending the four propositions intends to point toward that which is penetrated, rather than the means by which one penetrates; it merely negates what is incorrect without asserting what is correct.

If you can recognize it directly and immediately, you will transcend words and sever all conceptualization, surpassing thought and emotion;
entering from this point is like a fine horse that, upon seeing the shadow of a whip, at once enters the correct path—is this not a joy? Those without wisdom do not understand this.

If one wishes to take [them] away, they are taken for the sake of mutual desire; yet if one wishes to bring them, there is nothing to be brought, and if one wishes to take them away, there is nothing to be taken.

Because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are non-existent, and because all dharmas are unobtainable; thus, all dharmas do not perish. Mahāmati, why is this so?

I shall now speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed listen and receive it with reverence. The Buddha said to him:
Wisdom is of three kinds; how is the distinction between the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) established?

What are these three? They are the inferior, the intermediate, and the superior. The inferior [stream-enterer] has at most seven more births; the intermediate has three or five more births before attaining parinirvāṇa; the superior attains parinirvāṇa in that very same birth.
These three types possess three fetters (*saṃyojana*)—inferior, intermediate, and superior. What are these three fetters? They are as follows:

The three fetters—satkāyadṛṣṭi (view of a self-identity), vicikitsā (doubt), and śīlavrataparāmarśa (clinging to precepts and rituals)—are distinguished by their progressive advancement toward the attainment of arhatship, O Mahāmati.
There are two kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi: that which is innate (*sahaja*) and that which is conceptual (*parikalpita*).

Just as with the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there arises a clinging to the various conceptualized natures (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); yet, because those [conceptualized natures] do not exist, [the clinging is abandoned].
It is neither non-existent nor existent, because it lacks the characteristic of real false imagination;

yet, due to the attachment to the characteristics of the various imagined natures of self-nature by the ignorant, it is like the mirage that a thirsty deer perceives as water. This is the view of a self in the body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) which is falsely imagined by the *srotāpanna*;
by means of the realization of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), they grasp the absence of intrinsic nature and thereby sever their long-standing attachment born of ignorance.
The Dharma must be universally known; even minor virtues of humans and devas are not to be abandoned, let alone the teachings of the Śrāvakas.
Practice must reach the ultimate; even the provisional vehicles of the partial and gradual are not to be rejected, let alone the teachings of the Śrāvakas.
Thus, "practice must reach the ultimate" refers to one's own cultivation (sva-caryā), while "the Dharma must be universally known" refers to the transformation of others (parārtha).
Therefore, Mahāmati requested the Buddha to explain the Dharma of the four fruits, saying:
"Srotāpanna—'srotāpanna-gati' refers to both the fruit and the path toward it; the same applies to the subsequent stages up to Arhatship.
By way of expedient means, other sutras may refer to the 'Path,' which is merely the cause, and do not grant it the name of a 'fruit,' as it has not yet reached ultimate realization."

This is because they have ultimately reached the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding the "distinctive common characteristics," this refers to the fact that each of the four fruits (*phala*) and so forth possesses both common and distinct characteristics.
Having distinguished them thus and known them as such, one subsequently explains this Dharma to sentient beings;
therefore, it is said: "the characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness and the purification of the two kinds of hindrances."

Thus, from the realization attained through the four fruits up to the ultimate penetration of the inconceivable realm that transcends all signs of the stages, one proceeds by means of this superior advancement.

Therefore, as it corresponds to the fruition, all dharma-gates—like a *maṇi* jewel—are fully manifested therein, because during the causal stage one has universally known and universally studied them all. By means of everything...
The Dharma-realm serves as an inexhaustible body and wealth to sustain all sentient beings; this concludes the request for its exposition.

In the Buddha’s response, he first explains in detail the characteristics of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Regarding the phrase "at most seven more births" (the meaning of the terms is explained elsewhere):

because these refer to the afflictions of thought (*klesha*) severed from the first fruit upward, there are various explanations concerning the number of births one may still undergo. Now, in this context...

This statement is made hereafter to clarify the previous analysis of the natures of the three faculties (*indriya*). Regarding the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), they are precisely the afflictions to be abandoned upon entering the first fruit (*phala*);

thus, there is a difference between the detailed and abbreviated enumerations, such as the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Furthermore, it is said that these fetters are categorized as superior, middling, and inferior based on the person;
those who progress upward and attain arhatship possess the full realization of their abandonment at this stage.

There are three types of abandonment and four types of transcendence (as explained at length). This current discussion concerns the nature of the faculties of great transcendence. Regarding the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*):

it refers to the view that takes the five aggregates as a self and its master. This is divided into two kinds: innate (*sahaja*), which arises simultaneously with the body like the aforementioned view of a self-body;
and conceptual (*vikalpita*), which arises based on views like the subsequent view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Therefore, it is said to be "like a condition."
"Arising and so forth" refers to the fact that because one relies upon dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one gives rise to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Regarding the phrase "because it does not exist," this correctly explains the aforementioned "body-view of the imagined nature. Since there are four views where there were originally none, these are unreal marks of imagined construction;
just as with that dependent origination, the deluded person, through their own imagination, gives rise to various kinds of imagined constructions.
Because of their attachment to intrinsic nature, they are likened to a mirage in the heat; it is not water, yet they perceive it as water—this is its characteristic.

When those who grasp at the absence of nature through the realization of *pudgala-nairātmya* (the selflessness of persons) do so, they are those progressing toward the first fruit (*prathamaphala-pratipannaka*), for by observing through *pudgala-nairātmya*, they realize that there is fundamentally no nature, and thus their delusions are severed.
What is called "ignorance" refers to defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*).

(1) Mahāmati, as for that which is innate: it is the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of the *srotāpanna*, because the four aggregates (*skandha*)—both one's own body and those of others—are devoid of the characteristics of form;

because form arises from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*); because they are mutually dependent causes and conditions; and because the primary elements and form do not aggregate [into a substantial entity].
The stream-enterer (srotāpanna), by contemplating the categories of existence and non-existence, does not manifest the view of a self-body; thus, this view of a self-body is severed.
When craving is severed, it does not arise again—this is called the characteristic of the view of a self-body, Mahāmati. As for the characteristic of doubt:

because one has attained the characteristic of the correct vision of dharmas, and because the two previous kinds of deluded views of a self-body have been severed, doubt regarding dharmas does not arise, nor does one give rise to another teacher elsewhere.
To perceive things as pure or impure is called the characteristic of doubt; this is severed by the Srotāpanna.
Mahāmati, what is meant by the Srotāpanna not grasping at precepts? It means that because he clearly perceives the characteristics of suffering in the places of rebirth, he does not grasp at them.
Mahāmati, "grasping" refers to the fool who resolutely undergoes ascetic practices for the sake of seeking the pleasure of the requisites of life and thus seeks rebirth.

He does not grasp at them, except for the practice of upholding the factors of morality through skillful means—characterized by the dharma-signs of outflow-free phenomena that are free from false discrimination, superior to self-awakening, and detached from [worldly] dedication.
This is called the *srotāpanna* grasping at the signs of morality; it is the severing of the *srotāpanna*.

When the three fetters are severed, greed and delusion do not arise. If a *srotāpanna* were to have this thought: "These various fetters are not accomplished by me," then there would be [a further state].
Second, there is the fault of falling into the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the failure to sever the various fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Regarding the innate view of a self (*sahaja-satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), it fundamentally arises based on one’s own and others’ bodies. Since the body consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and four of these aggregates are formless, one investigates by inferring from form;
thus, through three general principles, the characteristics of the body cannot be found when seeking them. This refers to the arising of form.
1. Because there is the primary (bhūta) and the derived (bhautika), if one were to separate the primary from the derived, the latter would not exist;

thus, they are one. 2. Because they are mutually dependent causes for one another, since the primary elements and the derived matter are mutually dependent causes, they fundamentally lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
3. Because the great elements and form do not aggregate, their nature is without combination. Observing the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in this way:

Since neither existence nor non-existence can be apprehended, what is there for the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) to rely upon? Therefore it is said that in the chapter on existence and non-existence, the view of a self does not manifest.
Once the view of a self is severed, craving also does not arise; thus, the craving and other afflictions produced by the view of a self are also severed. Regarding the characteristic of doubt:
the text explains doubt by way of its opposite, "not doubting," meaning that one has attained the dharma and perceives its characteristics well. This refers to the first [stage].
When a person on the path of fruition has thoroughly understood the Dharma of the Four Truths without delusion, they possess the characteristic of "good vision.

Because the two previous types of deluded views regarding the self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have been severed, they are no longer obscured; they naturally and clearly distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.

They no longer give rise to the notion of a teacher among other outsiders—regarding them as either pure or impure—and thus they harbor no doubts concerning the Buddha regarding what is wholesome or unwholesome.
This is also because the characteristic of doubt does not arise; when it does not arise, the three fetters (saṃyojana) are definitively severed.

Since the fundamental afflictions of views are severed simultaneously [with the other two], the statement here that they are "severed first" is made to indicate the sequential order of the characteristics of the afflictions. As for attachment to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), this refers to regarding what is not the true path as the path.
However, a person who has attained the first fruit (srotāpanna) does not cling to such precepts, for they clearly perceive the realms where those precepts lead to rebirth.
Because it is characterized by suffering, one sees that its karmic fruit is merely the toil of ascetic practices; therefore, one does not take them up again.
This further explanation of "taking up" clarifies the error of the non-Buddhists' adoption and practice [of such disciplines], such as observing the precepts of the cock or the dog.
As for those who seek rebirth for the sake of various objects of pleasure, this means they rely on the five desires and other such requisites as pleasure, which is not the same as *samādhi*.
Regarding such "pleasure," even if one seeks its fruit of bliss, what substance actually exists therein? One does not adopt these precepts because they lack substance;
yet one does not disparage self-restraint, for it is also the cultivation of actual practice. Therefore it is said:

"Excluding the dedication toward the excellence of self-awakening" means that those very practices cultivated as causes are dedicated toward the fruit, being untainted (*anāsrava*) in their characteristics and conduct.

Furthermore, one also upholds the "limbs of morality" (*śīlāṅga*); "limbs" refers to constituent parts, such as the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) or the fivefold morality (*pañcāṅga-śīla*), and so forth.
Although one does not grasp those [other categories], one does grasp these; for according to the Great Teaching, this too constitutes grasping.
Moreover, regarding the "three fetters," they consist of views (*dṛṣṭi*). Because views are severed, craving, delusion, and the like do not arise; thus, within views, there is volition (*cetanā*).
Furthermore, one should not again give rise to the thought, "I have not accomplished these fetters. This refers to those among the *srotāpannas* who have not attained full realization;
they say, "I have not accomplished them," which means "I do not possess them. This immediately falls into the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*).
To have a self is the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which remains as the first fault. If the root is not eliminated, the branches will persist.
By what means could one depart [from existence] without also severing the various fetters? This would be a double error.
Generally, for anyone who holds such a view, it is impossible to say they do not fall [into error] while being able to sever [the fetters]. (2)
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has spoken of many kinds of craving. Which among these is the craving that must be severed?

The Buddha told Mahāmati, “It is the fondness for women, being entangled in and greedily attached to them through various means, performing evil deeds of body and speech, and experiencing pleasure in the present while planting the seeds of future suffering.
That [craving] does not arise. Why is this? Because one attains the correct reception of samādhi.”
Because of delighting in this, that abandonment does not lead to Nirvana; rather, it is the abandonment of craving, O Mahāmati. What, Mahāmati, are the characteristics of a Sakṛdāgāmin?
It is one who suddenly illuminates the characteristics of form, the characteristics of the arising of false discrimination, and the characteristics of views, so that they do not arise;

because of well-perceiving the characteristics of the progression of dhyāna, he returns once more to this world to reach the end of suffering and attain Nirvana. Therefore, he is called a Sakṛdāgāmin. What, Mahāmati, is an Anāgāmin...?

Anāgāmin refers to one who, having seen the faults of the arising of the nature and non-nature of form in the past, future, and present, no longer gives rise to deluded thoughts through the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and because they have severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*), they are called Anāgāmin.

Mahāmati, Arhat refers to one who, by means of the powers and insights of the various dhyānas, samādhis, and liberations, realizes that afflictions, suffering, and deluded thoughts are without intrinsic nature; therefore, they are called Arhat.
Since the Buddha has taught that the meaning of "greed" (*rāga*) is manifold, he asks again which kind of greed is to be abandoned.

When the Buddha mentions its most prominent forms, it implies that the others should likewise be eliminated; thus, his intention lies in providing instruction and admonition. This is why it is said, and so forth.
That one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) is forever free from female bodies and birth in the four miserable realms is because they have been able to sever [the roots of existence].
Its root is what is called the experience of present pleasure which sows the seeds of future suffering; it all originates from this.
Yet, present pleasure is not necessarily pleasure, for future suffering is indeed suffering. Thus, both pleasure and suffering are suffering—is this not something to be scrutinized?
If so, by what means can one change this? Only the bliss of samādhi can do so.
