The *Yì* says: "Because one attains the bliss of samādhi and right reception (*samyak-samāpatti*), one does not give rise [to further existence].

Thus, even if one were to take that away and give it here, one would still be unable to exhaust the root of craving and attachment. Therefore, it is further said: "Not seeking nirvana, but severing craving to perfect *bodhi*.
This means that while suppressing the root of self-love may be considered nirvana, one must necessarily eliminate both the branches and the root together before reaching the ultimate conclusion.
Ultimately, one must sever what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* calls the "mechanism of lust," ensuring that even the nature of this mechanism is severed so that it no longer exists;

in this, one perceives the Tathāgata’s skillful guidance. Next, the identity of the two fruits is clarified: after the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), when one again contemplates the True through the conditions of further reflection, there is only the single contemplation of emptiness, which suddenly illuminates the five aggregates (*skandhas*) such that their material characteristics and delusive thoughts are seen as distinct from those of the first fruit. Thus, one cultivates the four practices.

Because of contemplation, one attains the name "sudden. Regarding the non-arising of the characteristics of birth and views: this means that the various fetters are the characteristic of birth, while deluded conceptualization is the characteristic of views;
because these do not arise, one relies solely on untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

Thus, one clearly perceives the characteristics of the stages of dhyāna and advances in severing the thoughts of desire until reaching the exhaustion of the six grades [of the first dhyāna]. Because there remains only one more birth, it is called "coming suddenly."
Regarding those who have reached the end of suffering in this realm and are equal to *anāgāmins*: they contemplate that the characteristics and nature of form are neither existent nor non-existent;
being non-existent, they are empty. There is only the addition of the distinctions of the three periods of time. Thus, one perceives the faults of arising;

having recognized them as faults through the two aforementioned marks, one cuts them off so they do not arise again. Therefore it is said: "to prevent delusive thoughts from arising" and "because the fetters are severed. This refers to the latter [of the two].

The three grades of abandonment refer to the Arhat, who—by means of the wisdom and concentration cultivated through the various dhyānas, samādhis, and so forth, as well as the dharmas realized therein—clearly perceives that the three paths of afflictions, suffering, and so on are not inherently existent;
having exhausted the volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) of the two upper realms, he realizes the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). (3)
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, the World-Honored One speaks of three kinds of arhats. To which of these does this refer?

World-Honored One, is it the śrāvaka who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility, or is it a bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifesting as an arhat through skillful means, or a transformation buddha created by a buddha?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “It refers to the śrāvaka who has attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility.”

It is not for others; rather, it is because of their practice of the bodhisattva path, their skillful means of emanating Buddha-transformations, and their original vows, that they manifest birth within the great assembly to adorn the Buddha’s retinue.

Mahāmati, in the realm of conceptual construction, various teachings are expounded—such as attaining fruits and attaining dhyāna—yet since those who enter dhyāna are entirely free from them, one manifests the attainment of self-mastery.

The attainment of the fruit through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the mind is called "attaining the fruit. Furthermore, Mahāmati, those who wish to transcend the realms of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) should abandon the characteristics of what is directly perceived by their own minds.
Mahāmati, it is not the case that one transcends the direct perception of one's own mind through the meditative attainments of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-samāpatti*); why?
Because there is still the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*). At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
And he spoke in verse:
"The various dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the formless attainments, the samādhis, and the cessation of all sensation and perception—all these are merely the mind's measure; they do not exist.
The fruit of stream-entry, the once-returner, the non-returner, and arhatship—these are likewise the delusions of the mind."

When the practitioner of dhyāna severs both the meditation and its objects, knowing and seeing the ultimate truth, this is merely the measure of delusive thought; if one awakens to this, it is liberation.
This third section distinguishes the names and characteristics of the four fruits, both in their commonality and their particularity, in order to clarify the provisional and the real.

Since the first three fruits can be understood by implication when the fourth is mentioned, only the ultimate one is shown here. As for what are called the "three kinds," they are listed as in the sūtra; now, regarding what is said...
Because it is one of the three [vehicles], it is said that the śrāvaka attains the path of the single vehicle of tranquility, and not others;

this means they do not include the other two types of provisional practices. As for the term "single vehicle," it refers to one of the three vehicles, not the single vehicle as revealed through the ultimate opening and manifestation.
If one speaks of it in relation to bodhisattvas in a hidden sense, it may also refer to the skillful means and original vows, which are the remaining two types.
By virtue of his original vows, he manifests the adornments of arhats as members of the Buddha’s retinue; this refers to what is known as the "convergence of shadows and echoes.
When he speaks of attaining fruits or attaining dhyāna within the realm of deluded thought, it is said for the purpose of causing sentient beings to practice and realize these states.
Although he speaks of attaining dhyāna, he does not abide in dhyāna, even as he conforms to it.

The manifestation of the mind-measure (cittamātra) results in the attainment of the fruit, yet one does not abide in that fruit; therefore it is said that "the practitioner of dhyāna enters dhyāna and is entirely detached.
This means that the "practitioner" is the person who enters, and "dhyāna" is that which is entered; because one does not give rise to attachment or relish [in the state], one is entirely detached.
By analogy, the attainment of the fruit should likewise require detachment; thus, this is not the same as the practice of actual realization.

Since one abides in neither of these two, this is precisely the transcendence of dhyāna; therefore, next the characteristics of the transcendence of dhyāna are shown so that one may abandon that [lower state] and attain this [higher state].
Thus it is said: "Desiring to transcend dhyāna... Here, "dhyāna" refers to the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless concentrations.

When one is detached from the marks of the self-manifesting cognition (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), and the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*) reaches its ultimate limit, then there is Tathāgata-dhyāna. Such is cessation.

One might ask: "Does not the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) also transcend the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*)? Therefore, [the text] further distinguishes it, saying: "No;

because therein still exists the grasping for the cessation of perception and feeling, that too is the measure of the mind. Thus, one must be entirely free from all of these. When one seeks that which transcends, that which is free, or that which has ceased, none of them can be apprehended.
As the *Awakening of Mahāśrī* (*Mahāśrī-vivaraṇa*) says: "The illumination and the illuminator are simultaneous."

"Quiescence (nirvāṇa) may perhaps be attained through this. The verse states, "The various dhyānas, the four immeasurables," and so forth, which praises the aforementioned arising of the characteristics of dhyāna.
Regarding the phrase "the mind measures that which does not exist," the word "that" (*tat*) is profoundly worthy of reflection.

The verse states, "The fruit of Srotāpanna and so forth," which praises the aforementioned four fruits of liberation; yet, to dismiss them as "great" [in a derogatory sense] does not avoid confusion. This is so.

Therefore, one must transcend both the practitioner of dhyāna and the dhyāna itself, as well as that which enters and that which is entered, the objects of focus for dhyāna, and the realization of the cessation of suffering and the knowledge of its origin through the vision of the True Dharma—all these are but the mental constructs of deluded thought within the nature of quiescence.
If one awakens to the fact that nothing exists, then ultimate liberation is attained, yet it is an attainment wherein nothing is attained. (4) ○ Right.
Chapter Thirteen.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of awakening: the awakening of investigation and the awakening that establishes through the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of conceptualization.
Mahāmati, the awakening of investigation refers to that which investigates the nature and characteristics of self-nature, being free from the four [extremes].
The non-apprehension of these positions is called the "investigation of awakening," O Mahāmati. Regarding those four positions:

they are defined as being free from identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, and both existence-and-non-existence and neither-existence-nor-non-existence, as well as permanence and impermanence; these are called the four positions, O Mahāmati.
Being free from these four positions is called "all dharmas," O Mahāmati. One should study and practice the investigation of all dharmas through these four positions.
As stated previously, if awakening constitutes liberation, then the path of awakening is likewise vast.
If its characteristics are not clearly defined and its principles are not fully exhausted, how could one hope to reach liberation? Therefore, the two types of awakening are further clarified.
Although their names are listed as if they were distinct—true and false—the concluding text states: "The Bodhisattva achieves..."

These are all what the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) contemplate; yet because the ultimate and conventional truths differ, the first is the awakening to the ultimate truth, and the second is the awakening to the conventional truth.
This is truly because the Bodhisattva contemplates the ultimate without abandoning the conventional, and illuminates the conventional without omitting the ultimate.
Relying on one to practice both, and cultivating both to manifest the Middle Way—though the ultimate and conventional [differ], [they are unified].
When differences are found to accord with reality, only then can it be called "correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*).

Regarding the statement within the explanation of characteristics that "if one contemplates the self-nature of the nature of awakening," "awakening" (*jue*) is synonymous with "contemplation" (*guan*); this means that by contemplating the self-nature of the nature through reality, one speaks from the perspective of the fundamental source.
Furthermore, when it says, "these four lines of observation apply to all phenomena," it speaks from the perspective of the derivative manifestations. These two perspectives are unified.
To speak of it is to contemplate the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena;

this nature is primordially devoid of characteristics and cannot be analyzed or discriminated by means of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), such as identity or difference. Therefore, it is said that through selection, it is found to be beyond the four propositions and unobtainable.
If one were to ask: "Is this nature identical? Is it different? Is it both? Is it neither? Or is it permanent, or impermanent? [it remains beyond such conceptualization].

These fall within the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), yet they are not the means by which the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*) is realized. Since all [propositions] are now sought and found to be unobtainable, one is thereby free from those four propositions;
thus it is said that "those four propositions" refers to the four propositions to be abandoned, such as identity (*ekatva*) and difference (*anyatva*).
These four propositions are precisely the means by which one abandons them. Furthermore, it is said that these four propositions are termed "the abandonment."
"All dharmas" refers to that which can transcend, and having transcended, returns to the source to accord with the nature (*dharmatā*).

To speak exhaustively according to principle, what is there that is not transcended, and what is there that is not identical? If one contemplates in this way, then that which transcends and the act of transcending spontaneously vanish and merge.
As stated in the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*, once one has transcended the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), this state alone is called "non-existence" (*amātra*).

Because all phenomena are subject to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one knows that when ordinary beings perceive them through their deluded minds, they fall into the views of the four extremes;

when those of the Two Vehicles contemplate them, they merely distance themselves from existence and so forth. Now, speaking from the ultimate perspective, they are all equally transcended in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*).

In short, as long as even a single trace of passionate conceptualization remains unexhausted, it is not yet the present awakening. Therefore, the exhortation concludes as follows: "Thus, these four extremes..."
This refers to removing the instruments that perceive objects upon the sensory realms; if the perception of objects is truly removed, one returns to the fundamental wondrous clarity.
All dharmas are nothing but the single nature of awakening (*bodhi*), and this nature of awakening is itself without self-nature—it is merely a provisional designation. (1)
Mahāmati, what is the awakening that consists in the grasping, attachment, and establishment of the characteristics of false discrimination?

It refers to the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination—namely, solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—which are unreal; it is the establishment based on the attachment to the characteristics of the four great elements, as well as to propositions, reasons, and examples, which are all unreal.
This is called the awakening that consists in the grasping, attachment, and establishment of the characteristics of false discrimination.

These are called the two kinds of marks of awakening. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes these two marks of awakening—the mark of the selflessness of persons and phenomena—and thoroughly understands skillful means, they attain the awakening of non-existence, observe the stages of practice, and enter the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Therein, they attain one hundred samādhis, attain the samādhi of differentiation, see one hundred Buddhas and one hundred bodhisattvas, and know the limits of the past and future.

Each [bodhisattva] illuminates the events of a hundred kalpas and a hundred buddha-fields; they know the characteristics of the progressively higher stages (*uttarottara-bhūmi*), possess the excellence of great vows, and attain mastery over spiritual powers.
They receive the empowerment of the Dharma-cloud (*dharmameghābhiṣeka*) and shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening.

With their minds firmly bound to the ten inexhaustible phrases, they mature sentient beings through various transformations, adorn themselves with the light of radiance, and attain the samādhi of the noble bliss of self-awakening.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should be skilled in the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
How does a Bodhisattva become skilled in the primary elements and derived matter? Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva forms this realization regarding those who perceive ultimate truth (*paramārtha*):

"Those primary elements are unarisen. Having observed that those primary elements are unarisen, he observes in this way; having observed, he realizes that names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) are [unreal].

The limits of false conceptualization are the limits of what is manifested by one's own mind; external natures are neither existent nor non-existent. This is called the limit of conceptualization as it appears from the mind.
That is to say, when observing the three realms, one perceives that the nature of the four great elements and derived form is free from the four extremes. It is pure and detached from "I" and "mine.
It abides in its own segments according to the true characteristic and its own specific characteristic, established through the self-characteristic of non-arising.

Second, regarding the establishment of awakening: this refers to apprehending through the characteristics of false conceptualization (*parikalpita*) and thereby establishing the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);

it is in this manner that one awakens (the meaning of "awakening" will be explained later). Now, as for what has been awakened to previously, all things are devoid of characteristics, and thus even the worldly four great elements cannot be found.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva relies upon the nature of the four great elements—solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion.

Although the five-membered syllogism—consisting of the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and so forth—established by positing the four great elements is ultimately unreal, it is nevertheless established for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Thus, the two modes of the ultimate and the conventional do not obstruct one another, and through this, the gateway of the transformation of reality is established;
such is the general purport. Furthermore, statements such as "conceptual construction is unreal" all [arise] from... [the perspective of ultimate truth].

He is not a bodhisattva. If a bodhisattva establishes the characteristics of the two types of awakening by means of the subsequent realization, because they are established through the initial awakening, they know the characteristic of non-self in persons and phenomena;
because they are established through the subsequent awakening, they realize the characteristic of non-self without departing from persons and phenomena.
Therefore, it is said that those who thoroughly understand skillful means possess the awakening of non-existence; this awakening is itself the two kinds [of realization].
After *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) have passed through the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), one finally attains entry into the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Regarding the visions of Buddhas and other phenomena within samādhi, these are all described as being "a hundredfold" in the First Stage, "a thousandfold" in the Second Stage, and "ten-thousandfold" in the Third Stage; these are all teachings concerning the progressive increase in excellence along the Path.

As for the Ten Inexhaustible Phrases (*daśākṣaya-pada*), according to the "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, when abiding in the first stage, the Joyful (*pramuditā*), there are ten kinds of inexhaustibility.
Regarding the passage on "the limit of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-pada*) and so forth: it is also like the ten vows of Samantabhadra’s practices, all of which speak of being inexhaustible.
By binding the mind with these virtues, one matures sentient beings and causes them to attain these marks of benefit; thus, the practices and vows of a Bodhisattva reach their consummation.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the following section provides a retrospective explanation of the characteristics of the four great elements and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*); although they were briefly established previously, they have not yet been fully explained.
To explain this thoroughly, it is shown again in two parts. First, clarifying the capacity for contemplation (*vitarka-vicāra*), it says: "The Bodhisattva makes such an awakening," and so forth.

That the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are non-arising in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the underlying principle (*yukti*). This also follows from the preceding discussion on observation and awakening. However, the principle is not that the four great elements do not exist;
rather, it directly reveals their signlessness (*animitta*), hence they are said to be "non-arising. This is precisely what the Bodhisattva brings about.

Thus, one contemplates non-arising as arising within non-arising; this is because there are the names and characteristics of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) due to the conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*) of their limits.
That is to say, each of the four great elements has its own names and characteristics, which are the limits of conceptual proliferation.

Furthermore, investigating the source from which the four great elements arise, they are also the limits of what is manifested by one's own mind; that is to say, the triple world is nothing but mind (*cittamātra*).

It is so. It is precisely because one awakens to the fact that the four great elements are nothing other than manifestations of the mind, and realizes that external natures have no inherent nature, that this is the contemplation of the nature of the four great elements as being devoid of created form (*rūpa*).
To contemplate their nature as devoid [of such form] is to realize that they are unborn according to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

By means of these four propositions, one thoroughly purifies the four great elements; thus, the four great elements themselves are perfectly free from the four natures. From this, one is detached from "I" and "mine."
Thus, because all things are detached from detachment, they return to their original state; because they return to their original state, each phenomenon (*dharma*) does not lose its own essence.

Therefore, it is called the "suchness-mark" (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*). The abiding of self-marks in distinct segments refers to the "same-mark" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), while the abiding of self-marks in distinct segments refers to the "different-mark" (*viśe�ṣalakṣaṇa*).
When these natures of sameness and difference do not obstruct one another, this is precisely non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Through such characteristics, this wisdom capable of awakening is formed (2).
Mahāmati, how do the four great elements give rise to derived matter? It is said: from the great element of the delusion of moisture, the internal and external water element arises;
from the great element of the delusion of capability, the internal and external fire element arises; from the great element of the delusion of movement... [the wind element arises].

When the internal and external wind-elements arise, they sever the false conceptualization of form; yet the great elements give rise to the forms of the internal and external earth-elements, as well as space.
Clinging to these as false truths, the five aggregates accumulate and the four great elements produce derivative matter.

O Mahāmati, because consciousness delights in various traces and objective realms, one continues into other realms of existence. O Mahāmati, this includes the four great elements such as earth and their derivative matter.

The four great elements have conditions that are not those of the four great elements themselves. Why is this? It is because they arise from the conjunction of nature (*svabhāva*), form (*saṃsthāna*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), place (*deśa*), action (*kriyā*), and means (*upāya*).
Great Wisdom, when nature, form, characteristics, place, action, and means are combined, there is production;
it is not that which is formless. Therefore, the externalists' false imaginings regarding the marks of derived matter produced by the four great elements do not belong to me.
Next, to clarify the phenomena that are to be awakened to, we again refer back to the preceding text to investigate and explain their characteristics.

Regarding those four great elements (*mahābhūta*), from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), these four great elements are "those" four great elements, and ultimate truth itself is also referred to as "those.

As for the statement that the four great elements give rise to derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), this means that the great elements act as the producers (*janaka*), just as previously described in terms of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion.

This is so because the four great elements serve as the basis for what is derived from them, as in the case of the internal and external water-elements and others mentioned later, which are collectively termed "form" (rūpa).

According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, however, they arise through mutual interaction; for instance, it says: "Because luminous awareness and empty dullness depend upon one another, they produce agitation, and thus there is the wind-circle," and so forth.
In the present context, since each element is produced according to its own kind, the moist great element gives rise to water.
The great elements and so forth are, at first glance, distinct in their textual descriptions, yet in principle they all interpenetrate.

Generally speaking, when we speak of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), none arise without depending on their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to manifest their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). From their initial emergence, they progress toward manifestation; these characteristics are formed by conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) as secondary developments, arising from seeds.
Thus, the generation of the myriad categories of things is rooted in the single mind. That which is moistening, capable, mobile, or obstructive each [functions according to its specific nature].

This is explained according to the respective natures and portions of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Furthermore, it is quite reasonable to speak of the fourfold division of afflictions (*kleśa*) in terms of moisture and so forth;
therefore, each is called "false conceptualization" (*vitarka*) and "great variety. All of these arise from the primary elements (*dhātu*).
Once they have become manifest, they constitute the internal and external four great elements, which are the sentient beings themselves.
The primary retribution is the internal, and the secondary retribution is the external; both pervade all things and coexist with space.

Therefore, it is said that "form and space coexist," etc., which further implies the two great elements of space and consciousness. Regarding space, as previously mentioned, it is space that enters into the category of form;
yet externalists become attached to this as a false truth, speculating on its existence or non-existence.

Having already refuted the section on arising as before, he continues by saying: "The aggregates (*skandha*) arise from the collection of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).

Because of these aforementioned four great elements and derived matter, the five aggregates exist; because of the aggregates, the six sense bases (*āyatana*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) arise therein, following that same sequence.
Therefore it is said: 'Consciousness arises dependent upon various traces and objective spheres (*viṣaya*),' meaning..."
Because the six consciousnesses enter, exit, and traverse the objects of their sensory realms, they are further termed "traces.

It is precisely because these consciousnesses cling to delusive objects that illusory karma is formed, whereby the six destinies continue in succession. As for the term "the rest," it refers to those within the six destinies where one serves as the basis and the others are called "the rest.
Furthermore, it is said that the four great elements—earth and so forth—and the derivative matter possess the conditions of the four great elements.

This indicates that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not produce [phenomena] alone, but must be accompanied by conditions (*pratyaya*), yet they do not reside exclusively within those conditions;

therefore, it is said: "It is not those four great elements, nor the conditions. Why is this so? The following text investigates and explains its meaning: "Nature" (such as the nature of moisture) refers to the cause (*hetu*);

"form and appearance" (the color and characteristics of the four great elements), "location," and "functional application" refer to the conditions (*pratyaya*). If there were no cause for arising, then even with conditions, [phenomena] would not be produced.
Furthermore, because they do not arise, they are called "great elements" (*mahābhūta*). If these great elements do not arise, they do not exist within conditions (*pratyaya*).

If forms were necessarily produced through the combination of various conditions such that they were not formless, then they would likewise exist within conditions. Since they neither exist nor do not exist, they are fundamentally without real nature (*svabhāva*).
That which arises from a lack of nature is precisely the manifestation of the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). As for what is called "external":
Regarding the statement, "The conceptualization of a path is not the self," this is a refutation based on the preceding discourse concerning attachment to false truths;
it does not mean that these four great elements and their derivative forms are different from the conceptual constructions and discriminations of non-Buddhists.

Therefore, it says, "it is not the self. Alternatively, some claim this is a doctrine of the non-Buddhists, asserting it is not our own Dharma; because of this single phrase, they have all lost their way.
Our school now maintains that one should carefully examine the underlying principle; why needlessly be confused by the literal phrasing?

Although this is so, how can it be that the Wei translation speaks of "the externalists' false discrimination regarding the four great elements and the four sense-objects as being non-self," whereas in our own Dharma there is no such discrimination?
To explain it directly as we have done above does not contradict it; moreover, the wording and meaning of the two translations are not without points of agreement.
Because they differ, one should know that this text is not necessarily exhaustive; it relates significantly to the intent of the teaching, so let us examine it further (3).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates (*skandha*). What are the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates? They are the five aggregates. What are the five?

They are form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Among them, four aggregates are non-material (*arūpin*): namely, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Mahāmati, as for form (*rūpa*), it consists of the four great elements and the derivative forms, each having its own distinct characteristic.

Mahāmati, it is not that non-form (*arūpa*) possesses the number four in the manner of space. For example, just as space transcends numerical characteristics and is detached from numbers, yet through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) one speaks of "one space";

so too, Mahāmati, the aggregates (*skandha*) transcend numerical characteristics and are detached from numbers; they are free from existence and non-existence, and detached from the numbers of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are what are spoken of by the speech of foolish commoners, not that of the noble sages. Mahāmati, the various forms and images of the noble ones are like illusions, free from the conceptualization of difference or non-difference;
they are also like dreams, reflections, or the body of a person, being free from difference or non-difference.

Therefore, Mahāmati, the way the noble wisdom approaches is that the manifestations of the false imaginings of the aggregates (*skandha-vikalpa*) are called the "characteristic of the self-nature of the aggregates. You should eliminate them.

Having taught the dharma of tranquility after the cessation of all cessations, Mahāmati spoke of the purification of the view of selflessness in phenomena and the severing of all heterodox views regarding the Buddha-fields.
When he taught this dharma of tranquility, [beings] entered the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Having entered the Immovable Stage, they attained mastery over immeasurable samādhis, obtained the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), and through the attainment of the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), they realized the ultimate power and clarity of their own nature.
Just as the great earth supports and nurtures all sentient beings,
so too does the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva universally rescue and benefit all sentient beings.
Next, the self-nature and characteristics of the five aggregates (*skandha*) are explained.

Since the fundamental numerical principle of the aggregates is non-numerical, when one speaks of the essence of the aggregates as being fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*), the principle for both the sage and the ordinary person is one; there is no need to abandon the aggregates in order to seek reality.
The text first mentions "number" because form (*rūpa*) and the non-form aggregates each have four counts. Therefore, it says: "Those four aggregates are non-form," and further: "Furthermore..."
Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) each have distinct characteristics;

that is, because the four great elements differ, they are collectively termed "form," and thus form also possesses four [aspects]. Next, regarding "non-enumerable" (*asaṃkhyeya*): both form and formlessness are non-enumerable.
Furthermore, for the sake of convenience, this is demonstrated by way of formlessness; therefore it is said that there are not four enumerations of formlessness, being like space.
Emptiness correctly states that the four formless aggregates (*arūpin-skandha*) are fundamentally not four; they are like empty space, which is also fundamentally not one.
To "transcend number" means to be free from numbers such as one, ten, hundred, and thousand. To transcend is to go beyond the mutual dependence of the many and the few;
yet number and non-number are still not free from number. Only when one transcends them is the essence itself non-numerical, as in the case of what is called "Buddha."

The body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories. It is further said that it is immeasurable; having transcended all measure, there is nothing it does not encompass and nothing it does not transcend.
Yet, when one deludedly speaks of "one empty space," how could this be what is meant by empty space? Such is the case with the combination of the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth.
Speaking from the perspective of the aggregates themselves, they properly belong to the realm of numerical characteristics; yet, in their ultimate sense, they have transcended and departed from them.
If one examines the substance of the aggregates (*skandha*) as it truly is, what is one and what are four?
Since the aggregates and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, there is no suffering to be abandoned; how then could there be any question of number or non-number?

Thus it is said: "Detached from being and non-being, etc. This means one does not fall into existence, non-existence, or the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*), just as space is beyond numbering. Number...

Regarding "characteristics," the following section contrasts the sage with the ordinary person to demonstrate the transcendence of characteristics: it means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas realize the aggregates (*skandhas*) are like illusions;
although they manifest various forms and images, these are free from the conceptual constructs of difference or non-difference. Therefore, they do not give rise to views such as oneness or otherness.
This principle is likewise true for the appearance of a human body within a dream or a reflection. By clarifying this through such reasoning, then—

Because the Noble Ones approach [reality] through wisdom, they are free from the notions of difference and non-difference; whereas ordinary people, because of deluded manifestations, fall into numerical characteristics and fail to realize that which is beyond number.
Although there is a distinction between delusion and awakening, the principle of the aggregates (*skandha*) remains the same;

thus it is said that "the Noble Wisdom approaches them as the same, while the aggregates appear through false imagination. This means that their underlying principle is one. Therefore, the concluding exhortation states: "Know that one need only eliminate delusion."
Since the very substance of the aggregates (*skandha*) is originally quiescent, perception is said to be a quiescent dharma.

Furthermore, the mention of "Buddha-fields" in order to sever all views of external paths is intended to demonstrate that Buddhas, Māras, and followers of external paths have never existed apart from one another.
Moreover, it is said that "the time of teaching quiescence" refers to the moment of realizing the principle; it is a teaching without words, wherein no dharma is perceived.
Because it can be attained, one perceives the purity of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) and enters the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Attaining through non-attainment, one acquires immeasurable samādhis and all other dharma-gates, universally saving all classes of beings, just as the great earth supports and nurtures all things.
(4) This concludes the fourteenth chapter.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvāṇa taught by the various non-Buddhists. What are these four? They are: (1) the nirvāṇa of the self-nature of things being neither existence nor non-existence;
(2) the nirvāṇa of the non-existence of the nature of various characteristics; (3) the nirvāṇa of the realization that the self-characteristic of self-nature is neither existence nor non-existence;
and (4) the nirvāṇa of severing the continuity and flow of the aggregates' own and common characteristics. These are called the four kinds of nirvāṇa of the various non-Buddhists.
“Nirvāṇa is not what I teach, Mahāmati. What I teach, Mahāmati, is that the cessation of the conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*) is called nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, do you not establish the existence of the eight consciousnesses? The Buddha said: “I do establish them, Mahāmati. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“If they are established, why is it that one is liberated from the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) and not from the seven [other] consciousnesses? The Buddha told Mahāmati: “It is because...”

Due to causes and their corresponding objects of perception, the seven consciousnesses do not arise independently; rather, consciousness arises through the attachment to segmented objects and the nourishment of habit-energies (*vāsanā*).

It arises from the conditions of the thought that clings to "self" and "mine" in conjunction with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the mental faculty (*manas*), producing an indestructible semblance of a body.
Furthermore, due to the storehouse consciousness taking its own mind-manifested objects as its cause and object of perception, the collection of minds arises through mutual interaction and clinging.
For example, it is like the waves of the ocean; when the wind of objective realms manifested from one's own mind blows upon them, they arise and cease in the same way.
Therefore, when the *manovijñāna* ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

I do not possess the nature of nirvana through the activity of its characteristics or through false conceptualization; such is the nature of the *vijñapti-mātra* consciousness. When this ceases, my nirvana occurs.
That which serves as the cause and the object-condition for the formation of the body, along with the mental tendencies (*āśaya*), is the mind that acts as the support for consciousness.
Just as waves do not arise when the great flow of water is exhausted, so too, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) ceases, the various forms of consciousness do not arise.
Permanence, bliss, self, and purity are called *nirvāṇa*, wherein nothing is not ultimate; how could it be exhausted by a single path or a single aspect?
However, this [definition] takes the cessation of deluded conceptualization and consciousness as *nirvāṇa* specifically to refute the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

They reckon that there are four kinds of *nirvāṇa*: essential nature (*svabhāva*), self-nature (*svabhāva*), non-essential nature (*asvabhāva*), and so forth, as will be shown according to the subsequent verse.

The text states: "To falsely calculate that which is produced by nature as being the agent and the mark of *nirvāṇa*—that is, to regard the marks of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and so forth as *nirvāṇa* because they are 'non-nature' (*aniḥsvabhāva*)—or alternatively, to reverse the preceding [view] and take 'nature' (*svabhāva*) and so forth to refer to what is non-existent;

thirdly, to combine and oppose the two preceding views while calculating only a single capacity for cognitive perception; and fourthly, to calculate the marks of the various aggregates and their fluxes."

The commentary on the section concerning "severance" states that because all those who stubbornly cling to a self and persons do not depart from deluded consciousness, the Buddha spoke directly in terms of the extinction of deluded conceptual consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*) in order to refute external views and reveal the correct teaching. This does not mean that the *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata is limited to this alone;
however, by speaking of the extinction of consciousness, there is nothing it does not encompass. When the words are near yet the meaning is far-reaching, this is what is seen here.

Regarding this, Mahāmati’s intention was as follows: he harbored a doubt regarding the statement that "consciousness ceases," wondering whether it meant that the eight consciousnesses are not established, saying, "Is it that you do not establish the eight consciousnesses?
or whether it meant that the seventh consciousness does not cease, saying, "How can one be free from the mental consciousness if it is not the seventh consciousness?
The Buddha’s answer was that he indeed establishes the eight consciousnesses, because they are the fundamental source of all consciousnesses.
Because it is not subject to extinction, yet it is not that the seven consciousnesses do not cease; therefore it is said:
"Due to their causes and their objects of attachment, the seven consciousnesses do not arise. This means that what the seven consciousnesses grasp at is merely the self.

Since the causes and objects of those consciousnesses reside entirely within the six consciousnesses, when the six consciousnesses cease, the seven consciousnesses likewise do not arise. It may also be understood thus.
Because the cause resides in the eight consciousnesses while the conditions reside in the six consciousnesses, it is both extinguished and not extinguished.

Regarding "the mental consciousness," this section below generally demonstrates that the various consciousnesses are mutually dependent; they have never failed to coexist, such that their essence is one while their manifestations differ.
There are four points from which this does not deviate: first, because the mental consciousness arises from attachment to the divisions of objective realms, the six consciousnesses thereby [arise].

First, it arises from the six sense-objects; second, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) nourish the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and since the *manas* is conjoined with it, the six consciousnesses do not depart from the seventh and eighth consciousnesses;

third, it arises through the causal conditions of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that clings to "self" and "what belongs to self"—that is, the seventh consciousness which grasps at "mine" arises from conceptualizing those causes and those conditions.
Furthermore, the seven consciousnesses are not separate from the six consciousnesses. Fourth, the "unbroken body-form" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the eighth consciousness.
Because it takes as its object the manifestations of one’s own mind, it is the eighth consciousness;

because it relies upon the six consciousnesses as the cognizing subjects to again take as objects the manifestations of one’s own mind, these are the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). It is through this clinging that the six [consciousnesses] arise.
The "aggregation of consciousness-minds" (śikṣa-citta-puñja) refers to its ability to synthesize all minds; thus it is called a "mind-aggregate.

This means that the eight consciousnesses and the six consciousnesses arise from one another in a reciprocal manner; therefore, we know that the true nature of these various consciousnesses is one of mutual dependence.

Furthermore, there is the principle of "root and branch": viewed from the root, they evolve and manifest from the eight consciousnesses; viewed from the branch, they arise based on the proximate support of the six consciousnesses.

Therefore it is said: "They turn and depend on one another, like the waves of the ocean. Here, the ocean is used as a metaphor for the eight consciousnesses, and the waves for the six consciousnesses.

Taking the six sense-objects manifested by one's own mind as their boundary-condition (ālambana), the wind blows upon the ocean of the eight consciousnesses, causing the waves of the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna) to arise.
Thus, whether these various consciousnesses arise or cease, they exist solely in dependence upon the ocean.
The analogy of wind causing waves to surge through successive stages makes the meaning even clearer;

thus, the core point is reiterated and clarified as follows, without mentioning the cessation of the eight consciousnesses. From a logical standpoint, that which arises through mutual dependence must likewise cease through mutual dependence.

Therefore, although the eight consciousnesses themselves arise [from conditions] and would also cease, the text speaks of the cessation of the *manovijñāna* (seventh consciousness) here for the sake of brevity, referring to what is most proximate.

Thus, when all deluded thoughts and consciousnesses cease, there is only that which arises without cause; since it has no source from which it arises, it likewise has no destination from which it ceases.
This is the Tathāgatagarbha-consciousness, which is neither born nor extinguished—the ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

The verse states, "I am not of the nature of *nirvāṇa*," which correctly means that I do not regard the self-nature (*ātman*) and so forth as *nirvāṇa*, but rather [the cessation of] the burning heat of deluded thought alone.
The cessation of consciousness is *nirvāṇa*. This *tathatā* (suchness) is that which is known through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Regarding its cause and its object of attachment:

it is said that the seven consciousnesses arise from the causal conditions of the *manas* (mind-organ), thereby forming the six consciousness-bodies; therefore, when the six consciousnesses cease, the seventh consciousness also ceases accordingly.
Speaking of its own fundamental nature, that which serves as the cause for them is the eighth consciousness, the *ālayavijñāna*, which acts as the basis for all consciousnesses.

Because it is the support, this [seventh consciousness] likewise takes the eight consciousnesses as its cause. The passage on "the flow of the water-element being exhausted" and so forth uses a metaphor to clarify this meaning, which is the reverse of what was stated above.
Above, it was said that because the six consciousnesses cease, the seventh consciousness does not arise;

here, it is said that because the flow of the seventh consciousness is exhausted, the waves of the six consciousnesses do not arise. Thus, the dharma and the metaphor mutually clarify one another. Now, as for the water...
Because they are exhausted, the waves do not arise; when consciousness ceases, nirvāṇa manifests. One should reflect deeply upon the locus of this principle.

[End of] Chapter Fifteen. Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the general characteristics of the discrimination of the self-nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). If the self-nature of conceptualization...

Mahāmati, you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have well distinguished the common characteristics of penetration; you have transcended false imagination and attained the noble realization of self-awareness.
You have clearly seen that the external paths of non-Buddhists lead to commonality, and you have severed the false imaginings of grasped and grasper.

You understand that the various marks of dependent origination are themselves the nature of false imagination, and thus you no longer engage in further false imagining. Mahāmati, what is the penetration through the discrimination of the nature of false imagination?

Mutual discourse, the conceptualization of verbal expression, the conceptualization of things spoken of, the conceptualization of characteristics, the conceptualization of benefit, the conceptualization of self-nature,

the conceptualization of cause, the conceptualization of views, the conceptualization of accomplishment, the conceptualization of birth, the conceptualization of non-birth, the conceptualization of continuity,

and the conceptualization of bondage and non-bondage— these, Mahāmati, are called the general characteristics of the differentiation of the self-nature of conceptualization. What, Mahāmati, [is the specific characteristic]?
"Discursive thought regarding speech (*abhilāpa-vikalpa*) refers to the attachment to the sounds of various exquisite melodies and songs as being beautiful music;
this is called discursive thought regarding speech. Mahāmati, what is discursive thought regarding the objects expressed (*abhidheya-vastu-vikalpa*)?

It means that there are objects expressed which possess an intrinsic nature known by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*); based upon those, discursive thought regarding speech arises. This is called discursive thought regarding the objects expressed, Mahāmati."
What is the conceptualization of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vikalpa*)? It refers to the various attachments to the very things described, such as the mirage of a deer-thirst;
that is, the conceptualization of all natures through their characteristics of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—this is called the conceptualization of characteristics.

Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of benefits (*guṇa-vikalpa*)? It refers to the delighting in various kinds of gold, silver, and precious jewels—this is called the conceptualization of benefits, Mahāmati.
What is the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*)? It refers to the false view of conceptualizing that "this is its intrinsic nature, it is thus, and it is not otherwise";

this is called the conceptualization of intrinsic nature. Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of cause (*hetu-vikalpa*)? It refers to the appearance of causal characteristics through the discrimination of existence and non-existence regarding causes and conditions;
this is called the conceptualization of cause. Mahāmati, what is the conceptualization of views (*dṛṣṭi-vikalpa*)? It refers to [the views of] existence, non-existence, or oneness...
The false discrimination of views, Mahāmati, refers to the conceptual attachment to the false imaginings of externalists regarding difference, simultaneity, and non-simultaneity;

this is called the false discrimination of views. What is the false discrimination of establishment? It is the formation of a definitive doctrine based on the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self"; this is called the false discrimination of establishment. What is the false discrimination of origination?
It is the attachment to the arising of existence and non-existence as having intrinsic nature; this is called the false discrimination of origination.
Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of non-arising? It refers to the fact that all natures are fundamentally unarisen and lack seeds;
that which arises from causes and conditions is a body without cause. This is called the discrimination of non-arising. Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of continuity?
It refers to their mutual continuity, like gold and thread. This is called the discrimination of continuity. Mahāmati, what is the discrimination of bondage and non-bondage?
This refers to the attachment to the causes and conditions of bondage and non-bondage, such as the skillful means of a person regarding whether one is bound or liberated;

this is called the discrimination of the imagination of bondage and non-bondage. Regarding this, all foolish commoners discriminate its self-nature and general characteristics, clinging to existence and non-existence.

The faculty of deluded conceptualization is one; however, according to the various circumstances encountered, its calculations are immeasurable. Briefly stated, twelve types are presented to highlight the major points.
Yet, when investigated to the ultimate, there is nothing that is not delusion. To know this and remain undeluded is what is valued.
When discrimination awakens and is able to sever itself, even discrimination itself vanishes—this is the great purport. The text first provides a general clarification of discrimination.
Furthermore, regarding what is called "the nature of conceptual construction" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it is one of the three natures;

it does not exist in isolation, for the meanings of all three are fully present within it. This also expands upon the meaning of the three natures. If one can discern this well, one will not be deluded by it;

thus, by abandoning conceptual construction, one is able to reach the self-realized state of the noble ones (*ārya-gocara*) and clearly perceive the commonalities with those non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
The ultimate limit of these realms is nothing other than the delusion of the grasper and the grasped (*grāhya-grāhaka-vikalpa*).
As will be explained later, although there are various kinds [of phenomena], they do not, in total, transcend the delusion regarding the sense faculties and their objects.

Once one realizes that the grasper and the grasped are empty, delusion is severed; other dependent originations (*pratītyasamutpāda*) likewise no longer arise. Now, I shall illustrate this with a single analogy.
Dependent origination is like the great earth, and false conceptualization is like the seed; the practices arising from self-nature are like branches and leaves.
It is clearly visible that once the root is severed, all other delusions will naturally vanish. Next, the text is explained by listing its twelve terms individually.
Regarding the "self-nature of the phenomena spoken of": as for all the phenomena spoken of, one must exhaustively investigate their very source.
The nature [of things] is known only by the wisdom of the noble ones; ordinary fools do not understand it, but merely give rise to conceptualizations based on those phenomena.

These conceptualized appearances—such as the characteristics of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion that exist upon the phenomena described—are grasped and clung to by the ignorant through the perception of a mirage by a thirsty deer. They fail to know that their nature is fundamentally unified and identical.
The same applies to the conceptual attachment to the imagined nature; this nature is itself the dharma.

Regarding the phrase "clinging to this as self-nature," "clinging" (*dhāraṇa*) means to grasp; it refers to giving rise to a fixed view of self-nature toward all dharmas, grasping them as being thus and asserting that all else is not.
This is no different from a false view, because one clings to the nature as being real. Therefore.

"Discrimination" refers to the false conceptualization of dharmas such as existence and non-existence arising from causes and conditions, wherein one falsely perceives that each has its own distinct causal characteristics;
this too is a false and deluded view. "Discrimination" does not transcend views such as existence and non-existence, as is the case with the conceptual attachments of externalists.
"Non-arising discrimination" means that all natures are fundamentally unarisen. Directly...
This means that originally there is no nature of arising, like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit;
yet, if one perceives something as having arisen, one reckons it to be produced from no-seed causes and conditions, which is a body of causelessness.

Regarding "successive false conceptualization," this refers to those things that are successively continuous, meaning that the mind and those phenomena arise together in succession, like gold threads. According to the Tang translation, it says:
They are mutually interconnected like gold and thread; if one takes the thread as the string, then one should take the gold as the needle, for these two things are not used in isolation.

Thus, there is a mutual continuity between them. Regarding the deluded thoughts concerning "bondage" and "non-bondage," and the attachment to the causes and conditions of bondage and non-bondage—although various versions differ, one should rely on the present text.
To speak of this according to principle: the Dharma is fundamentally free from attachment; how could there be sentient beings who are bound?

It cannot be said that such [beings] do not exist, for they fixate upon and cling to views regarding the causes and conditions of bondage and non-bondage, and thus all constitute deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
This is like a person employing skillful means: it is only through the functional activity of a single individual that distinctions such as "bondage" and "liberation" arise.

This deluded thought may also be described as being "bound yet not bound," yet those who cling to it—such as people today who are firmly attached to sounds and forms while claiming to be free from attachment—are the very pinnacle of such delusion. Other instances can be inferred, so they are omitted here;
generally speaking, because one calculates that nothing exists outside of existence and non-existence, the conclusion is thus stated. (1)
Mahāmati, those who are attached to dependent origination cling to various kinds of imagined self-nature.

Like a magical illusion, it manifests in various forms; through the delusions of ordinary people, these various different illusions are perceived. Mahāmati, illusion and the various forms are neither different nor not different.
If they were different, illusion would not be the cause of the various forms; if they were not different, then [illusion] would be... [the various forms].
Although there are various [aspects], they are without differentiation; yet one perceives them as differentiated. Therefore, they are neither different nor not different.

For this reason, Mahāmati, you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should not harbor attachments to the imagined nature of dependent origination—which is like a magical illusion—as being either different or not different, existent or non-existent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
When the mind is bound by objects, consciousness and cognition follow along; yet, when there is nothing whatsoever, the wisdom of supreme equanimity arises.
While the imagined nature exists through conceptualization, it does not exist within dependent origination.

Or, if one grasps dependent origination as being non-conceptual, then the various constituent parts that arise would be like a magical illusion and would not constitute those characteristics; if there were various conceptualizations, they likewise would not be established.

Since the preceding section’s analysis of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) had not yet clarified that which is clung to, the following section clarifies that dependent origination (*paratantra*) is like an illusion, thereby demonstrating that the basis of deluded thought (*vikalpa*) is fundamentally empty. Thus it is said:

"clinging to dependent origination" uses "illusion" as a metaphor for the various bodies of dependent origination, and "body" as a metaphor for deluded thought. Ordinary fools do not understand this; they merely see...
Because people do not know that these various manifestations are illusory, it is shown to them that the illusion and the various manifestations are neither different nor non-different.

This can be understood by examining the preceding examples. In general, this reveals that phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because they are falsely conceptualized within dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are ultimately unfindable.
Therefore, one should not form attachments to them as being different or non-different, existent or non-existent, as stated in the verse at the beginning of the text.
The four lines of this verse, which universally address both delusion and awakening, express the essential meaning of the single stanza:

"When the mind is bound by objects" refers precisely to how external objects are able to bind because the mind is deluded. As previously stated, the twelve kinds of false conceptualization all arise from being bound by external objects;
yet, what binding power do external objects actually possess? It is just like being turned by things due to the inversion of the mind.

Therefore, even when objects are transformed, they have never truly been transformed. Perception and wisdom are fundamentally not two separate dharmas; because perception follows after objects, wisdom is transformed into perception.
If one realizes that phenomena are non-existent and reaches the most supreme state, then perception is again transformed back into wisdom.
Thus it is said: "When equalizing wisdom arises, one immediately turns away from deluded thoughts and returns to the self."

Awakened noble wisdom is this [very thing]. Regarding the statement that "the nature of false discrimination exists," there are sixteen lines of verse below which explain the two aforementioned natures.
Among these, the first eight lines state that the dependent origination of false discrimination consists of things that exist in mutual relation;

since existence and non-existence cannot stand together, where there is existence, there must be a metaphor. Of these, the first four lines concern the dharma: if the nature of false discrimination possesses various [manifestations], then...
Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) should not be something that can be apprehended, nor should it give rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by depending upon dependent origination.

If one holds that conceptual construction is what grasps those objects and thereby constitutes conceptual construction, then since dependent origination itself is not conceptual construction, how could it possibly constitute conceptual construction?
The latter four lines are a metaphor, meaning it is like a phantom person created by illusion.
If various constituent parts have already arisen previously, they do not depend upon illusion to subsequently come into being—this is like the first two lines mentioned above.
If the various [parts] exist because of that illusory appearance, then since the false imagination itself lacks variety, the false imagination would also fail to be established.
This, in turn, reverses the latter two lines above to demonstrate that all are unobtainable; for this reason:
If one examines this, if one exists and the other does not, then two dharmas cannot be established. If there were two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), those natures would necessarily be contradictory;
how then could two separate dharmas combine to form a single conceptual construction? When sought through investigation, it cannot be found;
therefore, it has no real nature. (2)
Those marks are faults that all arise from the bonds of the mind; they are delusions (vikalpa) that lack knowledge of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
These various natures of delusion are themselves that delusion of dependent origination. Regarding the delusion of dependent origination, there are three types:
the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and the delusion of arising without cause. When the conventional truth is severed, it is the realm of the sages.
For example, when a practitioner of yoga contemplates a single object, various appearances manifest; yet in that [object], there are no signs of various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

It is just as various colors appear through the conceptual construction of cataracts, yet the cataract itself has no color; it is not that color is absent, but rather one fails to realize the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) [of the perception].
Furthermore, just as refined gold is free from all impurities and the sky is free from clouds and mists, so too is the purity of non-conceptualization.
There is no nature of false imagination, yet there is the establishment of that dependent origination; both its affirmation and its denial arise from false imagination.
If one destroys false imagination, then if there were no nature, there would be the nature of dependent origination; if there were no nature, there would be nature;

and if there were nature and no nature, they would arise based upon false imagination as their cause. Thus, one obtains the characteristics of that dependent origination, and names and characteristics constantly follow one another to give rise to all false imaginings.
Ultimate non-attainment means that once all deluded thoughts are transcended, wisdom becomes pure; this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The following eight phrases further state that these two are mutually dependent for their formation. Furthermore, there are two parts:

first, the initial four phrases directly demonstrate the point, stating that those characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) constitute a fault because they are bound by the mind; thus, they become faults due to mental bondage.
This is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). If conceptual construction were separated from dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there would be nothing known.

It is precisely upon conditions that conceptual construction arises. The subsequent four lines conclude the meaning; specifically, the first two lines conclude the second point previously discussed, and the latter two lines conclude the first point previously discussed.
To speak from this perspective: conditions do not condition themselves; they are established through conceptual construction. Conceptual construction does not [condition itself].
Perception arises from dependent origination, yet conceptualization, though mutually dependent in appearance, has never truly existed as prior or subsequent;

conversely, when each is seen to be independent, both are found to be ungraspable. Thus, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—the two previously established—are the very source from which the false and the correct emerge.
That there are causes and conditions, and that there is cause and effect, is the conventional truth.
The realization that causes and conditions are unobtainable—that which is neither arising nor non-arising—is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
To directly calculate that things arise without a cause is the doctrine of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Because it is contrasted with the former two, the non-Buddhist view constitutes the third.

If one asks whether this is of the same category as the non-Buddhists, I say: no. It is correctly stated that the Buddha-dharma clarifies only the two truths; to abandon these is [to fall into error].

When external calculations reach this conclusion and subsequently establish the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), they refer to them as "discursive thought" (*vikalpa*) and "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

This means that discursive thought and conventional truth are precisely the former two natures. Because these two are severed, the realm of the sages (*ārya-gocara*) is established as the [third] nature.
It may also be said that the "discursive thought" and "conventional truth" spoken of by these outsiders differ from the two truths taught by the Buddha.

Thus, whether ultimate or conventional, there is nothing that is not the true truth (*satya*). Based on the teachings, it is clearly explained that the seven and two truths are fully possessed [as follows].

For example, regarding the "practices of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-kriyā*), there are four similes below; these are used in sequence to illustrate the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). The first simile states:
"The practices of cultivation" are like the ten kinds of universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatana*) in dhyāna—namely, blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth—all of which pervade a single [object].
The essence of all objects is fundamentally one; it appears as various forms because of the mind’s conceptualization. This is illustrated by the analogy of deluded imagination (*vikalpa*);

the only difference is that the former [the yogin] relies on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the latter [the ordinary person] relies on the formation of delusion. Regarding the analogy of various cataracts for dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):

cataracts are originally devoid of color, yet colors appear through false vision. Thus, what is not color is the reality of color. Likewise, the characteristics of dependent origination are unreal when not awakened to.
The two analogies, such as refined pure gold and so forth, both illustrate the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Because those two natures do not exist therein—just as gold is free from impurities and space is free from obscuration—it is said that the purification of delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is likewise so.
This explains that the nature of delusive conceptualization does not exist; it is not merely that it should not be fixedly existent, but furthermore...

One should not definitively establish that [things] do not exist, nor definitively establish that they exist; for one who falls into the view that they definitely exist, they fall into the error of reification (*samāropa*), and one who definitively establishes that they do not exist falls into the error of denial (*apavāda*).
Both are destroyed by false conceptualization (*parikalpita*). Therefore, it is next explained that neither is established individually:

if false conceptualization were without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) while dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*) existed, then there would be existence where there is no intrinsic nature, and thus the principle of "no intrinsic nature" would not be established. There is [existence].

The principle that "existence arises from non-existence" is not established; one should also conversely state that if dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) were without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), yet the nature of false discrimination (*vikalpa*) exists, the case would be analogous.
Furthermore, it is said: "Depending upon false discrimination, one attains that dependent origination.

Since the meaning of dependent origination is not established, characteristics and names always arise in mutual succession, giving rise to various false discriminations; and false discrimination, in turn...
Since neither [of these] can be established through exhaustive investigation, as they all lack substantial meaning, it is said that they are ultimately unestablished.
When a single thought is severed, one transcends all delusive imaginings; thus, wisdom becomes pure and principle becomes manifest. (3)
Delusive conceptualization consists of twelve links; dependent origination has six aspects. Self-awakened knowledge is thusness itself, for it is without differentiation.
The five dharmas constitute reality, while self-nature is threefold. One should discern these through cultivation; they do not transcend suchness.
All various marks and dependent origination are termed the arising of delusive conceptualization. Those various marks of delusive conceptualization arise from that dependent origination.

When awakened wisdom thoroughly examines that which is without conditions and free from conceptual construction, it is established as being devoid of intrinsic nature; how then could there be conceptual construction?
One awakens to those very conceptual constructions by establishing the two natures through conceptualization. Conceptual construction manifests in various ways within the pure realm of the sages.

Conceptual construction is like the colors of a painting; dependent origination is reckoned as conceptual construction. If conceptual construction were something other [than this], one would rely upon the treatises of the non-Buddhists.
Conceptualization (vikalpa) is said to arise from the cause of what is conceptualized; when one is free from these two types of conceptualization, such is the accomplishment [of reality].
The first two lines of the verse summarize the two numbers and unify them into one, as in the twelve [bases] listed above.

Since it is already stated that they are merely conceptualization, yet described as dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), the six numbers do not exceed the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya). This is like the statement regarding the conceptualization of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-vikalpa*), which refers to sound.
If "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refer to the four great elements, they correspond to the four objects such as form (*rūpa*); other cases may be understood by analogy with these various objects.
Alternatively, those who explain this through the six causes do not realize self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). As for "suchness" (*tathatā*), it refers back to the wisdom of self-awareness;
knowing that which is known [by others] is called "suchness. Although the objects of knowledge are manifold, the wisdom of self-awareness [perceives them as they are].
Thus, there is no distinction; by extension, it can be said that the so-called five dharmas and three natures are all likewise real.
This is because a great practitioner, through non-conceptual wisdom, clearly perceives that all phenomena are none other than suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, it is said that they do not transcend suchness. Yet, although they do not depart from suchness, names, marks, and conceptual constructions are not lacking in even a single dharma.

Furthermore, it says: "The various characteristics and the characteristics of dependent origination. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) in relation to dependent origination, the wording is still somewhat brief;
it explicitly states that both the various characteristics and names are equally dependent origination. Those names and characteristics all give rise to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
The next two phrases refer to the dependent origination of false conceptualization, which arises through mutual interaction; this is to be observed with awakened wisdom (*buddhi*).

When the perception of conditions is utterly absent, that which is realized through supreme self-awareness and distinguished by the practitioner is the sole *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).
It stands utterly detached and does not conjoin with any deluded thoughts; since this nature is itself without nature, even awakening itself vanishes.
Therefore it is said: "Once perfected, there is no nature. How could there be the awakening of deluded thoughts? This is awakening and its object.

When deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is simultaneously dispelled, one may say that this concludes the preceding section and gives rise to the subsequent one; thus, all following phrases are none other than explanations of delusion based upon awakening.

This is stated as: "That deluded conceptual nature establishes two natures," namely, the two kinds of nature consisting of the nature of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) and the nature of things and characteristics (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, these various deluded conceptualizations do not exist separately [from awakening], for they are entirely manifested within the realm of the Sage.
Because it is central, it is like the colors in a painting arising from what was originally no form or image;

that which was originally no form or image is the realm of the sages, whereas the presence of forms and images is mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Conceptual construction is rooted in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and dependent origination is fundamentally without discrimination.
One generates conceptual construction by calculating [the nature of] dependent origination; such is the nature of conceptual construction. If it were otherwise than this...
"Discursive thought" (*vikalpa*) refers to the speculative calculations of non-Buddhist treatises; therefore, it is called discursive thought.
To say that what is conceived arises from the conjunction of views—that is, arising from the combination of three conditions—is not the True Teaching.

"To be free from the two types of discursive thought" is a summary of the two self-natures (*svabhāva*), collectively termed discursive thought; when one is free from them, they become the [true] self-nature. (4) The sixteenth chapter concludes here.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).
