If you explain the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the Single Vehicle, I and the other bodhisattvas will thoroughly realize the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization and the Single Vehicle through our own insight, without depending on others, and thus penetrate the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
“Wisdom, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this; I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: “That which was known by previous sages has been transmitted from one to another; it is the absence of self-nature in false discrimination (*vikalpa*).

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, in a solitary and quiet place, observe through their own self-awakening (*pratyātma-adhigama*), not relying on others, having transcended false discrimination based on views.”
Ascending and entering the stage of the Tathāgata is called the characteristic of the noble wisdom of self-awakening, Mahāmati. What is the characteristic of the One Vehicle?
It refers to awakening to the path of the One Vehicle; this is what I call the One Vehicle. How does one awaken to the path of the One Vehicle?
It means that when the false imaginings of the grasped and the grasper cease to arise in their true state, this is called awakening to the One Vehicle, Mahāmati. This is the One Vehicle.
Awakening cannot be attained by any others—such as non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or even Brahmā kings—but only by the Tathāgata;
for this reason, it is called the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Now, regarding the fact that the Buddhas of the three periods attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, if we discuss it according to its designations, we speak of it as the *dharmakāya*, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, *prajñā*, *vimukti*, and the two virtues of wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*).

While these are distinct names spoken of differently, if one speaks in terms of principle, they are but one. Thus, although the dharma-gates are profound and vast, difficult to fathom, from the perspective of ultimate truth, they are simply unity.

The essential point of the discourse in this sutra concerning the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) and the awakening to the path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is nothing other than the non-substantiality of false discrimination (*vikalpa*).
It further states that in the state of suchness (*tathatā*), false discrimination does not arise;

if one can realize this through practice and directly accept it as one's own responsibility, then the unsurpassed path of awakening in the stage of the Tathāgata is not far to return to. Furthermore, it says:
That one attains penetration into the Buddha-dharma not through others is precisely because these two dharmas are the fundamental nature of all virtues.
Regarding the statement that "what was known by former sages has been transmitted from one to another," these two phrases are truly not easy to clarify.
Yet, when it comes to what is known and what is transmitted, it is said to be nothing more than "delusive thoughts having no inherent nature. Often, when people nowadays hear this—
To insist that there is no principle more profound than this is to fail to realize that the way of the transmission between Buddhas and patriarchs lies precisely here.
Nevertheless, this merely indicates the point of entry; one must know that apart from the naturelessness of deluded thoughts, there exists a reality beyond them.
This must be attained through personal realization, for it is not something reached by words; therefore, one should practice alone in a quiet place.
Advancing toward the realization of this single point, one truly knows that this matter cannot be misrepresented; otherwise, how could it be easily discussed?
What is called the characteristic of the One Vehicle is not something existing apart from wisdom;

rather, within the very state of the faculties and objects—the grasped and the grasper—it is, in its own essence, suchness as it is, free from the arising of deluded thoughts, ultimately quiescent, and without even a hair’s breadth of duality or opposition.
This characteristic constitutes the realization of the path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); such is all there is to it, Mahāmati.

Regarding this realization of the One Vehicle, when contrasted with other ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to distinguish who attains it or not, it is found that—with the sole exception of the Tathāgata’s solitary awakening of the One Vehicle—none others attain it.

Nevertheless, there are those at the initial stage of the Perfect and Sudden [teaching] who share the same destination as the Buddha and likewise attain realization; however, the text is brief on this point.
1. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, for what reason do you teach the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and not the one vehicle (*ekayāna*)?

The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Because they lack the nature of attaining parinirvāṇa by themselves, I do not teach a single vehicle for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it is because of this [lack of self-nature] that there is no one vehicle.”
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain liberation through the Tathāgata’s skillful means of subduing them and bestowing tranquility; it is not by their own power.

For this reason, the One Vehicle is not taught to them. Furthermore, Mahāmati, because they have not severed the habitual tendencies of afflictions and karma, all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not taught the One Vehicle;
they do not realize the selflessness of phenomena and have not transcended the realm of birth and death.

Because of death, the three vehicles are taught, O Mahāmati. When all those [practitioners] have severed the afflictions, faults, and habitual tendencies, and have awakened to the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), they sever the afflictions, faults, and habitual tendencies.

Having awakened to the non-substantiality of attachment to the flavor of samādhi within the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), and having awakened to it, they further enter the supramundane, most excellent untainted realm to fulfill all requisites.
When one attains the inconceivable and sovereign Dharma-body of the Tathāgata— at that time, the World-Honored One,
wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The vehicle of the devas and Brahmās, The vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, And the vehicle of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas— I have taught all these vehicles."

As long as there is a mind that revolves through the various vehicles, it is not ultimate. When that mind is extinguished, there are no vehicles nor those who ride them; there is no establishment of vehicles.
What I teach is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), for the purpose of guiding sentient beings. Thus, I have provisionally distinguished and taught the various vehicles. There are three kinds of liberation:
liberation from the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), liberation from afflictions, and liberation through wisdom. Through these, one becomes utterly detached.
For example, a piece of wood floating on the ocean constantly turns with the waves; so too it is with the ignorant śrāvaka, who is tossed about by the winds of signs.
As they give rise to afflictions and extinguish them, their habitual tendencies remain.

Being deluded by the "flavor" of attachment to the bliss of samādhi, they dwell in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), neither attaining ultimate liberation nor yet regressing. They obtain bodies of various samādhis and do not awaken for even an eon.
For example, it is like a person who is intoxicated; only after the alcohol has worn off does he awaken. The awakening of the Dharma is likewise: one attains the supreme body of a Buddha.
Next, [the questioner] asks about the Tathāgata’s intention in teaching the three vehicles rather than the One Vehicle.

The Buddha answers that for three reasons he does not teach the two-vehicle persons the One Vehicle: because they are those whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa by themselves, they are unable to realize the fundamental [nature].

"Coming to quiescence is one" means that when it is said, "The Tathāgata provides the skillful means of subduing and bestowing tranquility," this refers to those who do not understand that birth-and-death is fundamentally empty;
they must await the bestowal of the Dharma of subduing to attain liberation, and thus do not emerge through their own power—this is the second point.
Furthermore, the statement "because the afflictive obstructions, karma, and habitual tendencies have not been severed" refers to the preceding text.
What is called "the non-cessation of both active afflictions (*kleśa*) and latent tendencies (*vāsanā*)" refers to the third [obstruction].

Because these latent tendencies and other afflictions are not severed, ignorance (*avidyā*) still persists; because one does not realize the Bodhisattva’s mark of selflessness (*anātman*), one does not transcend birth-and-death with physical limits (*bhavasaṃsāra*).
Therefore, the Three Vehicles are taught to guide them. The passage beginning with "all those aforementioned" serves as a counter-illustration to clarify this point.
Regarding those who lose the correct teaching and attain the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the meaning of their severance of afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth is entirely the reverse of the above:

because they have severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions, they are no longer intoxicated by ignorance; because they do not cling to the flavor of the bliss of *samādhi* as having intrinsic nature, they awaken to the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).
In terms of stages, from the initial self-realization up to the ultimate stage of the Tathāgata, it is all thus.
This means that the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) is precisely the entry into the Dharma-nature land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*) and the reception of the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*).
Even up to the supreme untainted realm, which is the ultimate Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*) where all requisites are fulfilled, the two adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*) are complete.
One shall then attain the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, which is the ultimate One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The first six lines of the verse praise this aforementioned One Vehicle.
Because it is not otherwise, it is said: "up to the point where the mind still functions.

This means that even if the Tathāgata were to have a mind that could still function, he would not yet be ultimate, let alone those of other vehicles. Because this transformation has reached its limit, all mental measures (*cittamātra*) are extinguished;
there is neither a vehicle nor a rider, and there is no vehicle to be established—this is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). If...

"When one looks toward the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, that [other teaching] is general while this is specific; that is general in opening and revealing the three vehicles, whereas this is exclusively the ultimate Buddha-realm.

Although they are thus distinguished, there is no difference in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), for it serves to guide sentient beings. This verse summarizes the preceding passage concerning the three [vehicles];

by contrasting the three kinds of liberation with the single dharma of selflessness (*anātman*), the identity of the Great and Small Vehicles, and of the Three and One Vehicles, is established therein.

This is distinct; yet when one speaks of afflictions (*kleśa*) and wisdom (*jñāna*), etc., then delusion and wisdom are equal, and bondage and liberation are non-dual—is this not the liberation that is their transcendence?
It is like the metaphor of wood floating on the ocean, which illustrates the *śrāvaka*:

though they rely on the ocean of the eight consciousnesses and are not moved by the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), they drown in the pit of the three unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*), being distracted by the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*).
Because the mind has not yet departed from the shadows of dharmas and phenomena, it is said to be "drifted and tossed by the winds of signs.

Furthermore, because one has not yet severed fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), one is deluded by residual afflictions (*vāsanā-kleśa*). Thus, while attached to the bliss of samādhi, there is no further progress;
one dwells in the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) without returning, remaining in the body of samādhi for kalpas on end.

Because awakening occurs, it is further compared to a cloud: just as a person intoxicated by the wine of ignorance must wait for kalpas for their faculties to transform before they can arouse the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta), so too must the wine be digested before one awakens.
This is precisely what is meant in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* regarding the five sons of the Buddha arousing the aspiration;
this is a teaching that uses the path of instruction to refute [the notion of inherent awakening], yet it is not necessarily the whole truth. That awakening...

The Dharma is likewise: as the verse above states that by awakening to the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) one will ultimately attain the Dharmakāya of a Tathāgata, it says, "one attains the supreme body of a Buddha" (2). This concludes the seventeenth chapter.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "The characteristics of the differentiation of the mind-born body (manomaya-kāya) and its supernormal powers."
"I shall now speak; listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). What are the three? They are: the mind-made body produced by the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi;
the mind-made body produced by the realization of the self-nature of dharmas; and the mind-made body produced by conformity to the species [of beings]."

Regarding the practitioner who cultivates the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) born of the absence of volitional effort: one who understands the characteristics of progressive advancement from stage to stage realizes three kinds of bodies.
Mahāmati, what is the mind-made body born of the meditative absorption in the bliss of samādhi? It refers to the third, fourth, and fifth stages;
because of the meditative absorption in the bliss of samādhi, one gives rise to various forms while abiding in the tranquility of one’s own mind within the ocean of the mind.

The non-arising of the characteristics of the billowing consciousnesses, knowing that the nature of the objective realm is a manifestation of one’s own mind, and understanding it to be neither existent nor non-existent—this is called the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body) of the correct attainment of the bliss of samādhi.
Mahāmati, what is the *manomaya-kāya* of the realization of the self-nature of dharmas?

It refers to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), where through observation and realization, one perceives that all phenomena such as illusions are entirely non-existent; the body and mind undergo transformation and attain the state of being like an illusion.
The samādhi of obscurity and the other gates of samādhi possess immeasurable marks, powers, and masteries of clarity;
they are as adorned as exquisite flowers, swift as one’s will, and like illusions, dreams, the moon in water, or reflections in a mirror.

Neither created nor created-from-conditions, yet like all that is created and from conditions, they are fully adorned with all varieties of physical forms and limbs, entering into and penetrating the great assemblies of all buddha-fields.
Because it is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is called the "mind-made body born of the realization of the self-nature of phenomena" (*dharma-svabhāva-avabodha-manomaya-kāya*).

Mahāmati, what is the "mind-made body born of the lineage, arising spontaneously and without effort" (*jāti-sahaja-anābhoga-manomaya-kāya*)? It refers to the realization of all Buddha-dharmas and the characteristic of the joy of self-attained realization;
this is called the mind-made body born of the lineage, arising spontaneously and without effort. Mahāmati, regarding these three types of bodily characteristics...
"One should observe, awaken to, and train in this. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"It is not my Great Vehicle; it is neither speech nor letters. It is not the truths, nor liberation, nor is it a realm of non-existence."
However, regarding the adornment of various *manomaya-kāyas* (mind-made bodies) attained through mastery over the samādhis of the Mahāyāna:

previously, it was stated that the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) constitutes the culmination of attaining mastery over the *manomaya-kāya*; now, by taking the ultimate limit of its categories to be the Buddha-stage (*buddha-bhūmi*), the beginning is also clarified.
Furthermore, the names and numbers of the metaphors used here correspond to those in the preceding text, differing only in their degree of detail.

The distinction between them is essentially that the upper and lower stages manifest one another. The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanation of the Words) states that the practitioner clearly understands the characteristics of progressive advancement from the first stage upward;
this is precisely what is clarified here through the three types [of progress] across the beginning and end of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Since awakening to phenomena corresponds to the eighth stage, the single type of "homogeneous" (*jāti*) progress increases spontaneously. Thus, the ten stages are divided into distinct portions.

"Equanimity" (*sāmya*) mostly refers to the state of universal penetration (*samantaka-bhūmi*), which is also explained as the path of instruction (*śikṣāmārga*). In the commentary, it says "the correct reception (*samyag-upabhoga*) of the bliss of *samādhi*":
here, *samādhi* takes the determination of nature (*niyata-dharma*) as its bliss, for it is distinct from feelings such as suffering or pleasure; thus it is called "correct reception.

In terms of stages, this refers to the *śūnyatā-samādhi* from the third stage (*bhūmi*) upward; the reason other stages are not mentioned is for the sake of brevity. This pertains to the Bodhisattva...
Because they are Bodhisattvas, they do not share the characteristics of the three vehicles; they are unmoved by the winds [of external objects], and their various minds are tranquil.
When the mind is free from variety, and because those various [appearances] are themselves the tranquility of one's own mind, it is said that they "abide in the ocean of mind.
Since they differ from ordinary beings, the waves of the six consciousnesses do not arise, and they fully comprehend all objective realms.
To know that external natures are non-existent because they are merely manifestations of one's own mind is the first mark of the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*);

this is clearly revealed in the commentary on the passage regarding the awakening to the self-nature of phenomena. As for the statement "phenomena are like illusions" and so forth, it means that because all phenomena are understood to be like illusions, they are non-existent;
yet, because the body and mind are likewise illusory, they can undergo transformations without obstruction—this is the third [mark], that of being like an illusion.
The "obscuration, immeasurable marks, power, mastery, and clarity" refer to the dharma-gates obtained through samādhi, which are like the adornments of exquisite flowers.
Their bodies are as swift as one's will and unimpeded like illusions or dreams;

because they are not substantially created by the four great elements, they are said to be neither created nor created-from-elements, yet they are not non-existent as illusory, provisional manifestations.
Regarding the phrase "because of characteristics, like the primary and derived elements, one penetrates all forms and so forth as being the self-nature of phenomena":

this means that the Bodhisattva penetrates the self-nature of phenomena by means of their being like an illusion, thereby establishing the basis of emanation; this is what is called the meaning of awakening to the self-nature of phenomena.
As for the expression "arising together with all categories," regarding the awakening to all Buddha-dharmas, the two preceding [emptinesses] and the illusion are still [the objects of realization].
Because one now awakens to the Middle Way between the two extremes, all dharmas are called the Buddha-dharma; since the Buddha-dharma is not something other, it is said to be "attained by oneself.
This bliss of self-attainment is the ultimate of all joys, hence it is called the characteristic of bliss.

In its meaning, this corresponds to the eighth stage and above, where one attains the samādhi of the single body and the infinite bodies, universally manifesting like reflections appearing in a mirror; therefore, it is called a "seed."

Because it arises simultaneously with its object and does not depend on mental attention (*manasikāra*), it is called "without effort" (*anabhisamskāra*). Alternatively, if the character "effort" (*abhisamskāra*) is attached to the following term, it still does not entirely escape the need for mental attention;
this is merely stated by way of analogy, as can be understood from the exhortatory text.

Regarding the first four lines of the verse, they concern the Tathāgata’s self-realization which is free from characteristics; therefore, everything is expressed in terms of "non-. This means that although [the preceding] was analyzed as such...
The Mahāyāna is not that which I ride; what I ride is free from all names and marks, without realization and without attainment, yet it is not that there is no realm that can be shown.
Therefore, it is said to be "not spoken," nor is it [expressible by] letters and the like.

Furthermore, the words and phrases of "speaking" and "letters" may be applied to correspond with the three tracks (*triyāna*). When these three tracks are harmonized, they constitute the single Great Vehicle. Thus:

The first phrase does not mean that one abandons [the One Vehicle] and fails to mount it; rather, as previously stated, since the nature of the One Vehicle is fundamentally extinguished and non-existent, how could the designations of three vehicles be permitted?
Nevertheless, because of the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, one "mounts" what is not a vehicle.
This refers to the subsequent four phrases, which concern the transformative function after fruition: within a single moment, one mounts the Mahāyāna and the three types of Great Vehicles.
Therefore it is said that the texts concerning "mastery over samādhi" and so forth do not manifest in sequential order, but rather all at once;
as explained above regarding the correspondence between stages and capacities, each approach has its own appropriate application. [End of] Chapter One.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, if a man or a woman commits the five deeds of immediate retribution, they do not enter the Avīci Hell. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One! Indeed."
However, the Buddha, having received the request for instruction, told Mahāmati: "What are the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karmāṇi*)? They are:

killing one's father, killing one's mother, harming an Arhat, causing schism in the Saṃgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind. Mahāmati, what is the mother of sentient beings? It is craving (*tṛṣṇā*) that leads to further rebirth;
it is accompanied by greed and delight, and stands as the mother. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is established as the father, which gives birth to the village of the sense-bases (*āyatana-grāma*)."

To sever the two roots is called "killing father and mother. When those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not manifest, yet their poison flares up like that of a rat, to ultimately sever all phenomena is called "killing an Arhat.
What is meant by "breaking the Sangha"? It refers to the ultimate severance of the accumulation and aggregation of the various aggregates (*skandha*) characterized by distinct marks;

this is called "breaking the Sangha. Mahāmati, one who does not realize that external objects—whether of specific or general characteristics—are merely the manifestations of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*).
The seven bodies of consciousness are ultimately severed through the three liberations and the absence of tainted conceptualization; the Buddha calls these seven kinds of consciousness "evil minds.
If a man or woman commits this act of shedding the blood of a Buddha, it is called one of the five *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses, and it is also called "the immediate" (*ānantarya*).
[The World-Honored One asked: "How is it that a man or woman who commits the five *ānantarya* karmas does not enter the Avīci hell?"
The five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*) represent the ultimate limit of perverse evil.

They are called "deeds of immediate retribution" because at the time of committing these evils, there is no interval due to the intensity of the mind. The Tathāgata once spoke of this in passing, saying:
"There are those who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution yet do not enter the Avīci hell. *Avīci* is synonymous with "immediate" (*anantara*).

Mahāmati, not yet having attained realization, questioned [the Buddha] on this matter. In the Buddha’s response, he first enumerated the names based on phenomena (*dharma*), and then examined and explained them by means of the principles (*dharma*).
Although the sequence of names followed a reverse order, the underlying principle was actually in accord with the natural order.

The reason for speaking in this way was to demonstrate that phenomena have no fixed names and that principles have no fixed explanations; whether something is "reverse" or "accordant" depends upon the mind and not upon the phenomena themselves, while good and evil depend solely upon reality.
Not only the names, but even the provisional designations used for evil are intended to elucidate the ultimate truth;

are not the five acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma) all, in fact, called the marks of liberation? The Buddha’s teaching possesses profound significance. When Mahāmati asks his questions, the principle is not in vain:
that which he calls "craving for further rebirth" refers precisely to the craving within the present moment of the twelve links of dependent origination.

Furthermore, because it undergoes rebirth and possesses the sense of "arising" together with future craving and delight, it is established as the mother—just as the mother gives birth—or perhaps the character "established" (*li*) is an error for the character "arise" (*sheng*). Since craving must necessarily precede ignorance, ignorance is established as the father;
from this, craving gives rise to the village of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the twelve sense fields (*dvādaśāyatana*), and so forth.
If one cuts off the root of craving and so forth, this has the same meaning as harming one's parents.

Those underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not manifest, just as when an Arhat has already severed the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), the "rat-poison" may still arise among various phenomena (the meaning of "rat-poison" is explained separately).

The phrase "various phenomena" refers to the fact that while residual habits (*vāsanā*) still remain, there are various kinds of phenomena that are non-defiled ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*). If [one reaches] the ultimate...

To sever those habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is precisely what constitutes the meaning of "harming the Saṃgha of Arhats. Because the name "Saṃgha" is established through the harmony [of its members], to sever the harmony of the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) is termed "schism in the Saṃgha.

Not realizing that external phenomena—both their specific and general characteristics—are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, one remains deluded regarding the eight consciousnesses and retains only seven;
thus, taking the deluded awakening of the seventh consciousness to be the "Seven Buddhas" is the [erroneous] doctrine.
Since nothing other than untainted conduct (*anāsrava-caryā*) can sever it, one employs the wisdom of the three liberations (*trivimokṣa*) to sever those seven consciousnesses.
Since all these are called "ultimate," they must be explained in their most extreme sense;

thus, they do not merely consist of the untainted [wisdom] of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), nor do they stop at the mere meaning of "shedding blood. While the untainted is fundamentally wholesome, why is it described as "evil"?

Regarding "conception" (*saṃjñā*), it refers to the evil mind that accords with the various matters [of the five actions]. Each matter of the five immediate actions (*pañcānantarya*) is also an action (*karman*).
Furthermore, it is said that "immediate" (*ānantarya*) means that such actions are equal to the immediate wisdom (*ānantarya-jñāna*) at the time of realizing the true Dharma;
according to the latter sense, the retribution is also called "equal," meaning it is identical to the action and no different from it. (1)
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are external *ānantarya* [sins of immediate retribution] which I shall now expound.
Having heard this meaning, you and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will not fall into delusion in future ages. What are the five *ānantarya*? They are the *ānantarya* previously mentioned;
if one commits these, one will not attain the *ānantarya-dharma* [the realization of the Truth] in each of the three liberations (*vimokṣa*), with the exception of...

Beyond this, there are other instances where the power of transformation manifests immediate realization (*ānantarya*). This refers to the transformative power of Śrāvakas, the transformative power of Bodhisattvas, and the transformative power of Tathāgatas.
For those who have committed an act of immediate retribution, these powers manifest as such a realization in order to eliminate their doubts and remorse and to inspire them toward awakening.
There is no one who, having performed an act of immediate retribution, does not attain [realization] through such a manifestation of power.

In the intervals between these states, one removes the realization that [objects] are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, becoming free from the delusions regarding body and wealth, and free from the grasping at "I" and "mine.
At times, by encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one is liberated from the delusions concerning the continuity of existence in other realms of rebirth.
Then, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Craving is called the mother, and ignorance is the father; the consciousness that perceives objects is the Buddha, and the latent proclivities are the Arhats;

the accumulation of the aggregates is called the Sangha. One who severs these in immediate succession is said to have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, yet they do not enter the Avīci Hell.

The following section further clarifies the distinctions between the provisional and the real regarding external uninterrupted karma (*ānantarya-karma*), as well as the differences in whether it is extinguished or not, and whether one progresses or regresses.
"External" is contrasted with "internal"; that which precedes is designated as internal, referring to the internal mind, while actual deeds are designated as external, referring to external matters.
If one hears that the retribution for external uninterrupted karmic deeds does not fail to manifest, then one will neither fall into false views nor be deluded.
Because it was explained previously, it is said that one does not fall into delusion. What was previously stated refers to the uninterrupted practice regarding matters discussed at other times.
One who practices externally cannot attain [realization] internally; one who attains internally is able to eliminate what is external.
Therefore, it is said: "If one practices this," and so forth; that is to say, if one truly practices these external uninterrupted karmas, then they do not [occur].

Within the attainment of the three liberations, the dharmas such as the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*) are also like those who practice internally and do not obtain external retribution;
they merely involve the alternation of the adverse and the compliant. Having excluded these, there arises subsequent provisional practice (*upāya-caryā*).

This means that when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest provisional paths of non-interruption, they must necessarily lead toward the ultimate reality; for those who practice provisionally are easily transformed, whereas those who act according to reality are difficult to transform.
This is done to manifest traces that are easily transformed, so as to cause them to eliminate doubt, repent their transgressions, and resolve their minds toward awakening.
One might ask: "If that is so, can a practitioner who has actually committed such acts—like Māndgalyāyana—have the fruits of their immediate karma (*ānantarya-karma*) extinguished? I reply:

I only fear that their doubt may not be truly eliminated or that they do not truly repent their transgressions. If they were able to do so, who would say it were otherwise? However, this has not yet occurred.

Since there are those who actually perform such karma yet fortunately escape its retribution, it is said that "there is none for whom the commission of an *ānantarya* act [necessarily results in retribution].
This statement serves to rectify the false view that cause and effect are not infallible. The term "unilaterally" (*ekānta*) refers to karma that is certain;
excluding cases where the subsequent result is uncertain, it is not unilaterally fixed. There are three reasons why it is not certain.
Therefore it is said: first, by removing the notion that objects are external manifestations of one's own mind, one realizes that arising and ceasing are merely mind;

second, by departing from delusions regarding the body, wealth, and so forth, one does not perceive a body internally nor perceive wealth and such externally, thereby abandoning the grasping of "I" and "mine" and realizing that even conditions for committing heinous acts are empty;
or third, when occasionally encountering a virtuous friend, they are exhorted [to practice].
Third, by exerting the power of guidance, one causes the retribution of deluded thoughts regarding other realms of existence not to continue.

If these three [factors] are abandoned, it is not seen that there is anything capable of extinguishing karma; thus, karma is determined. Furthermore, since karma has degrees of lightness and heaviness, transgressive evil is fixed, whereas other karma is not fixed.
If one follows the teaching of the *Naxin* (納心), regardless of whether the karma is light or heavy, as long as one attains...
As for this principle, it is fixed; one cannot make it unfixed. Although it may appear unfixed when one has not grasped the principle, it remains fixed nonetheless.
Other karmic matters should be inferred accordingly; the principle of evil karma cannot be discussed in general terms, yet it is approximately like this.

The verse states, "Awakening to objects, consciousness is the Buddha," meaning that consciousness is that which is capable of awakening to objects. To take consciousness as the Buddha is to sever [the cycle] through non-existence.

The "outflows" (āsrava) are precisely what harm the Buddha; their sequential abandonment refers to the fact that craving and so forth must necessarily be severed by means of the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga).
Furthermore, because they are severed, one attains "sequential abandonment";
although this occurs simultaneously, the mention of "sequence" is merely a description based on the process. (2) ○ This concludes the second section.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening.
World-Honored One, what constitutes the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Awakening to the non-existence of self and dharmas, fully understanding the two obstacles, being free from the two kinds of death, and severing the two afflictions—this is called the Buddha’s knowledge and awakening. [This is not] the case for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
One who attains this Dharma is also called a Buddha; for these reasons, I preach the One Vehicle.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of selflessness, severing the two obstacles and afflictions, and being eternally free from the two kinds of death—this is called the Buddha’s awakening.
What was previously described as the path of awakening to the One Vehicle was still a brief explanation;

it has not yet been stated what dharma is to be awakened to, what delusion is to be severed and abandoned, or what principle is to be realized. Therefore, [the interlocutor] requests that the Buddha explain this.
Regarding this awareness, the Buddha answered that awakening to the two kinds of selflessness constitutes "awakening," while knowing the two obstacles constitutes "knowledge.
Because one awakens to the selflessness of persons and phenomena, one is freed from the two types of death: the death of the分段 (paricchinna) realm and the 變易 (pariṇāma) realm.

Because one knows that the two obstacles are fundamentally empty, the two afflictions are severed; thus, the two obstacles are identical to the two afflictions, though they may be distinguished otherwise. As for the afflictions...

"Affliction" (*kleśa*) and "cognition" (*jñeya*) are called the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). Ignorance regarding views (*dṛṣṭi-moha*) and ignorance regarding thought (*bhāvanā-moha*), and so forth, are called the two afflictions (*kleśa*). Although their names are general and specific respectively, their essence is in fact not different.

If one explains them according to the characteristics of the three dharmas: that which realizes the non-selfhood of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*) is the path of no-action (*an-akarma-patha*), because where there is a self, there must be action;
thus we know that the severing of the two obstacles and the two afflictions is the state of being without affliction (*a-kleśa*).

The path that eliminates affliction is free from the two kinds of death; this is the path of no-suffering. Since one has ultimately departed from the three paths, the three virtues are ultimately revealed.
Although the three virtues are not explicitly mentioned, by speaking only of what is abandoned, that which is realized can be known.

This also demonstrates that there is realization without anything to be realized, and attainment without anything attained. Thus, the path of awakening of the One Vehicle resides solely in the Buddha.
As stated in the preceding chapter, it is said that even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who attain this Dharma are also called Buddhas;
this, moreover, is a statement made by way of concession.

The intended meaning is that if those of the two vehicles can be called Buddhas upon attaining this Dharma, then by extension, even ordinary beings of the six realms and non-Buddhists who attain this Dharma would likewise [be so called].

Fundamentally, there is no difference; it is only because their aspirations are small and inferior compared to others, and they are unable to exhaustively realize the selflessness of phenomena and persons, that it is said:
"For this reason, I preach the One Vehicle. Only the Buddha alone attains this text.

This is similar in wording to what the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states—that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is attained by all three vehicles—yet the underlying intent differs. (And so forth. Furthermore...
I grant it to them for fear that those of the Two Vehicles might disparage themselves;
I take it away from them for fear that those with superior pride might become indiscriminately arrogant. Although this is so on the surface, in the ultimate sense, there is neither gain nor loss.
[End of] Chapter Three.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for what reason did the World-Honored One proclaim these words among the great assembly:
'I am all the Buddhas of the past, and through various births, I was once [the Buddha] Māndhātṛ'?"

The *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speaks of the Cakravartin King, the six-tusked elephant, the parrot, Śakra-devānām-indra, the Rishi Sunetra, and others such as these across hundreds of thousands of lifetimes. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Because of the four kinds of equality, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words among the great assembly: 'In that time, I was Krakucchanda...'"

Regarding the fourfold equality of Kanakamuni and Kāśyapa Buddhas—namely, equality of letters (*vyañjana*), equality of speech (*vāk*), equality of dharma (*dharma*), and equality of body (*kāya*)—it is called the fourfold equality because of these four kinds of equality.
For this reason, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words among the great assembly:
"What is the equality of letters? If a letter designates me as 'Buddha,' that same letter also designates all [beings]."
The self-nature of those syllables of all Buddhas is without differentiation; these are the equality of names and so forth. What is meant by the equality of speech?

It means that just as my sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds arise as the characteristics of speech, so too do those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas likewise give rise to sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds as the characteristics of speech;
they are without increase, without decrease, and without differentiation.

What is the nature of the *kalaviṅka*-like Brahma-voice? Regarding "the body and so forth," it means that there is no difference between myself and the Buddhas' Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and Form-body (*rūpakāya*), including their marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
However, for the sake of taming sentient beings of various dispositions in their respective realms of rebirth, one manifests various distinct form-bodies;
this is what is meant by "the body and so forth. What is meant by "the Dharma and so forth"? It refers to myself and...
That Buddha attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; briefly stated, the unobstructed wisdom of the Buddha-dharma is called the fourfold equanimity.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaimed these words amidst the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni—I speak of these four as being equal to myself, declaring them to be my sons.
This is because there is no Tathāgata of the three periods of time who is not identical to me; for since the principle is ultimate, all matters are without distinction.
Therefore, it is said that "I am all the Buddhas of the past," and also that "I receive various different births."
Now, since he is called "Buddha," it follows that his name, speech, and body are identical in all respects; yet why is it that their physical forms differ?

This is because Mahāmati raised his question by holding to these two extremes, and the Buddha directly informed him with the teaching of the fourfold equality—namely, the equality of letters, the equality of speech, the equality of dharmas, and the equality of bodies. "Equality" here means sameness. Therefore, this is the case.
This demonstrates that the principle is the same, thereby answering the question posed above regarding the Buddhas of the past. Furthermore, it says:
"Except for the sake of taming those various sentient beings who differ according to their respective realms of existence," as previously stated in the *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
This answers the question posed above regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Nevertheless, there remain [the categories of] "equal" and so forth, which are not [the intended] objects.
By thoroughly contemplating that which is equal as the equality of inequality, there is nowhere one does not encounter equality.
Although traces may differ according to the various capacities and conditions of beings, their ultimate destination is but one.

This is what is meant by saying that the three periods of time are spoken of for the sake of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and not because Bodhi has coming, going, or the present. Other versions take the four kinds of equality as the esoteric meaning.
The Master [Vasubandhu] held that because [the teachings] exist in that [context] but not here, the ancient masters established four kinds of underlying intent (*abhiprāya*), of which this is one.
By this it is clarified that until one reaches the ultimate fruit, there may be differences; but once the ultimate is reached, there is nothing that is not entirely equal.
As for the sixty-four kinds of *brahma-svara* (Brahma-voice), they are as described in the *Guhyakapada-sūtra*.

Regarding the statement (and so forth) that there is no difference between the *dharmakāya* and the *rūpakāya*: this means that all Buddhas possess both the birth-body (*janmakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and it is for this reason that they are equal.
Furthermore, while the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are always identical, the *nirmāṇakāya* is indeterminate according to conditions;

yet even though it is indeterminate, because the three bodies are one in essence, there is likewise no distinction. Other passages may be understood accordingly, but as for what is called "the Buddha-dharma":
Unobstructed wisdom means that upon attaining these four equanimities, one encounters no obstacles regarding any of the Buddha-dharmas,
nor does one become confused about the similarities or differences in the Tathāgata’s manifestations and traces (1).
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what the World-Honored One has said—
that from the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, not even a single word was spoken therein, nor has it been spoken, nor will it be spoken,
and that this is not the teaching of the Buddha— World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for what reason did you say this?"
Regarding the statement that "this was not spoken by the Buddha," the Buddha told Mahāmati: "I speak thus because of two dharmas. What are these two dharmas?

They are the dharma of self-attainment through realization (*pratyātma-adhigama-dharma*) and the dharma that has existed from the beginning (*pūrvasthita-dharma*). These are called the two dharmas. It is because of these two dharmas that I speak in this way.
What is the dharma of self-attainment through realization? It is that which the Tathāgatas have realized, and which I also realize."
This is without increase or decrease; it is the ultimate realm of the Dharma realized by oneself, free from verbal conceptualization and the two paths of letters.

What is meant by the "primordially abiding Dharma"? It refers to the ancient path of the sages, like the nature of gold, silver, and so forth—the Dharma-realm that is eternally present whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear. It is like the path leading to a city.
"Suppose, Mahāmati, a man traveling through a vast wilderness were to see a level, direct path leading toward an ancient city;
he would then enter that city and enjoy all manner of pleasures as he desired. What do you think, Mahāmati? Did he create that path and the various pleasures within the city?
He replied, "No, Blessed One. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "I and all the Buddhas of the past abide eternally in the Dharmadhātu."

It is likewise so; therefore it is said: "From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken therein, nor has one been spoken, nor will one be spoken.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"From the night I attained enlightenment until the night of my parinirvāṇa, throughout this interval, I have not spoken anything at all;
for the Dharma realized by myself abides of its own accord. Therefore, I say that there is no difference whatsoever between those Buddhas and me."
Now, what was previously shown still involves the traces of words; it is not yet the state where words are extinguished and traces are obliterated in their equality.

Therefore, Mahāmati again asks about the meaning of "not having spoken a single word from beginning to end," asserting that this teaching of non-speaking is the Tathāgata’s intended meaning, which brings forth the subtle mystery of the Tathāgata’s silence and now culminates in ultimate equality.
As stated in the text, when the Buddha replied, he said: "It is because of two dharmas that I speak thus:
namely, the dharma of self-attainment, which is the name for the realization of the ultimate, and the dharma of primordial abiding, which is the designation for the virtue of nature.
The realization of the ultimate is the virtue of nature; the virtue of nature is the realization of the ultimate. The principle is one and the same. Indeed, it is only through realization...
The ultimate limit is that there is neither "that" nor "this," for its essence is without increase or decrease; therefore it is said: "That which the Tathāgata attained, I too have attained.
Because this is the final consummation, its nature is devoid of [dualistic] separation. Thus, it transcends speech and words, as well as the two paths of the speaker and the spoken.
It is not only beyond the wondrous words of personal realization; even if one were to express it through various means, it remains ineffable.
Furthermore, there is that which cannot be understood through explanation: it is like a person eating honey; although its sweetness can be described, the reason why it is sweet cannot be explained.
It is like a fish in water; although its coldness or warmth can be known, the reason for that coldness or warmth can only be known by the fish itself.
Only when each realizes it for themselves—like two mirrors reflecting one another, merely pointing directly—is the truth attained.
Indeed, it is because the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-guṇa*) is naturally and inherently present, not something produced through artificial effort;
therefore, it is said that the Way of the ancient sages is precisely the Dharma in which the Buddhas of the past fundamentally abide.

This is illustrated by the analogy of the nature of gold and silver, which are inherently firm and solid, not something obtained through smelting or refining. Thus, the Dharma-realm is eternally abiding. It is as if a Tathāgata were to appear...
The phrase "the world and so forth" refers to their conjunction. That is to say, whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature and characteristics of phenomena remain eternally as they are;

one cannot even increase or diminish them, much less speak of or demonstrate them. Regarding the two statements that the *dharmadhātu* is eternally abiding—one from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*) and one from the perspective of principle (*li*)—this is why the analogies used for their conjunction differ.
Furthermore, it says: "It is like the road leading to that city," and so forth.
Furthermore, these two metaphors together illustrate that two dharmas ultimately converge into a single principle:

the "ancient city" with its level ground and direct path represents the *dharmatā* (the fundamental abiding nature); the person who travels it and arrives represents the dharma of self-attainment through conditions.
Because this direct path exists inherently, one is able to follow it and enter; having entered, one dwells in peace. Since these are not external objects, it is said:
If one asks whether that person constructs such a path and so forth, the answer is "no," because it is said that all things are inherently possessed (*prakṛti-stha*).
This uses an analogy to show that the nature of the two dharmas is primordially existent and is beyond the reach of verbal expression.

Thus, the reason why not a single word was spoken throughout the Great Canon of Teachings over fifty years is not that nothing was spoken; rather, it means that what was spoken did not reach [the ultimate nature].

This, too, involves the dispatching of words; yet when there is neither word nor non-word, there is no speech and no trace. The principle of all Buddhas of the three periods of time returns to a single standard;
thus, there is neither equality nor inequality, which is why it is called ultimate equality. The verse commentary is self-evident.
(2) ○ This concludes Chapter Four.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested of the World-Honored One:

"I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all dharmas, so that I and other Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas may depart from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now explain it for you."
You say that Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"There are two kinds of bases for this world, namely: reliance on existence and reliance on non-existence. These fall into the views of being and non-being, and they do not depart from the characteristics of what is to be abandoned.
Mahāmati, what is meant by the world relying on existence? It means that the world arises from causes and conditions; it is not that it does not exist."
"Mahāmati, that which has arisen is not non-arisen; those who speak thus, Mahāmati, are speaking of a world that is without cause. Mahāmati, how does the world rely on what is non-existent?

It is because, having first experienced the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, one subsequently engages in false conceptualization and attachment regarding the existence or non-existence of the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Mahāmati, if one does not grasp at the existence of a nature, it is because the characteristics of nature are quiescent."
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of all Tathāgatas do not grasp the nature of greed, anger, and delusion as being either existent or non-existent.

To hold views of existence or non-existence is the biased conceptualization of ordinary worldlings; to be free from the marks of existence and non-existence is the orthodox essence of the Buddha-dharma.
If one does not distinguish their bias, how can one know what is orthodox? Therefore, Mahāmati requested that the existence and non-existence of existence be explained.
To contemplate the nature of phenomena is to depart from those biased views and reach the true path. Within this, first two kinds of reliance on meaning are shown, stating:
"There are two kinds of worldly reliance," and so forth. Generally speaking, the emotional perceptions of ordinary beings never stand independently;
not relying on existence, they become attached to non-existence. That which is pointed to as existence or non-existence is the objective realm upon which they rely, and it is not merely...
To rely [on these] alone, yet again fall into the view that nature is not desire, while regarding desire as pleasure—such a view is necessarily biased;

being fundamentally unable to leave it behind, one forms the notion of having left it. This is called "not leaving while having the appearance of leaving," which is the same as the previous passage concerning "not emerging while having the perception of emerging.
The phrase "How is it worldly? and so forth is an inquiry and explanation; it refers to the calculation of those who rely on existence.

There is the world produced through causes and conditions; both this production and that which is produced exist. Yet, to preclude the notion that they do not exist, it is said: "It is not that they do not exist.
From existence comes production, meaning that the world produced is indeed existent and not non-existent.

"From existence comes production" means that the productive causes and conditions are indeed existent. Therefore, the Buddha refuted [this view], saying: "This is the theory of no-cause (*ahetuvāda*). For the world exists.
Since there is no necessity for mutual dependence, according to their reckoning, if existence arises from existence, then conditioned phenomena would have no cause;

that existence without a cause is already a false view. As for those who reckon in non-existence—claiming that one first experiences the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, and subsequently falsely reckons that this nature is "not-nature," and that "not-nature" is non-existence—the Buddha refutes them, saying: "If [it were so]..."
"Grasping at the nature of existence" means that there was first something accepted and subsequently something rejected; this indicates that there is still grasping, not a lack of grasping.

If one does not grasp, then its nature and characteristics are fundamentally quiescent, like those of the Tathāgatas, who do not grasp at the nature of greed, anger, and delusion as being either existent or non-existent, and thus do not grasp at existence or non-existence therein.
Only then can it be said that they do not grasp. Thus, while the two vehicles originally seek to sever and destroy [defilements], this [state] is identical to the Tathāgata’s non-grasping;
for this reason, the honey is used as a metaphor for their intent, so as to cause them likewise not to grasp (1).

"Mahāmati, among these, what is it that destroys? Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if one no longer grasps at the nature of greed, anger, and delusion after having previously grasped them, is that it?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! You understand it thus.
Mahāmati, it is not only the nature and non-nature of greed, anger, and delusion that constitutes 'destruction'; it applies to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even the Buddhas as well."

This is what constitutes their destruction. Why is that? It is because neither the internal nor the external can be apprehended, and because the nature of the afflictions is neither different nor non-different.
Mahāmati, greed, anger, and delusion—whether internal or external—cannot be apprehended; for the nature of greed, anger, and delusion is bodiless and without grasping.
This is not the destruction [brought about] by Buddhas, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas; rather, it is the realization of the self-nature [of these states] by Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
Because liberation from both bondage and its cause is non-existent by nature, Mahāmati, if there were one who was bound, there would necessarily be bondage, for that is the cause of bondage.
Mahāmati, to speak in such a way as to negate [these] is called the characteristic of non-existence.

The Tathāgata, intending once more to calculate that which is not spoken by means of questioning whether this exists or does not exist, and whether it is grasped or not grasped—asking among these what constitutes "destruction"—Mahāmati replied according to the sequence previously explained:
that non-grasping is the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), and this is precisely the meaning of destruction.
The Buddha confirmed his statement, yet within that confirmation there was a discourse of affirmation and negation, suppression and indulgence; such is the purpose of the seal.
Regarding the appropriateness of what was said during our conversation, that which "subverts" [the view] is because the argument of "non-appropriation" is overly broad (*prapañca*).
If one were to claim that even the Buddha would not appropriate [anything] simply because it is non-appropriation, how would this differ from [the opponent's position]?

Therefore, it is said that it is not merely the nature or non-nature of greed, hatred, and delusion that constitutes their subversion. Why is this so? [As follows: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "所者何下" (Why is this so? Below...).*
This correctly distinguishes it from the "characteristic of difference," which refers to the statement that [the self] is not apprehended at first glance;
yet, because the reasons for their being different are distinct, it says, "Because internal and external are unobtainable," and so forth.

This means that the Buddha is able to fully comprehend the nature of all afflictions, such as greed, anger, and delusion, as being neither different nor non-different from internal and external phenomena. Since their nature is fundamentally empty, no real body can be apprehended.
In this way, because one does not grasp [at them], one is not like those who hold that there is a definite destroyer; thus it is shown by covering [the point] and concluding:
"Neither the Buddha, nor the Śrāvakas, nor the Pratyekabuddhas are the destroyers, because their original nature is primordially liberated. Since there is no liberation, there is no bondage.
Since both bondage and the cause of bondage are without intrinsic nature, they are all unobtainable. If, regarding greed and hatred...
If the nature of delusion first experiences [an object] and subsequently does not grasp it, then one has already been bound; therefore it is said, "If there is one who is bound," and so forth.
This means that bondage is the fruit, and since every fruit must have a cause, one should point to craving and the like as the cause.
Since that which is bound must necessarily undergo destruction, it is said: "To speak thus of destruction is called the characteristic of non-existence; this must be annihilation."
Falling into the view of emptiness, one destroys [the teachings]; this refutation of such loss is as follows (2).
Mahāmati, for this reason I say that it would be better to grasp a person-view as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the view of emptiness based on the overweening pride of non-existence.
Mahāmati, this "overweening pride of non-existence" is called destruction and falling into self-[clinging].
Mutually seeing one another and hoping for [something else], they do not know that what they see is the manifestation of their own mind;

they perceive external natures as impermanent, subject to momentary succession and destruction, a continuous flow of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) that undergoes transformation and cessation. These are devoid of the nature of words and are false appearances—these are called "the destroyers.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Existence and non-existence are two extremes; even the sphere of the mind must be purified of those spheres.
When the mind is equanimous and tranquil, the nature of the object of apprehension ceases, yet it is not that nothing exists; all things are suchness (tathatā). Such is the sphere of the noble ones:

unconditioned yet manifesting through birth, and having been born, they again cease. Conditioned by causes and conditions, existence is neither existent nor non-existent, and it does not abide within my teaching.
It is not produced by non-Buddhists, nor by a Buddha, nor by me, nor by any other causes and conditions. How can it be attained?

Since there is no one who assembles the causes and conditions, yet one speaks of existence, this is the arising of false views and conceptualizations regarding the birth of phenomena, calculating them as either existent or nonexistent.
If one knows that there is nothing produced and likewise nothing extinguished, and contemplates all this as entirely empty and quiescent, one is free from both existence and nonexistence.
Having thus corrected their error, he spoke with utmost severity to disparage it, saying: "It would be better to hold the view of a person as vast as Mount Sumeru.

By using that which is supremely great to illustrate that which is supremely small, he shows that the error of the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) is far worse than the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*).
For while the evil of the view of a person has its limits, the view of emptiness held by those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) leaves no phenomenon ungrasped.

To abandon these is what is called "destruction. As for those spoken of as having "overweening pride" (adhimāna), all who grasp at even a single dharma as being supreme and thereby form views and arrogance are precisely those who have not attained what they claim to have attained, and have not realized what they claim to have realized; such are the people referred to.
Those who fall into the views of self-characteristics and common characteristics and harbor expectations are fundamentally attached to existence, and it is for this reason that they are rebuked.
Those who hold the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) possess but a single capacity; because they are unable to forget existence, they must negate existence in order to establish non-existence.
Thus, failing to realize that external phenomena are merely manifestations of one's own mind, they perceive external natures as impermanent and regard them as subject to destruction.
Conversely, it is revealed that if one awakens to one's own mind and ultimately remains unattached, then both emptiness and existence will vanish. Furthermore, it is said: "Detached..."
Those who harbor deluded conceptualizations regarding words are likewise attached to the marks of words; because they necessarily seek to depart from these marks, this constitutes a failure.
If one realizes that the nature of words is itself devoid of marks, this is liberation—so what is there to depart from?
Even these marks of words originally possess no fixed nature. The verse states, "Existence and non-existence are the two extremes," which summarizes the above.
Relying on existence and non-existence, one merely reaches the two extremes;

yet at their ultimate limit, there is fundamentally only the single mind, which is the realm of the self-manifestation of one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*). Now, these two extremes and the single mind are originally not far apart;
it is simply by purifying those two views and deluded thoughts that the mind and its objects become equal. When not even a single dharma is perceived as obtainable, then there is stillness.
"Extinction is the absence of the nature of grasped objects" means that, as stated above, there is no grasping;
because one does not grasp that nature of objects, although it is extinguished, it is not non-existent, and although it exists, it is not something other.
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are entirely suchness (*tathatā*). What is called "the realm of the noble ones (*ārya*)" is precisely this: there is arising without seeds.

The preceding verses summarize these two types of reliance; since their meanings do not transcend the worldly calculation of existence and non-existence based on causes and conditions, they are refuted by the True Teaching. Therefore, it is said that one does not abide in my teaching.
Whatever I call "arising phenomena" is not created by a Buddha, nor by outsiders, nor produced by a self (*ātman*), nor by any other distinct cause; rather—
Because things arise from the conjunction of primary causes and conditions, they are said to be "arisen through the collection of causes and conditions.

However, speaking from the perspective of what has arisen itself, one cannot say it is non-existent; yet, when seeking that which collects them, it cannot be found, meaning it was fundamentally non-existent from the start.
How could one then further negate existence by asserting non-existence? Thus, we know that erroneous conceptions of both existence and non-existence are all merely deluded imaginings.

If one realizes that birth is without anything born and cessation is without anything ceased, naturally and wondrously harmonizing with emptiness and stillness so as not to fall into existence or non-existence—this is the correct response to the request. (3) ○ This concludes the fifth chapter.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me and for all bodhisattvas the characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate principle (*tattvapraveśalakṣaṇa*).
If the characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate principle are skillfully distinguished, I and the other bodhisattvas will penetrate these characteristics;
having penetrated these characteristics, we shall swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and not follow after [deluded] awakening."
“Regarding thought, the various Māras, and the non-Buddhists,” the Buddha said to Mahāmati, “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;

I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “All Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas have two kinds of general characteristics:
namely, the penetration of the ultimate principle (zongtong) and the penetration of the teaching (shetong). Mahāmati, as for the penetration of the ultimate principle, it means:

Based on the attainment of the characteristics of one's own superior progress, being far removed from the conceptualizations of speech and letters, one proceeds toward the outflow-free realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
This stage of self-awakening is characterized by its own intrinsic nature, which is far removed from all false and deluded perceptions; it subdues all externalists and the hosts of Māras.

Being based on the illumination and radiance of the path of self-awakening—this is called the characteristic of the penetration of the ultimate principle (*zong-tong-xiang*). What is the characteristic of the penetration of the teaching (*shuo-tong-xiang*)? It refers to the teaching of the nine... [the nine vehicles].
The various teachings of the schools transcend characteristics such as difference and non-difference, existence and non-existence;
through skillful means, they accord with sentient beings and teach the Dharma as appropriate so that they may attain liberation—this is called the characteristic of the penetration of teaching.
Mahāmati, you and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study this. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

Regarding the doctrine and the characteristics of the common teaching on dependent origination: one should clearly perceive and correctly discern the teachings themselves, not following various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
Since there is no such thing as a truly existent nature, how could false imaginings arise?

To understand that "non-nature" is liberation, one observes the characteristics of the continuity, increase, and the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), which are based on the two views and inverted ignorance.
First, regarding the truth of ultimate reality, which is nirvana free from fault: one contemplates that worldly delusions are like illusions, dreams, and plantain trees;
although greed, anger, and ignorance exist, in reality there is no person, and all aggregates (skandhas) arising from craving are entirely like illusions and dreams.
To skillfully transform and guide others, one must master both the essence (*zong*) and the exposition (*shuo*); only then can one lead beings to the Way.

For the essence is the foundation of the Way, while the exposition is the manifestation of the teaching. The essence serves to clarify the goal; if the goal is not clarified, one loses the destination to which one should return.
The teaching serves to explain the principle; if the principle is obscured, one remains bewildered regarding the entrance. Therefore, the essence must be mastered.

If one’s exposition does not accord with principle, it will inevitably be obstructed despite its refinement; if one’s exposition accords with principle but fails to penetrate the essence, it may be eloquent yet lacks substance.
Indeed, if the exposition is not penetrating, the essence has not been reached; if the essence is not penetrated, the exposition is not clear.
These two truly complement one another as the Way, serving as the manifestations of concentration and wisdom, and of liberation and practice.
This is the standard. Mahāmati requested an explanation of the characteristics of the *zongtong* (penetration of the essence), yet he did not mention the *shuotong* (penetration of the expression);

this was to highlight the essentials, for once the *zongtong* is established, the *shuotong* is inherently contained within it. In the response, both are mentioned because they must be paired to be complete.
There are three levels of *zongtong*: the supreme, the intermediate, and the next level below that; the text describes them as "attaining excellence through self-realization."

Regarding those who are free from the conceptualizations of speech, words, and letters, they are said to be "oriented toward the outflow-free realm" (*anāsrava-dhātu*) and further described as having the "characteristic of supreme progress.
Such individuals are those who have realized the Dharma as it is realized by the Tathāgata, and like Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and other great beings, have deeply entered the sphere of the Tathāgata;
they represent the ultimate pinnacle of the "penetration of the essence" (*zongtong*). As for the phrase "oriented toward the outflow-free... [the text continues].

The outflowing realms (*āsrava-dhātu*), the stages of self-awakening (*svasaṃbodhi-bhūmi*), and their respective characteristics are precisely the Dharma-gates realized by Bodhisattvas dwelling in the stages of awakening,
such as the various Dharma-gates obtained by Sudhana from his spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*,

which assist his progress. Furthermore, it is said that "the light of the realm of self-awakening shines forth" means that, with the exception of the aforementioned eight ultimate fruits (*phala*), all that is capable of being brought forth [is included].
To realize that one’s own radiance shines brilliantly, equal to that of the patriarchs of antiquity who transmitted the lineage and clarified the Way, is yet another level.
Although these three types differ, they all consist of self-attainment and self-awakening;

however, there are variations in depth and distance, in the capacity for subduing [delusions], and in what is required or not required. One thereby knows that these are all the characteristics of the thorough penetration of the school (zongtong).

This matter is truly not easy to discuss; that people nowadays have not yet attained even a small measure of realization in this regard, yet claim to have "mastered the essence" (zongtong), is an error—or worse, a deception.

As for "mastery of the exegesis" (shuotong), since this relies upon the teachings, there is no need to differentiate it as distinct [from the essence]; nevertheless, it is not without degrees of depth and shallowness.
To speak of the ninefold division of the scriptures (*navāṅga*) is to refer to the twelvefold division of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), excluding the *nidāna*, *avadāna*, and *upadeśa*.

If one deliberates on these three points, they still involve both the minor and the major; thus, the nine divisions of the teachings also possess both general and specific aspects, as well as progressive and regressive applications (and so forth).
By means of these teachings, one guides and benefits those with various capacities; yet, one must still distinguish between difference and non-difference.

That is to say, only after one has personally abandoned the four attachments can one then, according to suitability, provide the fourfold teaching for others—this is what is meant by "skillfully distinguishing the characteristics of phenomena."
Only one who remains unmoved within the ultimate truth (paramārtha) may be said to have succeeded; otherwise, it is indeed difficult.
Regarding the first three lines of the verse, they are explained here according to the general characteristics of the school’s doctrine. To speak briefly:

"not following various conceptualizations" means that one who has attained the two general characteristics does not follow the conceptualizations of non-Buddhists (tīrthika) nor the [false] nature of reality held by foolish commoners.
Regarding these deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*): how do they arise?

To explain the origin of the perceptions and thoughts raised by the preceding inquiry, it is said that one may take non-existence to be liberation, or give rise to dualistic views regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), or take "oneness" to be the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), or take the absence of transgression to be nirvāṇa;
the characteristics of these are set forth later in the section on "views of nirvāṇa."

Since these are all views of inverted ignorance, when one observes those deluded imaginings as being like illusions, dreams, or plantain trees through the perspective of our present school’s tenet, one does not follow after them.
Although there are the obscurations of greed, anger, and delusion, this explains the meaning of their being like illusions:
although the three poisons exist, the person who possesses them does not; it clarifies that since there is no one capable of giving rise to them, there is nothing that can arise. Furthermore...

Since the arising of craving and so forth is illusory, the aggregates produced thereby are likewise so; as these two aspects mutually clarify one another, their illusory nature becomes even more manifest.

"How does unreal conceptualization arise? What kind of phenomena are called unreal conceptualization, and within what kind of phenomena does unreal conceptualization occur?

"Bhagavān, why is it that the proliferation of false conceptualization arises from attachment to the various natures of unreal objects within the divisions of the sense-bases (*indriya*) and their causal characteristics, rather than arising from attachment to the characteristics of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
