Why is it that they do not arise? It is because the false imaginings of existence and non-existence do not arise.
When one realizes that external appearances—whether as entities or non-entities—are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, false imaginings do not arise.

Mahāmati, I say that for other ignorant people, who are attached to the various characteristics and natures of false imaginings, various false imaginings arise based on the objects of karma appearing before them.
One who exhausts deluded conceptualization must reach its ultimate limit; one who demonstrates true nature must exhaust its source.
For when the source is exhausted, true nature naturally manifests; when the limit is reached, where can deluded conceptualization exist?

Thus, Mahāmati requested an explanation of the characteristics of unreal conceptualization, asking three questions in total: first, how does conceptualization arise? Second, what is it... [the third question follows].
The Dharma is named "delusive conceptualization. [The Buddha] was asked three times, "In what does one delusively conceptualize? and he answered in succession to explain. First, he answered:

The Buddha’s words below further restate the meaning of the preceding section to generate the intent of the subsequent question.

As for "production" and "non-production," this means that within the fundamental state there are originally no two [realities]; it is only through awakening that one realizes they are not produced. Because the ignorant claim they are produced, it is said that the deluded conceptualizations of existence and non-existence do not arise.

Thus, in the passage beginning with "because they are not produced," in contrast to those of inferior capacity below, these are considered "awakened ones" because they have thoroughly understood the delusions of existence and non-existence.
Because thought does not arise, one realizes that the external world—whether it appears as existent or non-existent, being or non-being—is merely the manifestation of one’s own mind.
When natural false conceptualization does not arise, this very state of non-arising is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for there is no ultimate truth existing apart from this.
Other deluded beings do not realize this principle because they perceive through various false conceptualizations of their own minds.
Because of signs, when one perceives activities before oneself, there arises the false conceptual attachment to various external objects;
this is what constitutes unreal meaning, for there is no separate unreal meaning that arises. Therefore, I say that other ignorant people likewise [perceive] it as such.
Because it does not arise, that which is unreal is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); because it arises, it is [conventional].

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the state beyond substantiality; when examined through two perspectives, there is from the outset no fixed dharma. It is only due to the difference between delusion and awakening that there is birth or non-birth.
How can a fool abandon the attachment to views of "self" and "what belongs to self," and leave behind the errors of agent, action, and causal conditions, thereby attaining awakening?

Through the transformation of the body and mind resulting from the cessation of the mind that measures its own delusive imaginings, one ultimately and clearly understands all stages and the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.

Being free from the five dharmas, the three natures, and the delusive imaginings regarding objects and views, for this reason I say that delusive imaginings arise from attachment to various unreal meanings;
by knowing the meaning of reality as it is, one attains liberation from the various [projections] of one's own mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Causes and conditions give rise to this world; it is born of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Attached to the four positions, people do not know my penetrating realization.
The world is neither born from existence, nor is it born from non-existence; it is not born from both existence and non-existence, nor is it born from neither existence nor non-existence."
Regarding all causes and conditions, how is it that the deluded imagination of fools is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent?
By observing the world in this way, the mind turns away from [grasping at] a self, and one realizes that all natures are unarisen because they arise from conditions.
Since everything produced by conditions is a product, it does not exist as an intrinsic entity; for an entity does not arise from itself, as there would be the fault of duality in such an entity.
Because there is no fault of duality, an existent nature cannot be apprehended.
According to the previous response, since fools are consistently immersed in delusion, by what means could they be freed from all views of error?
Since they do not abandon the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," the causal conditions of agent and action and so forth are all merely erroneous characteristics; thus, it is further shown:
To awaken to the fact that one’s own deluded thoughts are merely the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*) means to realize that all delusions are simply the measure of one's own mind.
Thus, whether in existence or non-existence, confusion or awakening, everything is but the mind; it is not turned by external objects, but rather can turn external objects.

Through this, body and mind undergo transformation, and through the awakening to one's own former delusion, one attains ultimate clarity and understanding of the meaning of all stages (*bhūmi*), reaching the state of Suchness (*tathatā*).

When one arises from the realm of self-awakening and departs from the five dharmas, the self-nature, and the objects of conceptualization regarding superior states—wherein seeing objects is itself called the conceptualization of names and signs—then since that which is to be remedied has been abandoned, the remedy itself also vanishes.

If even the five dharmas are transcended, how could one not transcend the views of attachment to "I" and "mine"? This is specifically a general demonstration, from the root, of departing from such faults.

Having already separately analyzed and refuted the characteristics of causes and conditions, as well as the agent and the action, in accordance with the subsequent verses, the conclusion is shown by saying, "For this reason," and so forth.
This means that if one follows the meaning of unreal conceptualization (*vikalpa*), then conceptualization arises;
however, if one accords with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) through knowledge of reality as it is, then liberation is attained. Thus, the conceptualizations of one's own mind can be understood.

Nevertheless, the distinction between "real" and "unreal" is merely a conventional designation based on the nature of phenomena and cognition; it is nothing more than a provisional name established according to circumstances.
From the beginning of the verse up to the line "no intrinsic nature can be found," the verse praises the transcendence of the relationship between agent and action within causes and conditions.
Within this, first, by investigating causes and conditions, it says: "All causes and conditions, etc."—meaning that among all worldly phenomena, there is none that does not arise from them.
Those who give rise to false conceptualization regarding dependent origination cling to the four views—existence, non-existence, and so forth—within the dharma of dependent origination;

because they do not understand the principle of non-arising through which the Tathāgata has attained penetration, it is said that "the world is neither produced nor [unproduced]," etc., which means to depart from the four views by abandoning attachment to their inherent nature.
Furthermore, it says, "All causes and conditions," etc., which continues to refute the previous [notions of] existence and so forth.
The four propositions are likewise conceptual constructions; they are not merely "not non-existent," etc., but rather the abandonment of attachment to the characteristics of the four propositions.
This is as fully explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding the two kinds of emptiness—of nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

When one thus contemplates the world and the mind undergoes transformation to attain selflessness, it means that by transforming the mind’s dual attachments to nature and characteristics, one attains the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness: of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). All natures...

that is to say, since the dharmas of worldly dependent origination are fundamentally unarisen, the faults of [imputing] "agent" and "action" or "cause" and "condition" are spontaneously transcended. (2)

One does not grasp meaning by means of words, but enters into meaning through words, just as a lamp illuminates forms. Although the previous statement that "suchness is equal to the limit of emptiness" is the ultimate expression regarding principle, it still falls within the realm of mental construction (*cittamātra*); how much more so with other verbal explanations? Because there was a question and answer concerning the relationship between words and meaning, the following first clarifies the meaning of words individually: [The text continues: "Words are like a finger pointing at the moon; they are not the moon itself. Furthermore, since all phenomena are ultimately ungraspable, words cannot reach their limit. Therefore, the Tathāgata taught that words are empty and without self-nature, yet he did not say that meaning is non-existent. Why? Because if meaning were non-existent, then even if one were to abandon words, one would have no basis for attaining liberation. Thus, while words are empty, meaning is not non-existent. Therefore, one must exert oneself. This is the spirit of the Way. One must not be indolent. If one is indolent, one will perish. Therefore, one must be resolute. This is the power of the mind. Therefore, one must be courageous. This is the virtue of the sage. One must not be timid. If one is timid, one will be subdued. Therefore, one must be brave. This is the courage of the hero. One must not be cowardly. If one is cowardly, one will be crushed. Therefore, one must be bold. This is the majesty of the victor. One must not be weak. If one is weak, one will be broken. Therefore, one must be firm. This is the integrity of the noble one. One must not be fickle. If one is fickle, one will be scattered. Therefore, one must be stable. This is the constancy of the steadfast one. One must not be unstable. If one is unstable, one will be lost. Therefore, one must be settled. This is the peace of the enlightened one. One must not be restless. If one is restless, one will be agitated. Therefore, one must be calm. This is the tranquility of the peaceful one. One must not be turbulent. If one is turbulent, one will be disturbed. Therefore, one must be serene. This is the clarity of the pure one. One must not be turbid. If one is turbid, one will be defiled. Therefore, one must be clear. This is the purity of the stainless one. One must not be impure. If one is impure, one will be stained. Therefore, one must be clean. This is the cleanliness of the pure one. One must not be dirty. If one is dirty, one will be sullied. Therefore, one must be bright. This is the brightness of the luminous one. One must not be dark. If one is dark, one will be obscured. Therefore, one must be radiant. This is the radiance of the brilliant one. One must not be dull. If one is dull, one will be dim. Therefore, one must be brilliant. This is the brilliance of the wise one. One must not be ignorant. If one is ignorant, one will be blind. Therefore, one must be clear-sighted. This is the vision of the awakened one. One must not be blind. If one is blind, one will be lost. Therefore, one must be seeing. This is the sight of the enlightened one. One must not be sightless. If one is sightless, one will be trapped. Therefore, one must be free. This is the liberation of the liberated one. One must not be bound. If one is bound, one will be confined. Therefore, one must be released. This is the release of the released one. One must not be confined. If one is confined, one will be imprisoned. Therefore, one must be open. This is the openness of the open-minded one. One must not be closed. If one is closed, one will be shut in. Therefore, one must be expansive. This is the expansiveness of the vast one. One must not be narrow. If one is narrow, one will be cramped. Therefore, one must be broad. This is the breadth of the wide one. One must not be cramped. If one is cramped, one will be restricted. Therefore, one must be spacious. This is the spaciousness of the spacious one. One must not be restricted. If one is restricted, one will be limited. Therefore, one must be infinite. This is the infinity of the infinite one. One must not be limited. If one is limited, one will be finite. Therefore, one must be eternal. This is the eternity of the eternal one. One must not be finite. If one is finite, one will be transient. Therefore, one must be constant. This is the constancy of the constant one. One must not be transient. If one is transient, one will be fleeting. Therefore, one must be enduring. This is the endurance of the enduring one. One must not be fleeting. If one is fleeting, one will be momentary. Therefore, one must be timeless. This is the timelessness of the timeless one. One must not be momentary. If one is momentary, one will be ephemeral. Therefore, one must be permanent. This is the permanence of the permanent one. One must not be ephemeral. If one is ephemeral, one will be impermanent. Therefore, one must be indestructible. This is the indestructibility of the indestructible one. One must not be destructible. If one is destructible, one will be perishable. Therefore, one must be immutable. This is the immutability of the immutable one. One must not be mutable. If one is mutable, one will be changing. Therefore, one must be unchanging. This is the unchangeability of the unchanging one. One must not be changing. If one is changing, one will be shifting. Therefore, one must be unshakable. This is the unshakeability of the unshakeable one. One must not be shakable. If one is shakable, one will be wavering. Therefore,

The combination of the conceptualization of words, which arises in dependence on the throat, lips, tongue, and other such locations, as well as the conceptualization of discourse regarding "self" and "other," is called speech (*vāc*).
Apart from these two, there is a distinct phenomenon that manifests and is called meaning (*artha*).

Therefore, it is said that one must realize through direct experience (*sākṣātkriyā*) that which is free from all characteristics of conceptualization and characteristics of speech; only then is it truly so named.
The "good meaning" (sany) is not so; it is merely words. Therefore, next, to clarify the way of practicing the seal (mudrā), it says:
"In such a meaning, alone in a quiet place," and so forth. "Alone" means being without counterpart; "in a quiet place" means that both thought and perception are severed.
In such a place, one follows what has been heard to turn toward what is called *tathatā* (suchness) as it truly is.

When one contemplates and cultivates through observation the meanings of terms such as "limit" (*koṭi*) and so forth, each condition is individually realized by self-aware wisdom that accords with *nirvāṇa*, causing all things to harmonize and coincide.
One turns away from the habitual tendencies of speech and conceptualization, returning the body to the realm of self-awakening.
Thus entering into the superior progressive meaning and characteristics between each stage (*bhūmi*), this is called "skillful in meaning. However—
One who is skilled in meaning (*artha*) must certainly be skilled in speech; however, one who is merely skilled in speech is not necessarily skilled in meaning.
Therefore, to clarify both skill in speech and skill in meaning together, it is said: "Observe speech and meaning, and observe meaning and speech. They are neither different nor non-different.
This means that if speech were different from meaning, one would not be able to discern meaning by means of speech; yet, if one enters into meaning through speech, they cannot be separate.
Just as a lamp’s illumination of form is a cause that is not distinct from it, yet one should also say that the lamp can illuminate form while form is truly not the cause of the lamp;
likewise, words enter into meaning while meaning is truly not the words—this too is not a unity.
Examining it thus, they are neither different nor non-different; being fundamentally without intrinsic nature and free from all conceptual discrimination, who could possibly [grasp them]?
Is the meaning determined by words? If it cannot be determined by words and meanings, then even the nature of letters—which is beyond verbal expression—is already such;
how much more so the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)? Yet, to interpret it in this way alone is not yet called "skillful" (1).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding non-arising, non-ceasing, intrinsic nature, nirvāṇa, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, the mind, self-nature, and so forth—due to attachment to the meanings of words based on conditions, there arise various views of establishment and denial.

Based on these, false imaginings of difference are established, such as the manifestation of various illusory signs; just as with various illusions, foolish ordinary beings produce false imaginings of difference.
This is not the teaching of the noble sages. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Those who establish all phenomena through conceptual proliferation based on verbal expression—because of such establishment, they fall after death into the hells or the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Therein, there is no self, nor are the aggregates (*skandha*) themselves the self; yet it is not as those conceptual proliferations imagine, nor is it the case that there is no self."
All things possess a nature that is merely the false imagination of the ignorant; yet, as they perceive it, all should see the Truth.
All dharmas are without intrinsic nature, and both purity and defilement are entirely non-existent. They are unreal just as they are perceived, yet they are not nothingness either.
For those who cling to verbal designations, even the sacred teachings cannot avoid falling into the fault of nihilism;

therefore, it is said that they are "unborn, unceasing, intrinsically nirvāṇic," and so forth—all of which are merely conventional names for the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). If one asserts that these exist substantially, one falls into the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*);

if one asserts that they definitely do not exist, one falls into the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). How much more so for other cases? Thus, the words differ and the conceptual constructions differ.
"Delusive conceptualization" refers to the construction of various distinct conceptualizations based on the establishment of linguistic designations;
one then falsely discriminates these as having distinct characteristics when they appear in various ways like illusions.
One never realizes that although they appear diversely as illusions, they lack any reality—just as the Tathāgata’s diverse verbal teachings merely employ provisional names to guide sentient beings.
Those born as ordinary and ignorant fail to understand and thus grasp [these things] as real; they are not sages or worthies.
To do otherwise would constitute slanderous delusion; this is omitted from the text for brevity. The verse says:

"Regarding those who engage in conceptual proliferation through speech, while it is not necessarily an error to establish various phenomena by means of speech, it is because they establish them through such false imaginings that it becomes slander."
This would indeed be an error; therefore it is said that one falls into the *niraya* (hell) upon death.
Now, there is no sin greater than disparaging the Vaipulya [sūtras] and slandering the *Prajñāpāramitā*; thus, to receive this retribution now is not an error.

Regarding the three verses beginning with "In the aggregates (*skandha*) there is no self," following the previous refutation of externalist calculations, these are further employed to demonstrate the characteristics of falling [into error]. It is said that within the aggregates there is no self.
It is said: "To say that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are not identical to the self" is a general and concise statement; it should be understood as encompassing both existence and non-existence.

These do not go beyond the four types of views, all of which ultimately fall into the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); therefore, he directly refutes them by saying: "Nor is it the case that they are merely false conceptualizations.
This means that while it is not like those aforementioned views of a self, it is also not the case that there is no self at all—thus, one is free from both self and non-self.

Furthermore, it is said that the view that "all things possess an intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is the eternalist view (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). If an intrinsic nature truly existed, one would necessarily have seen the Truths (*satyadarśana*);
yet, since they have not seen the Truths and still claim there is an intrinsic nature, this is merely a false conceptualization (*parikalpa*).

Furthermore, it is said that the view that "all phenomena lack an intrinsic nature" is the nihilistic view (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Since nihilism implies that nothing at all exists, [the author] refutes this, saying: "It is not as you say."
He perceives that such views are not as they claim; for these views are unreal. Both the notions of annihilation and permanence are not correct views.
Since there is no dharma to be seen, how could there be permanence? (2) [End of] Chapter Eight.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of knowledge (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).
If you and the other bodhisattvas skillfully discern the characteristics of knowledge, you will be able to penetrate those characteristics and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Mahāmati, that knowledge is of three kinds: namely, worldly (*laukika*), supramundane (*lokottara*), and supremely supramundane (*lokottaratama*).
What is mundane knowledge? It refers to all non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings who cling to the notions of existence and non-existence. What is supramundane knowledge?
It refers to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who fall into the hope and clinging for self-characteristics and common characteristics.
What is the supreme supramundane knowledge? It refers to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas who contemplate the dharma of non-existence and perceive that which is neither born nor extinguished.
O Mahāmati, the stage of the Tathāgata, which is free from the categories of existence and non-existence, arises spontaneously through the realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena.

That which is subject to arising and ceasing is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which is neither arising nor ceasing is wisdom (*jñāna*). Furthermore, that which falls into the characteristics of the signless and the fallen into the various causal signs of existence and non-existence is consciousness;
that which transcends the signs of existence and non-existence is wisdom. Furthermore, that which nourishes and develops signs is consciousness.
The characteristic of cultivation is wisdom.

Since nothing is equal to knowledge for discerning the truth and falsehood of all phenomena and clarifying the right and wrong of words and meanings, the Tathāgata, without waiting for a question, spoke thus:
"I shall now explain the characteristic of knowledge; listen, O son of noble family. As for that which knows:

The term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) has both general and specific applications. In its general sense, as in common worldly usage, it may be applied to anything that can be termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*), such as the eight consciousnesses and so forth.
In its specific sense, however, consciousness reaches its ultimate limit in the ordinary mind, whereas knowledge reaches its ultimate limit only in the Sage.

Therefore, when speaking in terms of knowledge, there is no phenomenon that is not [knowledge]; when speaking in terms of consciousness, there is no phenomenon that is not [consciousness]. If you wish to know this:

To discern right and wrong regarding all phenomena depends solely upon the clarity of one’s wisdom and cognition. Initially, it is said that there are three kinds of wisdom based on the ten realms (*daśadhātu*).

When speaking of "wisdom" (*jñāna*), "cognition" (*vijñāna*) is implied; when speaking of "worldly wisdom," both are included. Regarding "existence and non-existence," these refer to the two views (*dvaidhī-dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding "self-characteristics and common characteristics," this refers to the observation of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) as having existence by those of the Two Vehicles.
The general and specific characteristics are as previously analyzed (*etc.*). Regarding the statement that the wisdom of the highest degree concerns "the dharma of non-existence":
at the ultimate limit of principle and wisdom, there is nothing by which it can be named; thus it is forcibly indicated as the "dharma of non-existence.
Since it is called "non-existence," what is there to be observed? To contemplate and clearly realize that all dharmas are ultimately empty is precisely to see the Unborn (*anutpāda*).

The categories of "arising" and "non-extinction," which are free from existence and non-existence, and all their various alternative names and distinct explanations, ultimately converge upon this principle.
Furthermore, the specific presentation of these names and characteristics serves as a foundational basis for subsequent comparative analysis.

Since wisdom is taken as internal realization, all [realizations] arise from what is personally attained; there is nothing else such as so-called "non-arising" or "non-extinction. This is the self-awakened sagehood.
Although the meaning of "the realm of wisdom" (*jñāna-gocara*) is still general, it is specifically distinguished by means of three pairs of opposites:

that which pertains to the nine realms, such as arising and ceasing, belongs to consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which pertains to the Buddha-realm, such as non-arising and non-ceasing, belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*).
While this encompasses both the general and the specific, the present intent lies in the specific; in terms of the teachings, this is also a correspondence between the partial and the perfect.
As for "illumination" (*vidyā*), the first three belong to consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone; only the perfect [nature] is termed the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the mention of the "characteristic of cause" within both the characterized (*sanimitta*) and the uncharacterized (*animitta*), this is based on the principle that each of the three pairs universally encompasses both cause and effect. It is specifically mentioned here to show that while the former mostly follow from the cause and the latter mostly follow from the fruit, the text is merely abbreviated.
As for the characteristic of nourishment (*puṣṭi-lakṣaṇa*) being consciousness, this is strictly in reference to the absence of [clinging to] persons and phenomena.
What I stated previously—that which is called "matter and so forth nourishing the mind"—is precisely this meaning.
Generally, whatever relies on external objects to sustain that which is internal is consciousness (*vijñāna*);
only that which requires no external support or dependence and attains itself within is wisdom (*jñāna*) alone. (1)
Furthermore, there are three kinds of wisdom: namely, knowing arising and ceasing; knowing specific and general characteristics; and knowing non-arising and non-ceasing.
Furthermore, the characteristic of non-obstruction is the sphere of wisdom, whereas various obstructed characteristics are consciousness.

Furthermore, the characteristic of the means of production arising from the conjunction of the three factors is consciousness, while the characteristic of the self-nature of the means when no factors are present is wisdom. Furthermore, the characteristic of attainment is...
The characteristic of consciousness cannot be apprehended; this is the self-attained realm of noble wisdom, which neither issues forth nor enters, being like the moon in water.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

Gathering [objects] is consciousness (*vijñāna*); not gathering them is wisdom (*jñāna*). To observe all phenomena and penetrate their non-existence, thereby attaining the power of mastery—this is called insight (*prajñā*).
That which is bound to objects is the mind (*citta*); that which arises from conceptualization and perception is wisdom.
From this, the non-existent and supreme insight are born. Mind, thought, and consciousness are far removed from discursive thinking and perception.
Having attained the state of non-conceptualization, O Son of the Buddha—not a Śrāvaka—you possess the supreme, progressive patience and the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom.
Born from the sublime ultimate truth, you are entirely detached from all spheres of activity. I possess three kinds of wisdom that reveal reality;
therein, I fully embrace all conceptualizations and thoughts regarding the various natures. This wisdom is not shared by the followers of the two vehicles, as it is free from all that exists.
Attached to intrinsic nature, [the teaching] arises from the various śrāvakas; transcending all mind-only (*cittamātra*), the Tathāgata’s wisdom is purified.
Next, regarding the elucidation of the three wisdoms: based on what a single person knows, there are three illuminations. The subsequent verse refers to the three [wisdoms] known by the Tathāgata.
Just as one possesses five eyes, yet in reality that which is able to know is one, it is therefore the same as the previous [case].

If one distinguishes them by their characteristics as they still penetrate both the shallow and the deep, yet again, because the ultimate wisdom is specifically revealed through three meanings, it is called the "unimpeded characteristic" (*anāvaraṇa-lakṣaṇa*).

This refers to the equality of wisdoms; that is, because the three preceding wisdoms are fused and merged into a single mind, there is no opposite of defiled obstruction—this is what is meant by "consciousness.
Regarding the statement that the conjunction of the three factors gives rise to the "expedient characteristic" (*upāya-lakṣaṇa*), it is as explained previously.

The arising [of consciousness] through the conjunction of the three conditions—faculties, objects, and so forth—is the characteristic of *upāya-vijñāna* (expedient consciousness), not the characteristic of *svabhāva-lakṣaṇa* (intrinsic nature).

If it were the characteristic of intrinsic nature, then the numinous awareness of a single thought-moment would not depend on conditions for its arising; therefore, it is said that "unconditioned expedients" constitute the characteristic of intrinsic nature.
This is wisdom (*jñāna*). To grasp characteristics is consciousness (*vijñāna*); not grasping characteristics is wisdom. The characteristic of wisdom is one and the same. However...
Because one perceives that there is detachment from [phenomena], there is a distinction between attainment and non-attainment;
this is precisely the meaning of what is said in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*: "Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory," and so forth.

That which is called the Tathāgata’s self-realized realm of noble wisdom is such that all that the Tathāgata has revealed is entirely free from the three characteristics of obstruction and so on, yet it is also not separate from obstruction.
Because its equal realm cannot be described by name or form, it is said to neither emerge nor enter; like the moon in water, it is neither identical to nor separate from it.
This can be known through wisdom but is difficult to demonstrate with words.

The verse states, "The accumulation of karma constitutes consciousness," which briefly summarizes the two meanings of the superior wisdom and consciousness. The meaning of "accumulation" is as explained above; here, the eight consciousnesses are taken as [the basis].

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the ultimate limit of consciousness; when it reverses its orientation upward and does not engage in grasping or accumulation, it becomes wisdom (*jñāna*), which is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha.

The verse concerning the observation of "non-existence" and so forth refers to the progressively superior wisdom (*uttarottara-jñāna*). Furthermore, "wisdom" is also called "insight" (*prajñā*), and "consciousness" is also called "mind" (*citta*);
these are all synonymous terms. Therefore, it is said: "Binding to objects is the mind," and so forth—the meaning of these four lines has been explained previously.
To understand these words: that which arises from conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*) by the wise; it is the transformation of conceptualization into wisdom.
As for "mental consciousness and cognition," this refers to *vijñāna*. To be "far removed from the phenomena of thought and ideation" means that wisdom is attained.
When one attains the state of non-ideation, one transforms *vijñāna* into wisdom; this is the Bodhisattva, not the Śrāvaka—this is the beginning of what is called wisdom. It is supremely tranquil.
The "advanced patience" (*kṣānti*) is precisely the Tathāgata’s attainment of the wisdom of the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti-jñāna*), which marks the culmination of verbal knowledge.
Because it arises from the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), its sphere of activity is entirely free from all [conceptual] attachments.

Regarding the verse stating, "I have three kinds of wisdom," these three objects of knowledge are those revealed by the Tathāgata; thus, although they involve the arising and ceasing of what is known, [they are ultimately beyond such fluctuations].

These are also all the true *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, namely what is called "opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" (*buddhajñānadarśana*); and what is called in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* "the three knowledges in a single mind.
In that [text], the preceding two [knowledges] are reiterated through the categories of "conception" (*saṃjñā*) and "thought" (*cetanā*) to manifest the ultimate knowledge (*atyanta-jñāna*).

This is because ordinary beings grasp at the nature of arising and ceasing through deluded thought and conception, whereas the followers of the Two Vehicles do the opposite; therefore, [they do not attain it].
If one is associated with detachment from all possessions yet still clings to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this is merely the wisdom of the śrāvaka.
If the Tathāgata’s ultimate wisdom is pure, it transcends all mental measures (*cittamātra*);
how could it be merely different from the worldly wisdom of the two vehicles? (2) This concludes the ninth chapter.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are nine kinds of theories of transformation among the non-Buddhists; from these views of transformation, [the following] arise:

namely, transformation of shape and location, transformation of characteristics, transformation of causes, transformation of becoming, transformation of views, transformation of nature, transformation of clearly manifest conditions, transformation of clearly manifest actions, and transformation of things. Mahāmati, these are called the nine kinds of transformation.
Based on this, all externalists give rise to theories concerning existence, non-existence, birth, and transformation. What is meant by "transformation of form and location"?

It refers to the perception of different forms and locations; for example, when gold is transformed into various vessels, diverse forms and locations appear, yet the nature of the gold does not change.
The transformation of all natures is likewise. Or there are externalists who act as follows:
These are false imaginings, even up to the false imagining of the transformation of things; for they are neither identical to nor different from the false imagining itself.
When phenomena undergo change or remain unchanging, it is not that the reality is different, but rather that those who perceive it differently see it as such.

This is like the nine theories of transformation held by non-Buddhists—such as the theories of shape, characteristic, cause, and formation—which do not transcend the four great elements and the five aggregates.
Regarding these dharmas, because one perceives their characteristics of arising, ceasing, and change, one reckons that there is transformation (*pariṇāma*).

However, the True Teaching speaks of "dependent origination," "being like an illusion," and "the manifestation of one's own mind," asserting that external natures have no self-nature and are unchanging.

Thus, it has never definitively declared what is heterodox or orthodox, or gain or loss; this is seen therein. As for "form" (*ākṛti*), it refers to the various perceptions of spatial locations; this is the explanation of the text.
"Manifestly" refers to the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing; "mutually" refers to causes that gradually mature; "forming" refers to the necessity of decay following formation;

"perceiving" refers to the transformation of things according to conditions; "changing" refers to the inexhaustible succession of births; "conditions" refers to the transformation and cessation caused by causes and conditions;
"acting" refers to the non-eternal nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); "evident" means they are clearly visible; furthermore, it is called "dividing."
The logical necessity of the theory that [the self] arises from seeing the causes is that which gives rise to existence and non-existence;

that is to say, whether it be the non-existence of what already exists or the existence of what was previously non-existent, these are all modes of transformation that ultimately resolve into nothing but existence and non-existence.

To explain the term "transformation of form and location" (rūpa-sthāna-pariṇāma), according to the subsequent verse, it refers to the locations of the physical forms of the four great elements and the various sense faculties.

Furthermore, when one observes that its form changes according to time, one says there is transformation; yet the spirit-self (*ātman*) does not change. It is like gold being transformed into various vessels:

because the vessels are of many kinds, their distinct appearances manifest, but the nature (*svabhāva*) of the gold does not change. It is further said: "The transformation of all natures is likewise.
This serves as an analogy for other characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and all phenomena (*dharma*), showing that their transformation and shifting are also like this.
However, this does not mean that its nature undergoes transformation. [The text] first refutes their position by citing the fallacy of the preceding analogy:

it is like gold transforming into various vessels, which refers to what the aforementioned sutra calls "gold ornaments. The original analogy is one of neither identity nor difference, yet they reckon it as being different;

furthermore, because they take its unchanging nature to be "identity," we know that they— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Awakening of Faith* or a similar treatise concerning the relationship between the Absolute and phenomena. The translation reflects the philosophical nuances of the Chinese terminology.)
To say that "identity" and "difference" arise from false conceptualization (vikalpa): for this reason, the fixed positions of identity and difference cannot logically coexist;
yet the principle of neither-identity-nor-difference is inherently and eternally harmonious.
Now, by using this harmonious principle to refute those fixed positions, one distinguishes between the gains and losses regarding the internal and external [realms]. (1)

In this way, one should understand that all transformations of nature—such as milk turning into curd, wine, or the ripening of fruit—are merely the false conceptualizations of transformation held by the non-Buddhists (tīrthakaras).
In reality, there is no such transformation, whether in terms of existence or non-existence.

Mahāmati, it is only through the habitual cultivation of their own false conceptualizations that ignorant beings give rise to [these notions]. Mahāmati, there is not a single dharma that is ever born.
If one perceives the cessation [of things] as being like the arising of forms seen in a phantom or a dream—at that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The transformations of shape, location, and time, the four great elements, the sense faculties, and the intermediate state arise gradually through false conceptualization; they are not the domain of the wise."
The Supreme One [teaches] that dependent origination is not as it is imagined by them; rather, worldly dependent origination is like a city of the Gandharvas.
Next, following this analogy, he refutes all [theories of] transformation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth. First, he indicates this through a simile, saying:

"One should know that [the claim] that things such as milk and curd ripen gradually in succession is likewise not so; it is merely a conceptual construction of transformation. This is established by reasoning.
Because that which is seized is fundamentally without reality, it is said: "That also has no transformation," and so forth.
Since phenomena such as existence and non-existence are all manifestations of one's own mind, external natures lack inherent existence;

they are merely like illusions. How, then, could there be any real transformation of milk into curd and the like? Therefore, the concluding passage says: "Thus, the ignorant and so forth" refers to those who perceive things as existing.
That which arises, ceases, and undergoes transformation is entirely due to the nature of one's own deluded imagination and is produced by past habitual tendencies;
it is not a real dharma-substance. Furthermore, it is said that there is no dharma whatsoever that arises or ceases.

When one perceives the arising of forms like a phantom or a dream, this precisely means that because they are fundamentally unreal, they appear like phantoms or dreams; no real dharma ever arises or ceases, yet they appear as such.
The analogy of illusions and dreams—such as milk turning into curd—is that there is fundamentally no transformation; the principle is likewise so.
Extending this reasoning, it may be said that while the ignorant perceive things like illusions as undergoing arising and ceasing, they do not perceive arising and ceasing as being like an illusion.
If one perceives them as being like an illusion, then there is no arising or ceasing; how could there be any transformation? Thus, within arising and ceasing, there is no arising.

Those with false views belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Those who give rise to conceptual attachment based on seeing arising and ceasing are followers of external paths (*tīrthika*).
Those who see things as like illusions and dreams are practitioners of universal contemplation.

Those who see that all phenomena are manifestations of their own mind and realize that external natures have no inherent nature are the true followers of this sutra. Thus, it is clear that the Buddha-dharma differs from the teachings of external paths.
The verse states that "form, location, and time undergo transformation. This is a brief summary of the meaning of the aforementioned transformation of form;

furthermore, the term "time" may also encompass other [factors], as there is nothing that is not subsumed within time. The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is called the beginning of transformation, and it is considered preeminent among dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the like.
This is because the Buddha perceives dependent origination as being like an illusion or a magical creation; thus, it is said to be like a city of the *gandharvas*.

(2). Chapter Ten. At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the meaning of the continuity of all dharmas and the meaning of liberation.
If you skillfully distinguish the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas, both I and [others]..."
All Bodhisattvas are skillfully proficient in the expedient means of all continuities and do not fall into the attachment to the characteristics of the literal meaning as it is spoken;
they are adept in the characteristics of continuity and non-continuity regarding all phenomena, as well as in the departure from verbal expressions, letters, and false conceptualizations;
they travel through all Buddha-fields, possessing the power of mastery over the infinite assemblies and the great supernormal powers.
Holding this seal, they manifest various transformations and illuminate with radiant light; their awakened wisdom skillfully enters the ten inexhaustible phrases.
Their practice is without artifice, like the sun, moon, mani-jewel, and the four great elements. In all stages, they are free from the marks of their own deluded imaginings;
they perceive all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, and so forth. They enter the body of the Buddha-ground and, in accordance with the realms of all sentient beings, [manifest accordingly].

He preaches the Dharma to them as is appropriate and guides them, causing them all to dwell securely in the realization that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, free from the categories of existence and non-existence, as well as the deluded conceptualizations of arising and ceasing; thus, their bodies become increasingly sublime.
Dharmas have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and from the beginning have never possessed the characteristics of either continuity or non-continuity.
The conceptualization of continuity and non-continuity arises because of persons; it is due to these verbal expressions that their meaning is produced.
Thus, "continuity" is the deluded imagination (*vikalpa*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while "non-continuity" is a synonym for liberation (*vimukti*). Regarding this continuity...
Those who have fully realized the absence of continuity are those skilled in expedient means;
those for whom continuity arises due to what was originally without continuity are those whose emotional attachments are deep. If one can sever it with even a single thought, one attains liberation.
How sublime are these words! Are they not the very foundation for liberation from birth and death? This is why Mahāmati requested that all dharmas be explained.
Regarding the meaning of continuity (*saṃtati*) and liberation (*vimukti*): liberation is the opposite of continuity.

Within this context, the preliminary prayer and invocation consists of both self-practice and the practice of transforming others. Regarding self-practice, the phrase "if one discriminates well" and so forth refers to attaining benefit through teaching;
that is, by means of teaching, one attains discrimination, and through discrimination, one attains thorough understanding.
Those who fall into attachment to the meanings as they have been explained will encounter the views regarding those meanings later in the text.

Because one skillfully understands the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) and awakens to the state that is free from the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of words and letters, one is able to increase the Path according to circumstances.

Therefore, it is said that by means of the seal of the sovereign power of the *abhijñās* (superknowledges), the *dhāraṇīs*, and the universal movement throughout all Buddha-fields, one attains the merit [thereof].
The "Dharma-gate of Virtue" refers to the various transformations and so forth, which give rise to all manner of emanated functions.
The names and meanings are as set forth elsewhere (*etc.*). As for the phrase "lacking expedient practice," this refers to the absence of developed expedient practices.

It is like the sun and moon traveling through space without any point of attachment; it is like a *maṇi* jewel manifesting according to conditions without intrinsic nature; it is like the four [elements]... [and so on].
That they are vast and pervasive yet do not obstruct one another is the mark of the Bodhisattva’s transformative path;
as for the successive stages of realization and entry, it is said that one must "separate from the marks of one's own delusive thoughts.

According to the subsequent text, each stage (*bhūmi*) has its own marks of delusive thought, all of which must be abandoned until reaching the ultimate entry into the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), where one’s own practice and vows are fulfilled.

In the section on "fulfilling the transformation of others," the manner in which objects are enticed and benefit is brought about is also roughly as described above regarding the characteristics of the benefits obtained;

therefore, it says, "in the realm of all sentient beings, etc. The meaning of the different terminology is that one does not subsequently fall into attachment to the literal meaning of what was said, and once the merit of transformation is attributed to oneself, the *dharmakāya* of both self and others becomes further enhanced and more sublime.
(1) The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "So be it; we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "All dharmas are like [an illusion]..."

The continuous attachment to the meaning of what has been taught consists of: the continuous attachment to signs; the continuous attachment to conditions; the continuous attachment to existence and non-existence;
the continuous attachment to the delusive conceptualization of arising and non-arising; the continuous attachment to the delusive conceptualization of cessation and non-cessation;
the continuous attachment to the delusive conceptualization of vehicles and non-vehicles; and the continuous attachment to the delusive conceptualization of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The continuity of attachment to the specific characteristics of each stage; the continuity of attachment to one's own false imaginings;

the continuity of attachment to the uninterrupted succession of false imaginings regarding existence and non-existence; the continuity of attachment to the false imaginings of externalists based on the categories of existence and non-existence;

and the continuity of attachment to the uninterrupted succession of false imaginings regarding the three vehicles and the one vehicle. Furthermore, Mahāmati, this and other [views] belong to ordinary, ignorant beings themselves.

The continuity of false conceptualization occurs because of this succession; thus, the delusions of the foolish and ignorant are like a silkworm making a cocoon, binding themselves with the threads of their own conceptualization.
They bind others as well, clinging to the characteristics of the continuity of existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, therein there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity, because all phenomena are seen as quiescent and the production of false conceptualization does not arise.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva perceives all dharmas as quiescent. Next, Mahāmati, he realizes that external natures—whether existent or non-existent—are merely manifestations of his own mind and are ultimately non-existent.
By conforming to and investigating the measure of what is manifested by his own mind, he sees that all natures are without marks (*animitta*).
Because he perceives the continuity [of these marks] as quiescent, he is free from the characteristics of continuity or non-continuity regarding all dharmas.

In the reply, the characteristics of all continuities are first demonstrated by stating that they are "immeasurable. This means that internally there is the single body, and externally there are the myriad phenomena;
from the vastness of empty space to the minuteness of a single speck of dust.

Whether speaking of the coarse or the ultimate ineffability, when one traces the attachment of the mind, there is nothing whatsoever that is not a continuity. Therefore, it is said: "In accordance with the meaning spoken, one calculates and clings [to it]."
This refers to what is called "generating understanding according to words. Within this, there are three parts. First, regarding worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*):

it means that characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)—namely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—and conditions (*pratyaya*)—namely the objects of perception (*ālambana-viṣaya*)—as well as existence and non-existence, arising and non-arising, and so forth, all have mutually contradictory meanings, yet they continue in succession to form attachments.
The intent is that although the deluded thoughts of ordinary fools may not [directly] concern the nature (*dhātu*),...
They are equally attached [to existence], and furthermore, they are attached to non-existence; their attachment to signs does not cease, and other meanings are to be understood by analogy with this.

Next, regarding what is called "transcendent phenomena" (*lokottara-dharma*): "vehicles" refers to the three vehicles, while "non-vehicles" refers to the removal of those vehicles—namely, the paths of humans and devas—and the conditioned and unconditioned, which refer to the two types of liberation and the specific characteristics of each stage (*bhūmi*).

"Delusive conceptualization" refers to the attachment to signs within one's own stage, which is to say, the craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). Thirdly, speaking in terms of the contrast between ordinary beings and sages:
"one's own delusive conceptualization" refers to the mundane dharmas of the preceding stage; "immediacy" refers to supramundane dharmas;

the categories of existence and non-existence refer to what non-Buddhists rely upon, namely the views of annihilationism and eternalism; and the three vehicles and the one vehicle exclude that which is attained through self-realization. If...
To act with the expectation of a counter-measure is likewise a state of deluded conceptualization; it is a continuity that is not severed.

This and other such [states] refer to the fetters of ordinary, ignorant people, which were previously distinguished and refuted. The word "this" (*ci*) specifically refers back to the disciples of our own internal teachings (*neijiao*), whose attachments are often still light.
Next, the ordinary ignorant ones are specifically refuted; this refers precisely to the non-Buddhists (*waidao*), whose attachments are even more severe. Therefore, it says they are "like silkworms."
One may spin a cocoon but cannot emerge from it oneself; in the end, one merely returns to the continuity of existence and non-existence.

Yet, if one were to exert oneself for a moment so that a single thought of their past seeds could be severed, it is not necessarily the case that this would not be reversed. Within that state, there is also no subsequent [arising].
Next, to clarify the wisdom of non-continuity: when about to clarify the severance of wisdom, one must first demonstrate that the objective realm is empty, so that the realm...
Although it is not non-existent, even wisdom does not sever this wisdom; yet, although it possesses the power to sever, it is only because the object is non-existent that it is designated as "wisdom.
Therefore, it is said: "Within that, there is also neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity," referring to the objects.

This means that as clarified above, all characteristics of continuity are merely false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*); they are called "continuous" while fundamentally lacking any characteristic of continuity.

Because it is the continuity of reality, when one sees that all phenomena (*dharma*) are quiescent and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise, then the object accords with the wisdom (*jñāna*).
It is further said that this is the wisdom that realizes the non-existence of external natures and so forth;

for even if one realizes these characteristics, if one does not subsequently engage in contemplative observation, one cannot sever [the grasping toward] those objects. Thus, when one perceives the continuity as quiescent, one attains clear comprehension.
When there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity, then wisdom accords with its object.

Although the phrasing suggests a temporal sequence, in reality, at the single moment of severance, all views are extinguished and one is liberated. Furthermore, it is said that there is no characteristic of non-continuity;
this means that if even one [characteristic] were to remain, it would still constitute continuity. Therefore, both must be discarded for it to be truly so.
The discourse on tranquility reaches this point and is called "the cessation of words" (2).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, therein there is neither bondage nor liberation; others fall into error because they do not realize as it truly is that there is neither bondage nor liberation.
Why is this? Because among all phenomena—whether existent, non-existent, both, or neither—not a single sentient being can be apprehended.
Therefore, furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three continuities for the foolish: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as craving for future existence accompanied by delight.
Because they continue by means of these, there is the continuity of the realms of existence (*gati*). As for that continuity, Mahāmati, it is the continuity of the five realms of existence.
Mahāmati, when continuity is severed, there is no continuity; it is the characteristic of non-continuity. Furthermore, Mahāmati, [it concerns] the threefold conjunction.

When one clings to the means of practice as a conceptual attachment to the continuity of consciousness, there is the uninterrupted arising of the continuity [of consciousness] through the conditions of the threefold conjunction.
When the conditions for consciousness are severed by the view of liberation from all three, then no continuity arises.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Unreal conceptualization is said to be the characteristic of continuity."
If one knows that true nature of the web of continuity, then one severs the ignorance regarding all natures and abandons adherence to mere verbal expressions;
just as a silkworm weaves a cocoon and entangles itself, so too are fools bound by the delusions of their own conceptualizations, failing to discern the continuity [of existence].
The following section is a re-explanation based on the meaning of bondage and liberation. However, since non-continuation constitutes liberation, then continuity is bondage;
these share the same underlying principle. When both are simultaneously negated, they both vanish, thereby manifesting the sense of their ultimate identity.
Thus it is said, etc. Since there is fundamentally no bondage from the outset, what liberation could there be? Only true wisdom can accord with this.
As for the rest who fall into not awakening to reality as it is—such as the partial, small, ordinary, and external—they possess both bondage and liberation, yet neither is ultimate.
Why is this so? [The text] below interrogates and explains by presenting the intent behind both existence and non-existence:
because regarding all phenomena, if they exist, there are sentient beings who can be bound; where there is bondage, there is liberation. If they do not exist, the opposite is true.
Since this is now explained from the perspective of the subsequent [state], there is neither bondage nor liberation. If so, what was meant by the previous mention of "liberation"? It is said:
it was spoken in contrast [to bondage] for the purpose of severing the continuity [of delusion]. Once liberation is attained, one spontaneously accords with the One Suchness (tathatā);
how could the distinction between bondage and liberation remain? Furthermore, it was said that "fools possess three continuities"; this also serves to clarify the meaning established above.
Regarding the various continuities (*saṃtati*), when speaking specifically in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), one does not know that the reason for their continuity lies herein and not therein;

therefore, the meaning of the three types of continuity is further set forth: First, in terms of the three paths (*trivartman*), this refers to greed, hatred, and delusion, which are the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three times.
Because of these, there is the continuity of the realms of existence (*gati-saṃtati*); "existence" (*bhava*) here refers precisely to karma, which continues.
The five destinies are the fruition (*vipāka*), yet since both [fruition and its cause] are simultaneously discarded, it is said...

(as above). Second, regarding the meaning of the conditions of the threefold harmony, as explained previously: when one employs the condition of skillful means (*upāya*), there arises attachment to the characteristics of consciousness, which continues in uninterrupted succession.
Because these two continue in an unbroken stream, it is called "skillful means and attachment."
Thus, there is continuity, and existence is also karma. If the three conditions combine and then separate, the continuity of consciousness is severed;
that is, at the point where the three combine, one sees the three liberations, for there is no liberation apart from them. Therefore, when there is continuity, [new birth] does not arise;
it arises only by means of conditions. When consciousness is severed, the conditions depart; yet in all cases, consciousness is primary. As the verse says: "No..."
Regarding the meaning of continuity and non-continuity in true reality and delusive conceptualization, it is nothing other than the distinction between the real and the delusive.
Because it is delusive, there is continuity; because it is real, its severance can be known. Thus, true reality is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena;
how could there be room for continuity or severance within it? Therefore, what is called "severance" is merely spoken in contrast to the delusive; in principle, it is simply this.

Since speech is fundamentally without continuity from the outset, what discontinuity could there be? If one realizes that speech is devoid of cognition regarding all natures, then one sees that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent;

what we call "discriminative cognition" arises merely from the delusion of ordinary fools who, following words and grasping at them, become confused upon encountering objects and falsely reckon them to be continuous.
This is due to a lack of investigation. If one looks back in this way, where is there any continuity?
If it does not continue, it is severed. If there is that which appears to be observed yet is not severed, it is because the path of observation lacks strength.
(3) ○ This concludes the Eleventh Chapter.
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught— that by means of various conceptual constructions one conceptually constructs various natures,
yet those natures do not exist, being merely the nature of conceptual construction— World-Honored One, if it is only the nature of conceptual construction and not the nature of intrinsic reality,
such that they are mutually dependent, then, according to what the World-Honored One has said, there would be no such thing as the non-substantiality of affliction and purification."
"Is it not so? Because all dharmas are of the nature of false imagination and lack intrinsic nature," the Buddha told Mahāmati, "it is so, it is so, just as you have said.
Mahāmati, the nature and self-nature of false imagination as it is imagined by the ignorant is not real;
rather, this imagined nature has no characteristic of an existent self-nature."
Is it not the teaching on the self-nature of deluded thought that exhaustively describes the root of illusion and unreality?
If one realizes that the nature of deluded thought is "no-nature," then since its root has perished, its branches will naturally fall away. It is like flowers in the sky:
once the cataract is cleared, the flowers vanish of their own accord; how much less could they possess any individual self-nature? Therefore, it is said: "By means of that..."
Those various deluded imaginings do not possess that respective nature; their own-nature is merely the nature of deluded imagining itself.
This is because the preceding passage contains the statement regarding the continuity of various deluded imaginings;

thus, Mahāmati, taking the meaning of the text into consideration, establishes the foundation for further posing a challenge. The phrase "those various" specifically refers to the characteristics of the various continuities, which are [the objects of] deluded imagining.
For this reason, it is said that by means of various deluded imaginings (*vikalpa*), one imagines the nature of various phenomena;
yet those phenomena are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and are merely attributed to deluded imagination. Nevertheless, there may still be doubt, such as:

"If the nature of things is merely deluded imagination and not an inherent nature belonging to those phenomena themselves, and if intrinsic nature exists only in dependence upon deluded imagination, would this not be the same as worldly convention?"
"Does what the Venerable One has taught regarding the dharmas of affliction and nirvāṇa, defilement and purity, etc., also entail the fault of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)?

Since all dharmas are merely the self-nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and are fundamentally without nature, this objection intends to challenge [the teaching] by asserting that while all dharmas lack intrinsic nature, false discrimination possesses intrinsic nature. In the Buddha’s response, he first confirms this statement.
The meaning established above—that those [dharmas] lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—serves as an analogy for the fact that afflictions and other phenomena should likewise lack intrinsic nature;
this is what is meant by saying that all dharmas have no intrinsic nature. It is not correct to say that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) possesses intrinsic nature.
Therefore, the Tathāgata directly declares that conceptual construction also lacks intrinsic nature, stating: "It is not like the nature of foolish commoners."
The delusion regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) is truly a veil;

that which is now called "delusion" is precisely what is taught for the wise to awaken from their confusion—namely, the teaching of detachment from the delusion that regards [phenomena] as having real intrinsic nature. Therefore, one should not equate this with the delusion of ignorant people who calculate an intrinsic nature and regard it as real.
Furthermore, it is said: "This delusive intrinsic nature has no characteristic of an intrinsic nature."
However, to say that they lack a real nature is simply to say that they are entirely without nature. If one knows they are without nature, how could delusive thoughts exist?
One might ask: "Are there then two kinds of delusive thoughts? I reply: Delusive thoughts are fundamentally one; the difference lies between the ignorant and the wise.

For the ignorant person, who regards them as real, their delusion is difficult to eliminate. For the wise person, who knows them to be empty, their delusion is easy to transform. Now, I am acting for the sake of the wise.
This explains why they are distinct (1).

Mahāmati, regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of noble wisdom—wherein there is noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom—it is through such intrinsic nature that one knows it.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "If it is by means of the noble [path], with noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom..."
The divine eye is not of the nature of the fleshly eye; its intrinsic nature is known in this way, unlike the deluded imaginings of foolish people.

World-Honored One, why do foolish people not awaken to the reality of the noble nature by departing from such deluded imaginings? World-Honored One, that is neither inverted nor non-inverted. Why is this so?
It is because they do not awaken to the nature of the noble reality; they do not see that which is free from existence and non-existence.

Because of their characteristics, O Blessed One, even the noble ones do not perceive things in this way; they do not take the objects of false conceptualization as objects by way of their own intrinsic characteristics.

O Blessed One, those [characteristics] also appear as the nature of self-nature and the nature of false conceptualization, yet you do not speak of them as having causes or being causeless, because that would entail falling into the view of intrinsic characteristics. Their objects are different; they are not like those [false conceptualizations].

“World-Honored One, there would be the fault of infinite regress because one would not perceive the self-nature and characteristics of the nature of consciousness. World-Honored One, furthermore, the nature of consciousness is not the cause of the nature of false imagination;
for what reason is it that one falsely imagines, rather than being free from false imagination, yet knows false imagination as it truly is?”
Fearing that they might not yet have attained awakening, the Tathāgata again used the self-nature of the noble nature as a metaphor to instruct them, saying:
"Just as the noble wisdom possesses the self-nature of the noble nature, so too should you know; by analogy with the noble vision, there exists the noble eye of wisdom.
That which knows the self-nature of the noble nature is what the noble person truly knows and truly sees. This is the first [knowledge].
Because the nature of all phenomena is neither existence nor non-existence, one should know that false imagination is likewise to be understood in this way; thus it is said:
"The nature of suchness. When one knows this intrinsic nature, the Tathāgata has fully revealed his own realized realm, which may be called clear indeed.
Thereupon, Mahāmati attained a lucid understanding and said: "If it is truly as the noble ones know it, and not as ordinary people know it..."
The noble vision is not the ordinary vision; thus, it is not like the deluded imaginings of the foolish.

Having deeply attained realization, he again addressed the World-Honored One to challenge his doubts and resolve his knots. His exposition consisted of five successive layers, describing how the foolish depart from their deluded imaginings.
The Buddha remained silent, sealing his approval without offering any further interrogation; thus, one knows that his explanation was quite appropriate for the noble ones.

Regarding the initial statement on the mind: since ordinary beings do not awaken to the reality of the nature of the sages, by what means could they possibly be free from the difficulty of delusive thoughts?
From this point downward, there is a sequence of alternating doubts and explanations, totaling three such pairs.
The intent is that this lack of awakening is a state of inversion; therefore, the explanation says: "That is neither inverted nor non-inverted. Why is this so? [The following text follows.]
Furthermore, he provides a self-examination and explanation: because one does not perceive the nature of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is not that there is no inversion;

yet, because one does not see [the truth] apart from the marks of existence and non-existence, one sees according to the facts, and thus it is not an inversion. He further states: "The noble ones do not see in this way either.

Regarding the phrase "delusive conceptualization according to the facts," his intention is that seeing according to the facts is considered non-inverted, yet even the noble ones [do not see it in that way].
"It is not as in the case of seeing through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); rather, it should be understood as being free from inversion. Furthermore, the commentary explains:

"Because one does not take the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of objects as an object, it is said that although the Noble Ones do not see things in such a manner, they are not turned by the self-characteristics of objects;
therefore, they are not inverted. It further states: "That [self-nature] is also the nature of self-nature (*svabhāva-svabhāva*), etc., meaning that it does not function as an object."

That which is transformed yet not inverted refers to the fact that for the noble ones, there has never been an absence of *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) and *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected intrinsic nature).

If the noble ones possessed this *svabhāva*, then foolish commoners would certainly possess it as well; therefore, it is said that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined intrinsic nature) manifests in this way.
Furthermore, the commentary explains: "It is not because of the absence of causes" means that the Tathāgata indeed possesses *svabhāva*.
Because he does not speak of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as being either caused or uncaused, he does not fall into the view that intrinsic nature is real.
Since they [the others] speak of causes and speak of the absence of causes, they fall into the views of self-nature and characteristics.

Therefore, what the Tathāgata perceives as a distinct realm refers to a realm different from the realm perceived by ordinary people; it is not a realm characterized by their various distinctions. Thus, he concludes with a refutation, saying:
If such an infinite regress were to follow, then all the doubts previously raised would instead become faults;
therefore, it is said that there is no infinite regress, as the single nature of non-awakening (*abodha*) itself exhausts the matter.

Furthermore, these marks of non-awakening—the nature of false conceptualization (*vikalpa-svabhāva*)—do not arise because of the characteristics of that nature of self-existence, but are simply false conceptualization itself. Thus, he returns to the fundamental tenet to resolve the difficulty.
It is asked: "How does one come to know, as they truly are, both the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and that which is not conceptual construction?
What is this 'how' that refers back to the preceding difficulty regarding how fools are [caught up in] conceptual construction? (2)
“World-Honored One, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is different from the characteristic of self-nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). World-Honored One, they do not share a similar cause;
how is it that the imagined nature and its characteristics are each non-imagined, yet foolish commoners do not know them as they truly are?

Nevertheless, for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon their imaginings, you say that things exist according to the characteristics of their imaginings, though they do not exist as they truly are. World-Honored One, for what reason do you deny that sentient beings exist?”
There is no attachment to the self-nature of perceived objects, nor attachment to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom;

yet, falling into the view of existence, one speaks of the emptiness of dharmas as being without intrinsic nature, while [simultaneously] speaking of the self-nature of things as the reality of noble wisdom. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"It is not that I teach the emptiness of dharmas as being without intrinsic nature, nor do I fall into the view of existence when speaking of the self-nature of things as the reality of noble wisdom. Rather, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon their fear."

Because of the fear-inducing nature of words, Mahāmati, sentient beings have from time immemorial clung to the characteristics of the self-nature of things (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), and have clung to the characteristics of the objects of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna-vastu-svabhāva*).
To counteract this, I teach the Dharma of emptiness. However, Mahāmati, I do not speak of the characteristics of the self-nature of things;

rather, Mahāmati, I abide in the emptiness of reality as it is personally realized (*pratyātma-yathābhūta-śūnyatā-dharma*), which is free from the appearances of delusion and free from the views of existence and non-existence regarding the manifestations of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-bhāva-abhāva*).
Having attained the seal of the three liberations as they truly are, one attains the realization of the self-nature of phenomena through the observation of dependent origination;
thus one abides apart from the views and signs of existence and non-existence.

To provide a detailed explanation, he first summarizes by indicating two distinctions: namely, the distinction between false imagination and reality, because their nature as unreal and real, respectively, is different. From himself...
Because their natures and characteristics differ, and because awakening and non-awakening are distinct, this is why they are considered dissimilar causes.
Such is the characteristic of the self-nature of false conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): that which is empty yet capable of awakening is the non-conceptualization of the wise;
that which is real yet lacks awakening is the failure of the foolish to know things as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*). Therefore, he asks again: "How is it that each of these is not [the same]?"
Regarding the phrase "each and every [of] false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and so forth," it means that within the two aforementioned differences, each is not itself a false conceptualization.

To further explain by correlating the difficulties of the ignorant and the wise, it says: "Thus, for the sake of sentient beings being free from false conceptualization," and so on. The meaning is this:

although the ignorant and the wise differ, one cannot claim that they differ from false conceptualization based on their personal differences; however, the ignorant person... [does not...
