For one who is not obscured by emotional afflictions, what worry need there be regarding failing to depart from this? This is the profound intent of the Tathāgata for the sake of sentient beings;
however, since the previous [teaching] has already negated the "real existence" of foolish people, he should not again provide them with such discourse.

Since the principle does not permit him to explain it on his own, he specifically entrusts Mahāmati to bring it forth; yet even this is spoken by virtue of the Buddha’s power. World-Honored One, why is this so?

Therefore, the following section further challenges that partiality and falling into extremes: "If, as you say, false conceptualization is unreal, why do you again negate the biased views of existence and non-existence?
To cling to the self-nature of this matter constitutes using reality to challenge the unreal.
This refers to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), as previously clarified regarding the sphere of the self-nature of noble wisdom; herein, one calculates [the nature of things].

If one clings [to these views], one falls into the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, if one asserts that the teaching on emptiness is a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) while contradicting what has been taught regarding the reality of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), then existence and non-existence would be in opposition.
In the Buddha’s response, he first simultaneously dispels those objections by stating that it is "a phrase free from fear.
This means that sentient beings have, since beginningless time, feared emptiness and clung to existence; because they fear emptiness, the noble wisdom is taught for their sake.
One guides them by means of the nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). Now, the object of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) is neither existent nor non-existent;

yet because beings cling to existence, they give rise to clinging to signs and views. Therefore, one preaches the Dharma of emptiness to remedy this. Thus, whenever emptiness or existence is preached, it is invariably for the sake of sentient beings;
never has it been said that there is a real dharma of existence. Hence it is said: "I do not speak of the characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*)."

To demonstrate the Dharma of abiding in oneself, it is said: "I abide only in the attainment of the *yathābhūta-śūnyatā* (emptiness as it truly is), which is the primordial, ultimate, and wondrous emptiness (*atyanta-prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
Because I do not fall into heterodox categories, I am free from the signs of delusive conceptualization;

because I always abide in the Middle Way, I am free from views regarding the existence or non-existence of what is manifested by one's own mind. Furthermore, it says: "Attaining the three gates of liberation," etc., refers precisely to this.
What is established therein merely clarifies the three aforementioned meanings (3). [End of] the twelfth section.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding the statement that "all dharmas are unarisen," a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not establish this as a thesis (*pakṣa*). Why?
Because the thesis consists in the non-existence of all intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), and because their causes are characterized by arising; thus, it is said to be one.
The thesis that "all phenomena are non-arising" is itself undermined by that very thesis; for if all phenomena are non-arising, then that thesis must also be non-arising.

Since that thesis arises in dependence [upon its object], it is undermined. Furthermore, because that thesis of non-arising enters into all phenomena, it cannot be established as a non-arising characteristic.
Thus, one who establishes the thesis that "all phenomena are non-arising" has their own statement undermined. Mahāmati, existence and non-existence do not...

Mahāmati, if one were to establish a thesis based on the non-arising of all natures— that is, establishing a thesis because the characteristics of existence and non-existence of all natures are unapprehendable—
then that thesis would be undermined, because the characteristics of existence and non-existence do not arise.
Furthermore, one should not establish such a thesis, as it involves the many fallacies of the five-membered syllogism and because the reasons are mutually contradictory in their characteristics.
Because it is a mere fabrication, one should not establish a formal thesis (pakṣa),

such as "all dharmas are unarisen," "all dharmas are empty," or "all dharmas lack intrinsic nature" (niḥsvabhāva). Mahāmati, rather, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should speak of all dharmas as being like illusions or dreams—
appearing and yet non-appearing— and because they perceive the faults of conceptualization and awakening, they should speak of them as one.
All phenomena are of the nature of illusions and dreams; this is taught except for the purpose of removing the state of fear in foolish people.
Mahāmati, do not let foolish people fall into the views of existence and non-existence, lest they become terrified and turn away from the Mahāyāna.
Since all dharmas are unarisen, speech and conceptualization are entirely cut off; once speech has ceased, how much more so can one falsely establish a thesis?
When those non-Buddhists establish the thesis of "non-arising," they produce further branches and leaves precisely where there is no arising;
this is what makes it untenable. This is why the Tathāgata cautioned the Bodhisattvas: "One should not establish such a thesis. All.
Because there are many contradictions and errors. Why is this? [The text] below interrogates and explains its meaning, stating: "The thesis is that all natures are non-natures.
The intended meaning is as follows: A thesis must necessarily have a proponent. If the thesis is that all natures are themselves non-natures, where is the meaning of that thesis located?
Generally speaking, the term "unborn" is established in dependence upon "birth. Since it exists in relation to its opposite, it is not [ultimately real].

First, it is incorrect to establish the thesis that the meaning of production is itself non-production through self-destruction. Furthermore, according to your position, that which is unproduced must necessarily be included among all phenomena;
if it were identical to other phenomena, it would possess the characteristic of destruction, and if it lacked the characteristic of destruction, it could not be called "unproduced.
Since both positions are untenable, this is the second reason why it is incorrect. Moreover, it is said:
Regarding "neither existence nor non-existence gives rise [to anything]": previously, one simply took non-existence to be non-arising;
yet even if one were to shift this position and claim that all natures, whether existent or non-existent, are equally non-arising, this too is not the case.

Even if one further adds that both the nature and characteristics of existence and non-existence are unobtainable, the meaning of "non-arising" itself cannot be established as a formal thesis (*pakṣa*), for the reasons already refuted in the third point. This is what is called the "fivefold division."

Regarding the phrase "because there are many fallacies": this refers precisely to the fact that when establishing a thesis for the opponent through a series of shifting reasons (*hetu*), various distinct characteristics arise, resulting in many fallacies (the meaning of which is set forth separately).
Furthermore, because it falls into the error of implying purposeful activity (*kṛtakatva*), it is subject to the same criticism as this [previous point]; thus, it should not be the fourth [position].
Moreover, it is said: if one posits that all phenomena are unarisen, or that they are emptiness, or that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and so forth—if all these were established...
If the thesis (*pakṣa*) contradicts both name and reality, how could there be a thesis established through emptiness or the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*)?
Since it is not fixed as one, there ought to be many theses; yet if there could be many theses, then there should not be only five.

However, below this, the Bodhisattva himself further resolves these doubts and demonstrates the principles of what may and may not be asserted, such as when he says: "All phenomena are like illusions."

If it is argued that dreams are not non-arising, then since their characteristics are not permanent, there must likewise be a fault; why single out and criticize only those who establish the thesis of non-arising?

Therefore, it is said: "Because of the faults regarding manifest and non-manifest characteristics, as well as seeing and cognizing. This means that when an illusion manifests, it exists, and when it does not manifest, it does not exist;
likewise, when one speaks of dreaming, one sees while deluded, but upon awakening, it is no longer seen—all these are faults of impermanence.
To sever this doubt, it is said: "I shall explain that which is of the nature of an illusion or a dream; its nature being free from existence and non-existence, there is no fault.
However, one must further examine whether this is appropriate or not, and thus it is said: "This may be explained only for the sake of removing the state of fear in foolish people.
For those who are foolish fall into the views of existence and non-existence; if they were to hear that things are of the nature of illusions or dreams...
If one were neither existent nor non-existent, one would then fear existence and fall into the error of rejecting the Mahāyāna;

therefore, it should not be said that by this reasoning, even when teaching the Dharma, one need only examine the capacities of sentient beings to know what is beneficial or harmful—how much more so when establishing a tenet based on such teaching, which could it possibly be changed? (1)
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Without intrinsic nature, without speech, without objects, and without continuity—those deluded fools imagine them like corpses.
All dharmas are unborn due to false discrimination; they do not belong to the tenets of the non-Buddhists, for ultimately there is no nature produced by causes and conditions."
For those whose wisdom realizes that all phenomena are unborn, no conceptualization arises, because the causes for such [conceptual] positions have been extinguished through awakening.
It is like one with cataracts seeing the false appearance of falling hairs; attachment to their nature is likewise.

The foolish, through their perverse deluded imaginings, construct the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). They construct the intrinsic nature of things and, by reflecting upon that constructed intrinsic nature, give rise to further conceptualization.

When signs and phenomena give rise to verbal teachings, the mind becomes disordered, extremely agitated, and trembling; yet the Son of the Buddha is able to transcend these, remaining far removed from all false conceptualizations.
What appears as water is not truly water; such perceptions arise from thirst and craving. Thus are the delusions of the foolish, but for the noble ones it is not so.
The vision of the sages is pure, born of the three liberations and samādhis; they remain far removed from arising and ceasing, wandering in the realm of non-existence.
Practicing that which is non-existent, as well as neither-nature-nor-non-nature, from the equality of nature and non-nature the noble fruit arises.

What is meant by "nature and non-nature," and what is meant by "equality"? It means that when the mind does not know the internal or external and is utterly agitated, if one can destroy that [agitation], the mind then sees equality.
The verse states: "There is no intrinsic nature and no speaker. This recapitulates the statement that all phenomena are unarisen.

Since there is no intrinsic nature, there is no speaking; since there is no speaking, there is no objective entity; and since there is no objective entity, there is no conventional designation of continuity.
Thus, both the root and the branches are fundamentally unarisen. Yet, those deluded fools establish dogmatic tenets through their false imaginings, like a corpse rising once more to commit evil.
If an awakened person were to believe that all things are thus non-arising, how could this be a tenet attained by the non-Buddhists?
This doctrine of non-arising is intended, for the time being, to refute the various non-Buddhists; it cannot be discussed on the same level as ordinary conventional views.
Ultimately speaking, the nature is fundamentally non-arising, yet it is accomplished through conditions, and even those conditions are unattainable; therefore, it is the wisdom of awakening.

If one does not even form the notion of non-arising, how much less would one form the notion of arising? Since both arising and non-arising are non-arising, how could one establish a thesis in opposition to arising?
It is like a person with cataracts looking downward to distinguish between what is correct and what is erroneous;

the falling hairs seen by such a person serve as a metaphor for that which is non-existent yet appears to exist. Indeed, the three realms of existence are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature, being merely products of deluded conceptualization.
Fools manifest false and deluded views, positing various characteristics, things, and intrinsic natures within the three realms of existence where nothing truly exists.
Furthermore, they give rise to conceptual constructions through discursive thought, establishing verbal teachings based on these characteristics and things.

These verbal teachings are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*). When the mental ground becomes agitated and reaches a state of extreme trembling, this constitutes the most severe form of distraction.
The phrase "the Son of the Buddha who is able to transcend" refers to the Bodhisattva’s ability to depart from this nature.
By stating that it is "not water," yet there is the "perception of water" and a "craving for its weight," the analogy of the thirsty deer is used to illustrate what is to be abandoned.

When the Sage perceives the purity and so forth, he further speaks of the meaning of the non-arising of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and the arising of wisdom; this is the wisdom of the three liberations (*vimokṣa*). Samādhi is meditative concentration (*samāpatti*); concentration is...

Because wisdom (*prajñā*) and the arising-and-ceasing of phenomena are opposites, they constitute the Path (*mārga*). Therefore, when concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom arise, arising-and-ceasing are abandoned.
The Noble Ones (*ārya*) wander within and cultivate this [Path] such that it is like empty space; thus, there is nothing whatsoever.

Since existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended, nature (*prakṛti*) is non-nature (*aprakṛti*), and in their equality, one returns to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is that from which the fruit of Buddhahood arises. Furthermore, it is asked: "What is it?"
Regarding the nature of existence and non-existence, one further investigates the reason why they are equal; this essential point does not transcend the two minds of delusion and awakening.

Because of delusion, one fails to know that the internal and external are of one suchness, and thus one drifts and wavers between existence and non-existence. Consequently, there arise views of "nature" and "non-nature.
If one can destroy those views, one returns to the fundamental mind and perceives equality. (2) *Note: The original text contains a parenthetical number "(二)" indicating the second section.*
This concludes the thirteenth chapter.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught—that wisdom does not apprehend objects of perception—this is the establishment of the measure of designation (*prajñapti-mātra*).
It is comprised within the establishment of designations, yet it is also the non-apprehension of what is grasped."
Because there is no grasping of non-nature, cognition does not arise; it is merely a conventional designation.
Why is it that, Blessed One, cognition does not apprehend because the self-characteristics and common characteristics of non-awakened nature are neither different nor non-different?

Or is it because cognition does not apprehend due to the obscuration of the various natures and intrinsic characteristics of self-characteristics and common characteristics? Or is it because of mountains, crags, stone walls, earth, water...?
Is it because of obstructions such as fire or wind that knowledge does not arise? Is it because of being too far away or too close that knowledge does not arise?
Or is it because of old age, childhood, blindness, or the impairment of the sense faculties that knowledge does not arise?

World-Honored One, if knowledge does not arise because one does not perceive whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are different or not different, then one should not speak of "knowledge," but rather of "non-knowledge," since there is an object that is not apprehended.

Therefore, if various kinds of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) are not apprehended by cognition because their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are obscured, that too is not a lack of cognition;
it is not that cognition does not exist. World-Honored One, because there is such an objective field (*ālambana*), cognition arises. It is not that [the object] lacks an intrinsic nature;

because one encounters that objective field, it is called cognition. This is like [the case of] mountains, rocks, walls, earth, water, fire, or wind, whether extremely distant or extremely near, or for those who are aged, young, or blind.

That which is obscure, where the faculties are incomplete and wisdom is not attained—this too is not wisdom; it should rather be called non-wisdom, because there is an object that cannot be apprehended.
There is knowing and one knows, yet that which knows what is known is the deluded consciousness of an ordinary person. It is non-knowing...
To know while being without a knower is the true knowledge of *prajñā*. Indeed, to know while being without knowing means there is nothing that is not known;
yet to know while being without a knower implies their characteristics are mutually lost. As it was previously stated in the *Mahāmati-sūtra*: "One does not apprehend characteristics; this is wisdom.
Judging by the meaning of these words, it is because one does not apprehend the characteristics of the perceived object (*ālambana-viṣaya*) that it is called wisdom.

As the Blessed One said, "equality" refers to the fact that when there is an object of apprehension, the wisdom that takes it as its objective support—that is, the wisdom which is capable of knowing it—is not obtained, and thus it is not seen.
Since the result is not seen, what is called "wisdom" is merely a provisional designation established within the measure of conceptual construction (*prajñapti-mātra*);
it fundamentally lacks any reality. Therefore, it is said that "that which is grasped is without intrinsic nature."

This means that when the grasper and the grasped are subsumed, they are simply the faculties and their objects; since it is said that these lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are all unapprehendable.
How could there be cognition within them? Therefore, cognition does not arise; it is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) established by analogy.
Generally, the purpose of posing questions through various points is to destroy false cognition and reveal true cognition; thus, each instance initially takes up false views as a basis for doubt.

Regarding the statement that "wisdom does not apprehend because it does not perceive whether the self-characteristic and common characteristic of the nature [of objects] are different or non-different":
this means that one is entirely unaware of whether the nature of what is grasped possesses self-characteristics and common characteristics that are either different or non-different;

is it therefore the case that wisdom does not apprehend? If that were so, then there would be no wisdom at all, because it would fail to apprehend those characteristics within the objective sphere of its focal point.

The summary question states, and so forth: "Furthermore, it is said that because the specific and general characteristics (svalakṣaṇa and sāmānyalakṣaṇa) mutually obscure one another, this refers to those various [characteristics] wherein their respective natures further conceal each other.
Because they mutually usurp one another as described above, cognition does not attain certainty;

it is like the doubt regarding what is truly the case. One must correctly understand that phenomena lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). If this is not called 'cognition,' what else could it be? Therefore, we know."
In this context, the fact that the message has already been revealed while still posing a question is merely a rhetorical device.
Furthermore, when it is said that "wisdom arises because there is an object-field (*ālambana*)," this specifically means that wisdom arises because there is an object-field as its cognitive content;

it does not mean that the nature of that [object] is entirely non-existent. Rather, the cognition that accords with the object-field is what is termed "wisdom," and this necessarily involves the union of the subject and object.
Therefore, if there is cognition, it is still [a cognition] that takes obstructions as its object; it is not the wisdom of solitary illumination (*prajñā*).
According to the formal explanation below, this serves as a reductio ad absurdum (*prasanga*), making the meaning of the hypothetical assumption clear.
That which is extremely near yet unseen is the eyelashes; that which is small yet unseen is an infant; the rest of the text is self-evident. (1)
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not as you say. It is not that non-wisdom is wisdom; it is not that wisdom is not non-wisdom.
I do not speak thus with concealment regarding the objects of perception. Wisdom does not apprehend them because they are merely conventional designations and mental constructs.

One should know that the manifestation of one's own mind is the measure of reality, and that external natures—whether existent or non-existent—do not exist. Because such things are not apprehended, wisdom does not function within that [dualistic] appearance."

The wisdom that accords with birth and the three liberations is also not to be grasped as non-delusion; for it is produced by the beginningless habit-energy of the false discrimination between existence and non-existence.
Because such knowledge is itself ignorant of the object, the delusion regarding the characteristics and nature—or lack of nature—of external things is not severed.
Consequently, one establishes and speaks of the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind, clinging to and conceptualizing the marks of "self" and "mine."
Failing to realize that what appears is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, one gives rise to false conceptualization regarding the radiance of gnosis;

because of such conceptualization, one perceives external natures as being either existent or non-existent, and failing to find them through investigation, one relies upon the view of nihilism. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
When there are objects of perception, if wisdom does not examine them— this lack of wisdom is not true ignorance but is called "conceptualization" (parikalpa)—
and when wisdom does not examine the nature of non-differentiation, nor the obscurations of delusion, nor the distant and the near, this is termed "false wisdom" (mithyājñāna). Furthermore,
when the faculties of the old and the young are dull and wisdom does not arise, yet the actual reality (*tattva*) exists, this too is called false wisdom.
In the response, he first dispels that objection, saying: "It is not so;
one directly addresses the point of the question and knows only the wisdom of having wisdom, yet never knows the wisdom of having no wisdom, which is the ultimate wisdom. Therefore, it is said:
"Non-wisdom should be wisdom," meaning it is the wisdom that is not wisdom, and since the essence of wisdom is furthermore unattainable, it is further said: "Not non-wisdom."

This is still a general explanation; however, if one follows the Tiantai school’s reliance on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to clarify the nature of wisdom, it means that what is called "the wisdom of non-wisdom" is emptiness, while "the wisdom of wisdom" is the conventional (provisional).
It is not merely the absence of the former two types of wisdom; rather, it directly manifests the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the Middle Way.
These three wisdoms are attained within a single moment of mind; though attained, there is no attainment. Thus...
One cannot attain emptiness, one cannot attain the provisional, and one cannot attain the Middle Way; the fusion and dissolution of these three wisdoms constitutes wisdom.
Furthermore, it is said that "not attaining characteristics" is wisdom—all of this is its underlying principle.
When I speak of "not being thus" as a concealed teaching, I do so to repeatedly dispel their objections; for the Tathāgata’s teaching is a direct teaching, a manifest teaching.
How could there be that which is fundamentally without reality, yet merely established through concealment and provisional designation?

Nevertheless, it has indeed been taught through concealment, as in the subsequent passages. It is simply that when concealment is appropriate, one conceals; when manifestation is appropriate, one manifests.
This is not a case of concealment here, for it reveals that what appears to the self-mind is the measure of existence and non-existence; below this, true wisdom is correctly revealed.

It is also said that realizing the existence or non-existence of objects is merely the measure of one's own mind. That external natures have no inherent nature means knowing that all phenomena are fundamentally empty.
To know in this way is to know without knowing; because the object cannot be apprehended, it is not called a failure to understand.
Since the nature is fundamentally empty and there are no phenomena outside the mind, they cannot be apprehended. This "non-apprehension" is wisdom.
Since the object of knowledge (*ālambana*) does not arise, and the wisdom regarding that object also does not arise—both being non-arising—their essence is fundamentally empty.
This accords with the three gates of liberation, such that even wisdom cannot be attained as a self-entity. Thus, true knowing is like this;
how can one speak of knowing or not knowing, or of attainment and non-attainment? To say it is "not false conceptualization" is to distinguish it [from deluded thought].

False cognition refers to that which is not identical to deluded thought; rather, it is the cognition of mere objects arising from the habitual tendencies of beginningless existence and non-existence.
Although one can thus cognize those objects, because one does not know this for oneself, one loses one's wisdom to external things.

Consequently, if the false conceptualization of the existence and non-existence of external objects is not severed, one falls into the view of eternalism. This is established as the manifestation of one’s own mind through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The "speaker" refers to one who establishes discourse based on what was previously called the manifestation of the measure of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*).

Thus, existence, non-existence, and so forth are all the measure of one's own mind and are mere conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Because they grasp at and cling to the signs of "I" and "mine," they fail to realize that these are the manifestations of their own minds;
consequently, they do not sever their conceptualization of external objects and falsely reckon them as permanent.

When one perceives through subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), seeing that there is the capacity for subject and object, this transforms into the *nirmāṇa-rūpa* (illusory manifestation), giving rise to conceptual discrimination and false imagination regarding external existence and non-existence.
Where there is something known, there is something unknown; thus, at the point of what is not known, one reckons it as the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

Therefore, it is said that within the *nirmāṇa-rūpa* of wisdom and so forth, one fails to realize that the very state of being unable to apprehend [an object] through observation is precisely [the truth].
The verse stating, "Wisdom should properly contemplate this," correctly praises the meaning of the aforementioned "wisdom not being attained.
It does not mean that one fails to perceive or mistakenly understands its cause; rather, it refers to what is called "ignorance" by those who speak of false conceptualization.
Furthermore, when it says, "In reality, there is *yǎnyán* (radiant glow)," it specifically refers to the profound stillness of the various sense faculties (*indriya*).
The phrase "and so forth" indicates that although such a person does not perceive [the object], they actually possess knowledge; yet this is also false knowledge and not correct knowledge.
(2) ○ This concludes the fourteenth chapter.
The General Meaning of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Fascicle Four;
The General Meaning of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Fascicle Five.
Part Three of the First Chapter, "The Essence of the Heart of All Buddha-Speech" (Continued).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings are turned around by beginningless false, evil, and perverse conceptualizations.
As they are thus turned around, they do not properly understand the thorough penetration of one's own school (*svapratyātma-gati*) or the thorough penetration of teaching (*deśanā-gati*).

Because they are attached to external natures and characteristics manifested by their own minds, they cling to expedient teachings and fail to correctly discern the pure characteristics of the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) within the thorough penetration of one's own school. Mahāmati!

He addressed the Buddha, saying, "Truly, it is as the World-Honored One has taught. I only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain for me the *sūtrānta-yukti* (the teaching of the scriptures) and the *tattva-yukti* (the teaching of the ultimate truth), so that I and other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas may become proficient in these two teachings.

Thus, in future ages, ordinary people, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas shall be unable to find any deficiency in them. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well."

"I shall now explain this for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of teachings:
the teaching of the common discourse (*deśanā-pāṭha*) and the teaching of the ultimate realization of one's own school (*sva-pratyātma-gati*).

As for the teaching of the common discourse, it refers to the various collections of sūtras taught according to what is appropriate for the minds of sentient beings; this is called the teaching of the common discourse. As for the teaching of the ultimate realization of one's own school..."
This refers to the practitioner who, having abandoned the various delusive imaginings manifested by their own mind, does not fall into the categories of oneness, otherness, both, or neither;
who transcends all mind, mentality, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*); who personally realizes the realm of the noble ones (*ārya-gati*);

and who is free from the views of causal origination and the characteristics of signs—realms that cannot be known by any heterodox teachers, *śrāvakas*, or *pratyekabuddhas* who have fallen into the two extremes. This, I say, is called "self."
"Mahāmati, the penetration of the essence of the Dharma is called the characteristic of the penetration of one's own school and the penetration of teaching;
you and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study this. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

I maintain that there are two kinds of "pervasion" (*sāmānya*): the pervasion of the ultimate principle (*tattva*) and the pervasion of verbal expression (*vākya*). These are taught for the sake of instructing the ignorant and for practitioners of the ultimate principle, respectively.

The characteristics of the pervasion of the ultimate principle and verbal expression have already been explained in detail in the preceding text. The reason they are mentioned again here is simply that while the former pervasion applies to all three vehicles (*triyāna*), this [latter] pertains only to the Buddha;

thus, the capacity of the recipient (*adhikāra*) and the response (*pratisaṃvid*) differ. Furthermore, the former was the teaching, and this is the ultimate principle; subsequently, the latter reverses the former. Moreover, the former... [text truncated].
Because the Buddha himself recounted this for the sake of the assembly, there are such statements as "delusive thought" and "revolving," which serve to introduce his teaching.
Thus one should know that this dharma has never been absent even in ordinary beings; it is only because they are deluded and revolving that they do not know its entire reality.
As for "revolving," it means being deluded regarding one's own self, whereby one turns inward toward the external and clings solely to what is manifested by one's own mind as being outside.

Because the characteristics of nature and other such realms also involve attachment to expedient verbal expressions, one cannot comprehend the marks pervaded by the fourfold negation within the fundamental source of one’s own mind, O Mahāmati;
for this reason, he makes his inquiry, saying that [the teaching] does not fall short.

If it is claimed that while the penetration of the principle (*zongtong*) is present, the penetration of the teaching (*shuotong*) is absent, the deficiency lies in the guidance; if the penetration of the teaching is present but the penetration of the principle is absent, the deficiency likewise lies in the guidance.
The deficiency lies in one’s own practice; however, if one is fully proficient in both, that deficiency will not be found.

In the answer, the mention of "proficiency in two kinds of dharmas" refers to the *siddhānta* (the ultimate realization) which does not exceed self-attestation, and the *deśanā* (the teaching) which explains the dharma manifested by the single mind for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
This is why the Way of all Buddhas is the same, as expressed in this sutra by the phrase "equality of dharmas."
The *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Sūtra of All Equipments) is so called because the aforementioned nine divisions subsume all phenomena;

yet, in the final analysis, they all return to being in accord with principle and responsive to capacity—this is what is meant by "sūtra. Since the Dharma of self-realization is fundamentally inexpressible, it is manifested through the practitioner to show its characteristics;
thus it is said: "Free from the various delusive thoughts that are manifestations of one's own mind," and so forth. This means that [one does not perceive external objects].

Falling into the four propositions, false discrimination does not function; when false discrimination does not function, one transcends all mind and consciousness to reach the realm of self-realized sagehood.
How, then, is this demonstrated? It is simply said to be the departure from the characteristics of views formed through causes.
For all conditioned phenomena, it can be said that they are established through various causes and conditions and thus possess the characteristics of views. Now...
The realm of self-awakening is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and transcends causes and conditions; it is the characteristic of non-characteristics—how could there be anything seen therein?
Therefore, it is said that this is to be "separated from," as it is not something known by ordinary people, externalists, or those of small capacity who have fallen into the two extremes.

Thus it is said, and so forth. The verse speaks of "the ignorant" (*bāla*), referring to those at the initial stage of practice. This teaching is universally applicable and is not necessarily directed exclusively toward one specific group.

For beginners, these are spoken in contrast to the "principle-vehicle" (zongtong). Although this principle-vehicle is for the purpose of practice, if it were not expressed through speech, how could it demonstrate that principle?

Thus, it must also be explained—though this is a general statement—that those who follow faith and delight in extensive hearing are [the vehicle of] phenomena (faxing), while those whose principle is profound contemplation are [the vehicle of] principle (zongshen). [End of] Chapter Fifteen.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One once said:
'Regarding the various discursive arguments of worldly treatises, you must be careful not to study or associate with them; for if you do so, you will embrace craving and not embrace the Dharma.
World-Honored One, why did you speak thus? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Worldly discourse is of many kinds..."

Through the collection and adornment of phrases, meanings, causes, conditions, and parables, they entice and delude foolish ordinary people who do not enter into the reality of their own direct realization.
Unaware that all phenomena are but the deluded inversions of their own minds, they fall into the two extremes;

thus, being ignorant and confused, they destroy themselves, continue through the succession of various realms of existence, fail to attain liberation, and are unable to realize that [all things] are manifestations of their own minds.

Because measurement does not transcend the false conceptualization and attachment to external natures and self-natures, the various discursive explanations and debates of worldly discourse do not escape birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress, nor the deception, delusion, and confusion [of cyclic existence].

Mahāmati, Śakra Devendra extensively explained many treatises and composed his own work on phonology; among those followers of worldly treatises, there was a disciple who possessed the form of a dragon.
The image went to the palace of Śakra-devendra to establish the essential tenets of our school and to destroy Śakra’s thousand-spoked wheel.
[Śakra] vowed, "If you do not follow me, I shall cut off my head one by one as an apology for being defeated. Having made this vow, he used the Dharma of Śākya to subdue Śakra.
When Śakra fell into defeat, [the image] destroyed his chariot and returned to the human world. Such, Mahāmati, is the worldly discourse.

The treatises on logic, rhetoric, and ornamentation—even those of animals—can, through various phrases and expressions, delude the gods and asuras, causing them to become attached to views of arising and ceasing;
how much more so for humans? Therefore, Mahāmati, one should distance oneself from worldly discourse, for it brings about the causes for the arising of suffering.
Be careful not to study or frequent such worldly treatises, Mahāmati.
Mahāmati, those worldlings speak only of the objects perceived by the body. Indeed, there are hundreds of thousands of such worldlings;

however, in the future, during the final five hundred years, because the causes and views of evil conceptions will flourish, evil disciples will receive and propagate these various phrases, expressions, causes, analogies, and ornaments of the worldlings' treatises that destroy the true compilation.
Mahāmati, when discussing the matters of the non-Buddhists, they are attached to their own causal conditions and lack any independent realization.

Those non-Buddhists have no treatises of independent realization; regarding other worldly discourses, they extensively explain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of phenomena and characteristics, yet they possess no independent realization and do not even recognize that these are merely the worldly discourses of the ignorant.
Now, the Way consists of both the orthodox Way and the heterodox Way, while discourse consists of both worldly discourse and non-worldly discourse.
Although these do not coexist—being like water and fire—they have nonetheless always proceeded side by side in the world, like the mingling of incense and rancid herbs in a single vessel.
Therefore, the Tathāgata cautioned him, "Be careful not to be clever," and it was because of this that Mahāmati subsequently questioned him.

This clarifies that practicing [the teachings] is not what is meant by "receiving and practicing"; for if one receives and practices those doctrines, one will thereby bring about one's own destruction.

Consequently, there arise the various realms of existence and the subsequent characteristics of faults described below; thus, the text concludes by refuting such errors, and so forth. Śakra Devānām-indra and others cite these examples to demonstrate the fault.
As for those who assume the form of a dragon, it is likely because one who is not a dragon cannot ascend to heaven; therefore, [they do so].
When the Dragon-body (Nāga) went to seek out debate and establish a philosophical tenet (*siddhānta*), in all such debates one must first establish a tenet as a premise;
this "premise" (*yao*) should be pronounced with a level tone, meaning "to summarize.

Thus, when a proponent of the *Śāstra* uses that very treatise to raise a challenge and falls into defeat—that is, fails to prevail—O Mahāmati, the worldly treatises are mentioned again below to establish that treatise.
It is established that what is spoken of as the "body-consciousness" refers to the sphere of perception regarding the aggregate-body (skandha-kāya).
Although that worldly treatise contains hundreds of thousands of verses, its ultimate tenets do not transcend emotional consciousness; how could it know of any other path?
Fifty years later, those who destroyed the compilation—referring to the *Vajrapuṇyadatta-śāstra*—stated that the human lifespan was one hundred [years].
The lifespan is divided into two parts: in the first fifty years, the power of the teaching is strong; in the subsequent fifty years, the power of the teaching gradually diminishes.
This refers to the time when the True Dharma is about to perish. Alternatively, "ten" should be a scribal error for "one hundred.
Because they destroy the Tathāgata’s collected True Teaching, they act as Māras and outsiders; this is because the causes of evil perceptions have become prevalent.
This refers to those who, due to inverted and evil conceptualizations, hold false views regarding the causes of suffering;

because they perceive the world as flourishing, various evil factions adopt and practice their doctrines, thereby bringing about their own downfall. Thus, Mahāmati, the following summarizes these faults and censures them:
"To cling to one's own causal conditions" refers to what was previously explained as the perception of the body; yet they are unable to manifest their own direct realization.
Therefore it is said that there is no self-communication [of truth], and for the most part it is merely like this (1).

At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if the various phrases, flavors, causes, and analogies used by non-Buddhists in their worldly treatises lack self-communication and are merely attachments to their own particular matters, then the World-Honored One also speaks of worldly treatises as being of various kinds."
The various assemblies gathered from other regions—gods, humans, and asuras—extensively expound immeasurable varieties of phrases and expressions;
yet is this not their own conventional understanding? And does it not also fall within the category of the wisdom and discourse of all non-Buddhists? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I do not speak of worldly treatises (lokāyata), nor of coming and going; I speak only of neither-coming-nor-going. Mahāmati, 'coming' refers to a destination."
That which arises through gathering departs and perishes; that which neither comes nor goes is neither born nor extinguished.

This is the meaning I teach, which does not fall into the categories of worldly discourse or deluded conceptualization. Why is this so? It is because one does not cling to external existence or non-existence, but dwells in the manifestation of one’s own mind, where the dualistic conceptualizations of the two extremes cannot turn it back.
One realizes that the characteristics of objects have no inherent nature and are but the perception of one’s own mind.
When manifestation is seen as the manifestation of one's own mind, false conceptualization does not arise;

when false conceptualization does not arise, one enters the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and this is called liberation. Mahāmati, I recall that once, while staying in a certain place, a world-theorizing Brahmin came to where I was.
Without first seeking an opportunity for conversation, he immediately asked me: "Gautama, regarding all things..."
When I was asked, "Is everything created? I replied, "Brahmin, the view that 'everything is created' is the first worldly doctrine.
He then asked, "Is everything uncreated? I replied again, "The view that 'everything is uncreated' is the second worldly doctrine.
He then asked, "Is everything eternal? Is everything impermanent? Is everything born? Is everything..."
"Is it non-arising? I replied to him at that time: "This is the sixth worldly doctrine. Mahāmati, he then asked me again:
"Are all things one? Are all things different? Are all things both? Are all things neither? Do all things arise and manifest due to various causes?
I replied to him at that time: "This is the eleventh worldly doctrine. Mahāmati, he then asked again: "Is it one..."
Are all things indeterminate, or are they all determinate? Is there a self, or is there no self? Does this world exist, or does it not exist?
Does another world exist, or does it not exist? Is there liberation, or is there no liberation?
Are all things momentary, or are they all non-momentary? Is there space, or is there analytical cessation, or is there nirvāṇa, O Gautama?
"Is it created by Dharmakāra or not? Is there an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or not? At that time, Mahāmati, I replied to the Brahmin:
"Such statements as these are all merely worldly treatises (*lokavāda*); they are not my teaching. These are your worldly treatises.
I teach only that the various evils of the three realms of existence have their cause in the beginningless habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of false discrimination. I was unable [to explain further].

One perceives that the manifestation of one's own mind gives rise to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the grasping of external objects, just as the doctrines of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim that the self (*ātman*), the sense faculties (*indriya*), and the object (*artha*)—these three—in conjunction, produce the self. This is not so, O Brahmin. I do not say there is a cause, nor do I say there is no cause;

I speak only of the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) established through the nature of the grasper and the grasped (*grāhya-grāhaka*), which is merely a conceptual construction. This does not apply to you or others who have fallen into the acceptance of a self.
That which can be cognized by those in the continuum—Mahāmati, nirvāṇa, space, and cessation—are not three distinct entities;
there are only three designations.

Next, to manifest the true teaching, within this section, Mahāmati first poses a counter-question to the Tathāgata, stating that [the Buddha] also speaks in the same manner as worldly convention; thus there are two parts.

[Objection: If [the Buddha] extensively expounds various dharmas for the multitudes of devas and humans in other regions according to their own inclinations, is this not also his own established doctrine?
Furthermore, how does it differ from the intellectual discourses and enumerations of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas)?

As the text says at length... [Response: In the answer, he first dispels the initial objection, saying: "I do not speak of worldly discourse (lokāyata). For those who engage in worldly discourse— *Note: This translation reflects the structure of the argument as presented in the source text, which addresses the distinction between the Buddha’s teachings and both his skillful means (upāya) for others and the doctrines of external paths.*
Regarding the teaching on coming and going: the Buddha speaks only of neither coming nor going;

therefore it is said that "coming" refers to the meaning of convergence, assembly, birth, and so forth—meaning that things arise through the meeting of conditions—and "going" refers to the meaning of dispersal and destruction—meaning that things cease when conditions disperse.
The Buddha’s teaching differs from this; thus, "neither coming nor going" is precisely "neither arising nor ceasing," which is my own [teaching].

In response to the subsequent objection, it is said that "not falling into the category of worldly discourse and delusive conceptualization" means that the two extremes constitute the category of delusive conceptualization.
To explain this by way of inquiry: if one does not cling to external existence or non-existence—which are merely manifestations of one's own mind—then one does not adhere to the two extremes.
Because of this non-adherence, one cannot be turned back by the delusive conceptualizations of the two extremes; thus, the characteristics of objects lack inherent nature.

Since non-nature is itself emptiness, what is there to transform? Because one realizes that [all things] are manifestations of one's own mind, the delusive thoughts that manifest from one's own mind do not arise.
Once one has understood that they are one's own mind, what further could possibly arise? Thus, the mind does not give birth to itself;
the mind does not cause the mind to revolve; the mind does not become attached to itself. How, then, could the mind again fall into its own mind? Therefore.
"One for whom false conceptualization does not arise accords with the characteristic of emptiness and enters the three gates of liberation;
how could such a person be the same as the non-Buddhists? Next, the treatise is cited directly to extensively distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox, stating: "I recall at one time...

[The phrase] "not requesting an interval" (*kongxian*)—where "interval" (*kongxian*) refers to a gap or leisure—is likely a formal protocol for requesting instruction, similar to the rites of propriety.
The words "I ask" are correct, yet he did not request them; that he suddenly has questions is how I hold him accountable.
Although his questions are many, I generally respond with worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*) as a means of rejecting them.
To say that such explanations are entirely worldly discourse is to suppress them by following the views of emotional attachment. Furthermore, it says: "It is not I."
What you have spoken is the worldly philosophy (lokāyata), which is why I exclude it. I speak only of that which is below:
namely, the Buddha’s own demonstration of the true teaching, which does not go beyond the three paths of cause and effect—namely, the afflictions such as beginningless falsehood;
the various evil causes of karma; the suffering of the three realms of existence; and the deluded mind giving rise to false攀缘 (pān-yuan) toward external natures.
All of these are teachings on the correct causes and conditions within our own school, not something known by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Furthermore, the phrase "as in the methods of the non-Buddhists" reiterates their calculations to contrast them with our own doctrine. Regarding the statement, "Cognition arises from the conjunction of the self, the sense faculties, and the objects":
according to the Tang translation, this means that cognition—namely, consciousness (*vijñāna*)—arises because of the conjunction of the self, the faculties, and the objects.
Some explain it as having a cause, while others explain it as being without a cause; the Buddha refutes all such divergent views, saying: "I do not speak of a cause, nor do I speak of no-cause;

I speak only of the nature of the grasped and the grasper within the realm of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). When one speaks of 'provisional designation' (*prajñapti*) and 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda'), it is never without a cause;
when one speaks of 'false conceptualization,' it is never possessed of a [transcendent] cause. It is simply that it is not like those [other systems]."
To say that [the self] exists is eternalism; to say it does not exist is nihilism. Therefore, it is said: "This cannot be realized by you or others who fall into the continuity of the view of self.

Thus, the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox is made. Those who hold to the view of self—some of whom originally lacked the character "view" (dṛṣṭi)—claim that because there is a self, there is grasping (*upādāna*), and because of the self, grasping arises;
thus they continue in a reciprocal succession. These are all followers of external paths (*tīrthika*).
Regarding the passage stating that "nirvāṇa, space, cessation," and so forth, the text appears to be isolated;

however, since non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) also inquire about these matters, why would they also be considered worldly treatises (loka-vāda)? Therefore, it is explained as follows: "The unconditioned dharma is fundamentally not threefold;
because they inquire about them by means of numerical categories, they are also worldly treatises. (2)
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time the Lokāyatika Brahmin again asked me:
"Is the existence of the three realms of being caused by ignorance, grasping, and karma, or is it without cause? I replied to him: "Both of these views are merely worldly discourse. He asked again:
"Are all natures included within specific and general characteristics? I replied once more: "This too is worldly discourse."
The treatise states: From the Brahmins up to those whose minds flow with false conceptualizations regarding external objects, all are proponents of worldly discourse (*lokāyatika*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time, the Brahmin of worldly discourse again asked me: "Is there anything that is not worldly discourse?
I am the founder of all non-Buddhist schools, who explains various phrases, flavors, causes, conditions, and parables as adornments. To this, I replied: [as follows].

When the Brahmin said, "There is that which belongs to you, yet is not yours," it was not that he lacked a thesis, nor that he failed to speak, nor that he did not utter various phrases and expressions adorned with causes and analogies.
When the Brahmin asked, "What is it that is not worldly discourse (loka-vāda), yet is not a non-thesis and not a non-speech?
I then replied to him: "Brahmin, there is that which is not worldly discourse, such as is found among you followers of the heterodox paths."
Because they cannot understand that external natures are unreal, and because they are attached to false conceptualizations and deceptions, they claim that "conceptualization does not arise.
[In truth,] it is through the realization of the existence and non-existence of what is manifested by one's own mind that conceptualization ceases;

when one no longer perceives external objects and conceptualization is forever stilled, this is called "non-worldly discourse" (*alokāyata*). This is my teaching, not yours, O Brahmin. Thus, he spoke briefly to him.
"O Brahmin, if consciousness comes or goes, dies or is born, experiences pleasure or pain, is immersed, sees, touches, or clings to various marks,
or to marks of conjunction and continuity, or if it is characterized by craving and causal attachment— such as these, O Brahmin,
are your worldly doctrines (loka-vāda) and not mine. Great Wisdom, such are the worldly doctrines composed by the Brahmins."
When asked this, I answered him in such a way that he immediately lit his lamp and withdrew without further protest. Reflecting upon my own realization, I thought to myself:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have emerged beyond ordinary realization; they speak of non-arising, signlessness, and causelessness, asserting that what appears as a sign is one's own deluded imagination, and that when such deluded imagination does not arise, [true realization occurs]."

Furthermore, he posed questions based on two or three points concerning the Buddha, intending that if the Buddha were to answer with the ultimate truth, he would fall into the trap of his own questioning;
thus, [the Buddha] likewise used worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*) to block his words, even saying: "The mental flow’s false conceptualization of external objects is entirely worldly discourse.
This was to align with what that person knew—that ordinary consciousness moves and follows after objects, clinging to them—without further inquiry.
Both the heterodox and the orthodox are driven by worldly discourse; thus, they are prevented from questioning the reason for it, as that discourse serves to block them.
Once their discourse is exhausted, they then first offer the request to refute worldly discourse.

When the Tathāgata says, "Existence exists, but it is not yours," he does so directly to differentiate [them]—this is the discourse used to open their minds. Each instance speaks of "non-existence" and so forth, which serves as the response.
The outsider’s words were likewise never intended to state the reality of things. When he requested it again, [the Master] said, "It is not that it is not the thesis (*pakṣa*).
This means: what is meant by "it is not that it is not the thesis"? It refers to the meaning of the current thesis and its statement.

Yet, [the Master] further suppressed him, saying, "This is not what you know," because [the outsider] is merely attached to false conceptualizations regarding external phenomena; it is not only that he does not... [understand].
