Third, when the two extremes of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) are manifested, the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) are found to be unobtainable.
Fourth, all forms of measurement fail to find what is established; this reveals that true *nirvāṇa* transcends all heterodox and external views.

Regarding those who are deluded about reality and should not accept [erroneous views]: it means that ordinary beings, being confused regarding the true principle, should not accept whatever they perceive, yet they nevertheless do so.
If one takes up [the practice] for oneself, then there is non-attachment to all things; this is the fifth.

Furthermore, one may also see this by reversing the meanings of the preceding five points (and so forth). Speaking from this perspective, all those things that obscure *nirvāṇa* should be abandoned; therefore it is said:
"Having abandoned those, one attains the noble Dharma of self-realization, whereby the unsurpassed and wondrous principle of the mind naturally manifests."
That which is called permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as the countless merits of intrinsic purity, are merely provisional designations applied to what is illusory;
speaking in terms of the ultimate, there is not a single dharma that exists. If there were anything to be attained, it would not be nirvana.

Furthermore, it is by being free from both self and other that one realizes the knowledge of non-attainment; thus, the realization of the two kinds of selflessness is itself the enlightenment that is realized.
The meaning of "Dharma" is as explained above. Attaining profound samādhis such as the "phantom-like" and others, one is detached from mind, thought, and consciousness;
all of this serves to manifest *nirvāṇa*. Now, to speak definitively of what is called *nirvāṇa*:
it is neither realization nor non-realization, neither attainment nor non-attainment, neither detachment nor non-detachment—wondrously transcending all, it utterly transcends the hundred negations.
The four natures being thus established is the ultimate treasury of the secret principle (3).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The various views of nirvāṇa held by the non-Buddhists arise from their own deluded imaginings; these are born of mental conceptions and lack the skillful means for liberation.

Being ignorant regarding that which binds and the binder, they remain far removed from wholesome skillful means. While the non-Buddhists harbor notions of liberation, true liberation never arises for them.
Their various intellectual systems lead to divergent paths, and what the non-Buddhists perceive is entirely devoid of liberation, due to their foolishness and false imaginings.
All the deluded non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) with their false views argue regarding the categories of agent and action, existence and non-existence; none of them possess liberation.

The foolish and ignorant delight in false conceptualization and do not hear the words of true wisdom. These three types of suffering are fundamentally rooted in reality, yet the cause for the cessation of suffering is [hidden].
It is like an image in a mirror: although it appears, it does not exist. Within the mirror of the mind of false conceptualization, the foolish perceive duality.
If one does not recognize the mind and its objects, then two kinds of false conceptualizations arise; once the mind and its spheres are understood, false conceptualization no longer arises.

The "mind" refers to the various characteristics of the distancing [of subject and object], where the perceived and the perceiver appear yet do not exist, just as the false conceptualizations of the ignorant regarding the three realms of existence are merely conceptualization.
External referents are entirely non-existent; yet through various manifestations of conceptualization, ordinary fools are unable to perceive this.
The sutra explains that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) ultimately does not transcend names; if one is separated from verbal expression, there is likewise nothing to be expressed.
The verses consist of two parts: the first four verses all state that externalist calculations have no liberation, and their meaning is as follows:
There are four [reasons]: first, the mind does not transcend conceptualization; second, one lacks skillful means; third, one relies solely on deluded conceptualization;
and fourth, one falsely views existence and non-existence. Speaking from this perspective, that which is called liberation is fundamentally no dharma at all;
it is simply the departure from deluded conceptualizations and the like—this is liberation. Next, it is said that ordinary fools cling only to false conceptualizations.

The preceding four lines mutually clarify their respective meanings: the Dharma does not transcend deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), for deluded conceptualization arises from verbal expression and is thus the root of the three sufferings;
true reality (*tattva*), being the opposite of deluded conceptualization, is the cause for the cessation of suffering.
If this is so, what further role do verbal expressions and true reality play? It is simply because ordinary beings, out of delusion, spontaneously give rise to preferences and aversions.
The intention behind this present teaching is to cause sentient beings to turn back from delusion and return to awakening. For example, consider an image within a mirror:
separately citing this analogy clarifies that the mirror represents the mind and the image represents the objective realm. Although the image appears, it has no substantial existence;

thus, one can understand that the objective realm is none other than the mind. While the mirror and the image are not two, the foolish perceive them as dual, asserting that they are the mind and the object.

Regarding the duality of objects: those who do not recognize the mind and its conditions—wherein conditions themselves are also objects—claim that the mind and objects are distinct because they fail to recognize this.
Since both the mind and objects arise from delusion, these two are but false imaginings. When one realizes them, they are non-dual, and thus false imaginings do not arise.
Because the mind itself is manifold, there is no separate objective phenomenon; though things appear, they are non-existent.

This is the fourfold analysis of the mirror and its image regarding manifestation and conjunction. That "the three realms of existence are merely conceptual construction" means that apart from conceptual construction, there is no further dharma.
As the sutras repeatedly state, conceptual construction never transcends names. Apart from provisional names, there is nothing to be spoken;
since there is nothing to be spoken, there is no dharma. Thus, conceptual construction arises solely from the mind, and liberation likewise [arises from the mind].
Liberation arises from the mind; it does not arise from the self. There is liberation because there was bondage, yet bondage does not bind itself; it is established by the mind.
If one realizes that the nature of the mind is fundamentally empty, then both bondage and the binder are liberated in their own place.
It is only because of this lack of understanding that delusive thoughts increase. Ultimately, it is nothing more than the single dharma of the mind, undergoing a process of inversion and reversal.
All of these are the Tathāgata’s demonstrations for people, intended to lead them to awakening and entry through the essential points.
(4) ○ The seventeenth chapter concludes here. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Volume Three, ends.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Volume Four, Chapter One:
The Essence of the Words of All Buddhas, Part Four.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
“I and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to be skilled in the self-nature of the Tathāgata, awakening ourselves and awakening others.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “Mahāmati, ask whatever you desire; I shall explain it to you according to your questions.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, a created thing, or is he uncreated? Is he a substantial entity, or is he a cause?”
"Is it the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? Is it that which is characterized (*lakṣya*)? Is it the teaching (*deśanā*)?
Is it that which is taught (*deśya*)? Is it awakening (*bodha*)? Is it that which is awakened to (*boddhavya*)? Are such terms and phrases different or not different? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding such terms and phrases, does not regard them as either entities (*bhāva*) or causes (*hetu*). Why is this? Because both [positions] entail faults."
Therefore, Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were a conditioned thing, he would either be produced or impermanent;
because of impermanence, all things would consequently be the Tathāgata—a conclusion neither I nor the Buddhas desire.

If he were not a conditioned thing, he would be unattainable, and thus skillful means would be empty, like the horns of a rabbit or the son of a barren woman, because of their non-existence, Mahāmati.
If there were neither phenomenon nor cause, it would be neither existent nor non-existent; if it were neither existent nor non-existent, it would transcend the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That which transcends the four propositions does not fall into the four propositions.
Because it does not fall into the four propositions, the meaning of the words of all Tathāgatas as apprehended by the wise is likewise so. The wise should [understand this].
"Understood.
It is indeed not easy to hear or see a Buddha, and it is even more difficult to know one, O Mahāmati. Thereupon, he clearly explained:
"Samyaksaṃbuddha means 'Perfectly All-Knowing' (正徧知). Furthermore, it refers to one who is skilled in the self-nature of the Tathāgata and has awakened through self-awakening."
Its intrinsic nature is the Dharmakāya; because the principle of cognition is one, they mutually manifest each other.

This textual basis comes from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and is intended for those of future generations who wish to properly understand the Buddha. Generally, it is explained by way of six meanings, namely:

"that which is created" and "that which is not created," and so forth. "Created" refers to the sense of cultivation, refinement, and construction; since this meaning encompasses both cause and effect, it subsequently relates to the causal stage of phenomena.
It is the fruit itself; because it is not produced, it is neither an effect nor a cause, and thus it is omitted from mention.

Furthermore, it is mutually presented with the text of the subsequent answer as referring to the body, marks, speech, and cognition. In all these cases, the rational nature (*dharmatā*) serves as the "characteristic" (*lakṣya*).
Regarding whether such phrases are different or not different, it refers to the Tathāgata’s self-nature in relation to activity and non-activity.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi-pada*) as being distinct, in the response to the objection, he first answers the question directly by stating it is neither a thing (*vastu*) nor a cause;
that is to say, it is neither cause nor effect. According to the subsequent inquiry and explanation, one could also say it is neither produced (*kṛta*) nor unproduced (*akṛta*).

This is because "effect and cause" carries the sense of being produced, whereas [the subject] is not produced; thus, both terms can be applied. However, to say they are both [produced and unproduced] entails error.

This does not merely negate the causal factors of things; it correctly states that if the Tathāgata were solely a causal factor of things, he would fall into the error of being a conditioned product (*kṛtakadoṣa*), and if he were not a causal factor of things, he would fall into the error of non-existence (*abhāvadoṣa*).
This fully exhausts the intended meaning of the text. First, by examining things through the negation of their causal status, it says:
"If the Tathāgata were such a thing," and so forth—meaning that if the Tathāgata must necessarily exist as a thing characterized by causes, effects, and so on.

If you claim that because they share the same nature as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they are impermanent, and because they share the same nature as all things, you say that all things must therefore be the Tathāgata—this is not what the Buddha intended, nor does the Buddha permit such an identification with those things.

To speak according to principle, even if one were to further seek commonality with all phenomena, it could not be found; how much less so when one does not desire it? Furthermore, this is merely a provisional examination of the error.

Thus it is said: by citing the effect, one knows the cause; therefore, the cause is omitted for brevity. Next, to examine what is not a phenomenon (dharma) through phenomena, it says: "If it were not something produced," and so forth.
This is simply an examination of the preceding phrase "not a phenomenon, not a cause," expressed with different terminology.

Therefore, it is stated in contrast by means of skillful means (*upāya*): if it is not something produced, then there is nothing to be attained; if there is nothing to be attained, then [there is] merit and wisdom.
Since all skillful means would be rendered as mere vain exertions, skillful means would then be empty, identical to a rabbit's horn or the son of Baṇḍī.
Speaking from this perspective, if one examines the essential substance of the self-nature *dharmakāya*, it cannot be categorized as cause or effect;
yet, if it is manifested through cultivation, it is not without causal activity. Thus, it is said that there is neither a causal factor with activity nor a causal factor without activity. Therefore—
Regarding the partial statements that it is neither existent nor non-existent, these are also briefly as explained above.

To say that the four propositions are worldly discourse means that the four propositions—existence, non-existence, and so forth—are conventional expressions. To transcend the four propositions is to not fall into the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of existence, non-existence, and the like;
this is what is grasped by the wise, namely the meaning of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body phrase (1).
Regarding what I have taught—that all dharmas are without self—you should understand this meaning: the nature of selflessness is itself without self.

All dharmas possess their own-nature (svabhāva) and do not possess the nature of another, just as with oxen and horses, Mahāmati. For example, the nature of an ox is not that of a horse, and the nature of a horse is not that of an ox;
in reality, they are neither existent nor non-existent. Yet, it is not that they lack their own-nature. In the same way, Mahāmati, all [dharmas]...
All phenomena do not lack their own characteristics; they possess their own characteristics, yet these are not the "self" that can be known by foolish people due to their deluded imaginings.
Thus, one should know that all phenomena are empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature.

In this way, the Tathāgata is neither different from nor non-different from the aggregates (*skandhas*). If he were not different from the aggregates, he would be impermanent; if he were different [from them]...
If these were two, they would have to be distinct, like the horns of an ox, because they are similar;
yet they are not distinct, because there are differences such as length. Thus, all phenomena are likewise, Mahāmati.

Just as the right horn of an ox is different from the left horn, and the left horn is different from the right horn, so too are length, shortness, and various colors each distinct. Mahāmati, it is the same for the Tathāgata.
Just as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are neither different nor not different [from them], so too the Tathāgata’s liberation is neither different nor not different from him.
It is by way of the name "liberation" that the Tathāgata is spoken of. If the Tathāgata were different from liberation, he would be constituted by material form;
because he would be constituted by material form, he would be impermanent. If he were not different, then when a practitioner attains realization, there would be no distinction [between them].

Because the practitioner perceives these as being differentiated, they are neither different nor not different; likewise, gnosis (*jñāna*) and its radiance (*arcis*) are neither different nor not different.

Since the preceding [section] concerned the non-difference and non-non-difference of the self-nature and characteristics of the Dharmakāya—which was general and comprehensive—the [following] section...
While the three virtues are fully elucidated, it is only by speaking in relation to the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth that their ultimate significance is reached.

First, regarding the *dharmakāya*, the text initially cites the phrase "all phenomena are without self" (*sarvadharma-anātman*) to establish the fundamental meaning of the *dharmakāya*. It then explains this itself, stating:
"The nature of non-self is non-self; that which is the 'self' of non-self is the true self (*tattvātman*). Therefore, this is spoken from the perspective of the true self.
It is said that "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) is spoken of in terms of the absence of a deluded self; thus it is called the "nature of non-self.
Therefore, it is said that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature and lack extrinsic nature. To know that all phenomena are the intrinsic nature of the Dharmakāya is to be free from delusion.
Furthermore, one should know that there are two kinds of intrinsic nature: the intrinsic nature that is solitary, unique, and beyond dependence, and this [latter] arising...
The self-nature of the mutual opposition between self and other that Buddhas and sentient beings alike possess arises from what they share;

however, since we are now addressing the primary meaning [of the distinction], it is not in relation to others that one speaks of the "absence of other-nature. This is because when "other" is mentioned here as the counterpart to "self," that "self" is thereby implied.
Thus, one should know that each of the two phrases has its own specific referent, just as the analogy of the ox and the horse makes this clear.

This is because the nature of the ox is supple while the nature of the horse is rigid, and thus they do not possess one another's qualities. Therefore it is said: "For example, it is not the nature of the ox, nor is it the nature of the horse.
This means that if it is not the ox-nature, it is the horse-nature; if it is not the horse-nature, it is the ox-nature. Since one exists and the other is absent, it is said:
"In reality, it is neither existent nor non-existent. Although these two are mutually absent, there is a single consciousness that knows them both.
If their natures are not different, it is further said that those [dharmas] are not without self-nature;
there are categories of dharmas that can be known through causes, and by analogy with their characteristics, it is also said that all dharmas are not without their own specific marks (*svalakṣaṇa*).

To have a self-mark means that while there are no dharmas without their own specific marks, there are likewise the specific marks of the *dharmakāya*. Thus, these two marks do not exclude or supplant one another, and from the beginning, neither has ever been hidden.
Furthermore, it is not something that can be known by ordinary, foolish people when it is said that "there is no self"; this refers to the foolish who deny the existence of the true self.

In this way, regarding the emptiness of all phenomena and so forth, as exemplified above by the teaching of non-self, one should understand that all these various names are likewise the Tathāgata’s own nature.
Next, in contrast to the five aggregates, it is correctly clarified that [the Tathāgata] is neither different nor [identical].
The aggregates (*skandhas*) are not different from suffering; their relationship with the *dharmakāya* is one of mutual opposition.

If one knows that they are neither identical nor separate, neither conjoined nor dispersed, then the essence of the aggregates is fundamentally integrated and is itself the *dharmakāya*, which cannot be transformed or eliminated.

Within this, first the position is established, then it is examined, and finally the three fetters are discussed. Regarding the statement that "expedient means are empty," it refers to the fundamental nature of the *dharmakāya*.
If the expedient means of signlessness were distinct from signs, then there would be no expedient means; thus, the characteristic that corresponds to it is neither different nor not different.
Furthermore, if there were duality, there ought to be difference. To demonstrate the two preceding meanings, it should not be further differentiated;
for if it were different, it would not be established as "neither different nor not different. Therefore, regarding the horns of an ox:

The first section, "Opening with Two Similes to Demonstrate," begins with the simile of the difference between a cow and its horns, which illustrates that while all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are distinct, their *dharmakāya* nature is identical;

therefore, it is said that "all phenomena are likewise. Next is the simile of the difference between a single cow and its horns, which illustrates that while the *dharmakāya* is fundamentally one, all phenomena appear distinctly; thus, the various differences in length and color are like the left [horn].

Regarding the differences in the preceding section, the concluding text makes it clear: within the discussion of liberation (*vimukti*), the Tathāgata is first established as being designated by the name "liberation.
This indicates that liberation is simply another name for the Tathāgata, as it is also the great function of the Buddha;
thus, it is explained in contrast to material form (*rūpa*). If the Tathāgata were distinct from liberation, then material form would have to be the Tathāgata, which is not the case.
If liberation were composed of material form (*rūpa*), it would necessarily be impermanent.
If it were not distinct [from the person], then just as a practitioner attains liberation, there would be no distinction between the person and the dharmas.

Furthermore, if one perceives a conceptual distinction, one cannot say they are one. However, when specifically contrasting the practitioner with [liberation], it is because the cause reveals the fruit, and thus they are one.

In the passage concerning the relationship between your *prajñā* (wisdom) and your *jñāna* (gnosis), when discussed in terms of their mutual opposition to cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the text merely provides a general illustration.

According to the underlying principle, it should be stated: "If they were different, then wisdom would exist apart from the removal of obstructions, just as water exists apart from [the absence of] water;

if they were not different, then how could the obstruction be identical to wisdom? Yet, in principle, one must understand that ice is neither identical to nor different from water. This can be understood.
The second [point] regarding the mind is attained:
that the Great Wisdom (*mahāmati*) and the *parikalpita* (the object of cognition) are neither different nor not different;

they are neither eternal nor non-eternal, neither agent nor action, neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), neither the perceiver nor the perceived, neither the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor that which is characterized, and they are not the aggregates (*skandha*).

It is not different from the aggregates, nor is it that which speaks or that which is spoken; it is neither one nor different, neither both nor neither, neither one nor different, neither both nor neither.
Because it is thus, it is entirely free from all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Being free from all means of valid cognition, there is no verbal expression.
Where there is no verbal expression, there is no arising. Where there is no arising, there is no cessation. Where there is no cessation, there is quiescence. Quiescence is itself...
Nirvāṇa by nature and intrinsic nirvāṇa are without objective basis and without cause; being without objective basis and without cause, they are without cognitive objectification (*ālambana*).
Being without cognitive objectification, they transcend all falsehood. Transcending all falsehood is the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata is the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Mahāmati, this is called the Buddha of the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Mahāmati, 'Buddha' or 'Samyaksaṃbuddha' refers to one who is free from all sense organs and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Completely free from all sense organs and means of valid cognition, Without objects and without causes, Already free from the cognizer and the cognized, And also free from the characteristic and the characterized."

Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), conditions (*pratyaya*), and the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*), no one can perceive their identity or difference. Since there is no perceiver, how could one make distinctions?

They are neither created nor uncreated; they are neither effects nor causes; they are not the aggregates, nor do they reside within the aggregates, nor do they exist as something else apart from them.

Furthermore, they possess no inherent nature (*svabhāva*) as perceived through deluded imagination (*vikalpa*). You should know that it is not that these phenomena do not exist; rather, the nature of these phenomena is likewise such.

Because there is existence, there is non-existence; because there is non-existence, there is existence. If there were no non-existence, one should not grasp at existence; if there were existence, one should not conceptualize it.
Whether regarding "self" or "non-self," if one lingers in and becomes immersed in the authority of verbal expressions, one ruins oneself and ruins the world by falling into the two extremes.
To thoroughly examine all faults and penetrate the self [of reality] is called right contemplation; thus one does not disparage the Great Teacher.

The reason why all three are neither different nor non-different is that their nature is harmonious and their principle is one. Because they are one, they are the Middle; because they are the Middle, they are the Sublime;
because they are the Sublime, they transcend the four propositions and verbal expression. Furthermore, to generalize and conclude this point:
it is said that they are "neither permanent nor impermanent," and so forth. In sum, these do not go beyond negating the two extremes to reveal the Middle Way.
The subject and object that manifest it share a single characteristic; they are not manifested through the four propositions, for even the cessation of words remains interspersed and disordered.
This demonstrates that the Dharma-gate is a harmonious fusion without fixed determination. As for the conclusion regarding the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it says:
"detached from all measures" (*sarva-pramāṇa-vinirmukta*). Now, to be detached from all verbal measures is simply the unborn, quiescent self-nature of *nirvāṇa*.
Having thus elucidated the principle of nature, he further summarizes and concludes by stating:

"Without affairs and without causes," and so forth, referring solely to the Dharma-body, which stands solitary and transcendent. Because it does not perceive any phenomena as objects of attachment or dependence, it surpasses all falsehood and is named Tathāgata-Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The term *Buddha* is repeated here; its translation is "Awakened One" (*zhījué*), indicating a distinction in the sense of realization.
The two preceding names have been concluded; to reach this point may be called the ultimate. Yet, it is further reiterated that one is "separated from all root-measures" (*mūla-pramāṇa*).
This collectively answers the intent of the inquiry: the ultimate destination is the self-nature of the *dharmakāya*.

The verse states, "Completely separated from all root-measures," etc., which reiterates the various preceding passages to collectively manifest the single characteristic of separation regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). It correctly [clarifies] the state of being entirely free.
The "Awakened One" refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*); the "conditions" refer to the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth—the conditions of objective apprehension.

These are spoken of in relation to the *dharmakāya* and perfect awakening (*samyagbodhi*) as being neither identical nor different, yet they cannot be perceived. Because the subsequent objection arises from this, it is said:
"If there is no one who sees, it is difficult [to explain]"—this is the difficulty. The meaning is that since everything is entirely detached, there is nothing at all; in what [could seeing occur]?
The statements that "discrimination is neither created nor uncreated," and so forth, are incomplete; they are of a diverse nature and do not convey a single meaning.
Furthermore, it is not the case that various phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as they are perceived through such false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, regarding that which is to be relinquished—which is difficult for those who rely on their own discriminations to understand—one should know that this is not a mere negation such as "non-existence" and the like. This is because, although [phenomena] are relinquished...

This means that although there are characteristics, they are not without conceptual differentiation, because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such that it is so of itself. Therefore, it is said: "Because existence exists, non-existence exists," and so forth.

Thus, existence does not differentiate from existence, and non-existence does not differentiate from non-existence; nor does existence differentiate from its own non-existence, nor does non-existence differentiate from its own existence.
This should be stated as: "Because of non-existence, existence does not exist. As for the phrase "existence exists," it may be used in a differentiated sense.
Because there is intentionality, although there is discrimination, it does not hinder one from being free from signs; yet, to preclude what is erroneous, it is said:
"If it were non-existent, it should not be received; since it is received, it exists. If it were existent, it should not be conceptualized; since it is conceptualized, one becomes attached.

Whether it be reception or conceptualization, they both involve the addition of emotional views upon the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena); this is why they are erroneous. Or, it may concern the self (*ātman*) or the non-self (*anātman*).

This collectively refutes their attachment by means of the negation of "self" and "what belongs to self," using the measures of speech and cognition (*vāg-pramāṇa*) to address those who remain mired in and submerged by clinging to the two extremes, thereby increasing or diminishing conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
this constitutes both self-destruction and the destruction of the world.

Regarding "liberation from all faults," the verse above [states] that the Buddha is free from all faults of sense organs and measures of cognition (*indriya-pramāṇa*), which likewise reverses the aforementioned state of being submerged.
To lose [the correct view] and yet observe correctly is what I have mastered; conversely, to hold to existence or non-existence is not called correct observation.
"Not slandering the Great Teacher"—"slander" (毀) here means to revile (謗); otherwise, one would indeed be reviling him. (3). This concludes Chapter One.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught that the sūtras uphold the doctrine of non-arising and non-ceasing, and as the World-Honored One has further stated that 'non-arising and non-ceasing' is another name for the Tathāgata—how is it, World-Honored One, that you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing because of the absence of intrinsic nature, or is it indeed another name for the Tathāgata? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“O Mahāmati, I teach that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, and that the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, if all dharmas are unborn, then the apprehension of dharmas cannot be obtained, because all dharmas are unborn.
If there were any dharma within names, I pray that you will explain it for me. The Buddha told Mahāmati: “Excellent, excellent!”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I say that the Tathāgata is not without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), nor is he subsumed under non-arising and non-ceasing.
Furthermore, because he encompasses all phenomena and does not depend on conditions, he is neither born nor extinguished; yet this is not without meaning."
Mahāmati, what I call the "mind-born Dharma-body" is a name for the Tathāgata;

that which is unarisen is not within the realm of any outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas of the seventh stage. Mahāmati, that which is unarisen is simply another name for the Tathāgata.
The scriptures contain many statements regarding "non-arising and non-ceasing," yet there are similarities and differences in how their meanings are interpreted;

these must be carefully examined. On this basis, Mahāmati raised a doubt concerning these two ends, asking whether they both signify the meaning of "lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) or whether they are different names for distinct meanings. The Buddha answered with the term "non-arising."
Because it is neither extinguished, it is neither existent nor non-existent; thus it is said that the categories of existence and non-existence do not manifest.
This serves to sweep away those views, and through these distinct names in the teaching, both [extremes] are attained.
Yet Mahāmati maintains that "non-manifestation" means non-arising; if all phenomena are grasped as unobtainable, they are simply non-existent. Therefore, he says: "One."
Because all phenomena are non-arising, this is understood directly through the meaning of non-arising and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Therefore, when [the interlocutor] requests another name for it, [the Buddha] distinguishes it by stating there is a specific meaning regarding phenomena. In the response, he first dispels that [wrong] view, saying:

"When I say that the Tathāgata is not without intrinsic nature, I am speaking of a different name; I do not mean that he lacks intrinsic nature. Furthermore, he says: "Nor does it encompass all phenomena."
This sweeps away the previous meaning of "supreme leadership. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "not depending on conditions," this means that it is not spoken in dependence upon arising and ceasing;
rather, it is stated as "non-arising and non-ceasing" to counteract and negate those [conceptions]. Nor is it without meaning, for it serves as the introduction to the formal answer that follows.
Thus it says: "That which I call the 'Mind-born Dharma-body' (manomayakāya) is a name for the Tathāgata"—the wording here is still brief.
It should be stated in full: "When I say 'non-arising and non-ceasing,' this refers to the meaning of non-arising.

That which arises from non-arising is the Dharma-body of all phenomena; these are merely different names for it. Therefore, it is called the 'Mind-made Dharma-body' (manomaya-dharmakāya), the name of the Tathāgata.
Only then does the repetition of the phrase "that which is non-arising" become meaningful; otherwise, this single sentence would have no basis for its arising.

However, this "non-arising" is distinct from the non-arising understood by Mahāmati. It is intended to reveal that all phenomena ultimately tend toward non-arising, which is the domain of the Tathāgata;
therefore, it is said that it is not the domain of any outsiders, nor even of Bodhisattvas up to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).
Since those at the seventh stage have not yet attained the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*), it is not their domain.
Thus, it can be known that this constitutes the eighth stage of non-arising; therefore, in the concluding response, non-arising is identified as an alternative name for the Tathāgata.
That "non-arising and non-ceasing" signifies both the specific meaning and the universal perfection, for its principle is one. (1)
Mahāmati, it is like Indra, Śakra, Purandara, and so forth— each of these things has many names,
yet those many names do not imply many natures, nor are they devoid of self-nature. In the same way, Mahāmati,
I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names in this Sahā world, which all foolish people [perceive].
Mahāmati, when people hear each of my names being spoken, they do not understand that these are alternative names for me, the Tathāgata. There are sentient beings who know me as the Tathāgata;
some know me as the Omniscient One (Sarvajña); some know me as the Buddha; some know me as the Savior of the World;
some know me as the Self-Awakened One; some know me as the Guide; some know me as the Broad Guide; and some know me as the Universal Guide.
There are those who know him as the Rishi; those who know him as Brahmā; those who know him as Viśeṣa; those who know him as Īśvara; those who know him as Jina;
those who know him as Kapila; those who know him as Bhūtakoṭi; those who know him as Candra; those who know him as Sūrya; those who know him as Īśa;
those who know him as Anutpāda; those who know him as Anirodha; and those who know him as Śūnya.
Mahāmati, there are those who know suchness; there are those who know the truths; there are those who know the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi); there are those who know the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
there are those who know nirvāṇa; there are those who know the eternal; there are those who know equality; there are those who know non-duality;
there are those who know the signless; there are those who know liberation; there are those who know the path; and there are those who know the mind-born (manomaya). Mahāmati!
These and other such three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names—neither more nor less—are known by all in this and other worlds as being like the moon in water, neither emerging nor entering.
Yet those foolish people, having fallen into the two extremes, are unable to know me;
nevertheless, they all pay me respectful homage and offerings, though they do not skillfully understand the meaning of the words and phrases.
Those who do not discern the destinies are said to lack understanding of their own self-attainment;
they are attached to various words, phrases, and chapters, conceiving of non-arising and non-ceasing as being without intrinsic nature.

They do not know the distinctions among the names and titles of the Tathāgata—such as Indra, Śakra, and Brahmā—and thus fail to understand that their own self-attainment ultimately converges upon all phenomena, yet they remain attached to whatever is spoken.
The following passage cites analogies to demonstrate the meaning of various names: "These various things" refers to the abode of Śakra, space, and even hands and feet;
each is designated according to its respective object to manifest a distinct name.
Thus, although Śakra has many names, the person is but one, and therefore there is no multiplicity of essence; rather, the meaning is manifested in accordance with the objects.
It is not that they lack intrinsic nature; the analogy with the Buddha is likewise. Thus it is said:

"In this Sahā world," and so forth, listing thirty-three names (fearing prolixity, I shall not explain them). At the outset, it says that fools all hear [these names] and each speaks of my name, implying that each name has its own distinct meaning.
Yet, if they do not understand that these are alternative names for me, the Tathāgata, they will not know that their substance is one and the same.
Regarding non-arising and non-ceasing, it is further said: "We all know that we ourselves are the wise ones who can understand this.
It is like the moon in water, which neither emerges nor enters; it is like the moon in space.

Just as the Dharma-body manifests in response to the water of sentient beings' minds, and just as the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) appears as a reflection that does not leave the water, it neither emerges nor comes from without.

Therefore, there is no entering; because there is no entering, there is no arising; because there is no emerging, there is no ceasing. This analogy is used to manifest the Dharma, and its principle is such.
This is merely a partial analogy; one must not cling to the analogy to the detriment of the Dharma.

It can be understood through the mind that those various deluded people who provide a distorted interpretation and remain ignorant do so because they fall into the two extremes, thereby being obscured regarding non-arising.

The Middle Way of non-extinction should fundamentally be understood as follows: just as worldly people may either perceive the Buddha through attachment to signs or claim that the Buddha has no form or characteristics, all such views fall into the two extremes.
Although they may offer worship, how could they recognize the reason why this is the true Buddha?
Furthermore, regarding those who do not skillfully understand, three faults are enumerated below: namely, not skillfully understanding the meaning of words and phrases.

1) To take [non-arising] as a single destination; 2) not to distinguish it as two; and 3) not to understand its own penetrating nature—these explain the three faults of clinging to various verbal explanations.

Regarding the notion that non-arising and non-ceasing constitute a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), this correctly explains that one has failed to understand the meaning and intent of non-arising, resulting merely in the establishment of non-existence. This also serves as a summary refutation of what was previously stated.
To understand the meaning without resolving it through interpretation and instead speak of its ultimate convergence and final destination as being identical with the self-nature dharmakāya—
this is what is meant by "failing to return to one's own self" (2).
Mahāmati, those deluded people speak thus: "The meaning is identical to the expression; there is no difference between meaning and expression.
Why is this? It is because they claim that since meaning has no body, there is no meaning other than the expression itself, and it is merely the expression.
Mahāmati, those of evil and scorched intelligence do not know the self-nature of expression, nor do they know that the arising and ceasing of expression does not apply to the meaning.
Mahāmati, when all verbal expressions are extinguished, one does not fall into the meaning of words; for, being free from both existence and non-existence, there is neither rebirth nor a body.
Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not teach a dharma that falls into words, because the existence or non-existence of words cannot be apprehended;
except for that which does not fall into words.

Based on the preceding discussion regarding the meaning [of words] and the demonstration of its gains and losses: first, it was stated that there is an absolute loss when "the meaning is like the verbal expression" (*yathā-vāda*).
Now, there are two kinds of meaning: namely, the meaning beneath the words (*vākya-artha*) which possesses a substantial body, and the meaning above the words (*vākya-ūrdhva-artha*).

Here, one merely knows the meaning beneath the words; since there is no further meaning beyond the words, it is said that "the meaning is like the verbal expression," meaning there is no distinct meaning apart from it.

"Body" (*kāya*) is synonymous with "substance" (*tattva*). To take the absence of body as the error while failing to recognize that the meaning of substance lies beyond words is to be consumed by evil views.
When correct wisdom does not perceive the intrinsic nature of verbal expression, one falsely imagines that there is arising and ceasing;
yet while the expression has arising and ceasing, the meaning has neither arising nor ceasing. How could these two ever be identical? It is simply like the meaning that lies beneath the words.
If one grasps its underlying principle, one does not rely exclusively on the literal words; it is as Vimalakīrti spoke regarding the meaning of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence, saying:
"The ultimate non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena is the meaning of impermanence," and so forth.

Furthermore, as the *Aṇḍabhūti-parivarta Sūtra* speaks regarding the meaning of birth and death, saying: "Birth takes non-birth as its meaning," and so forth. These are all meanings conveyed beneath the words.
How could the "destinies" (*gati*) ever be restricted to mere verbal expression? Next, it clarifies what constitutes falling into [conceptual extremes] and not falling into them:

relying on verbal expression leads to falling, whereas attaining the meaning leads to not falling. Regarding the first point: among all forms of verbal expression, there is none that does not emerge from the dharma of written characters.
Even if one claims there are no characters to be spoken, if one gives rise to attachment based on those words, this too is falling.

If one dwells only in "meaning" (*artha*), one does not fall [into conceptualization]. This meaning, which resides within the very essence (*tattva*), is eternally harmonious and transcends both existence and non-existence;
therefore it is said that it is "detached from nature and non-nature. Consequently, when it is expressed through words and emerges from characters, there is a source from which it arises.
Where there is arising, there is a body. However, this is not the case for "meaning"; thus, there is neither rebirth nor a body. Therefore—
Because the attainment of the "bodyless" (anātman) differs from what precedes it, the Tathāgata does not speak of dharmas that fall into words and letters;
this means that the Buddha has never, while attached to the marks of words and letters, spoken anything, for the existence or non-existence of words and letters cannot be apprehended therein.
This is what is meant by the passage below stating that "dharmas are apart from words and letters. Thus, is it then truly the case that the Tathāgata has nothing [to say]?
To speak of the heterodox is to say: "Eliminate [extremes] without falling into words; do not cling to the two sides of existence and non-existence.
Yet, for the sake of sentient beings, one also speaks of all phenomena. Furthermore, it is said: "It is not that the meaning of benefit is not taught"—this is what is meant.
To speak in terms of what is expressed: those who speak of existence or non-existence fall [into extremes]; it is the teaching of the Middle Way that is correct.
Those who do not fall are those who do not grasp at words as they are spoken; even if they are in the midst of [such discourse], they fall nonetheless.
However, one who understands the shifting transformations of existence and non-existence through the teaching of antidotes has never fallen from the beginning. (3)
Mahāmati, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata teaches a dharma that falls within the realm of words, they would be speaking falsely, for the Dharma is free from words.
Therefore, Mahāmati, we Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word, nor do we answer with a single word. Why is this?
Because the Dharma is free from words; it is not that there is no benefit, but rather that the meaning is expressed through conventional speech.
This is because of the false imaginings of sentient beings, Mahāmati. If one were not to speak of all dharmas, the teaching would perish;
if the teaching perishes, then there would be no Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas. If these did not exist, who would teach and for whom?
Therefore, Mahāmati, let Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas not be attached to mere words, but explain the sutras extensively through skillful means as appropriate to the occasion.

Because the afflictions and aspirations of sentient beings are not uniform, I and the Buddhas teach various dharmas for those beings of diverse understandings so that they may become detached from mind,
thought, and consciousness; it is not for the sake of attaining the state of self-realized noble wisdom.

The following section provides a counter-argument to establish the proof. To say that "the Dharma is apart from words" means that the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata is originally free from characteristics;
therefore, he does not cling to verbal explanations, nor does he cling to explanations that are wordless.
The reason for saying that not a single word was spoken or answered lies precisely in this. Nevertheless, it is through non-separation that there is separation.

To be detached from those words and letters that cling to signs—yet to be detached without being detached—means that words and letters are neither words nor non-words, neither letters nor non-letters. Thus, words and letters are detached in their very essence;

this is what the Vimalakīrti Sūtra means when it says, "The nature of words and letters is detachment, which is itself liberation. It is not that one speaks of liberation apart from words and letters.

Since "detachment" (*li*) and "principle" (*li*) differ in meaning while sharing the same character, one knows that the principle of phenomena is eternally harmonious; it is people who stubbornly cling to them.
If even detachment is not permissible, how much more so attachment? It is not that those teachings which provide benefit cannot be spoken;

rather, as stated above, anything that provides benefit—provided it does not fall into mere words—may be taught. The reason one must necessarily rely on verbal expression is for the sake of sentient beings.

Because of conceptualization, longing, and verbal expression, the Tathāgata relies upon them to treat the disease of delusion. When the disease of delusion is exhausted, verbal expression perishes of its own accord.
Nevertheless, one cannot abandon verbal expression because of conceptualization; for if the teachings were thus destroyed, who would speak and for whom?
"Who" refers precisely to that which we seek as a real self. If nothing at all existed, [who would teach?]

Who is it that acts as the savior, and who is it that is saved, such that the teachings are established according to the capacities of beings? This teaching and its non-teaching each have their own underlying intent; however, to give rise to conceptual understanding based on the literal words is not wholesome. Therefore, he warns against attachment to verbal expressions, so that one may depart from mind, thought, and consciousness. This is because [the teachings] are not for those who have attained the state of self-realized noble wisdom. Thus it is said: [The text continues with verses: "By means of various skillful means, I teach the Dharma to sentient beings; I do not speak of the ultimate reality, for it transcends all linguistic expression. Furthermore, it is said: "The Buddhas do not speak of the Dharma, nor do they hear it; It is only through the cessation of mind, thought, and consciousness that one attains Nirvana. This is because [the ultimate] is not something that can be grasped by the intellect. It is like the analogy of a person who, having been struck by a poisoned arrow, does not seek medical treatment but instead asks about the caste, name, appearance, height, and physical characteristics of the archer who shot the arrow. Because such a person is preoccupied with irrelevant matters, the arrow pierces deeper and deeper until they die. In the same way, if one does not seek the medicine of self-realized noble wisdom but instead pursues the proliferation of words and letters, one will surely fall into the error of clinging to the literal meaning. For this reason, the Tathāgata taught that one should not rely on words and letters. It is precisely because the ultimate truth is beyond the reach of speech that the Buddha spoke of "non-duality. If one relies on words and letters, one falls into the duality of existence and non-existence. Therefore, the Tathāgata taught that one should not rely on words and letters.
