The mind-consciousness of false conceptualization can be made to depart, but the state of self-awakened noble wisdom cannot be attained through external means;
it must be personally realized, for it is not within the reach of words. As it is said: "When ordinary sentiments are exhausted, there is no separate 'noble understanding'";
and again: "Where ordinary sentiments are exhausted, noble understanding stands forth clearly. These sayings come close to the truth. (4)

Mahāmati, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas realize that all phenomena are non-existent and are merely the manifestation of their own minds, they become free from the two kinds of false conceptualization.
Relying on the meaning and not on the words, if good sons or good daughters rely upon the words, they will destroy the ultimate truth for themselves and be unable to awaken others;
they fall into a succession of evil views and act as a burden to the masses.
It is said that those who do not correctly understand all dharmas, all stages (*bhūmi*), and all characteristics, nor the meaning of the words and phrases, will not know them;
whereas those who possess the nature of fully penetrating the meaning of the words and phrases regarding all dharmas, all stages, and all characteristics,
are able to delight themselves with the true bliss of signlessness (*animitta*) and, through the equality of the Mahāyāna, establish sentient beings, O Mahāmati.
To embrace the Mahāyāna is to embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas;
to embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas is to embrace all sentient beings; to embrace all sentient beings is to embrace the True Dharma;
and to embrace the True Dharma is to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed. When the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed, [the Buddha-dharma endures].

One who is thus able to understand and attain the sublime spheres of entry—such a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having attained these sublime spheres of entry, constantly attains transformation birth, establishes the ten powers of mastery of the Mahāyāna, manifests various forms and images, penetrates the physical types, aspirations, and afflictions of sentient beings, and teaches the Dharma according to reality.
"According to reality" means not differing from reality; it is reality itself.
That which is without coming or going, where all falsehoods have ceased—this is called reality as it is (*yathābhūta*).
O Mahāmati, sons and daughters of good family should not grasp at or adhere to what is merely expressed in words, for the true reality is beyond words.
Mahāmati, it is like a fool who, when pointed at an object by someone using a finger, looks only at the finger and does not perceive the actual object; such is the case with the foolish person.
Mahāmati, by following the finger of verbal expression and grasping at it with attachment, one never abandons it and can ultimately never attain the ultimate reality that transcends words.
Mahāmati, it is like an infant who should eat food that has been cooked; he should not eat raw food.
If he were to eat raw food, it would cause him to go mad, for he does not know the sequential skillful means required to cook it. Mahāmati, in this same way, [the unproduced] is not produced.

If one does not skillfully cultivate the means for non-extinction, it is unwholesome; therefore, one should skillfully cultivate the means and not follow mere verbal expression, which is like looking at the tip of a finger.
For this reason, Mahāmati, you should skillfully cultivate the ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*).

Ultimate reality is subtle, wondrous, and tranquil; it is the cause of nirvana. Verbal expression is conjoined with conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and conceptual construction is an accumulation [of conditions].
Regarding the true meaning of the great wisdom concerning birth and death: it is obtained from one who is "greatly learned.

To be greatly learned means to be skilled in the meaning, not merely skilled in verbal expression. One who is skilled in the meaning does not follow any of the scriptures or treatises of the various non-Buddhist paths;

neither does he follow them himself, nor does he cause others to follow them. This is what is called being a virtuous person of great learning. Therefore, those who seek the meaning [should follow such a person].
One should associate with those of great learning who possess the true meaning, which is the opposite of this; one should distance oneself from those who are attached to mere verbal expression.
Following the purport of the preceding text, in order to provide instruction and exhortation, it first speaks of relying or not relying on the meaning, as well as on what is wholesome or unwholesome.
Regarding the characteristics of skillfully diminishing and augmenting, it is said that all dharmas are non-existent;
this is spoken in contrast to those who cling to verbal expressions, for whom not even a single dharma exists, let alone any characters to which they might cling.

Since one is able to awaken to the fact that what appears to the mind is merely its own manifestation (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*) and is free from the two kinds of false discrimination—namely, the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*)—how could such a person not rely upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?

Therefore it is said: "Rely on the meaning, not on the letter. If a son of good family [were to] disparage those who rely on the letter, they would destroy the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) themselves.
However, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is truly indestructible; it is only when one clings to the letter that one deviates from its teaching and considers that destruction to have occurred.
Those who fall into a succession of evil views are as previously described regarding reliance on verbal expression.
To be continuously attached to this is what is meant by "good" and "not good. Regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and their chapters and phrases:
if one’s intention is good, then that which is good can be understood by relying on the meaning.

"All phenomena" refers to the teachings, principles, and so forth. "Grounds" (*bhūmi*) refers to the grounds of practice and stages; "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the characteristics of cause and effect. And as for...
Each and every one thoroughly penetrates the chapters and phrases, as well as the nature of detachment and the true meaning.
That which is called the "joy of non-characteristics" (*animitta-sukha*) and so forth refers to the complete accomplishment of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others.

While this establishes the matters pertaining to the fundamental fruit for sentient beings, because the ground of practice (*bhūmi*) also partially attains this function, it encompasses the Mahāyāna; and by encompassing the Mahāyāna, all [is encompassed].
There is nothing among ordinary beings or sages that is not encompassed by this; thus, it constitutes the True Dharma, the seed of the Buddha, and the supreme locus of entry.

This is precisely the state of bliss known through the noble self-realization of the sages. It is because one constantly manifests transformations for the sake of sentient beings that the affairs of a single lifetime are brought to completion;
this is truly due to the Bodhisattva’s initial engagement with the meaning of goodness, which transcends the marks of words, until its ultimate fulfillment in the function of transformation.
For this reason, he further demonstrates that which is "as it truly is" (yathābhūta) through three aspects: namely, the sense of non-differentiation;
the essence of neither coming nor going; and the cessation of all false fabrications in its functioning.

Although such distinctions are made, one should not adhere to them based on the words, for that which is true transcends all letters. Therefore, two metaphors are presented to illustrate gain and loss. First:
The analogy of pointing at an object with a finger illustrates that verbal expressions do not convey the ultimate reality;

the analogy of two infants eating food illustrates that while expedient methods for cultivating the Dharma exist, they all involve both gain and loss, a principle that is perfectly clear. Yet the foolish do not understand this:
they look at the finger instead of the object, and eat raw food instead of the cooked. All people today cling to verbal expressions and engage in lofty talk.
How many who possess rationality yet do not know how to truly cultivate themselves have failed to realize the truth and gone mad!
This is why the Tathāgata, unable to restrain himself, repeatedly instructed and rebuked them regarding the meaning of true reality (*tattvārtha*).
Those who should practice through skillful means (*upāya*) ought to follow the fourfold verse of Vimalakīrti concerning the bondage and liberation of true wisdom and skillful means.
(As stated above) it may also be said that cultivation is not without the principle of skillful means, and that there is no dharma that is not true. Such is the case;
the remaining text, which concludes by demonstrating faults and virtues, can be understood accordingly. Furthermore, it says: "The meaning of reality is obtained through much hearing (*bahuśruta*).
Here, "much hearing" refers to the excellence of the meaning, not merely to extensive learning. As it is said: "If one knows that the Tathāgata never speaks..."
"The Dharma is precisely what is called 'much learning' (paññā). (5) The second chapter concludes here.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, further empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, there is nothing extraordinary about Your World-Honored One’s teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is this? Because even all the heterodox teachers [do not teach] a cause..."
The Blessed One has also taught that space, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the realm of nirvāṇa are neither born nor extinguished.

The Blessed One, the Blessed One has also taught that the externalists claim the causes for the arising of all worlds, whereas [the Buddha] teaches that ignorance, craving, karma, and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) act as conditions for the arising of all worlds;
these are merely differences in names for those causes and conditions. External objects likewise have causes and conditions.

In this way, there is not even a grain of difference between the Blessed One and the non-Buddhists regarding such things as the Supreme Lord (Iśvara), the Sovereign of Beings (Puruṣa), and so forth—these nine entities being neither born nor extinguished.
The Blessed One also teaches that all natures are neither born nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended;
the non-Buddhists likewise teach that the four great elements are indestructible and that their intrinsic nature is neither born nor extinguished.
"The four great elements are always the four great elements, even as they circulate through the various realms of existence without abandoning their own nature;
the teaching of the World-Honored One is likewise so. Therefore, I say there is nothing extraordinary about it.

I only wish that the World-Honored One would explain the distinction by which it is extraordinary and superior to all non-Buddhists; for if there were no distinction, then all non-Buddhists would also be [enlightened]."
Because he is neither born nor extinguished, the World-Honored One has declared that it is impossible for many Buddhas to appear in a single world-system, as previously stated;
for if there were many Buddhas in one world-system, they would be indistinguishable from one another.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The 'neither-born-nor-extinguished' that I teach is not the same as the 'neither-born-nor-extinguished' of the non-Buddhists."
Why is this? Because those various non-Buddhists hold that there is a self-nature (*svabhāva*) which is unarisen and immutable;

I do not teach such a thing, as it would fall into the categories of existence and non-existence. Mahāmati, my teaching is free from the categories of existence and non-existence, and free from arising and ceasing.

It is neither a nature nor a non-nature, because it appears like various illusions and dreams; thus, it is not "non-existent. Why is it not non-existent? Because form (*rūpa*) has no characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
Because they encompass both the manifest and the unmanifest, and because they encompass both the grasped and the non-grasped, all natures are neither existent nor non-existent;
rather, when one realizes that these are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, conceptual construction ceases, and there is peace, happiness, and the eternal cessation of worldly affairs.
The previous statement regarding non-arising and non-ceasing was made strictly according to the direct teaching without yet distinguishing how it differs from the heterodox schools;
therefore, Mahāmati, empowered by the Buddha’s strength, again poses questions concerning their similarities and differences, setting forth four points in total:

first, he juxtaposes the cause posited by the heterodox schools—which they claim does not arise or cease—with the three unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*); second, he juxtaposes that [heterodox] cause with this [Buddhist] cause.
First, [the claim that] conditions arise together with the three [aggregates] from atoms and so forth; second, [the claim that] all natures are neither born nor extinguished;
third, [the claim that] the four great elements are indestructible; and fourth, [the claim that] these are all compared to and equated with the Buddha’s teaching, as stated in the text at length.

Therefore, it is said that there is nothing extraordinary about the Buddha’s teaching. Yet, the Tathāgata’s teaching is the Way of the Constant (nitya-dharma); how could it have any intentional design?
Regarding the phrase "Is it not marvelous? and "Mahāmati says this," these are not words spoken for his own sake;
they are simply addressed to the superior non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) to draw them toward [the truth]. Nevertheless, even those who do not know or understand may well call this "marvelous.
In the response, there is first a general repudiation of the non-Buddhists' erroneous claims, stating that the various non-Buddhists [assert] such things as "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
This refers to those who assert that all natures are neither arising nor ceasing and possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);

furthermore, they hold that the four great elements are eternal as the four great elements—such as earth being merely earth—and so forth, with each intrinsic nature remaining unmixed with the others. When combined with what was stated previously, they claim to attain the characteristics of non-arising and immutability;
thus, with a mind attached to existence, they reckon those natures to be truly existent, and because they are real, they are indeed existent.
Although it is said that destruction is neither arising nor changing, in reality it involves arising and ceasing, falling into the categories of existence and non-existence;
therefore, I say: "I do not thus fall into the positions of existence and non-existence. Regarding this, there are briefly three ways in which its explanation differs from others:

first, departing from the positions of existence and non-existence, as explained above; second, departing from arising and ceasing, as clarified in sequence below; third, being neither nature nor absence of nature.

It is said: "Various things such as illusions and dreams" means that what is now being described—like illusions and dreams—is not non-existent because something appears, yet it is not a real nature because it lacks reality.
Since it is not even a nature, how much less could it be like those [illusions] that fall into the trap of a real nature?
When one speaks of form (*rūpa*) being devoid of self-nature and being subsumed [under this category], it refers to the form of illusions and dreams.

The characteristic of the absence of intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended through grasping; for when one seizes upon an external object with a mind of attachment, it appears, whereas if one does not grasp it, it does not appear.
Thus, it is said that it "appears and does not appear" and is "grasped and not grasped.
By this analogy, all natures are neither existent nor non-existent; their nature is fundamentally empty, being merely the manifestation of the measure of one's own mind, just as it is.
This awakening, in which deluded thoughts do not arise and one dwells in peace, security, and joy, wherein worldly affairs are forever stilled—let us speak of this by way of immediate matters;
as for the profound principle, the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is attained from this point on.
How could it be merely like this? (1)
Foolish ordinary people cultivate practices based on false conceptualization, whereas the noble ones do not;

such unreal conceptualization is like a city of the Gandharvas or a magical illusion. Mahāmati, just as with a city of the Gandharvas or a magical illusion, various beings and merchants enter and exit;
yet foolish people, through their conceptualization, claim there is real entering and exiting, when in fact there is no one who enters or exits.
It is merely due to their false conceptualization that such ignorant, deluded worldlings give rise to the delusion of arising and non-arising;

yet for them, there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned. Like a person born from an illusion, they do not truly exist, whether in terms of arising or ceasing, because their nature is neither existent nor non-existent and is devoid of anything at all.
All phenomena are likewise thus, free from arising and ceasing, [yet] ignorant worldlings [perceive them otherwise].
Falling into the false arising of the delusions of birth and death is not the case for the noble ones;

that which is unreal is not so, yet it is not different from the delusion regarding the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of things. If the delusion were different [from that self-nature], one would be attached to all natures and self-natures and would not see tranquility.
One who does not see tranquility will never be free from delusion. Therefore, Mahāmati, there is no characteristic mark (*animitta*).
To see the superior is not to see the characteristic; seeing the characteristic is the cause for the arising of birth, and thus it is not superior.

Mahāmati, that which is signless (*animitta*) is where false discrimination does not arise, does not originate, and does not cease. I call this Nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, Nirvāṇa is like the vision of reality as it truly is;
it is the attainment of the Tathāgata’s own realized noble wisdom, having departed from the previously existing mind and mental factors of false discrimination. This, I say, is it.

Nirvāṇa. Third, to further demonstrate the meaning of being free from arising and ceasing: therein, first, it is clarified through a contrast between the unreal and the real. That is to say, ordinary beings take the activities produced by deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) to be real;
they do not realize that these are unreal conceptualizations, as is the case for the noble sages who do not [take] deluded conceptualization [to be real].

It is empty; yet while delusive thoughts are fundamentally one, the ignorant and foolish claim they are real, whereas the sages realize their emptiness. When one realizes emptiness, the nature of reality is present therein;

when one claims things are real, there is ultimately no reality to be found, as in the case of the city of Gandharvas and other such examples. Next, the analogy is used to clarify this; the text of the analogy is self-evident.
Regarding the statement in the Dharma that "fools give rise to delusions concerning non-arising and non-ceasing," this refers to those who are deluded.

To conceive of that which is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing as being non-arising and non-ceasing is an error; it results in being deluded about non-arising and non-ceasing by means of arising and ceasing itself.

To say that there is neither the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) therein—claiming that one does not abandon the conditioned—is to be ignorant of the reality of arising and ceasing;
and since there is no unconditioned, one is likewise ignorant of non-existence.
The reality of arising and ceasing is like seeing a conjured person enter or exit, yet in truth one does not know that there is fundamentally no entering or exiting.
Therefore, it is further stated collectively that "it is like the birth of a conjured person," etc., because the nature of illusion is non-nature and non-existent.
By means of this essence, one understands that all phenomena are free from arising and ceasing; thus, the manifestation of non-arising and non-ceasing is likewise like this.
This being so, the Dharma is fundamentally like an illusion, yet foolish people fall into views of arising and ceasing.

Those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are themselves fundamentally characterized by arising and ceasing, yet they conversely give rise to calculations of non-arising and non-ceasing; thus we know that ordinary people and outsiders are inverted from beginning to end.
How, then, could they be the same as [the Buddha]? Furthermore, the phrase "foolish ordinary beings" and so forth reiterates the previous distinction between the ordinary and the holy.
If it is claimed that deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) differ from reality in terms of being real or unreal, this is also not the case; therefore, it is said that it is "not so.
This means that the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and their own inherent nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) are neither identical nor different.

If they were truly different, then ordinary beings would remain stubbornly attached to their own inherent nature and fail to realize that this nature is fundamentally empty; consequently, they would not perceive tranquility and would ultimately never be able to transcend deluded thoughts.
Furthermore, by taking the meaning of "seeing the signless within signs" as superior, it follows that the real and the empty need not differ, and the holy and the ordinary need not be distinct.
However, because between signs and the signless the principle is easily transformed and delusion is easily dissolved, it is said that "seeing the signless is superior.
This means that those who see the signless perceive tranquility; therefore, their seeing is superior.
"Those who see characteristics where there are no characteristics" means that although fundamentally there are no characteristics, they perceive them as such;

thus they do not see tranquility, for this is the cause of rebirth. Therefore, their vision is inferior. By contrast, it is evident that those who see the absence of characteristics attain *nirvāṇa*, just as one who sees according to the true meaning [sees it].
Furthermore, "being free from prior deluded thoughts and mental factors" means that one has not yet seen [the truth].
Regarding the statement that all deluded mental factors prior to the nirvana of signlessness are abandoned:
although the phrasing is presented collectively rather than being answered individually, it can be understood by examining the text (2).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I refute the doctrine of arising and establish the principle of non-arising; I preach such a Dharma, yet the foolish cannot understand it.
All phenomena are non-arising, without intrinsic nature, and non-existent; like a *gandharva-city*, a phantom, or a dream, they have no inherent nature and no cause."

Since there is no arising and no intrinsic nature, for what reason is it empty? It should be explained that because the nature of cognition does not manifest apart from its conjunctions, it is therefore empty and unarisen.
I teach that "no intrinsic nature" means that while each individual conjunctive nature appears, it does not exist;
when analyzed, the absence of conjunction is not like the views of the non-Buddhists regarding dreams, illusions, falling hairs, mirages, or gandharva-cities.
The various phenomena of the world appear without a [perceptible] cause; thus, the proponents of causality are refuted and the meaning of non-arising is proclaimed.
To proclaim this non-arising is to ensure that the flow of the Dharma never ceases. This blazing [teaching] intimidates the proponents of causelessness and all externalists.
The verse states: "To eliminate those who propound arising. Although the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) have words regarding non-arising and non-extinction, in reality they involve arising and extinction;
thus, they merely establish a theory of arising. The Buddha’s teaching of non-arising and non-extinction, in contrast to them, carries the meaning of non-arising;
therefore, it is said that the principle of non-arising is established. The statement that "all phenomena are unarisen," etc., also brings forth other meanings.

Both "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) and "lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) can mutually clarify one another. That is to say, the meaning of "lack of intrinsic nature" is the meaning of "non-existence," which is the meaning of "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*);
"the city of Gandhāra" and so forth are the meaning of "illusion" (*māyā*). The text explains these in sequence.

The phrase "non-arising, lack of self-nature, etc. restates the previous inquiry. The phrase "because it is free from combination, etc. provides the explanation. First, the meaning of emptiness is set forth: regarding...

Because the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are devoid of the characteristic of conjunction, although there is cognitive awareness (*vijñapti*), its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not manifest. That which does not manifest is emptiness (*śūnyatā*);

that which is empty is non-arising (*anutpāda*). Therefore it is said: "For this reason, emptiness is non-arising. Furthermore, when I speak of "the absence of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), I am expounding the meaning of the lack of self-nature;
that is to say, although the nature of cognitive awareness manifests through each individual conjunction, its own intrinsic nature does not [manifest].
Because they can be apprehended, they are not non-existent; each follows its own meaning. Although the phrasing may appear contrary, the underlying principle is actually consistent.

This is not like the view of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who must wait for things to be analyzed into non-existence or for combinations to dissolve before they are empty. What the teachings refer to as the "four natures," "non-arising," and "illusory transformations are themselves empty" is precisely this.
The examples of dreams, illusions, and falling hairs serve to illustrate the meaning of being like an illusion. [End of] the preceding section.
To say that illusion has an intrinsic nature is to claim it is without cause; to say it appears without a cause is likewise intended to clarify that illusion is neither existent nor non-existent.

If illusion possessed an intrinsic nature, it ought not to be without a cause; yet since it occurs without a cause, its nature is not existent. If illusion were without a cause, its characteristics ought not to appear;
yet since its characteristics appear without a cause, those characteristics are fundamentally empty. Both [arguments] are thus established.
Because it reveals the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*), its refutations and establishments serve to subdue the heterodox arguments for a cause;
thus it is said that it "expounds the meaning of non-arising. Non-arising is such because it is without cause. The term "blazing" (*cīra*) signifies the flourishing of the True Dharma;
thus, the discourse on "cause and no-cause" is also, for the time being, like those heterodox schools who likewise maintain [theories of] non-existence.
As for the cause, it results in the view of annihilationism; however, it is said in general that the Buddha-dharma has never been biased from beginning to end.
It is only because [the teachings] clarify the internal by means of the external that there are such partial expressions regarding existence and non-existence.
(3) At that time, Mahāmati asked in verse:
"What is it? What is its cause? For what reason does it arise? In what place do they combine to produce this theory of non-causality?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
Observing that conditioned phenomena do not arise without a cause, but rather have causes, the views held by those who argue for their arising and ceasing were thereby extinguished.
At that time, Mahāmati spoke a verse and asked:
What is meant by "non-arising"? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature? Or is it that, in consideration of various conditions, there is a phenomenon called "non-arising"?
This name should not be without meaning; it is merely spoken for the sake of analytical exposition.
At that time, the World-Honored One again answered in verse:

"It is not that there is no nature, nor is it that there is no arising; it is not that one looks to various conditions, nor is it that there is a nature. It is called 'name,' yet it is not without meaning.
This is not the realm of any outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or those at the seventh stage. This is called the characteristic of non-arising."

Detached from all causes and conditions and free from all objective phenomena, there is only the subtle mind abiding; both the perceiver and the perceived are abandoned, and the body undergoes transformation accordingly.
I declare this to be non-arising, devoid of external nature, and without the grasping of a self-nature or mind.
Having severed all views, I declare this to be non-arising. Thus, one should discern the absence of self-nature, emptiness, and so forth.

It is not because of emptiness that it is called empty; it is because of non-arising that it is called empty. When causes, conditions, and numerical aggregates come together, there is arising and ceasing.

Apart from these various causes, conditions, and numerical aggregates, there is no separate arising or ceasing. If one were to abandon the causes, conditions, and numerical aggregates, there would be no other distinct nature.
To speak of identity or difference is the deluded conceptualization of externalists. The nature of existence and non-existence does not arise; it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Apart from these numerical transformations, none of them can be apprehended; there are only conventional designations that link together like a chain.
Apart from that causal chain, the meaning of "arising" cannot be found. Since arising has no intrinsic nature and does not occur, it is free from the errors of the non-Buddhists.
Next, a second set of questions and answers is presented, the first of which investigates the meaning of "causelessness. In total, four questions are posed, the intent of which is as follows:
"In what way? By what cause? For what reason? And in what place is this doctrine of causelessness formulated? The answer likewise contains four points;

specifically, the first phrase answers the location [of the doctrine], while the second phrase answers the manner in which it is causeless, stating that the Buddha-dharma is fundamentally not existent.

The first three phrases of the answer respond to the question: "What is the cause? [The response is] that it arises from that. The proponent of arising and ceasing answers with the fourth phrase: "For what purpose is it for the sake of extinguishing that view?
Next, in order to thoroughly investigate the meaning of non-arising, three points are established as questions:

namely, is it because of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), or is it because of "regarding" (*apekṣā*)? "Regarding" has the sense of "waiting upon"; that is to say, regarding those various conditions, there is something upon which one depends.
To answer the objection that there must be other dharmas apart from these three and that it would otherwise be meaningless, the response first negates what was asked;

this is because that which is "unborn" does not fall into the categories of existence or non-existence, as its nature is inherently such, and thus it cannot be designated by names—this is the initial negation showing it is not meaningless.
Following this is the formal response, which likewise contains three points: the first uses the stage of realization to manifest the correct state, which corresponds to the eighth bhūmi.
Because that which is attained is non-arising, it is called "not the realm of the seventh stage. This means that the principle of the Middle Way’s true reality is neither existence nor non-existence;
it is not the realm of ordinary people or those of the Two Vehicles. Second, because it is free from all conditions, it does not depend upon or await such conditions.

Yet, the dharma of causes and conditions has never been separate from them; it is simply said to be "non-arising," and by that very fact, it is naturally free from them. This is the uniquely subtle and wondrous path.
Because the mind that is attained through association is likewise unattainable as a state of non-conception, both subject and object are transcended.
Since the mind is thus, the body also follows suit; therefore, the Dharma-body becomes increasingly supreme.

Third, because internal and external natures are unattainable, externally there is no nature nor is there any non-nature to be attained, and internally there is no mind to be grasped or attained; thus, one and many are severed.
When all such views are equalized, all phenomena are quiescent. Thus, that which is non-arising has no intrinsic nature; because it lacks intrinsic nature, it is empty.
It is said to be "not empty" [in the sense of absolute nothingness], yet it is called "empty. This is merely to distinguish it from an emptiness that is a mere nihilistic negation;
it is simply called "empty" because of non-arising. However, as previously stated, if one speaks of its essential substance apart from conditions, it is likewise...
Because they do not depart from conditions, the enumeration of causes and conditions is a conjunction; subsequently, the very arising from conditions demonstrates the meaning of non-arising.
According to the subsequent text, the birth and cessation that exist through the conjunction of the factors enumerated in the twelve links of dependent origination are also non-arising.

Since both equally emerge from causes and conditions, they possess no distinct nature. If one were to fixate on them as being either identical or different, that would be the heterodox teaching of existence and non-existence.

The statement that "nature is unarisen," and so forth, correctly demonstrates non-arising by being free from the four extremes; because this non-arising is devoid of differentiation, it is said that "their enumeration is eliminated.
Regarding the phrase "there are only conventional enumerations such as transformation and so on": when contrasted with the truth of non-arising, these are merely conventional enumerations.
The intended meaning is that if there were no conventional enumerations, one would simply cease to exist; yet ordinary beings are inevitably submerged in birth by means of them.
The heterodox paths beyond this world fall into the pits of nihilism and eternalism; their continuous succession is like an unbroken chain, which is called "linked hooks.
Apart from this, there is no separate existence of birth or non-birth; therefore it is said that the meaning of birth cannot be apprehended.

Yet the Tathāgata demonstrates to the world the single principle of non-birth to shatter these views, so that by realizing birth as non-birth, one understands that the linked hooks are in fact without hooks. Thus, they are "hooks" [only in name].
Because the fetters are severed all at once and one enters the stage of neither arising nor ceasing, it is said that "arising has no nature" and "does not arise.
This means that although there is arising, it does not arise; this arising is itself non-arising.
Because it is neither identical nor different, it avoids the error of the fixed calculations of the non-Buddhists (4).
I speak only of dependent origination as a chain of causes and conditions, yet the foolish and ignorant cannot comprehend it.
If there were a nature of arising that existed apart from this chain of dependent origination, that would be a doctrine of causelessness, which destroys the meaning of the chain.

Just as a lamp reveals various forms through the chain of conditions, if it were so, then apart from the chain there would be no further natures or non-natures, and no arising whatsoever, being like the intrinsic nature of empty space.
If one is free from the chain of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is no further dharma of non-arising to be discriminated by wisdom that is attained by the noble ones (*ārya*).
That which arises or does not arise is itself the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
If those in the world were to observe this chain, they would all become free from the chain; from this, they would attain samādhi. Ignorance, craving, and karma—these are the internal chain.

The chain, the flint, the clay lump, the wheel, the seed, and so forth are called "external. If these were to possess an other-nature (*parabhāva*) while arising from causes and conditions, they would not have the meaning of a "chain" (*saṃkalana*);
thus, [the doctrine of dependent origination] would not be established. If, however, they arise without self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), for whom would there be a chain?

Because they arise through mutual succession, one should know that the meaning of causes and conditions—namely, the phenomena of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by the ignorant.
Apart from enumeration, there is no other distinct dharma; this is what is called "the absence of intrinsic nature.

Just as a physician treats various illnesses without having multiple theories—providing diverse treatments according to the differences in the diseases—I, for the sake of those sentient beings, destroy their afflictions and, knowing the superiority or inferiority of their faculties, teach them the gates of liberation. It is not that because the afflictions and faculties differ, there are various distinct dharmas.
To teach only the One Vehicle Dharma is precisely what constitutes the Mahāyāna.

Hereafter, the heterodox views are refuted to reveal the correct teaching. If one speaks only of the chain of dependent origination (*saṃkalana*) without mentioning non-arising (*anutpāda*), ordinary people will certainly fail to understand;
or if one posits a nature of arising apart from the chain of dependent origination, this reveals that all phenomena arise from a single source.

Regarding existence and conditioned phenomena, to claim they are without cause is to fall into the false doctrine of uncausedness (*ahetuvāda*), which destroys the meaning of the "chain of dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Just as a lamp reveals various forms without being identical to those objects yet being distinct from them, if this chain of dependent origination were to manifest in such a manner, it would be like the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who perceive various natures as existing separately and independently outside of causes and conditions. If that were the case...
Because its essence lacks intrinsic nature, it is without arising; that which has a nature like empty space accords with the True Teaching.
Therefore, one knows that if one abandons dependent origination to seek elsewhere for the wisdom of non-arising, there will be nothing revealed. Thus it is said: "Wisdom is without discrimination.
Furthermore, other designations such as "non-arising" refer to what is attained by the noble ones (ārya); these too are simply the non-arising of arising.
"Arising" is spoken of in terms of manifesting through realization. Furthermore, it is said:

"If those in the various worlds were to think that there could be one who contemplates in this way, then they would be situated in non-arising; this is called 'detachment' and is also termed 'samādhi.

This is spoken of in terms of manifesting through cultivation. Next, the Dharma is shown, which is twofold. First, establishing the internal and external to speak of causes and conditions, it says: "Ignorance, craving, and all karmas."
The "equal" refers to the twelve links [of dependent origination] as the internal fire-drill, while the external is used as a metaphor for the internal; thus it is spoken of in that way.
Next, one examines self and other to deduce the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), saying:

"If there were 'other-nature'—that is, if things arose from conditions solely through other-nature—then since conditions are not a causal chain (*saṃtati*), they would not be established in themselves. If there is no self-nature..."
Then, as for those external conditions acting as a hook-and-chain, one should likewise respond: "If there were only intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would not depend on conditions;
if there were no extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*), the cause would not arise from itself. The text has been abbreviated in both directions; this refutes the arising of things from self or other.
As for the phrase "because they arise through mutual succession," it means that if self and other were to arise through mutual succession—
The claim that the meaning of "arising through causes and conditions" is based on co-arising is also incorrect.

Just as the four great elements—solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—each possess their own intrinsic nature and are fundamentally without mutual combination, yet the ignorant and foolish form the false conception (*vikalpa*) of "produced phenomena," in reality, the nature of arising cannot be found;
this is the refutation of non-arising through co-arising. Apart from these enumerations, there is no distinct phenomenon; thus, it is simply causeless and non-existent.
How could there be arising from causes? Since all things are sought but cannot be found, it is said that they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), which means they lack the four types of nature.

This is like a physician treating various illnesses; this general analogy refers to the aforementioned dharmas. As explained above, the non-arising, emptiness, and illusory nature of phenomena differ according to the diverse faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings' illnesses.
It does not mean that the dharmas themselves are different; rather, it is because the faculties of the sentient beings' illnesses are different. If these faculties did not exist...
What distinction is there in the sublime Dharma? It is simply that only the One Vehicle is taught; thus, there are no various differences.
If there were no sentient beings, there would likewise be no Dharma. (5) ○ End of Chapter Three.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, all non-Buddhists give rise to the false discrimination of impermanence. World-Honored One, you also say that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing.
What is the meaning of this? Is it erroneous or correct? And how many kinds of impermanence are there? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All non-Buddhists..."
There are seven kinds of impermanence that are not the self-dharma. What are the seven? Some say that having created something and then abandoning it is called impermanence;
some say that the destruction of shape and location is called impermanence; some say that form itself is impermanence;
some say that the interval during which form undergoes transformation is called impermanence; and [some say] that its immediate disintegration of itself, like milk, is impermanence.
In the transformation of curd and so forth, impermanence is not visible in the interim; it is the destruction of all natures as they undergo transformation.
Some say that nature is impermanent; some say that the non-existence of nature is impermanent; and some say that the non-arising of all dharmas is impermanence.

Regarding the entry into the great wisdom-nature of all dharmas, "the impermanence of the non-existence of nature" refers to the four great elements and their derivatives, wherein their own characteristics are destroyed.
The great self-nature is unattainable; that which is unborn is not subject to impermanence. That which is not impermanent is not [merely] impermanent.
All phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—are unborn. Even when analyzed down to the subtlest atom, they cannot be seen;

this is the meaning of "unborn. It is not birth; this is called the characteristic of unborn impermanence. If one does not awaken to this, one falls into the view of all externalists regarding the impermanence of arising.
This is the meaning.
It is a natural principle that while those non-Buddhists are all heterodox, only the Buddha-way is uniquely correct.

If so, how does the fruit [of the Buddha-way] differ from that of the non-Buddhists? Is it because they consider it eternal? The non-Buddhists have also spoken of this as eternal; is it because they consider it impermanent?
The Buddha has indeed spoken of this before; how, then, does it differ from the heterodox paths? [The interlocutor asks:

"If the perversion of permanence is already clarified by the perversion of impermanence, why did Mahāmati request a further resolution? [The Master replies: The question can be understood from the text.
In the response, he first enumerates the seven heterodox meanings of impermanence; among them, only the view that "form undergoes transformation" is excluded.
In the constant [process], the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are briefly explained while the others are merely listed by name;

in the subsequent explanation, some [characteristics] may involve the refutation of [wrong] views while others do not, yet they do not follow a fixed order and do not appear simultaneously, as their sequence is manifested through their characteristics.

Regarding the phrase "in the interval of the transformation of matter" (*rūpa-pariṇāma-antara*): it refers to the state where, within the process of matter changing, there is a continuous and uninterrupted movement toward disintegration and destruction.
"Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) is like the process of milk turning into curd; the intermediate stages of change are so subtle as to be imperceptible.

It is only when things undergo destruction due to impermanence that one realizes the transformation of all phenomena—this is precisely their characteristic. First, regarding the explanation of "impermanence as having nature and lacking nature":
"nature" refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*); "destruction," however, means the absence of nature.

This is the meaning of impermanence (*anitya*). The phrase "the self-nature of the four great elements" (*catur-mahābhūta-svabhāva*) refers to the refutation of conceptual attachment. The intent is that since self-nature cannot be apprehended, how could there be any nature?
Since there is no arising, there is not even the existence of arising; how then could there be the destruction or impermanence [of what does not arise]?

That which is non-arising and impermanent is based on the previously mentioned names; furthermore, it is said that "entering into all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma-praveśa*) refers to the conceptualization of unity (*ekatva*).
Since all phenomena are fundamentally unborn, it is appropriate to say that they enter into the state of impermanence; yet, what is meant by "unborn"?
Once something is unborn, how can one speak of its impermanence? To rectify this through principle, it is said: they are neither permanent nor impermanent.
This is an ultimate statement that the unborn must mean that all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—are unborn. Whatever exists...
That which is unarisen may be called impermanent; yet if it does not exist, how can it be impermanent?

If you say that analysis down to the subtlest atom reveals nothing visible, and this is the meaning of "unarisen" rather than "that which arises," then there must be atoms that can be extinguished, which is precisely the same as the meaning of "arising.
What, then, is meant by "unarisen"? If one does not perceive this, then both existence and non-existence are equally unarisen.
To claim that the analysis of particles results in non-arising is precisely to fall into the eternalist view of the non-existence of arising (1).

Mahāmati, that which is "the impermanence of intrinsic nature" refers to the fact that the false imaginings of one's own mind are neither permanent nor impermanent in their essential nature. Why is this so?
Because, Mahāmati, the self-nature of impermanence is indestructible. Mahāmati, this excludes all matters concerning the impermanence of existence and non-existence.

There is nothing that can cause the nature of all phenomena to become non-existent. Just as a staff, a tile, or a stone breaks various objects, we see directly that each of these is not different from that nature.
Impermanence is a fact; it is not something produced by an agent. There is a distinction between the agent and the action: "this is impermanence" and "this is the object produced by the agent.
If there were no difference between the agent and the action, then all natures would be eternal, being without cause, and [the elements] would be the Great.
Wisdom [perceives] that all natures are without nature yet possess causes, which is not something known by ordinary fools.
If things were produced from non-causes or dissimilar things, then all natures would be entirely impermanent.

Since there is no distinction between the agent and the action, yet distinctions are nonetheless perceived, if natures were impermanent, they would fall into the category of being produced by causes; and if they so fell, [the fault of impermanence would follow].
If all natures were not ultimate, and if they fell into the characteristic of being causes for all natures, then that which is itself impermanent would have to be impermanent;
and because it is impermanent and impermanent, all natures would not be impermanent and would instead have to be permanent.

If impermanence were to enter into all natures, it would fall into the three periods of time: past form would be coexistent with destruction, and future form would be non-arising; thus, form would be non-arising.

Therefore, present form coexists with the characteristic of disintegration; yet as for form, it is a specific accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the self-nature of both the four great elements and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is indestructible.
Because it is neither distinct nor non-distinct [from its nature], all non-Buddhists maintain that the four great elements are indestructible.

Furthermore, the four great elements and derived matter within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) exist among the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and possess arising and ceasing, yet they are distinct from the four great elements and derived matter [as conceived by others].
Regarding what all non-Buddhists contemplate: they hold that the nature of the four great elements is impermanent, yet their own self-nature is indestructible.
As for this "impermanence of nature," it is as explained later: they merely calculate that while the phenomena of nature and non-nature are impermanent, nature itself is not.
Because it is impermanent, one simply negates it by means of the deluded conceptualizations of one's own mind;
this is not what is meant by the nature of permanence or impermanence. Why? Because while phenomena may be destroyed, their nature cannot be destroyed. Therefore, it is called "impermanence.

Since the self-nature is indestructible, how could one say that the nature itself is impermanent? As for that which is capable of destruction, its nature is indestructible; therefore, it is said to be "removed."
Impermanence and so forth are excellent precisely because the nature of impermanence is always co-existent with things; it is neither identical to nor separate from them.
It can cause things to be impermanent while not itself becoming impermanent, just as a staff, a tile, or a stone can destroy various objects while its own substance remains undestroyed.
It is also like the eight characteristics of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa). (And so forth. However, because this principle is not easily clarified, [the text] further...

He analyzes this argument repeatedly, stating: "It is directly perceived that each [entity] is not different [from its nature]," meaning that if the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were different from the phenomenon (*vastu*), then just as one perceives the phenomena themselves to have the nature of impermanence, one would not perceive any distinct characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) by which they differ.
Consequently, there would be no distinction between the agent and the object of action such that one could point it out and say, "This is impermanence" and "This is the phenomenon."
"How can there be impermanence such that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not destroyed? This is intended to address the opponent's objection.

Furthermore, the statement "the agent and the acted-upon are not different" reiterates the preceding argument. If they were not different, then just as all natures are eternal, they would likewise be without causal nature;
this uses the case of the eternal to illustrate the impermanent, demonstrating that all natures possess an intrinsic nature. Thus, all natures [would be eternal].
It is also clear that non-existence has causes; however, because its nature is subtle and hidden, it is not known by ordinary fools.
Therefore, one further verifies its necessary difference through empirical facts, saying: "Things do not arise from dissimilar causes.
This means that if there were no cause, nothing dissimilar could arise—just as when all natures are entirely impermanent, is this not [the case]?
If similar phenomena were to arise, one could verify that impermanence necessarily has a cause.

This conversely reveals that what was previously called "no difference" is in fact entirely characterized by difference; however, the former case directly manifests the nature of phenomena, just as a form possesses a shadow.
The deluded and ignorant fail to perceive this, seeing only the form while failing to see the shadow—this is using the permanent as an analogy for the impermanent.

Furthermore, as for the verification by facts: just as the distinct natures of the five grains are known to all, whether foolish or wise, this [argument] merely recognizes that impermanence has a nature, yet it does not clarify the reason for its loss;
therefore, I shall further refute it by saying: "If the nature were impermanent," and so forth.
For when one speaks of "nature," it must ultimately be unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), and what is unconditioned is permanent; if one speaks of impermanence, then...
To fall into the view that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are not ultimately real is to fall into the nature of a causal agent; because of this, one loses the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*).

Therefore, regarding the meaning of nature, it is said: "If [the self] were impermanent, it should be impermanent," and so forth. This means that "self-impermanence" refers to nature itself. Nature ought not to be impermanent;
if nature were impermanent, it would conflict with the characteristics of phenomena, and phenomena would consequently become contrary to their own nature.
This is stated as a concession because it would result in a counter-objection. Furthermore, it says:

"If the impermanent were to enter into all natures, one might fear that such an attachment leads to the objection that it must necessarily enter all natures, and thus fall into the error of the three periods of time; for how could its self-nature not be subject to destruction along with the destruction of its form?
Therefore, he further explains the reason why the self-nature [is not destroyed], stating: "As for 'form' (rūpa), it is an accumulation of the four great elements."
Regarding "differentiation" and so forth: if one speaks in terms of accumulation and combination, there has never been any difference;

yet if one speaks in terms of differentiation, there has never been no difference. Since both difference and non-difference are transcended, the self-nature of the four great elements and derived matter exists right here;
how could it possibly perish along with the derived matter? Those heterodox teachers reckon that nature is impermanent.

You are merely able to perceive the arising and ceasing within the four great elements in their undestroyed state and within the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) existing in the three realms of existence;
yet, when you seek to be free from these four great elements and derived matter, what further object could you contemplate to perceive the impermanence of the nature (*svabhāva*)?
You will ultimately fail to see it. This is because you do not realize that what is called the "indestructible self-nature" is not identical to derived matter.

Form is not separate from derived matter; it resides within the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which are fundamentally unborn. Therefore, it is said that the four great elements are unborn.
Because their self-nature and characteristics are indestructible, one speaks of the four great elements as being neither different nor non-different.
Thus, they possess no fixed nature. Because there is no fixed nature, they arise yet do not arise. Precisely because they do not arise, they cannot be destroyed, as in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
As for what Yan [Zongxin] so-called says, the doctrine that nature is impermanent falls into error;
because his arguments are extremely harmful to the truth, I have specifically devoted myself to refuting them (2).

Regarding "impermanence as the absence of initial creation": it is not that there are four great elements (mahābhūta) distinct from one another; rather, because each of the four great elements has its own distinct characteristics and specific natures, no differentiation can be found among them.
Since they are without such differentiation, these do not undergo further creation through two types of conditions, nor do they act [as agents].

One should know that this is impermanence. Regarding "impermanence as the destruction of shape and location": this refers to the fact that while the four great elements and the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) are not destroyed, their shapes and locations are destroyed.

Ultimately, there is no destruction. "Great Wisdom" (Mahāmati), "ultimately" means that even when analyzed down to the level of atoms and examined, one cannot find the destruction of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) or of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
As for the false view of distinct forms and locations—such as perceiving length and shortness—it is not the case that the four great elements themselves are destroyed;
rather, it is the perceived forms and locations that are destroyed. To say that "matter is impermanent" means that matter itself is impermanent; such a person [perceives] only form.
Abiding in impermanence, it is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). If the four great elements were impermanent, they would not be conventional designations (*vyavahāra*).

If conventional designations were not of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one would fall into the views of the worldly theorists (*lokāyatika*). All natures exist only as verbal designations; their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not perceived.

That which undergoes transformation and impermanence refers to the manifestation of a different nature of form (*rūpa*), such as gold being fashioned into ornaments, rather than the four great elements themselves.
When there is a transformation, it is not that the nature of gold is destroyed, but rather that the location of the ornamental object is destroyed;

likewise, it is the same for the transformations of other natures and so forth. When such various externalist views of permanence are burned by the fire of false conceptualization, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are not burned in their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If the destruction of each of their own respective characteristics were to occur, then the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced from the four great elements would have to be annihilated.
"Detachment from initial creation" (*ārambha-vivarjana*) and "impermanence" (*anityatā*), as well as "having created and then abandoning," are identical in meaning though different in name.
Because the sequential process of creating and abandoning at the beginning and end constitutes the sense of impermanence, it is said that one should be detached from initial creation and so forth.

"Initial" refers to the creation through the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); because one perceives their distinct characteristics, such as solidity, moisture, heat, and motion, each being separate.

Because they are not identical, one refutes [the notion of] difference by considering them as distinct directions; that is, one holds that the four great elements each have their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), yet the principle of their formation cannot be found through any differentiation.
Consequently, one abandons the notion of difference and instead calculates them as being of the same direction;

that is, one holds that while those [elements] lack differentiation, this [formation] likewise lacks both identity and difference. Therefore, even with the two skillful means (*upāya*) of identity and difference, one does not engage in further construction.
How much less could anything be established? There is nothing that does not take what was initially created as being correct and later rejects it;
since one's calculations are not constant, errors are formed through spontaneous operation without needing to be specifically refuted.

As for those who claim that impermanence consists in the destruction of spatial form, they mean that while the matter derived from the four great elements is truly indestructible, it is only its spatial configuration that is destroyed, and this difference in appearance is what constitutes impermanence.

In terms of its meaning, it is said that it is "ultimately indestructible. "Ultimate" (jing) means the extreme limit or the finality. This refers to analyzing derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) down to its most subtle limit;

even then, it cannot be destroyed. It is only by observing its destruction—that is, seeing its spatial dimensions such as length and shortness differently—that one speaks of its "destruction," for it is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) themselves that are destroyed. The phrase "the four great elements are not destroyed" refutes [this misconception], meaning that...
It is not that their substance is destroyed, but rather that the manifested characteristics of their form-locations are destroyed;
this means that when one perceives differences such as long and short, it is merely conventional enumeration and verbal expression. Therefore, it is said that they fall into the Samkhya system.

Furthermore, regarding the refutation of the claim that "form is impermanent," because its meaning is the opposite of the previous position, the argument is countered by stating: "In that case, it would be the form-locations that are impermanent," and so forth.
Each has its own partiality; regarding conventional discourse (*saṃvṛti*), some contradict it and others fall away from it.

To contradict it is to deviate from the mundane; to fall away from it is to stray from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Deviating from the mundane and straying from the ultimate are both not correct doctrines;

their error is one and the same. Furthermore, it is said that conventional discourse is not the true nature (*dharmatā*); this reiterates the previous fault by stating that because it is not real, there is only mere discourse, even though each [system] differs.
In calculating this, they differ; yet it is one in that the place where self-characteristics arise is not seen, as previously stated at length.
If even seeing the place of arising is not considered "non-destruction," how much less so can one speak of "destruction"?

Regarding the statement that transformation and impermanence mean the manifestation of a different nature of form (*rūpa*), this refers to the manifestation of the nature of impermanence due to the variation of derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*); it takes the manifest location as "destruction," not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The meaning of the analogy regarding destruction can be understood as being the same as before; the impermanence of shape and location is not separately refuted.
Such various [arguments] are collectively refuted below. Generally, all those views are expressed in terms of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);

they are not the discernment of true wisdom, but rather false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) superimposed upon those four great elements. Therefore, it is said that "the fire of false conceptualization burns the four great elements."

Furthermore, that which is called the "separate and non-separate" nature of self-characteristics cannot be destroyed; yet if it were destroyed, then the derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) would be annihilated, thereby falling into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Alternatively, if one perceives it as indestructible, one again gives rise to the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
Thus, the fire of false views burns the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), never coming to an end. (3)
"Mahāmati, the arising of my Dharma is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this? It is because external natures are not fixed;

I teach only the subtle mind of the three realms of existence, and not various characteristics that arise and perish due to the combination of the four great elements, nor the distinctions between the primary elements and derived matter.
One should understand that the two kinds of objects of false imagination—namely, the grasped and the grasper—are both false."

One who perceives that thoughts are free from the two views of external existence and non-existence, and realizes that they are the mere manifestation of one's own mind, understands that these conceptualizations arise through mental activity and do not arise without it;
such a person is free from the delusions of existence and non-existence regarding the nature of the mind.

All phenomena—mundane, supramundane, and the supreme of the supramundane—are neither eternal nor impermanent; yet, failing to realize that they are the manifestation of one's own mind, one falls into the two extremes.
All those of external paths who continue in evil views do not realize that these are their own deluded imaginings;

they claim that this world, the supramundane, and the supreme supramundane have no fundamental basis other than what arises from the discourse of deluded imagination—a truth which is not perceived by the ignorant and foolish.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
Free from the notions of initial creation, spatial form, difference, and the impermanence of matter, the Great Self-nature (mahāsvabhāva) remains as it is;
yet those outsiders, deluded by false imaginings regarding various natures, harbor the notion of impermanence and sink into manifold views.
Since for those outsiders there is neither arising nor ceasing, and the Great Nature is itself eternal, what is meant by their "notion of impermanence"?
"All is but the measure of mind; the two kinds of mental flow—the grasper and the grasped—are devoid of self or what belongs to a self.
With Brahmā as the root, the branches extend everywhere; thus I declare that all is but the measure of that mind."
The following section demonstrates the correct teaching’s differentiation from external views.

It means that if the self and dharmas arise from that which is neither permanent nor impermanent, then permanence and impermanence emerge from the same principle. This "one principle" refers to the essence (*tattva*);
"permanence" and "impermanence" refer to the functions of that essence. Because essence and function are mutually identical, permanence is itself impermanence, and impermanence is itself permanence.
"Permanence" refers to the fact that the external nature of these dharmas has never been determinate from the beginning;

therefore, it is said to be neither permanent nor impermanent to reveal the Middle Way. Since the principle of the Middle Way cannot be realized except through the wondrous mind, it is taught that the three realms of existence are but the subtle mind.
Regarding "the three realms," this refers to the measure of universal inclusion; regarding "the subtle mind," it refers to...

This Dharma, whose name is unfathomable, is precisely the mind itself; fundamentally, it has neither interior nor exterior, yet to speak of "external nature" is merely a provisional concession to delusion.
Furthermore, to speak of the "subtle mind" means that although the three realms of existence are vast, they are fundamentally rooted in this subtle mind;
within the sprouting of a single thought, there is no phenomenon that is not fully present. This is the great principle of the orthodox teaching, and it is precisely what this sutra expresses.
The reason why the mind is not described as having various characteristics of arising and ceasing is precisely to exclude external objects and directly manifest the rational nature;
therefore, those various marks of deluded thought are not mentioned. There are two reasons for this non-mention:
first, because the characteristics of intrinsic nature are indestructible, it is said that the four great elements combine to produce distinctions among the four great elements and their derivatives.
Because it is form, this implicitly indicates the meaning that the aforementioned self-nature is indestructible; therefore, no signs of arising or ceasing can be apprehended.
Second, because arising and ceasing are subsumed under the characteristics of delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it is said to be "delusive conceptualization.

The two kinds of things—subject and object—are such that the arising and ceasing of all phenomena do not transcend being subsumed under the two kinds of delusive conceptual things: names and appearances.
Now, in order to refute external objects, I do not speak of the reality of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

If one understands that these two types [of objects] are merely conceptual construction, then one will realize that apart from external existence or non-existence, there are no views of "being" or "non-being," but rather that all is but the manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*).
One who awakens in this way also knows that all conceptual constructions arise from the activity of thought; and from such thought-activity, further perceptions arise.
The grasping subject and the grasped object arise from the mind; thus, false conceptualization arises from the mind alone, for the nature of the mind has no inherent existence.

Therefore, one is also free from the false conceptualization of the internal mind. Yet, this does not mean that one ever abandons the performance of practice through false conceptualization; hence it is said:

"It is not that one does not perform practice, but rather that one is free from the false conceptualization within the nature of the mind. Thus, all things of both the mundane and supramundane realms—[are purified].
The Dharma returns to its original state as a single unity because it is identical to the Middle Way; therefore, it is said to be "neither eternal nor impermanent.
This refers to those who are capable of awakening. Those who do not awaken are said to fall into the two extremes and continue in evil views;

this is why these non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) constantly abide in deluded thought and fail to realize that their own thoughts are their own delusions. It is for this reason that ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) cannot leave behind the root [of affliction].
Yet there is no fundamental basis; this root pertains to both the mundane and the heterodox, as they are seen interchangeably.

Not knowing that the fundamental arises from this [consciousness], one merely follows words and conceptions to engage in various arbitrary reckonings; thus, it is only natural that one would claim that all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds arise from verbal discourse and false imagination.
As the verse says, "distant from initial creation," which praises the total transcendence [of such views].
"All views" and "all natures are indestructible," etc., are the verses summarizing the general refutation above.
This means that although they falsely imagine impermanence, the self-nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is not destroyed; thus it is said, "The great elements abide in their own nature.

One thereby knows that these non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) conceive the notion of impermanence regarding that which is fundamentally not impermanent, and thus sink into false views. Furthermore, it says: "Those various..."

Regarding the phrase "the non-Buddhists and others," this again covers the previous intention to demonstrate to those non-Buddhists that what they conceive—the reality of fundamental non-arising and non-ceasing—is such that its Great Nature remains eternally firm and unchanged. How can it be definitively claimed that they maintain the notion of impermanence?
Therefore, he restates their essential point, saying: "All is but the measure of mind," and so forth, which refers to the vision [of truth].
Whether these notions of the heterodox or the orthodox, or their presence or absence, all originate from the measure of the mind (*citta-mātra*) and possess no fixed reality.
It is because one wanders through the realms of consciousness with the two minds of arising and ceasing that there arise notions of impermanence.

If, however, one realizes that both the grasper and the grasped, as well as the faculties and their objects, are entirely devoid of self and what belongs to a self, then no such heterodox calculations can be found. All of this demonstrates the lack of fixed determination.
It is said that their sentiments are empty; they claim that Brahmā is the root of trees and so forth, asserting that Maheśvara first created sentient beings as the origin of all living things.
Thus, just as branches grow from the root of a tree, the manifestation of all delusive thoughts from the "Mind-Measure" (citta-mātra) is likewise so. (4) Chapter Four. Right.

Part Four of the First Chapter, "The Essence of All Buddha-Speech" (Continued).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) of all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

If one is skilled in the characteristics of the sequential continuity of the cessation-samādhi, I and the other bodhisattvas shall never recklessly abandon the gateway to the bliss of cessation-samādhi, nor fall into [the state of] one..."
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it;
I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain it for me.

The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the sixth stage, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); [this is not so for] Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage..."

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in every thought-moment, enters into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that is free from all characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). This meditative absorption is not that of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;

for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas fall into the perception of grasped objects and grasping subjects within the realm of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra-gati*), and their absorption is characterized by cessation.

Therefore, in the seventh stage, it is not a meditative absorption consisting of recollection, but rather one that attains the non-differentiated characteristic of all dharmas, as opposed to attaining various differentiated characteristics.

Because the nature of awakening is the correct realization (*samāpatti*) regarding the characteristics of the nature of all phenomena—both wholesome and unwholesome—therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no correct realization involving wholesome thoughts.
Mahāmati, in the eighth stage, the conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) of mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*) are extinguished for Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
From the first stage up to the seventh stage, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas contemplate the measure of the mind, thought, and consciousness within the triple world and remain detached from them.
Through the cultivation of false imaginings regarding "I" and "mine," they fall into the delusion of various external natures and characteristics;

these foolish people are directed toward the duality of their own minds—the grasper and the grasped—and remain ignorant and unaware of the beginningless faults of evil and the perfuming of false habitual tendencies.
The meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is one in name, yet how can its depths be discerned without inquiry?
The stages of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are one in their position, yet who could know the commonalities and distinctions of those who traverse them without explanation?
Therefore, Mahāmati asked: if the three vehicles enter the meditative attainment of cessation equally, why is there a sequence and difference in depth?
Passing through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there is a continuity characterized by both common and distinct aspects;

if one thoroughly understands these characteristics, then within the Great Cessation Samādhi (*mahā-nirodha-samāpatti*) one does not abandon [the path], and within the Lesser Right Attainment (*parītta-samyak-pratipatti*) one does not fall. This may be understood from the questions.

In the response, the characteristics of progress and regression at the intermediate stage follow many paths, generally comprising four meanings. First, by pairing the sixth and seventh stages to clarify their relative depth, the three vehicles (*triyāna*) are addressed in the sixth stage.
