They enter the meditative absorption of cessation together; however, because this stage is the most superficial, the concentration attained by the Bodhisattva does not yet differ from that of the two vehicles.

Regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage attain meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*) in every thought-moment," this means they enter and emerge from it without interval in each thought-moment, thereby abandoning all marks of intrinsic nature and self-nature.
As for "meditative equipoise," it refers to not grasping at any marks of subject or object; therefore, it is not the same as [the concentration of] the two vehicles.
One who rides upon the path of conditioned practice must extinguish all marks (*nimitta*) before attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, the seventh stage is called "non-recollection" (*amanasikāra*) meditative attainment; this means it is not the meditative attainment that dwells in recollection.

Furthermore, it is said that when one realizes the non-differentiated characteristic of all phenomena (*dharma*), one awakens to the fact that there is no difference between the nature and characteristics of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; it is not otherwise.
Because the followers of the Two Vehicles obtain only one or two aspects within that concentration, it is said that they do not "attain various characteristics by division.
This refers to the "samādhi of non-virtuous thought," meaning that even up to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), they do not abide in virtue, let alone in non-virtuous thought;
thus, it can be understood that this is the samādhi of undifferentiated characteristics. Based on this, [it is clear] regarding the seventh [stage].

Although it has already been stated that the [Bodhisattva] Grounds transcend the Two Vehicles and refer exclusively to Bodhisattvas, yet the Two Vehicles are again mentioned in relation to the subsequent grounds.

Now, seeking the meaning through reflection, this should be understood as follows: it is intended merely to distinguish the differing characteristics of the sixth and seventh grounds by way of their commonalities and differences regarding their presence or absence;
it does not mean that the latter stages do not also encompass the Two Vehicles. One may also consider that up to the sixth ground, they are all collectively termed "Bodhisattvas."

The point of distinction for the Bodhisattvas from the previous two vehicles is clarified by those with the eye of the teaching: they examine in detail the differences based on the seventh and eighth consciousnesses (*manas* and *ālayavijñāna*).

This is because the characteristics of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) within mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) have either been extinguished or not yet extinguished; thus, their transcendence and virtues differ.

Specifically, at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), the three vehicles extinguish the consciousness of deluded conceptualization, and thus possess only virtue. From the first stage up to the seventh, however, [the Bodhisattva]...
If one contemplates the stages while failing to extinguish and depart from them, yet is still able to practice, this remains within the interval between fault and virtue.
To practice by departing from the false imaginings of "self" and "what belongs to self" is virtue;

to fall into the various marks of external natures and be grasped by the dualistic mind of existence and non-existence as held by the ignorant is fault. That such faults arise is due to the influence of past ignorance and evil habits.
Because they are objects of perfuming, their superiority or inferiority can be known therein (1).
Mahāmati, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the eighth stage, as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, attain nirvāṇa because they are sustained by the awakening of samādhi;
therefore, due to the bliss of the gate of samādhi, they do not enter parinirvāṇa. If they were not so sustained, [they would reach] the stage of the Tathāgata.
Because they abandon all conditioned activities for the sake of sentient beings out of dissatisfaction, the lineage of the Buddhas would be severed.
Therefore, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, demonstrate the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata;

yet, being led by the attachment to the bliss obtained through the samādhi-gates of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, I have divided the seven stages [of the Bodhisattva] to cultivate the mind well.
By skillfully cultivating the characteristics of the mind, mental consciousness, and the conceptualization of "self" and "mine," as well as the grasping of persons and phenomena,

selflessness, arising and ceasing, and specific and general characteristics; and by means of the four kinds of unhindered analytical power, the gates of samādhi, and the sequential stages of the grounds, one enters the dharmas of the path in continuous succession,
so that the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not fail to perceive specific and general characteristics, nor fall into the evil scriptures of external paths at the seventh ground.

Therefore, Mahāmati, the sequential order of the stages (*bhūmi*) is established; yet in reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing, for it is nothing other than the manifestation of one's own mind.
This so-called sequential continuity of the stages and the various activities of the triple world are not perceived by the ignorant.
What is not perceived by the ignorant is that which I and the Buddhas teach as the sequential continuity of the stages and the various activities of the triple world.
The three vidyās, the eight stages, and the three vehicles all share the same nirvāṇa; yet, because there is a distinction between "taking it up" and "not taking it up," one is called a bodhisattva.
This refers to being sustained by the awakening of samādhi—specifically, being sustained by the power of the awakening of the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi).

Thus, although they enter the blissful gate of samādhi, they do not take up nirvāṇa. Conversely, those who do not sustain themselves [with such awakening] are distinguished precisely by that lack of sustenance.
Regarding the virtues of those who uphold [the Dharma]: if one is not satisfied with the stage of the Tathāgata, one's own practice will be deficient;
if one abandons all activities for the sake of sentient beings, one fails in transforming others. Since both self and others would thus be lost, the lineage of the Buddhas should be severed.
Therefore, the Buddhas manifest inconceivable merits in order to encourage and inspire [practitioners]. The followers of the Two Vehicles are the opposite of this.
This is why there is loss. I have divided the seven stages (*bhūmi*) below to summarize and indicate the underlying principle:

namely, that by categorizing the preceding and subsequent stages into distinct classes, one perceives the differences between the wholesome and unwholesome, the extinguished and non-extinguished, and so forth.

My intention is to cause one to skillfully cultivate the mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), whereby one penetrates the nature of consciousness as fundamentally empty and eliminates deluded imaginings. Skillful cultivation—
When one realizes that there is no self or what belongs to a self, and thus remains unattached to persons or phenomena, one then embraces the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

Not falling into the conceptual marks of arising and ceasing, or of specific and general characteristics, one becomes skilled in the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the power of certainty;

through the gate of samādhi, concentration and wisdom become equal, free from the fault of partiality or excess. Thereby, proceeding through the stages in succession, one enters the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) and advances further.

This refers to the provisions for the subsequent stage. "Not permitting bodhisattvas [to fall]" means not permitting those who are unwholesome to fall into the seventh stage, being encompassed by the two extremes and deviant paths of fools;
this is why the characteristics and sequence of this stage are established.
Regarding the statement that there are both wholesome and unwholesome aspects in cultivation: it is because detachment from signs is wholesome, while attachment to them is unwholesome.
For one who practices well, even the mind, mental factors, consciousness, the self, and what belongs to the self are sufficient as gateways for entering the Path;
yet for one who practices poorly, even dharmas such as meditative concentration and wisdom will not be free from partiality and error.

Thus we know that goodness and unwholesomeness reside in the person and not in the dharma. Therefore it is said: "In reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing, except for [the conceptualization of] the self."

Regarding "mental direct perception" (*cittapratyakṣa*) and so forth: this refers to the previously analyzed stages of sequential continuity and the various modes of activity within the three realms, such as the four *dhyānas* and eight *samāpattis*.

Although these progress from prior to subsequent states, they involve arising and ceasing; yet, apart from the establishment of one's own mental measure (*svacittamātra*), they are fundamentally non-existent in reality.
Nevertheless, the deluded do not perceive this and claim that these were established by the Buddha. How could this be so?

This is indeed the principle! Therefore, what I do not grant here is based on this reasoning: in all that the Buddha has taught, he relies entirely upon the mental capacity and conceptual distinctions of sentient beings;
as for the Buddha-dharma itself, what [independent] existence could there be in it? (2)
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are intoxicated by the intoxication of the bliss of the cessation-samādhi in the eighth stage of the Bodhisattva;

they are obstructed by the habitual tendencies of the self-characteristics and common characteristics of their own mind-manifestations, and having fallen into the views that grasp at the non-existence of persons and phenomena, they conceive of a false nirvāṇa through deluded discrimination.
They do not possess the awakening of wisdom that is true cessation. However, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattvas see [it as it truly is].
Through the joy of the gate of the samādhi of cessation, the fulfillment of original vows, compassion, great pity, and clear knowledge, one understands the ten inexhaustible phrases.

Because the conceptualization of nirvāṇa does not arise, and because that conceptualization of "having already entered nirvāṇa" no longer occurs, one is free from the conceptualization of grasping and the grasped.

One awakens to the fact that all phenomena are merely the manifestation of one's own mind; thus, conceptualization does not arise, and one does not fall into the domain of the mind, intellect, or consciousness.

The false imagination that clings to the characteristics of an external nature and self-nature apart from consciousness is not the cause of the Buddha-dharma; it does not arise, but rather arises in accordance with wisdom.
One attains the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, just as a person in a dream uses skillful means to cross water: before having crossed, they wake up;

having awakened, they reflect upon whether [the crossing] was real or unreal—it is neither real nor unreal. All else consists of the seeds of conceptualization arising from beginningless seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
Various habitual tendencies manifest as diverse forms and locations within the mind, thought, and consciousness, appearing like dreams and falling into the notions of existence and non-existence.

Fourth, regarding the "manifestation of the eight stages," there are both common and distinct aspects; according to the principles clarified by the Tiantai school, these should be divided into two types.
The first is that which is practiced in common with the Three Vehicles, wherein Bodhisattvas share in the realizations of the Two Vehicles yet do not escape certain faults—these are four.
First, being intoxicated by the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they are unable to transform others or benefit sentient beings.

Second, their own minds manifest as unwholesome, being obstructed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the self-characteristics and common characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.

Third, having fallen into [the view of] the non-self of persons and phenomena, they give rise to the view of grasping at phenomena and the view of attachment to the words of the True Teaching. Fourth, because they give rise to a notion of attachment toward *nirvāṇa*.
The statement that "non-ultimate quiescence and awakening are both as described in the text" (and so forth) refers to what is called "being dull and identical to the two vehicles.
This merely clarifies that within the shared stage there is progress and regression (and so forth).

Second, when the name "patience" (*kṣānti*) is established separately for the Bodhisattva, it is said that the Bodhisattva perceives the bliss of the gates of samādhi and so on, one by one reversing the aforementioned faults to manifest the grounds of the eight stages.
The meaning of the passage on the virtues of the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu can be understood through a sequential analysis of the text.

Since all delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) no longer arise, there is no further cause for their production; therefore, it is said that they are not caused by the Buddha-dharma. "Not arising" means that [delusion] does not arise unless it follows after wisdom (*jñāna*).
That is to say, when one takes the accomplishment of the Buddha-dharma as the cause, then [wisdom] arises; otherwise, it does not arise. Thus, it arises in accordance with wisdom.
That which is not [a self] likewise does not arise; thus it has never arisen, yet it has never failed to arise. It follows only the Way.
From the arising of birth to the non-arising of birth, one ultimately attains the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening—all of this is by means of this principle.

It is like a person in a dream; the lower analogy illustrates the aforementioned phenomena of self and other. The general meaning is that during the time of dreaming, it is not that awakening is absent.

Since there is already nothing [to be attained], it is neither real nor unreal; this is used as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), beginning from the vision of the Dharma and ending with the liberation of sentient beings.
This is because they are established through the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi).

Just as during a dream one performs actions, so too upon attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) revealed. It is like waking up and realizing there was nothing to be gained, yet saying that one has not yet crossed over.
The awakened one has not yet reached the other shore because their stage is not ultimate; "correct" or "erroneous" refers to examining its reality or unreality;
"neither correct nor erroneous" expresses the principle to its limit. Therefore, speaking from the perspective of self-awakening, who can say it is real?
Speaking from the perspective of dream-events, who can say it is unreal? To speak of anything else is to fall back into beginningless views.

To say that hearing, cognition, and consciousness arise from conceptualization (saṃjñā) is so; yet within the truly pure realm, there is neither Buddha nor birth—how, then, could there be the cultivation of causes to save sentient beings?
It is only because one has not yet returned to true purity and still possesses the beginningless awakening-consciousness as a basis for conceptualization that one arrives at the state of dreaming.
Because of these various habitual tendencies (vāsanā), there come to be various sentient beings.

When forms abide within their respective domains, one falls into the notions of existence and non-existence; thus, the mind, intellect, and consciousness manifest in accordance with dream-like phenomena.
If, through initial awakening, the consciousness caused by these notions is extinguished, then all dharmas become non-existent, such that upon awakening, none of them can be apprehended. (3)

Mahāmati, in this way, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva on the eighth bodhisattva stage perceives that the arising of false discrimination has been transcended from the first stage up to the seventh stage,
and having seen all dharmas as being like illusions and so forth, and having mastered the skillful means of the mind’s activity regarding grasping and what is grasped,
they cause those who have not yet attained the skillful means of the Buddha-dharma to attain it. Mahāmati, this is [the attainment].

The Bodhisattva’s skillful means for attaining nirvana are unimpaired; by departing from mind, thought, and consciousness, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

O Mahāmati, regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no sequential continuity; it is taught that all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are non-existent and that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is quiescent.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The Mind-Measure (*cittamātra*) is non-existent; this is the stage of abiding (*vihāra*) and the stage of Buddhahood. The Buddhas of the three times—past, future, and present—have taught that the seventh stage is the "Stage of Non-existence" (*nirābhāsa-bhūmi*), while the eighth and second stages are called "Abiding.
The stage of Buddhahood is called "Supreme Self-Aware Wisdom" (*pratyātma-jñāna*) and "Purity. This is my own stage, the most supreme place of mastery, pure and wonderfully adorned.
It shines like a blazing fire, its radiance pervading everywhere; its fierce flames do not damage the eyes. The wheel of transformation transforms the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
It manifests within the three realms of existence, and at times it manifests light therein to expound the vehicles (*yāna*), all of which are the stages of the Tathāgata.
The tenth stage is the first; the first is the eighth stage; the ninth is the seventh; and the seventh is likewise the eighth.
The second becomes the third, the fourth becomes the fifth, and the third becomes the sixth; what sequence could there be for that which is non-existent?

This section below combines with the preceding analogy, meaning that when this Bodhisattva perceives the arising of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it is precisely the analogy of the great river of birth and death within a dream.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, as he progresses to the seventh stage, he perceives all phenomena (*dharma*) as they truly are.
The skillful means of illusion and so forth is precisely the meaning of the skillful means of deliverance (*tāraṇopāya*).

Once one has brought to an end the mental activities of the grasped and the grasper through deliverance, this is the meaning of personally delivering oneself from all delusions regarding the faculties, objects, and so forth.

To employ the skillful means of the Buddha-dharma so that those who have not yet attained may attain it is to deliver others by means of one's own deliverance; it is just like causing those who have not yet crossed over to cross over.
This is the meaning: this is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya*) for nirvāṇa that is not destroyed;
it means that although the bodhisattva has attained nirvāṇa, they do not destroy the work of delivering sentient beings through skillful means.

To be free from mind, thought, and consciousness and to attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is to reach the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), where one attains the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*), such that upon awakening, there is no longer anything to be attained.
This is an analogy; furthermore, because it concludes by indicating the name of "patience" (kṣānti), it is said that one "attains the patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

This common and specific characteristic is not something recognized in the essential tenets of any single school or teaching alone. It is also seen that this sutra encompasses both the universal vehicle (pāramitā-yāna) and the specific vehicle; this is the third point.

Following the section on the "ultimate truth" (paramārtha), the text concludes by indicating the aforementioned characteristics of the stages (bhūmi), their sequential continuity, and so forth. Its textual passage is as follows:
In brief, one should properly say this: within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), where there is no succession, one speaks of succession;
within that which lacks continuity, one speaks of continuity; and within the absence of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one speaks of the quiescence of conceptualization.
This is because, within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), not even a single dharma can be apprehended, let alone succession or continuity. Nevertheless, [all these are taught].
Relying on the gateways of skillful means according to the mental capacities of sentient beings, one provisionally explains within that which is fundamentally non-existent: "This is your mind-only.
If this mind-only is exhausted, then the ultimate truth of emptiness is utterly devoid of anything whatsoever, like the great void where no bird tracks remain.
That which is called the teaching of "non-existence" and the "extinction of deluded conceptualization" is itself a provisional name within the absence of names and characteristics.

It is said that you are able to accord with this principle; "speaking of original non-speaking" means that the first eight lines of the verse first provide a general overview and then a detailed analysis.
The "detailed analysis" refers to the fact that while the seventh stage still retains the measure of mind (*cittamātra*), the eighth stage has nothing at all.

Thus, the boundaries are clarified by contrasting the seventh and eighth stages. Although the eighth stage is designated as "abiding exclusively," even though it has nothing at all, there is still a state of fixed abiding.
Only the name "Buddha-ground" (buddhabhūmi) is designated as supreme; thus, cause and effect are clearly distinguished.
While the explanations of the path of teaching differ, all subsequent passages describe the realization-path (sākṣātkriyā-mārga) of the Tathāgata-ground, which lacks a fixed sequential order.

The self-realized wisdom (*svasaṃvedana-jñāna*) and the purity [of the ground] are explained in separate verses regarding the excellence of the Buddha-ground’s virtues, such as the six meanings of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*); here, five of these are seen.
This refers to the wisdom of self-awakening and the renown of the Pure Ones; "the most supreme state" refers to auspiciousness.
The meanings of the remaining three names are clearly evident. Since these five qualities are fully possessed, how could they not be noble? (And so forth.
"Unfailing Eye" means that although the radiance of the Tathāgata is intensely blazing, it looks down upon all things with equal illumination.
A candle is not like the sun; its light is so overpowering that it blinds the human eye.

"The wheel transforms the three realms of existence" (*tridhātu*) is also called "wandering through," meaning that the Tathāgata wanders through the three realms to transform the worlds of the past and present, and to expound the various vehicles for the sake of the future.
Therefore, it is said that "in all those [realms], it is the stage of the Tathāgata. This, in turn, reiterates what was stated above regarding "at... [the verse].
Because the ultimate truth (paramārtha) has no sequential continuity, it is said that the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are themselves the first stage and so forth;
thus, by manifesting its perfect fusion through non-sequentially, one speaks of the extinction of true suchness (tathatā). What difference could there be in rank or position?
While the path of teaching (śāsana-mārga) certainly possesses sequence, [the ultimate reality does not]. (4) The above is Chapter Five.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, are the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha permanent or impermanent?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is neither permanent nor impermanent.
Why? Because both positions entail faults. If he were permanent, there would be the fault of being a creator; for what is permanent is said to be a creator by all the non-Buddhists."

That which is unconditioned is therefore neither eternal nor non-eternal; for there would be the fault of [the Tathāgata] being conditioned if he were eternal. If the Tathāgata were impermanent, there would be the fault of his being produced by causes.
The characteristics of the aggregates are devoid of intrinsic nature; if the aggregates were destroyed, the Tathāgata would be annihilated, yet the Tathāgata is not annihilated.
Mahāmati, all that is produced is impermanent, such as jars, garments, and so forth—all of them are thus.
If [the Tathāgata] were impermanent, all the requisites for omniscience and skillful means would be purposeless because they are produced;
furthermore, everything that is produced would be indistinguishable from the Tathāgata, as their causal nature would be identical.
Therefore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata is not permanent like space; if he were permanent like space, he would be self-...
Mahāmati, the equipment for the noble wisdom of awakening is devoid of objective referents;

it is like space, which is neither eternal nor non-eternal, because it is free from the faults of eternity and non-eternity, of identity and difference, and of both or neither. Therefore, it cannot be described. For this reason, the Tathāgata is not eternal.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were an unarisen eternal entity, he would be like the horns of a rabbit or a horse, since they do not exist.

Because [the Tathāgata] would be subject to birth and permanence, skillful means would be rendered meaningless; since there is the fault of [implying] both non-arising and permanence, the Tathāgata is not permanent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is another reason for knowing that the Tathāgata is permanent. Why is this? It is because the wisdom attained without interruption is permanent;
therefore, the Tathāgata is permanent. Mahāmati, whether the Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, phenomena remain fixed in their nature.
I have heard that the Pratyekabuddhas and all the Tathāgatas abide in the unconditioned, yet they do not dwell in empty space, nor is this realized by ordinary fools.
Although you have repeatedly spoken of the permanent and the impermanent, you alone have not yet clarified the fruit of the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata.
From the perspective of principle, that which is "constant" is in fact "impermanent. How could what has been explained previously fall outside of this?
If one does not clarify this separately, those who are deluded will remain ignorant; therefore, for the sake of those who have not yet understood, I shall first provide an answer within the text.

It is said that the fruit of realization is neither constant nor impermanent, because the principle realized transcends the hundred negations and is perfectly free from all faults, differing from those external [views].
Considering this, it is said that both [positions] are faulty when taken as dualistic extremes. Regarding the fault of having a permanent creator:
since even the Tathāgata is devoid of the mark of a self (*ātman*), how could he be subject to the fault of being a permanent creator or sovereign?
Furthermore, as for "permanence," all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) falsely conceive of a creator as permanent; such a state implies there is something produced, yet the Tathāgata—
Because it is said that the agent performs no action, [the Tathāgata] is both eternal and non-eternal; for an eternity characterized by action would entail error.
If the Tathāgata were impermanent, he would incur the error of being an impermanent agent. To speak truly, if he were impermanent, he would be identical to an agent.

If he were identical to an agent, he would possess the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) of the five aggregates (*skandha*); yet since those characteristics lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [he is not the aggregates].
If [the Tathāgata] were subject to destruction, he would be severed; yet the permanence of the Tathāgata should not be severed.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "all conditioned things are impermanent, like a jar or a garment," this means that if everything were to revert to impermanence—just like worldly objects such as jars and garments—it would imply that the merit of the Tathāgata’s cultivation of virtue is fruitless. Therefore, it is said: "The equipment of all-knowledge and skillful means."

All [phenomena] would then lack substantial reality; if they were identical to the "produced," then all produced things would be Buddhas, because there would be no distinct causal nature [to differentiate them].

Therefore, it is concluded [with the words] "and so forth. Although the nature-virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*) are perfectly complete and free [from extremes], and are said to be "neither of the two" (*ubhayābhāva*), the realization of the fruit (*phala-sākṣātkriyā*) may also be considered "eternal" (*nitya*).
However, since the meaning of "eternal" has many paths, one further negates the two kinds of non-meaning (*anartha*), namely:
It is said: "To claim that [the Tathāgata] is eternal like space and so forth is not correct. The eternity of space refers to its insentient, void, and non-existent nature;

it is not the same as the manifestation of the manifold virtues through the self-realized noble wisdom (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna*) of the Tathāgata. Even if one speaks in terms of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), emptiness transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and cannot be explained in a partial manner.
If it were the same as an unarisen eternity, then it would be like the horns of a rabbit or a horse, which are fundamentally non-existent."
If the meanings of "arising" and "lack of skillful means" were the same as the meaning of "permanent," then both [positions] would be faulty.
That being so, by what meaning is the fruit said to be the Tathāgata’s permanence? It is known through three meanings; therefore it is said: "The wisdom obtained without interval is permanent," etc.
This refers to the wisdom obtained by the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) at the final moment of the Vajra-like Samādhi; it is by this that [permanence] is revealed.
First, virtue is eternally constant because it is singular; second, because all phenomena are definitively established.
This means that all phenomena are definitively established within the principle of eternal quiescence; whether a Buddha appears or not, their intrinsic nature remains as it is.
It is only the Tathāgata who can manifest this, which is why it is called "constant. Third, because there is no interval or abiding, this refers to the lineage of the Tathāgata.
When the four dharmas are uninterrupted, one attains eternal abiding; this is not merely abiding in empty space.

Furthermore, the mention of the two vehicles indicates that each possesses its own lineage (*gotra*), thereby revealing the fruit through the cause. These three may also be meaningfully correlated with the Three Virtues (and so forth).

Mahāmati, the wisdom attained by the Tathāgata is perfumed by *prajñā*, not by mind, thought, or consciousness, nor is it perfumed by those aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Mahāmati, all that exists within the three realms of existence arises from unreal conceptualization;
the Tathāgata does not arise from unreal, false conceptualization. Mahāmati, it is because of two dharmas that there is permanence and impermanence, not otherwise.
Non-duality and the absence of duality are the tranquility of all phenomena, because there is no characteristic of dualistic arising.
Therefore, O Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is neither eternal nor non-eternal. As long as verbal discrimination arises, there is the fault of [clinging to] eternity or non-eternity;
for one whose discriminative awakening has ceased, the views of eternity and non-eternity held by the foolish are abandoned, and there is no lack of tranquility.

The wise are forever free from the habitual perfuming of permanence, impermanence, and neither-permanence-nor-impermanence. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"For those who lack the equipment for realization, there arises the fault of permanence and impermanence; if one possesses non-conceptual awakening, one is forever free from permanence and impermanence."
According to the thesis established here, there are various manifold meanings; yet when observing the virtues of one’s own mind, verbal expression is unattainable.
Since the impermanent is used to reveal the permanent, and dualistic phenomena are used to reveal non-duality, three further meanings are presented to clarify this:

namely, that what are called "the permanent" and "the double negation" (neither-nor) are all names for the ultimate fruit-virtue. While their specific meanings may be partial, their underlying principle is perfectly complete and one.
It is also said that the wisdom attained by the Tathāgata is that which has been permeated (*vāsita*) by *prajñā*;

this means that the wisdom of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) is entirely permeated and brought forth by the *prajñā* of inherent nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*). This is distinct from the mind-consciousness of the nine realms, which is permeated by the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth.
Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata does not arise from unreal, false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*), but arises solely from true merit.
Deheng [argues] that when one infers the effect from the cause, there is no deviation in principle; this uses the impermanent to reveal the permanent. Furthermore, he says:

"Because of two dharmas, there is permanence and impermanence; it is not that they are not non-dual. This means that if one takes birth-and-death and nirvana as two dharmas, then there is permanence and impermanence;
yet this is not what is meant by "non-duality," for the Tathāgata has already realized it.
All phenomena have a single characteristic, which is so-called "characteristiclessness. Because this is non-dual and quiescent, there are no two kinds of arising characteristics;
this is precisely what is neither eternal nor impermanent. While duality is manifested through non-duality, when speech reaches this point, it may be said to have exhausted its logical limits.
Yet, those who cling to words fall into conceptualization and discrimination, whereby both duality and non-duality arise.
Since even maintaining a state of non-forgetfulness while awaiting a response is still not tranquil, he further dismisses it by saying:

"Even up to the point where conceptualization arises through verbal expression regarding the existence or non-existence of phenomena, there is the fault of being either eternal or impermanent; therefore, words themselves must also entail the fault of being neither eternal nor impermanent.
Only when speech is cut off and discursive thought is extinguished, such that there is no longer any conceptual differentiation, does one leave behind all the views and faults of the foolish."
Setting aside the views of various schools, the text is abbreviated here; speaking in terms of mutual perspectives, this is the ultimate quiescent wisdom.
For one who has merely abandoned all views, even permanence and impermanence are not a failure of wondrous function—how much more so the "neither permanent nor impermanent"?

Alternatively, the original text contains many instances of the character "not" (不), which significantly deviates from the intent of the passage. The verse states that "the various requisites are without meaning," which means:
Since all that is not manifested through the cultivated virtue of the Tathāgata—whether it be permanence or impermanence—is fraught with faults, this constitutes the Sage superseding the ordinary.
If one is free from discriminative awakening and eternally transcends both permanence and impermanence, then this constitutes the sublation of emotional conceptualization by means of principle.
As for the tenets established therein, they are like the heterodox views of externalists regarding false permanence and the seven kinds of impermanence.

All these are what is called the meaning of manifold diversity. As for observing the mind with equanimity and realizing that it is the measure of one's own mind—when the measure of the mind is found to be non-existent, then birth-and-death and nirvana are fundamentally equal;
therefore, all verbal expressions are ultimately unattainable. (2) The above is the sixth chapter.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that the World-Honored One will further explain for us the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas).

Since there is no self therein, who is it that arises and who is it that ceases? How is it that foolish worldlings rely upon arising and ceasing, fail to realize the exhaustion of suffering, and do not recognize nirvana? The Buddha said: "Excellent! Listen attentively, Mahāmati, and I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied, "So be it. The Buddha spoke thus: "Mahāmati, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases arise from the discrimination of false conceptualization. They are like a dream or a magical illusion; they have no self-nature. Because of the habit-energy of beginningless ignorance, sentient beings perceive forms and characteristics, yet these are merely manifestations of the mind and have no external reality. It is like a person with cataracts seeing hairs or a net of flies; though they appear, they are empty and non-existent. So too, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases arise from the mind's own projections. There is no creator, no agent, and no one who undergoes birth or death. It is only because of deluded attachment that fools grasp at arising and ceasing, failing to understand the nature of suffering and remaining ignorant of nirvana."

He addressed the Buddha, saying, "So be it; we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "The Tathāgata-garbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, capable of universally producing all realms of existence. It is like an actor who manifests various roles;

though it is devoid of 'I' and 'mine,' because beings do not realize this, it arises through the conjunction of three conditions and skillful means. Outsiders, failing to realize this, falsely imagine it to be a creator."
Perfumed by beginningless false and evil habits, it is called the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).

It gives rise to the ground where ignorance dwells and coexists with the seven consciousnesses, like the body of waves upon the ocean, constantly arising without interruption. It is free from the fault of impermanence and free from the doctrine of self;
its intrinsic nature is stainless and ultimately pure.

The preceding text has already addressed the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas); yet Mahāmati again raises a doubt, his intention being this:
regarding the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, there is both delusion and liberation. In liberation, since there is no self, who is it that undergoes arising and ceasing?
In delusion, the foolish worldlings rely upon arising and ceasing; they do not realize the exhaustion of suffering and do not recognize nirvāṇa.
By what means can ordinary beings be born from birth-and-death? Thus he requests [the teaching] at length. In the Buddha’s response, there is first a general statement and then a specific one.

The general text contains both the principle and the analogy; it does not speak of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense-bases (*āyatana*), but directly declares the Tathāgata-garbha to be the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
For the Tathāgata-garbha is the root, while the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are the branches. By means of the branches...
It is not because the original state of delusion and enlightenment are mutually entangled that one ultimately cannot attain liberation;
rather, it is because one focuses on the fundamental and not on the derivative that delusion and enlightenment share a single principle.

Thus, beyond both delusion and enlightenment, there is that which has never been deluded or enlightened—the Tathāgatagarbha—which, following conditions, acts as the cause for both good and evil, universally manifesting itself.

Because they create all destinies and births, there is the distinction between delusion and awakening regarding the ten realms. Delusion constitutes birth and cessation; awakening constitutes non-self.

This is why affliction and wisdom are mutually inverted; though they alternate between existence and non-existence, their underlying principle does not contradict one another—this is the essential purport of the response to the question.
The phrase "like a performer" and so forth is an analogy that illustrates the preceding point. It serves as a metaphor for what follows.
Conditioned dharmas are like an actor manifesting various realms of existence, yet they are fundamentally devoid of self and what belongs to a self;
thus, the principle of arising and ceasing without self is contained therein, just as an actor can transform into various forms while having no self.
Next, there are two further distinctions: first, it is stated that the Tathāgatagarbha possesses both awakening and non-awakening, [the latter] being due to non-awakening.

Therefore, because there is arising and ceasing, it is called "non-awakening. The phrase "due to that" and so forth means that, through non-awakening to the nature of that storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is free from the three conditions, one falsely conceives of it as a self or as an agent. From this, there is arising and ceasing;

all of this proceeds from the perfuming of beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, whereby it transforms and is named the "consciousness-store" (*vijñānagarbha*), giving rise to ignorance (*avidyā*).

The term "abiding ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to its initial arising. When it functions together with the seven consciousnesses, including the manas, one can know that the remaining four abiding grounds of affliction arise again;
hence it is said, "like waves upon the ocean, the body constantly arises without interruption.

This means that from the root, which is the eighth consciousness, the branches extend down to the sixth consciousness; the "body" here refers to the bodies within the six realms of existence. Thus, starting from the branches...

To speak of it, there is nothing but the view of impermanence and self; however, if one returns to the principle of the *pitaka* through hearing the teachings and realizes that the fundamental nature is truly eternal, thereby departing from discourses on a self, then by merely removing its superficial branches, the principle naturally reverts to its source. Thus it is said:
"The self-nature is stainless and ultimately pure. This refers to the arising and ceasing of the eight consciousnesses. (1)
The remaining consciousnesses have arising and ceasing; the manas and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), moment by moment, possess seven causes.
They consist of unreal false imaginings that grasp at various objects and their diverse forms and locations, calculating and clinging to names and characteristics.

Failing to realize that these appearances of form are manifestations of one's own mind, they do not perceive suffering and pleasure, nor do they attain liberation from the entanglements of names and characteristics. Greed arises repeatedly, whether through causes or [conditions].
When those various feelings and faculties are clung to, they cease in succession and other delusions of one's own mind do not arise;

being unaware of pleasure or pain, one enters the attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) and the fourth dhyāna. The practitioner, having attained a true understanding of the reality (*satya*), conceives the notion of liberation.

Yet, because they have not departed from nor turned away from it, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). The seven consciousnesses continue to flow and do not cease; this is why [it is so named].

Because those consciousnesses arise by taking various objects as conditions, they are not the sphere of practice for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; yet, when one realizes selflessness and understands that the aggregates, elements,
and sense-bases arise through the grasping of both particular and universal characteristics, and perceives the Tathāgatagarbha, the five dharmas, the three natures,
and the selflessness of persons and phenomena are extinguished.
Next, regarding the statement that the various consciousnesses undergo arising and ceasing:

this refers to the fact that, apart from the [ālaya-]vijñāna, the manas and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) and so forth arise in every moment as a group of seven, necessarily occurring simultaneously. "Based on unreal conceptualization" refers to the six consciousnesses;

because the six consciousnesses grasp objects, there are various forms and locations, namely the six sense-fields (ṣaḍviṣaya). Once the six sense-fields have taken form, they manifest various names and characteristics.
If one does not realize that these forms and appearances are manifestations of one's own mind as the eight consciousnesses, then by means of the derivative one is deluded regarding the fundamental;

this "non-awakening" to suffering and pleasure refers precisely to the self-characteristic of the seventh consciousness. To say one does not awaken to suffering and pleasure is different from the sixth consciousness;
to say one does not reach liberation is different from the eighth consciousness. It is also said that [the seventh] does not experience suffering and pleasure because it lacks both cause and object.

The causes of *nirvāṇa* and so forth are precisely its meaning. However, when names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) arise together with the characteristic of craving (*rāga-lakṣaṇa*), they become the cause for the arousal of the six consciousnesses;
both that cause and its objective support (*ālambana*) are what is called the "characteristic of arising" (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the "characteristic of cessation" (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), it is said: those various faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*) cease, and perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), etc., do not arise in succession, leaving only the self-... [remainder].
When the subtle, deluded consciousness of the mind enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception— namely, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and the fourth dhyāna,
which possess only a single mental factor— and yet it is said that one does not know pleasure or pain, this is merely described as such by way of the "cessation of perception.
For practitioners who truly understand the noble truth of liberation, this refers to the śrāvakas' cultivation of liberation within this attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
"Perception is not ultimate cessation" refers to the general judgment and concluding answer that [the consciousnesses] are neither separated from nor do they cease to transform.

This is a general determination that among the aforementioned various consciousnesses, there are differences regarding whether they are separated from or not separated from, and whether they transform or do not transform; hence it says "not separated from and not transforming.

This means the *tathāgatagarbha*-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is not separated from the mental faculty (*manas*) and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), yet has never begun to transform, because it is endowed with...

This is because of the two meanings of "changing according to conditions while remaining unchanging. As for "transforming without being separated," this refers to the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness);

that is, the eighth consciousness, the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which contains all seeds. This is because it transforms without being separated from the storehouse consciousness, serving as the basis for the various consciousnesses.
To clarify that the seven consciousnesses both separate and transform, it says: "The seven consciousnesses flow and circulate without ceasing, yet they also separate."

Although the ālayavijñāna has never been separated from the seven vijñānas, the seven vijñānas themselves are separate; this is like the case where the emotional states are separated while the substance is not.
Furthermore, they are said to "transform" because the seventh vijñāna acts as the cause for the sixth vijñāna, and because that [sixth] clings to objects and gives rise to various conditions.
Thus, it is said that they flow and circulate without ceasing. As for the two vehicles, they merely know how to act in this regard.
"Conceptualizing liberation while not knowing the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*)—because the eight consciousnesses are truly indestructible—this is not their domain;
they do not realize [the truth of] non-self and so forth. This directly answers and concludes the question posed:

"If one does not realize non-self herein, and through the grasping of self-characteristics and common characteristics gives rise to the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, then this is still subject to arising and ceasing; it is not the exhaustion of arising and ceasing."

If one perceives the Tathāgatagarbha, then the five dharmas and the self-nature will all be devoid of the mark of self; how could the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases not be extinguished through their mutual [interpenetration]?
Thus we know that if one clarifies its beginning and end, they will naturally be eliminated. Therefore, the true reality of the beginning and end is manifested;
by clarifying this, the general and specific aspects are mutually connected, and the beginning and end reflect one another—this is the text of the Tathāgata’s response.
The essential meaning being such as this, how could one not investigate its beginning and end?

(2) The stages of the ground proceed in succession and advance further, such that the views of other outsiders cannot shake them; this is called abiding in the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
One attains the joy of the gateways to the thirteen samādhis, is sustained by the awakening of samādhi, and contemplates the inconceivable.

The Buddha-dharma consists of the gate of samādhi wherein one voluntarily does not accept the bliss of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), but turns toward the noble path of self-realization, which is not shared with any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or those who practice the paths of the various non-Buddhists;

it attains the path of the ten noble spiritual lineages (*āryagotra*) and the body of mind-born wisdom (*manomayakāya*) that is free from the functioning of samādhi. Therefore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who desires—
"O Mahāmati, those who seek supreme advancement should purify the Tathāgatagarbha and that which is named the Ālayavijñāna.

O Mahāmati, if there were no such thing as the Ālayavijñāna named Tathāgatagarbha, then there would be no arising and ceasing. Yet, O Mahāmati, all ordinary beings and sages alike possess arising and ceasing;

however, practitioners who have realized the noble path of self-awareness abide in the bliss of the present life and do not abandon their skillful means. O Mahāmati, this is the Tathāgatagarbha-Ālayavijñāna."
All that is perceived through the mental conceptions of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, though pure by nature, appears as impure because it is obscured by adventitious objects;
however, for the Tathāgatas of Great Wisdom, the Tathāgatas' manifest realm is like looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of one's hand.
Mahāmati, I shall establish this meaning through my supernormal power so that it may be excelled.
Queen Śrīmālā and the bodhisattvas endowed with sharp wisdom proclaimed and expounded upon the Tathāgatagarbha and the name Ālayavijñāna,
which co-arises with the seven consciousnesses; because śrāvakas cling to views and fail to realize the selflessness of both persons and phenomena,
Queen Śrīmālā, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, declared that the realm of the Tathāgata is not the realm of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists.
The Tathāgatagarbha and Ālayavijñāna are the sphere of wisdom accessible only to the Buddhas and to other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of sharp faculties who rely upon the meaning;
therefore, you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should diligently cultivate and study the Tathāgatagarbha and Ālayavijñāna, and do not merely be content with hearing and understanding them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The profound Tathāgatagarbha coexists with the seven consciousnesses; for those whose wisdom arises from the two kinds of grasping, it appears like a reflection in a mirror.
Those who observe reality as it is—unpolluted by beginningless habitual tendencies—see that all phenomena are ultimately without substance.
Just as a fool looking at the moon through a finger watches the finger and not the moon, those who are attached to names and words do not see my true nature.

The mind is like a stage performer, the intellect is like the assistant, and the five consciousnesses are their companions; together they observe the assembly of the audience through conceptualization.
Having realized this as previously explained, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*) and progresses sequentially through the stages, manifesting virtues according to their respective positions.

At this point, one becomes imperturbable against the views of other outsiders, attaining the eighth stage, the Immovable Stage (*Acalā-bhūmi*), where one finds the bliss of the path of thirteen samādhis.
It is on this very ground that one realizes ten kinds of samādhis, enumerated as listed separately; "one's own vow" refers to the original vow (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*).
Because of this original vow, one does not experience the bliss of samādhi nor abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), but rather arises in transformation to benefit sentient beings.

Regarding the "ten sages" (*daśa-ārya*): because they look toward the ultimate stage, they are called "sages" (*ārya*) and also "worthies" (*bhadra*), following the example of Samantabhadra. [This concerns] body, wisdom, and mind.
Those who are born obtain the three bodies, namely: one body and one wisdom, which are the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*; the "mind-born" (*manomaya*) refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Regarding those who have departed from the practice of *samādhi*, this still refers to the aforementioned mind-born [body], meaning that although it arises through *samādhi*, there is no further need for deliberate cultivation.
As for the instruction to purify what is named the *tathāgatagarbha* and the *ālayavijñāna*: the *tathāgata-garbha* is fundamentally nothing that can be [grasped].
That which is called the "storehouse of consciousness" (ālayavijñāna) when its coverings are purified is what is termed the "Tathāgata-garbha.

This is because the deluded consciousnesses that arise through transformation have no separate substance from it; they are merely its names. If the name "storehouse of consciousness" were not used, then upon the reversal of deluded consciousness, one would return to the principle of the original storehouse, which is free from arising and ceasing.
Thus, in all cases where the names of the true and the deluded are reversed, while the substance does not change—this is what is seen.
If this is so, then does it mean that the Sage has no arising or ceasing? Therefore, it is said: "Yes; all ordinary beings and sages alike possess arising and ceasing.
When speaking of practitioners, this refers specifically to the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*):

although the various sages at the causal stage have attained the noble bliss of self-awakening (*svasaṃvedya-ārya-sukha*), they do not abandon skillful means (*upāya*); therefore, they also possess arising and ceasing. This mention of "skillful means" is of two kinds.
That is to say, first is the skillful means of increasing the path through one's own practice, and second is the skillful means of benefiting sentient beings by transforming others;
both possess the sense of arising and ceasing. Since the followers of the Two Vehicles lack these skillful means entirely, they perceive what should be pure as being defiled;
therefore, it is further stated that "this Tathāgatagarbha," etc., meaning that although the Two Vehicles lack those [notions of] arising and ceasing, their mental conceptions [still persist].
As long as it is covered by adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*), its vision remains impure; this is not the ultimate purity of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, one should know that when it is said "purity of intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), it resides in the Dharma and not in the person. Furthermore, that which possesses arising and ceasing resides in the person and not in the Dharma.
To put it conversely, how could there be any fixed determination? It is precisely in this state of non-fixity that the principle lies.
It is further said: "The Tathāgata is the manifest realm," and so forth. This means that when the Tathāgata perceives the Tathāgatagarbha, it is not separate from the manifest realm;
it is utterly without concealment, yet without the characteristic of seeing—it sees without seeing, like fruit held in the palm of the hand.
Nevertheless, what exactly is this? Regarding this meaning, I shall cite the sutra below to provide explicit proof.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s teaching does not rely on external testimony; since it has already been explained extensively in that sūtra, this brief text may simply refer to it.
Moreover, because the text involves both affirmation and negation, it speaks by way of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
As for the statement that the Tathāgatagarbha and the various consciousnesses arise simultaneously, this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); as for the Śrāvakas—

This attachment to non-self—I have never known such a person who clings to non-self—who, being obscured by this very notion of self, does not possess the Tathāgatagarbha as their sphere of experience.
If the Tathāgatagarbha were characterized by non-self, then even "self" could not be apprehended;
therefore, the exhortation to cultivate awakening lies precisely here. Thus the verse says: "The Tathāgatagarbha is profoundly deep."
The term "and so forth" refers to the aforementioned *tathāgatagarbha-citta*. Because it is perfumed by beginningless evil habits, it coexists with the seven consciousnesses;
furthermore, through the two kinds of grasping—namely, self-characteristics and common characteristics—the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) arise.

However, if one perceives the *tathāgatagarbha* as being devoid of both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*), these cease. Therefore, it is said that "the wise are far removed from them," just like a mirror.
The analogy of the elephant appearing [in a mirror] illustrates the aforementioned dharmas. This means that the essence of the eight consciousnesses is originally devoid of substance;
yet, due to the false perfuming from beginningless time, the dharmas such as the seven consciousnesses arise, like the appearance of an elephant in a mirror.

If one observes according to reality and remains detached in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), then the phenomenon of the elephant is fundamentally empty; therefore, it is said that "all things are entirely without thinghood. Next...
A separate analogy of the finger pointing at the moon is presented to illustrate the gain and loss regarding provisional names and substantial dharmas;
if one cannot cast aside words to accord with the principle, it is just like looking at the finger instead of the moon.
The verse beginning "The mind is like a stage performer" follows up on the previous analogy and may be understood through reflection (3). [End of] Chapter Seven.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the ultimate characteristics of the five dharmas, the self-natures, consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness, so that I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may, throughout all stages, successively and continuously discern these dharmas and enter into all Buddha-dharmas. "To enter into all Buddha-dharmas" means...
"Up to the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, the Buddha said to Mahāmati: 'Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this!
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha: 'Yes, indeed; we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

'The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the two kinds of selflessness, and the characteristics of the various paths of discrimination—namely, names, signs, conceptualization, right knowledge, and suchness—if a practitioner cultivates these... "

Entering the Tathāgata’s own realization of the noble path, free from views of annihilationism, eternalism, existence, non-existence, and so forth, one dwells in the present manifestation of the blissful attainment of the Dharma.

Mahāmati, ordinary people do not realize that these five dharmas, the three natures, the two kinds of selflessness, and the external objects manifested by their own minds are merely the delusions of the ignorant;
they are not the [realization] of the noble ones. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how is this so?"
"Foolish people give rise to false conceptualizations, whereas the noble ones do not. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Foolish people are attached to conventional designations, names, and signs;

their minds flow and disperse accordingly. Once they have dispersed, they fall into various appearances and forms, giving rise to views of 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' and becoming attached to hopes and desires for exquisite forms.
Having become attached to these, because they are shrouded by ignorance, they give rise to defiled attachment. Once they are defiled and attached, greed and anger arise."
Karma born of delusion accumulates; having accumulated, it binds itself through false conceptualization, just as a silkworm produces a cocoon.

Thus one falls into the ocean of birth and death and the wilderness of the various realms, like a well-drawing wheel. Because of ignorance, one cannot realize that things are like illusions, mirages, or the moon reflected in water, and that their intrinsic nature is devoid of "I" and "mine.
One then gives rise to all manner of unreal conceptualizations regarding that which is free from both characteristics and the characterized.
Furthermore, arising, abiding, and ceasing arise from the false imaginings of one's own mind; they do not arise from a creator god (*īśvara*), time, atoms, or a supreme principle.
Foolish ordinary people follow after names and marks. Mahāmati, as for those marks: that which is illuminated by the visual consciousness is called "form" (*rūpa*);

that which is illuminated by the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses is called "sound, odor, flavor, touch, and phenomena" (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dharma*). These are what are called "marks."
Mahāmati, as for that which is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is the designation of various names and the manifestation of various characteristics;
just as there are names such as "elephant," "horse," "chariot," "infantry," "man," or "woman," these are called conceptual construction.

Although the five dharmas have already been clarified, they have not yet been analyzed according to the various stages (*bhūmi*) to demonstrate how one enters all Buddha-dharmas up to the stage of a Tathāgata;
therefore, he requests further instruction. In the response, the characteristics of delusion and awakening regarding the five dharmas are first shown in general:
it is said that when a practitioner enters [the path], these five dharmas are all characterized by awakening.
If practitioners and others reverse this [state] and fall into non-awakening (*abodha*), then these five dharmas are all characteristics of delusion; therefore, it is called "non-awakening.
Since those five dharmas and so forth are equal, one knows that dharmas have no self-nature (*svabhāva*); whether there is delusion or awakening depends on the person.

This merely initiates the thread of the discussion. As for the manner of entering [the path], the details will be fully seen in the subsequent text, where the inquiry and explanation first proceed as follows:
Separately, by means of names, marks, and so forth—these three—he demonstrates the characteristics of delusion regarding the dharmas of ordinary beings.

That is to say, based on the conventional designations of names and marks such as the six sense objects, various conceptual discriminations arise; the mind flows outward and cannot return to itself, falling into the views of "self" and "what belongs to self," and becoming attached through hope and expectation.
Thus, one regards wondrous forms as "wondrous" and coarse forms as "not wondrous"; yet this attachment constitutes the very substance of the coarse and the wondrous, which is fundamentally [empty].

"Melting through" (*rong-da*) refers to the immediate departure from the three realms of existence, which arise from deluded conceptualization (*parikalpita*). These are the afflictions (*kleśa*), such as ignorance and the various obscurations;
the "accumulated karma" (*karmopacaya*) refers to the karma produced by them; and "falling into the ocean of birth and death" refers to the retribution (*vipāka*).
The analogy of a silkworm making a cocoon illustrates being bound by one's own [delusions]; the analogy of a water-wheel (*ghaṭī-yantra*) illustrates undergoing the cycle of saṃsāra.
It is like illusions, mirages, and the like, which serve as metaphors for not knowing that the nature of illusion is free from "I" and "mine.

That which arises from all unreal false imaginings refers to the arising of various false imaginings regarding the names, marks, and characteristics of the six sense-objects, thereby forming the three paths.
Now, the essence of delusion is fundamentally unreal; it arises from illusory appearances, yet illusory appearances are fundamentally detached [from reality].
Therefore, when one is free from both the characteristic and that which possesses the characteristic, even arising, abiding, and ceasing cannot be apprehended; it simply returns to one's own mind.
Yet, the mind does not exist as a self-sufficient entity, nor does it arise from external causes or other factors;

rather, it arises through the attachment of foolish worldlings to names and forms. Thus it is said that foolish ordinary beings are those for whom names, forms, and false conceptualizations mutually give rise to one another.
Furthermore, it is because one does not understand illusory appearances that deluded thoughts arise; if one understands illusory appearances, deluded thoughts are immediately extinguished.
This is why this passage repeats the point. It further states: "Those appearances" refers to the two dharmas of name and appearance, which do not go beyond the six consciousnesses.
That which takes up the six sense objects is called "name," and that which is taken up is "appearance. This clarifies [the meaning].
To demonstrate and establish various names and characteristics is mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); therefore, it is said that "this is not different" and so forth.

Just as with the fourfold army—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—as well as names and characteristics such as "man" and "woman," once these have been established, one discriminates each part as being "thus" or "not different.
To give rise to fixed views regarding what is not a fixed dharma is nothing but conceptual construction. This is the meaning.
This is called the dharma of ordinary beings (1).
Mahāmati, for those of right wisdom, names and signs are unattainable; they are like passing guests.

Their various consciousnesses do not arise, they are neither interrupted nor eternal, and they do not fall into the stages of any externalists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, Mahāmati, Bodhi...
By means of this right knowledge, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva neither establishes names and signs nor fails to establish names and signs;
he abandons the two views of superimposition and denial. Knowing that names and signs do not arise, he is called "Suchness.
Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who dwells in Suchness attains the realm of non-existence, he attains the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Having already forever departed from all heterodox paths and evil destinies on the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), he correctly abides in the supramundane path;

through the maturation of the characteristics of all phenomena—such as the discernment of illusions and so forth—and by realizing the nature of phenomena for himself, he becomes detached from the characteristics of all deluded conceptualizations and views.
From this stage up to the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), throughout the interval between them, he possesses mastery over the power of samādhi.

Having blossomed through supernormal powers and attained the stage of a Tathāgata, they manifest various transformations and perfect illuminations to bring sentient beings to maturity, like the moon reflected in water.
Having thoroughly perfected and fulfilled the ten inexhaustible phrases, they expound the Dharma with analytical distinctions for sentient beings according to their various inclinations;
yet the Dharmakāya is free from mental constructions. This is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into that which is attained as Suchness (tathatā).
Next, regarding correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*), we clarify the characteristics of awakening by means of the Dharma of the noble ones (*ārya*). Thus it is said:
"Correct wisdom" and so forth mean that since those names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) are unattainable, the meaning of the equality of each resides therein.

Because they fundamentally lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), all are subsumed under awakening; not giving rise to views such as annihilationism or eternalism is what constitutes correct wisdom. As for the term "suchness," it transcends [conceptualization].

Regarding the statement that "the various consciousnesses do not arise": guests are like travelers on a road; this is used as an analogy for names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), which from the outset have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because the wise ultimately do not give rise to any conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) regarding them, it is said that "the various consciousnesses do not arise.

When the noble ones and sages perceive those names and characteristics with correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), they do so in exactly the same way. By means of this correct wisdom, the Bodhisattva... [does not...]
Regarding the establishment of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*): it is said that a bodhisattva uses right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) to shatter the delusions of names and characteristics;

yet, if one were to establish names and characteristics for oneself, they would not be extinguished and would instead become objects to be shattered. Thus, since it is called "right wisdom," is this not a name?
Since it is "neither interrupted nor eternal," is this not a characteristic? Therefore, it is said: it is not that names and characteristics are not established, but rather...
Since this right knowledge has already abandoned the two extremes and does not fall into the two types of denial, its nature is non-arising;
that which is non-arising is precisely the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness). When a Bodhisattva abides in suchness, they manifest the characteristics of what is attained through suchness.
Now, if it is called "suchness," how could there be anything attained? Nevertheless, by attaining through non-attainment, one also attains for both self and others.
Because it is the dharma of cause and effect, it is said that attaining the realm of non-existence is precisely the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Without departing, one departs; one departs from all external paths and evil destinies. Without dwelling, one dwells; one dwells in the correct path that transcends the world.
Without conceptualization, one conceptualizes; one discerns that all phenomena are entirely like illusions, yet there is nothing to be realized.
Furthermore, the realization of the nature of self-awakened dharmas is also free from all conceptualizations and views of distinct characteristics;

this refers to both the perceiving subject and the perceived object, as well as their distinct characteristics. This is what was meant in the preceding text by "the simultaneous departure from characteristics and views.

For a bodhisattva is about to progress from shallow stages to the profound, up to the ultimate limit; therefore, they must depart from everything—subject and object, identity and difference—altogether.
Entering into the one suchness is naturally so. As for the various merits, such as the power of samādhi, they are developed thereby;
both one’s own fruition and the establishment of others’ benefit proceed from it.

From beginning to end, the ultimate dharmakāya functions spontaneously in accordance with its nature, free from mental effort, and is accomplished as the single suchness. Therefore, it is called "this name."
The Bodhisattva enters into suchness as it is attained (2).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it that the World-Honored One [teaches] that the three natures enter into the five dharmas?
Are they each possessed of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The three natures and the eight..."
"Mahāmati, both kinds of selflessness are entirely contained within the five dharmas. Mahāmati, that which consists of names and signs is the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Mahāmati, when the mind and mental factors arise based upon that false imagination, they arise simultaneously, like the sun and its rays;

these various signs are each separately distinguished and maintained—this is called the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Mahāmati, as for correct wisdom and suchness (*tathatā*):"

Because it is indestructible, it is called "perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are eight kinds of discrimination regarding the false imagination of what is manifested by one's own mind;
namely, the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses.

Since their characteristics are unreal and are merely false imaginings, the grasping of both "self" and "mine" is extinguished, and the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*) arise. Therefore, Mahāmati, these five dharmas are for the śrāvakas...
The stages of self-realized noble wisdom of the Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas proceed in succession, and all Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within them.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the five dharmas are: marks (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Mahāmati, as for "marks," when locations, shapes, forms, colors, and so forth appear, these are called marks. If there is that which exists...
These characteristics—such as "bottle" and so forth—are designated as such and nothing else; this is called "name" (*nāma*) and "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*).

To manifest these various characteristics through manifold names regarding the mind and mental factors, such as "bottle" and so forth, is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*). That name and those characteristics are ultimately unattainable;

from beginning to end there is no realization [of them]. To be free from the mutual succession of all phenomena and to be detached from unreal discrimination is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*), which is the truth.
In reality, the ultimate self-nature is determinately unattainable; that is the characteristic of Suchness (*tathatā*), the point of entry for myself and all Buddhas.
For the sake of all sentient beings, I have accordingly expounded, established, and revealed it as it truly is.

By entering into that, one realizes perfect enlightenment, wherein neither annihilation nor permanence arises, and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not occur. This accords with the noble path of self-realization, which is distinct from all external paths and the Śrāvakas.

The characteristic that is not attained by the Pratyekabuddhas is called Right Knowledge; Great Wisdom is called the Five Dharmas, the Three Natures, the Eight Consciousnesses, and the Two Kinds of Selflessness.
All Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within these. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should study them through your own skillful means and teach others as well;
do not follow after others. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
And he spoke in verse:
"The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness—these encompass all that is named in the Mahāyāna.
The imagined nature consists of names and marks; the dependent nature consists of false conceptualization; and the perfected nature consists of correct wisdom and suchness."
Since the five dharmas have already been set forth, the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) is contained therein, as they are subsumed within them as previously explained.
