To teach that the mind and visual consciousness, etc., are extinguished and impermanent, or to teach that they are eternal while viewing them as *nirvāṇa*, is not the true vehicle;

thus the verse says, "The three vehicles are also non-vehicles. That which is not a vehicle is the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) for which they are given a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). Because it is the true Buddha, it is called the Tathāgata who does not perish.
It is precisely because it is not a [conventional] vehicle that it bestows the prediction of the One Vehicle, and it is precisely because it is the true Buddha that it is so named.

The statement that one is free from all faults and evils also simultaneously summarizes the first and last of the two answers, as well as the answer to the fourth question. The phrase "the wisdom arising from all Buddhas" summarizes the meaning of the first answer, which refers to the wisdom obtained from the initial arising [of the path] until its attainment at the Bodhi tree; the subsequent analysis follows this. The phrase "the wisdom of all Buddhas" summarizes the answer to the second question. That is to say, it refers to the wisdom obtained from the initial arising [of the path] until its attainment at the Bodhi tree; the subsequent analysis follows this. The phrase "the wisdom of all Buddhas" summarizes the answer to the second question. Thus, one speaks of vehicles as non-vehicles and nirvāṇa as non-nirvāṇa. The realms of desire, form, and existence, along with the views, refer to the four stages of abiding (*catur-vihāra-bhūmi*) mentioned in the verse.
That which arises from the mental consciousness refers to the fifth answer in the text, meaning that the mind [arises] by...
The eight consciousnesses arise because they are that upon which the manas (the eighth consciousness) dwells; thus, they are metaphorically likened to a house.
For this reason, it is inherently impossible to give rise to the nihilistic view (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) that the eight consciousnesses cease with the destruction of the body.

Furthermore, those who speak of impermanence regarding the cessation of the sixth consciousness and so forth, or who conceive of this as *nirvāṇa*, are all merely the delusions of ordinary people and non-Buddhists.
Because they perceive through conceptualization, they do not know the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*); it is for this reason that the Tathāgata speaks of him as being eternally abiding (5).

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha with a verse, asking:
Those bodhisattvas who are resolutely seeking the path of the Buddha—how should they regard the consumption of wine, meat, and onions?

I pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One, out of compassion, will explain this for us: how can these things, which are foul-smelling and loathsome, which bring ill repute, and which are the sweet delight of tigers and wolves, be eaten?
To eat them gives rise to various faults; to abstain from eating them is a source of merit and goodness.
"I only pray that you will explain to me the merits and faults of eating and not eating meat.
Having spoken this verse of inquiry, Mahāmati Bodhisattva further addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain to us the merits and transgressions of eating and not eating meat, so that I and all the other bodhisattvas may [act accordingly] in the present and the future."

For those sentient beings who harbor various desires for meat-eating, he teaches the Dharma through various distinctions so that those beings may direct their minds toward one another with compassion.
Having attained a compassionate mind, each becomes pure and clear regarding their own stage of abiding, swiftly attaining ultimate, unsurpassed Bodhi.
Even those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who have rested in their own stages shall also quickly achieve unsurpassed Bodhi. [He refutes] evil and heterodox arguments...
"Even among the various non-Buddhist practitioners who hold false views and are attached to the inversions of annihilationism and eternalism, there are still prohibitions against eating meat;
how much more so for the Tathāgata, the protector of the world, who has perfected the True Dharma—would he eat meat?
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you. Mahāmati replied:
The Buddha said, "It is so; receive my teaching. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat;

however, I shall now briefly explain them for you. That is to say, all sentient beings have, since beginningless time, been related to one another through a succession of causes and conditions, having served as one's six kinds of kin.
Because they should be regarded with the thought of kinship, one must not eat the flesh of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, oxen, or horses."
One should not eat meat because butchers sell it mixed with the flesh of humans, animals, and other beings; one should not eat meat because it grows from impure elements;
one should not eat meat because all sentient beings give rise to terror upon smelling its odor, just as dogs see the Caṇḍālas and Taṃbas and, loathing them, bark in a pack out of fear;
furthermore, [abstaining from meat] causes the practitioner to cultivate loving-kindness.

Because the mind does not arise [in purity], one should not eat meat; because it is what the foolish and ignorant crave, being foul-smelling, impure, and lacking a good reputation, one should not eat meat;
because it causes various mantras and rituals to fail to achieve success, one should not eat meat;

because those who kill living beings perceive their forms and give rise to consciousness, becoming deeply attached to its flavor, one should not eat meat; and because those who eat meat are [despised] by the devas...
One should not eat meat because it causes one to abandon [the precepts]; one should not eat meat because it makes the breath foul-smelling; one should not eat meat because it causes many evil dreams;
one should not eat meat because tigers and wolves will smell its scent in secluded forests; one should not eat meat because it leads to lack of moderation in eating and drinking;
one should not eat meat because it prevents practitioners from developing a sense of revulsion [for the world]. I...
I have previously stated that whenever one consumes food and drink, one should regard it as the flesh of one's own son or as medicine;
therefore, one should not eat meat. For there to be anyone permitted to eat meat is impossible.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhasūtaputra who ate various kinds of meat until he eventually ate human beings. His ministers and subjects, unable to endure this, plotted a rebellion and cut off [his reign].
Because those who subsist on their official stipends and eat meat have such faults as these, one should not eat meat.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all those who kill for the sake of profit slaughter and trade living beings;
those foolish beings who eat meat use money as a net to catch various meats. Those who kill do so either with wealth and goods or with hooks and nets.

Mahāmati, by taking those beings that move through the air, on water, or on land, and slaughtering or trading them for various kinds of profit, there is no meat that is not taught, sought, or imagined;
for this reason, one should not eat meat.
Mahāmati, at times I have spoken of prohibiting five kinds of meat, or restricted ten kinds; now, in this sutra, I [prohibit] all kinds in every way.
At all times, one should exclude [the consumption of] meat through skillful means and completely sever it.

Mahāmati, even the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have no food to eat, let alone fish or meat. Furthermore, because they proceed with great compassion, they regard all sentient beings as if they were their only son;
therefore, they do not permit the eating of a son’s flesh. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this...
Proclaiming this meaning, he spoke in verse:
"In former times, when they were my own kin, they were born amidst base, loathsome, and impure things mixed with filth; the mere scent of them would strike terror into everyone.
All meats, as well as onions, leeks, garlic, and various intoxicants resulting from heedlessness—these the practitioner always keeps far away."
Furthermore, one should always avoid sesame oil and beds with holes, for within them there are minute insects that are extremely terrified.
When food gives rise to heedlessness, and heedlessness gives rise to various perceptions, from those perceptions arises sensual desire. Therefore, one should not eat such things.
From eating arises sensual desire; desire causes the mind to become deluded and intoxicated; this intoxication increases craving, and one remains unable to be liberated from birth and death.
To kill sentient beings for profit or to purchase various meats with wealth—both are evil karmas that lead, at death, to falling into the Raurava Hell.
If there is no instruction, no perception, and no seeking, then the three kinds of "pure meat" do not exist; since they do not exist without a cause, one should not eat them.
For this reason, all those practitioners of the path completely distance themselves from such things, as all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, unanimously condemn them.

Passing from one state to another, they devour one another and die, falling into the class of tigers and beasts of prey—beings foul, filthy, and loathsome, who are born constantly ignorant and dull-witted.
They are mostly born among the Caṇḍālas, hunters, and Taṃbas; or among the Dāyinīs and various flesh-eating Rākṣasas, cats, and wildcats.
It is primarily among these that they are born, such as the Bound Elephant, Mahāmegha, and Aṅgulimāla.
Furthermore, in this *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, I have completely prohibited the eating of meat; it is censured by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas.
Those who eat it without shame will be perpetually dull-witted and obscured in every birth.

Having previously declared that one must abandon all thoughts of meat regarding what is seen, heard, or suspected, those who fail to realize this give rise to the habit of eating meat. Such faults are like those of lustful desire, for they obstruct the noble liberation.
Alcohol, meat, onions, leeks, and garlic are all obstacles to the Noble Path. Sentient beings of future ages will be deluded regarding meat and will say, "This is pure and without fault;
the Buddha permitted us to eat it. You should regard eating it as taking medicine, or like eating the flesh of your own son.
For those who practice contentment, give rise to revulsion, cultivate the alms-round, and abide in a mind of loving-kindness—I declare that they shall always remain free from attachment.
Tigers, wolves, and various other evil beasts can always dwell together; yet when they eat the flesh and blood of living beings, all such creatures are struck with terror.

Therefore, the practitioner of the Way, possessing a heart of loving-kindness, does not eat meat. To eat meat is to lack compassion and wisdom, to turn one's back forever upon true liberation, and to violate the outward signs of the Sages.
For this reason, one should not eat it, for it prevents birth among the Brahmin caste and in other places where practitioners dwell.
The wisdom and prosperity of a family arise from not eating meat.
After the Buddha had spoken on the chapter of the mind, Mahāmati again requested that he provide further instructions regarding wine, meat, and so forth to bring the discourse to its conclusion.
Indeed, the foundation of our Buddha’s teaching and transformation is the equality of the single nature; his heart is compassion as the embodiment of the same essence.
Since taking up the Way for the sake of others is the primary principle, nothing precedes purity and the avoidance of transgressions;
since saving sentient beings and delivering them from rebirth is the primary task, nothing surpasses the law of cause and effect regarding sin and merit.

Therefore, following the *Lengyan jing* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra), which establishes the orthodox teaching, it clearly elucidates the four kinds of solemn admonitions and the three stages of gradual progress; its warnings in this present scripture are even more earnest and thorough. This may well be so.
Using this to model the circulation [of the text]: first, he requests general admonitions; next, he requests specific admonitions.

In the Buddha’s response, seventeen reasons for why one should not eat meat are fully enumerated (etc.). Next, regarding the demonstration of the general and specific prohibitions, it is first stated that in the provisional teachings of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), five types [of meat] may be permitted—namely, those involving seeing, hearing, or suspecting slaughter—and all other [types] should be avoided accordingly.

Regarding the opening of the prohibition or the formulation of the ten types—such as humans, snakes, elephants, and so forth—it does not extend to other similar cases that ought to be permitted by general principle;
however, one must speak with particular caution, for these are merely prohibitions and there is never any explicit permission.
Even if there were a temporary expedient, it would be nothing more than a measure of necessity. Next, the text speaks of the expedients for exceptions provided in this sutra.
The statement that "all [meat-eating] is completely severed" may indeed be called profound and incisive; yet commentators still regard the prohibition against eating meat as a point of difficulty.

This is likely because the recorders stated, "In this sutra, bodhisattvas should not eat meat," and thus understood it as meaning that while the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) still permits [eating meat], this sutra merely prohibits it for bodhisattvas, while leaving the Small Vehicle intact.
Regarding those who claim that the teaching permitting [the consumption of meat] is an error of the commentator, I say it is not so.

It is correctly stated that the *Laṅkāvatāra* follows the four Āgamas; thus, it preserves the doctrine of gradual teaching (*anupūrva-vinaya*), which differs from the sudden prohibition in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
This serves to show that the section of this scripture belongs to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/ Fangdeng) class. As for what is meant by "preserving," it refers merely to its textual form. Why?
This means that one might still maintain the existence of such matters and consider them mere errors; yet this is not so. The Sūtra says, "All things are [empty]...
What does this mean? Alas! Great precautions have been established and strict regulations have been formulated, yet people in the world still transgress them;
how much more so when no warnings are provided? This allows us to see the profound depth of karmic habituation, reaching a point where some can never again [return to the right path].
To praise the holy life (brahmacarya) while causing others to enter into non-restraint—I know that such a person brings this fault upon themselves.
Nevertheless, this sutra states that all phenomena are merely manifestations of one's own mind.
If one understands that good and evil are solely the mind, how could one follow deluded thoughts while contravening the sacred teachings? Be cautious! Exert yourself! (13) [Right] Number Thirteen.
